artigo.texto: Impulsionada pela expansão do mercado de data centers e infraestrutura crítica pata TI, uma empresa de Joinville, no Norte catarinense, avança com novos projetos e planos de crescimento. Fundada em 2006, a Novalogic anunciou a assinatura de um contrato com uma gigante global de tecnologia e traçou como meta alcançar R$ 1 bilhão em faturamento até 2030. Atualmente, a receita da Novalogic está concentrada principalmente em três grandes pilares: 50% provenientes de obras para data centers, 30% de projetos de infraestrutura crítica (sistemas essenciais de TI) e 20% de obras verticais de alto padrão. Os data centers são estruturas que abrigam servidores, sistemas de armazenamentos de dados e redes. Este mercado tem crescido principalmente por conta das demandas da inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem, digitalização das empresas e necessidade crescente de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Empresa de Joinville mira expansão; veja fotos: Para sustentar o crescimento, a companhia prepara uma transformação operacional e geográfica. O plano prevê a descentralização da estrutura, com presença física mais próxima das obras e dos grandes projetos, inclusive em regiões consideradas remotas ou de difícil acesso. A estratégia inclui ainda investimentos em novas áreas e unidades operacionais no Nordeste, Sudeste, Centro-Oeste e Norte do Brasil. No Nordeste, a empresa já adquiriu uma área de 50 mil metros quadrados para a construção de uma unidade de grande porte: um novo data center no Ceará que deverá atender a alta demanda de operação no norte e nordeste do país. Em São Paulo, o grupo também ampliará sua presença com uma estrutura física em Alphaville, polo empresarial e tecnológico do país. “Crescer nesta velocidade também traz novos desafios. A expansão geográfica, a ampliação da capacidade operacional e o desenvolvimento de ativos próprios de longo prazo aumentam naturalmente a demanda por capital. O desafio é estruturar esse crescimento com disciplina financeira, preservando a solidez construída pelo nosso grupo e criando as condições para capturar oportunidades cada vez maiores e mais importantes”, afirma o CEO, Felippe Prates. Outra estratégia da Novalogic também é se aproximar mais ativamente em Parcerias Público-Privadas. A companhia identifica oportunidades em projetos de infraestrutura no Brasil e em outros países da América Latina.

artigo.texto: A Vertiv, empresa global em infraestrutura digital crítica, anunciou hoje sua participação no Data Center World Brasil 2026, evento que reunirá líderes, especialistas e empresas para discutir os principais avanços em Data Centers e infraestrutura digital, de 6 a 8 de outubro, no São Paulo Expo, em São Paulo, Brasil. Durante o evento, os participantes discutirão como a adoção da Inteligência Artificial (IA), a expansão das redes e dos Data Centers, o crescimento da computação em Nuvem e a Transformação Digital de forma mais ampla estão moldando as prioridades de infraestrutura em toda a América Latina. A agenda incluirá temas relacionados à energia, gerenciamento térmico, conectividade, continuidade operacional e requisitos de infraestrutura para ambientes de maior densidade. A Vertiv estará presente com um estande onde clientes, parceiros e profissionais do setor poderão se reunir com especialistas da empresa para trocar perspectivas e explorar oportunidades relacionadas a novas implementações, expansões e modernização da infraestrutura. A participação da Vertiv também incluirá sessões de networking de negócios com os principais stakeholders do setor. “A rápida adoção da IA, da Computação em Nuvem e o aumento da demanda por processamento estão levando as empresas a tomar decisões de infraestrutura que afetam sua capacidade de escalar, adotar novas tecnologias e manter a continuidade operacional. Isso significa avaliar como projetar e operar uma infraestrutura crítica capaz de responder às crescentes demandas por energia, gerenciamento térmico e disponibilidade”, afirmou Alex Sasaki, vice-presidente de Vendas da Vertiv para a América Latina. “O Brasil conta com diversos fatores de crescimento que impulsionam o mercado de Data Centers à medida que a digitalização avança em toda a América Latina. O Data Center World Brasil 2026 representa uma oportunidade para trocar perspectivas com os principais tomadores de decisão do setor e discutir as possibilidades que poderão moldar a próxima etapa de desenvolvimento da região.” Serviço Vertiv.com

artigo.texto: A produção tropicalizada de baterias garantirá a segurança da matriz energética brasileira De olho no potencial do país, fabricantes traçam planos de longo prazo para suprir o mercado de armazenamento de energia Atualizado Mercado ainda incipiente no país, as soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias, essenciais para garantir flexibilidade e segurança às redes elétricas, ganham um novo impulso com a queda no custo das baterias de íon-lítio no mercado internacional, com a maior facilidade de negociação nos contratos de energia e com a perspectiva de avanços no ambiente regulatório — inclusive com o esperado Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade destinado a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, agendado para dezembro. As ações dos fabricantes de tecnologia no mercado brasileiro focam estratégias de longo prazo, visando consolidar uma produção tropicalizada, como avalia Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da multinacional chinesa BYD no Brasil, que anunciou em fevereiro deste ano um investimento de R$ 500 milhões para a fabricação de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias — em inglês, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — no país. “Estamos falando de uma decisão de longo prazo”, define. “É um movimento baseado na confiança que temos no potencial desse mercado e na importância que o armazenamento terá para o futuro da matriz energética brasileira”, diz. Segundo Baldy, a estratégia visa desenvolver capacidade industrial local e, ao mesmo tempo, criar condições para que uma cadeia brasileira de fornecedores cresça junto com esse mercado. “Esse processo de nacionalização também permitirá atender aos requisitos previstos pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia para o Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade, ampliando o acesso dos investidores a linhas de financiamento do banco, tanto para projetos ligados ao leilão quanto para outras aplicações”, afirma. No leilão, há dois segmentos: armazenamento nacional, com exigência de, no mínimo, 15% de componentes locais, e geral, sem requisitos de nacionalização. A Contemporary Amperey Technology Co., Limited (CATL), outro superfabricante chinês de tecnologia, pretende fornecer para os dois. Para participar do leilão nacional, a CATL anunciou uma parceria estratégica com o Grupo Moura, um dos principais fabricantes de baterias do país, sediado no município de Belo Jardim (PE). “Para maximizar nosso impacto, estamos nos preparando ativamente, em conjunto com parceiros nacionais, para fornecer equipamentos credenciados, implementando plataformas avançadas de armazenamento com capacidade nativa de frid-forming [seguidores de redes]”, explica Ray See, vice-presidente de negócios para as Américas da CATL. Ele diz que, além de fornecer equipamentos, a parceria com o Grupo Moura visa integrar os sistemas de baterias localmente com um fabricante nacional e cumprir as regras de nacionalização previstas pelo governo federal. Para suprir o leilão de armazenamento geral, a CATL vai importar os equipamentos. Nos últimos anos, as vendas acumuladas de soluções BESS no Brasil somaram somente 1,9 GWh, dos quais 730 MWh foram comercializados em 2025, especialmente nos setores comercial e industrial. Nesse ano, os financiamentos registrados em BESS atingiram R$ 126 milhões. É um volume maior que o registrado em 2024 (R$ 117 milhões), mas que não reflete a real expansão da tecnologia no país, aponta levantamento do Clean Energy Latin America (Cela), uma boutique de investimentos do setor de energia renovável da região. “A expectativa é que os primeiros leilões dedicados exclusivamente ao armazenamento, previstos para 2026, marquem uma nova fase de escala para o segmento, com impacto direto nos volumes de financiamento”, confia Camila Ramos, diretora-executiva do Cela. “Podemos ter até um crescimento explosivo dos sistemas de armazenamento por baterias no Brasil nos próximos oito anos”, acredita Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). “A corrida das empresas estrangeiras e brasileiras por esse mercado deve movimentar mais de R$ 80 bilhões em investimentos até 2034”, diz. Só o leilão previsto para este ano deve destravar R$ 10 bilhões em projetos, estima Vlasits. Segundo ele, esse aumento dos negócios no setor de armazenamento de energia em baterias é movido pela redução de quase 70% no custo das baterias de lítio nos últimos três anos e a necessidade crescente de flexibilidade no sistema elétrico do país para gerenciar as diversas fontes de energias renováveis, como a solar e eólica. “Teremos muitos projetos dos fabricantes voltados para atender o setor comercial e industrial, além de projetos de descarbonização na região amazônica”, destaca. A WEG avalia que o potencial de negócios não se restringe apenas a grandes projetos. “Acreditamos muito também nas aplicações de médio porte, principalmente soluções BESS junto à carga e combinado com geração distribuída”, diz Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de automação e sistemas da WEG. “A bateria pode ajudar a superar gargalos de fornecimento de energia e limitações da rede, garantir backup e maior confiabilidade para o consumidor e permitir arbitragem de energia entre diferentes horários.” No início deste ano, a WEG anunciou a construção de uma nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Itajaí (SC), com financiamento de R$ 280 milhões do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. A nova unidade ampliará capacidade produtiva para até 2 GWh ao ano e deverá entrar em operação no segundo semestre de 2027, informa Johann. “Praticamente todo o sistema pode ser industrializado no país”, indica. “O principal componente que ainda depende de importação é a célula da bateria, cuja fabricação exige uma escala muito maior para se tornar economicamente competitiva.” Praticamente dominado por fabricantes de tecnologia de ponta e gigantes industriais, o mercado de BESS movimenta t

artigo.texto: A regional gaúcha da Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica Regional (Abinee-RS) realizou mais uma edição de sua reunião-almoço nesta terça-feira, em Porto Alegre, abordando as oportunidades a partir da instalação de projetos de data center no Rio Grande do Sul, além de empreendimentos ligados à tecnologia, como o cabo submarino Malbec, cuja chegada ocorre no município de Balneário Pinhal, no litoral Norte. Representantes do segmento industrial e do governo do estado, apresentando números do setor, estiveram presentes no evento. O CEO da Parks, Fabio Cierro, comentou a respeito do andamento do projeto de um data center de R$ 500 milhões no Distrito Industrial de Cachoeirinha, na região Metropolitana. Para o diretor regional e vice-presidente da Abinee, Régis Haubert, as oportunidades tecnológicas têm relação com o momento de transformação digital e inteligência artificial, e o RS pode se beneficiar com isto. “Basicamente, temos aqui no estado um fornecimento e uma capacidade de energia muito boas. Também não nos preocupa a questão da formação técnica, porque temos qualificação e formação profissional muito boa, tanto nos cursos de graduação, quanto nos tecnólogos. O que precisamos é, cada vez mais, agregar a produção local de equipamentos, para que possamos atrair a demanda de nosso próprio mercado”, disse Haubert. Questionado a respeito dos desafios climáticos, o diretor da Abinee disse que eventos naturais como o El Niño são cíclicos. “Precisamos nos adequar às condições e mitigar para evitar problemas”, salientou ele. O vice-prefeito de Balneário Pinhal, Jorge Fonseca, comentou brevemente sobre os bastidores que levaram à construção e implantação da estrutura da V.tal, e que fará a comunicação de dados de milhões de usuários dos serviços da Meta, como WhatsApp, Facebook, Threads e Instagram, aumentando a conectividade e confiabilidade da Internet. Este é o primeiro cabo internacional a atingir diretamente o território gaúcho. “Após esta surpresa inicial, acredito que estamos fazendo a lição de casa, que é entender um pouco de processos, se apropriar de situações e fazer com que Balneário Pinhal não seja apenas um local de passagem do cabo. Já visitamos estruturas semelhantes em Montevidéu a convite da Antel (companhia estatal de telecomunicações do Uruguai) e tivemos bons diálogos com o governo do estado. Temos áreas já com licenciamentos ambientais disponíveis e estamos em uma aproximação com a CEEE Equatorial para analisar a qualidade da energia. São fatores muito significativos para nossas pretensões”, salientou Fonseca.

artigo.texto: Last week, community members made it clear to the City Council at a public hearing that they don’t want more data centers in Denton. The next public hearing on a proposed data center moratorium occurs on Oct. 27 — and a possible moratorium could start in early December. In the midst of the public hearings for a pause on data center development, the council will be voting Oct. 13 on whether to amend the Denton Development Code and tighten restrictions to allow more public input on a project by requiring a specific-use permit. If the City Council approves the development code amendments, all data center developers would need to pursue a specific-use permit regardless of whether the zoning allows the new development by right. Those zoning areas include public facilities, heavy industrial and light industrial, both of which are mostly located on the western part of the city and along the highway, Angie Manglaris, the city’s assistant planning director, pointed out last week at a Planning and Zoning Commission meeting. The commission voted unanimously, 5-0, on Wednesday to offer the council recommendations to amend the city’s development code and strengthen data center regulations. “When it comes to specific-use permits, it’s not prohibited but it’s also not permitted by right,” Manglaris told the commissioners, referring to data center development. “… It requires further scrutiny, specifically as it relates to potential adverse impacts.” Earlier this month, Mayor Pro Tem Nick Stevens, who originally pitched the idea for a moratorium, pointed out while these development changes would be helpful, they’re “more helpful in making it perhaps a little bit more difficult so that there’s more scrutiny.” “I don’t know the last time a council ever denied an SUP,” Stevens said. “Now, historically in the past few years, I just don’t recall the last time an SUP had ever been denied.” Stevens stressed that the purpose of a moratorium is to evaluate whether projected infrastructure demand, environmental impacts and financial returns associated with Denton’s two currently approved data centers align with projections. “The purpose of the moratorium was so that we could study infrastructure demand,” Stevens said. “The development code changes are about planning and zoning ... and say nothing about our grid. They say nothing about water supply because that’s a capacity question, not a zoning question.” Several people spoke on Wednesday at the Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, encouraging city officials “to ensure our development codes protect our community from harmful developments and unsustainable practices,” as Denton resident Rachel Weaver said in her opening remarks. Weaver pointed to the rapid growth of generative AI that “has led to a profusion of new proposed data centers in Texas. “Within two years, our state could become home to more data centers than any other state in the nation,” Weaver said. “This has led to a desperate need for regulation awareness of the environmental impacts of data centers and the AI tools they support. Texans of all political stripes are rightly concerned about water use, electricity use, wastewater, air pollution, noise and loss of working lands that could result.” Weaver also offered solutions including: - Third-party independent studies on the impacts on neighboring communities and local insect and bird populations, especially during migration season. - Power and water usage caps, especially during times of extreme weather. - Disclosure of total water consumption that includes indirect via power consumption. - A notification radius for data centers that equal their impact radius. - A ban on data center development within 5 miles of residential structures and zoning. - Requiring decommissioning bonds, so that developers must pay the teardown costs should the facility be abandoned for any reason in the future. “We’ve had a history of radiopharmaceuticals leaving low-level radioactive waste and contaminated equipment for us to clean up,” Weaver said, referring to the former U.S. Radiopharmaceuticals site on Shady Oaks Drive. “Core Scientific has already gone bankrupt once in crypto mining — what assurances do we have that they won’t go bankrupt again?” Core Scientific originally opened a crypto mining facility in Denton in 2021, only to file for bankruptcy in 2022 and emerge from it in January 2024. In 2024, Core Scientific received council approval to shift from crypto mining to AI data computing, which allowed the company to expand its facility and power usage up to 391 megawatts. The expansion is currently under construction and not at full buildout yet, Denton Municipal Electric General Manager Tony Puente told P&Z commissioners Wednesday. The council approved QumulusAI’s modular 20-megawatt data center in January, but the company still hasn’t broken ground, Puente said. “But for all these facilities, the intent is that we’re going to be managing them as a separate load from the rest of what we consider our native load,” Puente said. “We’re managing them as a separate portfolio, really looking at real-time power, day-ahead power. We’re also buying power well in advance, up to three years through various financial transactions.” Puente said they established a large load energy cost adjustment that’s also separate from the native load that is reflective of the power that DME purchases to serve Core Scientific’s load. This includes a “pretty hefty demand charge base rate [that is] considerably more than what we charge the rest of our native loads,” he said. Neither Core Scientific nor QumulusAI was required to produce water or wastewater impact studies because they aren’t required by ordinance, according to a city spokesperson. artigo.texto: From Isaac Anumihe, Abuja As the world seeks to transit towards climate finance and support greenhouse gas emission reductions as well as accelerate transition to a low-carbon economy, Federal Government has approved the carbon market framework objectives. Speaking at the National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft host country approval criteria for Nigeria’s carbon market operations, in Abuja, Vice Chancellor, University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN), Professor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, said that the approval represented an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations in the country. Ortuanya, who was represented by the Director of Resource and Environmental Policy Research Centre, UNN, (REPRC-EfD), Dr Nnaemeka Chukwuone, stated that it’s against this background that the next official task is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent host country approval criteria. “These criteria will provide guidance on the eligibility, screening and assessment of carbon market projects. They will also clarify institutional responsibilities, approval procedures, measurement, reporting and verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards; alignment with Nigeria’s Nationally -Determined Contribution (NNDC) registry and transparency arrangements, and carbon accounting” he said The criteria, the VC explained, should be sufficiently robust to protect Nigeria’s interests while remaining practical, predictable and responsive to the realities of implementation. “I am glad that the development of the proposed host country approval criteria was guided by sound research” he said. Before she declared the workshop open, the Director General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Dr Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said that having approved the carbon market framework, the task before stakeholders is therefore clear — to establish post-country approval criteria that protect Nigeria’s national interests while providing the certainty that credible investors and project developers need. According to her, at the heart of the process is a simple principle that Nigeria must participate in carbon markets on terms that are credible, transparent, equitable and beneficial to the people. “Carbon projects must deliver genuine mitigation outcomes. They must contribute to sustainable development, respect host communities, and promote social inclusion and align with national climate and development priorities” she said. In his remarks, PEP’s Scientific Adviser, Professor Adeola Adenikinju, maintained that the global carbon market presents important opportunities for countries seeking to mobilise climate finance, support greenhouse gas emission reduction and removal, and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy. For Nigeria, he noted, these opportunities are particularly significant as it has become imperative for Nigeria to pursue economic growth, industrial development, and energy access and poverty reduction while responding to the challenges of climate change. In his opinion, a well-governed carbon market can help mobilise the resources required to support poverty reduction and grow economy.ENDS

artigo.texto: 2026 Fall Homeland | Data centers 101 Sally Scholle Follow The news about rampant data center development in Virginia has made its way across the country, penetrating areas where people never thought such structures would be introduced. Those who learn about what’s happening in those states often adopt one of two views: It won’t happen where I live, or I want to make sure it doesn’t happen where I live. Data center development is exploding in Virginia for several reasons: high quality fiber connectivity, proximity to Washington, D.C., available land and reliable, affordable electricity. These factors provide developers with nearly everything necessary for profitable data centers. At first, those living in western states weren’t too concerned with data center development in the east. However, now that data centers are either under construction or proposed in states including Wyoming, Colorado and Nebraska, new concerns are surfacing. Last year’s announcement regarding construction of a large data center near Cheyenne gained heightened concern with the discovery of an unusual bacteria strain in the wastewater that contaminated the sewer system. Although the bacterium occurs naturally in soil, it poses a threat to immunocompromised individuals. Colorado has numerous smaller-scale data centers, most of which are in the Denver area. As is the case in other states, local government entities are responding to public protest by limiting new construction and passing moratoriums. Nebraska is home to several data centers with more on the way. While Governor Pillen supports data center development, he recently created a task force to set guidelines and signed LB1261, which requires entities to create their own electricity. Most early data center developers kept projects quiet, perhaps because they anticipated public outrage and unified attempts to squash projects. Now that the proverbial feline has exited the bag, there’s widespread interest among rural citizens to make sure data centers don’t become a part of their landscape. The advent and rapid improvement in artificial intelligence (AI) is one a primary reason for data center proliferation. These information hubs have become a necessary evil for a world transfixed with services such as ChatGPT3, launched in November 2022. Insurance, medical facilities, bank fraud protection, rideshare services and even doomscrolling rely on AI, which in turn requires data centers. According to Cleanview (http://www.cleanview.co/data-centers/us), as of August 20206, there were 1,287 data centers currently operating in the U.S. That number might seem high, but there are already more planned. In a recent webinar on data centers, Matt Svetz, Penn State Extension, explained some of the reasons for data center expansion, especially in rural areas. It’s primarily because some data centers don’t require proximity to major population centers because they aren’t sensitive to latency (delays in transmission) in the same way as traditional data centers. “The main thing is access to electrical grid infrastructure,” Svetz said. “This is generally high-voltage transmission lines. They also want space because of the size of the facilities.” Data center developers want access to large land parcels for ease of design and construction. Depending on existing infrastructure, new structures may require a dedicated substation. “They’re generally looking for relatively flat large tracts of land,” Svetz said, “so they can potentially expand operations. They also want less disaster-prone areas. A lot of developers are looking for onsite generation solutions to get around delays in the grid. Data center developers are looking for quicker timelines than grid operators can provide for interconnecting them.” One of the biggest issues in early data center development has been non-disclosure agreements (NDA). These legal contracts are signed by developers and local officials when preliminary deals are made to prevent the public from learning details regarding proposed data centers. From the developer’s perspective, an NDA can prevent land prices from increasing and deter competitors from attempting to purchase land. However, for many communities, learning about data center plans after the fact quickly results in concerns about land, water, noise and electricity; all of which yield strong local opposition. This leads to public distrust, along with highly vocal and even stronger opposition. Michael Helbling, staff attorney, Penn State Center for Energy Law and Policy, explains that for most communities, ordinance provisions are the best way to manage data center development. Such ordinances can address topics such as data center siting, conditional use and special exceptions, land or lot size restrictions, setbacks, building height restrictions and requirements that developers submit plans. Many states’ laws prohibit exclusionary zoning, which means all lawful activities must be allowed – including data centers. However, location and manner of operation can be restricted. When citizens begin to challenge data center development as a unified body, they often lack guidelines. Community members interested in monitoring local data center development should, at the very least, become familiar with state and local permits required for development. Even if the data center is not in your immediate community, it’s worth attending meetings in neighboring communities to gain an understanding of what has been proposed, what local officials have acted on and what can still be done. In many cases, the answer to the last point is ‘a lot.’ “We’re seeing states take action on permitting (data centers),” Helbling said. “How will they be permitted, what kinds of tax breaks and incentives are they getting, and how can they be located? Will municipalities maintain control over siting, or will the state have some centralized ability to determine how they’re located?” Helbling often sees broadly defined goals, but goa

artigo.texto: UK engineers develop dense-fluid energy storage system suitable for low-elevation sites When engineers at RheEnergise popped champagne in January, they were celebrating a milestone most people have never heard of: 500 kilowatts of peak power from a pumped-storage hydroelectricity system. That technology has quietly underpinned the world’s power grids for over a century, accounting for more than 90 percent of global long-duration energy storage. But this version is different in one fundamental way. It contains no water. The fluid needed to be viscous enough to stay put during an accidental spill, yet flow as easily as water through pipes and turbines under normal conditions. The world’s biggest battery — and its biggest limitation Pumped-storage hydroelectricity runs on a beautifully simple principle. During off-peak hours, excess electricity pumps water uphill to a higher reservoir. When demand spikes, gravity pulls that water back down through turbines, generating power on cue. No combustion, no chemical degradation, no exotic materials. That simplicity has made PSH extraordinarily durable. By 2023, global installed capacity reached nearly 200 gigawatts — more than 90 percent of the world’s long-duration energy storage. No other technology comes close at that scale. The technology hits a hard geographic ceiling, though. “You need a suitable mountain, and you need to have a river running along the bottom,” says Tamas Bertenyi, cofounder and CTO of RheEnergise. “You also need an alpine valley you can dam up, and there are just not a lot of sites where you can do that.” Flat countries, rolling hills, densely populated regions — all effectively locked out of the world’s dominant storage technology. That’s the problem RheEnergise set out to solve, according to IEEE Spectrum. A fluid 2.5 times denser than water — and engineered to behave like it The company’s answer is a proprietary substance it calls High-Density Fluid: a mineral-rich suspension 2.5 times denser than water. “It is so dense that if you threw a block of concrete into a pool of the fluid, it would float,” says Bertenyi. That density is the point — more energy potential per unit of height, which means lower hills can do work that mountains once monopolized. Developing the fluid was harder than it sounds. RheEnergise worked with the University of Exeter, where cofounder Richard Cochrane was a professor of renewable energy systems, to engineer something satisfying two almost contradictory requirements. The fluid needed to be viscous enough to stay put during an accidental spill, yet flow as easily as water through pipes and turbines under normal conditions. The solution was a shear-thinning, non-Newtonian formulation. At rest, the fluid is thick; under pumping pressure, its viscosity drops sharply — behaving, hydraulically, much like water. The mixture is 80 percent solid particulates by mass, suspended rather than dissolved. Spill it, and the particles simply dry and settle rather than seeping into soil or groundwater. What the pilot project actually looks like The pilot system, now running in the UK, keeps a deliberately low profile — literally. An upper reservoir sits at 80 meters of elevation. Two-and-a-half-meter fiberglass pipes carry the fluid down to a lower reservoir that Bertenyi describes as “basically a large swimming pool.” Both are buried underground, connected by steel pipe in a closed loop. Above ground, almost nothing is visible. Only the powerhouse — housing the turbine, pump, fluid-management system, and electrical controls — breaks the surface. For communities sensitive to industrial infrastructure, that near-invisibility could matter considerably. In January, the system hit its headline milestone: 500 kW of peak power. Modest, but it proves the concept works at real scale. The commercial ambition is far larger — RheEnergise envisions projects using two to four 5 MW modular turbines each, putting the target operating range at 10 to 20 MW per site. The company aims to deliver its first fully commercial system by the end of 2028. Why gentler slopes could change where energy storage is built The physics are straightforward. Higher fluid density means the same energy output is achievable from lower elevations and shallower gradients than traditional PSH demands, expanding the viable site map dramatically. “Given the system can generate the same energy output from gentler slopes and lower elevations than traditional pumped hydro, it makes far more sites viable worldwide — including low hills and urban fringe areas — not just mountainous regions,” says Professor George Aggidis, emeritus professor of energy engineering at Lancaster University. That matters for the broader grid challenge. Batteries are fast and modular, but cost-effective long-duration storage — the kind needed to balance renewable generation across eight to ten hours or more — remains elusive at scale. “Batteries alone can be expensive” for that role, Aggidis notes. RheEnergise’s target customers reflect the opportunity: independent power producers, utility companies, and energy-project developers all need exactly this kind of flexible, location-independent storage. The road to commercialization — and the competition waiting None of this arrives without friction. Aggidis is direct: “Larger scale deployment will require substantial civil works, permit requirements, and engineering coordination. This is more complex than plug-and-play battery systems.” Capital intensity and long lead times are familiar obstacles for any infrastructure-scale energy project. The competitive field is also crowding fast. Sodium-ion and flow batteries are modular, quick to install, and falling in cost. Compressed-air storage, hydrogen, and thermal storage all compete for the same long-duration market. artigo.texto: Gotion has begun delivering its Gotion Grid 5MWh energy storage systems to the Nefertiti and Horus projects in Egypt, an infrastructure that will become one of the largest independent energy storage facilities on the African continent, the deployment began on September 28 with the simultaneous departure of 50 heavy-duty trucks from Gotion’s facilities in Jinzhai and Nantong, China. The trucks are transporting units developed by the company for large-scale electrical storage applications, designed to improve the stability of power grids and facilitate the integration of renewable energy. Gotion promotes energy storage systems for Egypt’s grid The Nefertiti and Horus projects represent Egypt’s first standalone, large-capacity energy storage facilities, the infrastructure will be developed by AMEA Power, built by China Energy Engineering Group, and equipped with Gotion’s technological solutions. The integration of these systems will strengthen the stability of the Egyptian electricity grid through more efficient management of energy generation and consumption. Furthermore, it will facilitate greater integration of renewable sources such as solar and wind power, reducing the variability associated with these resources, the project aligns with Egypt’s energy transition goals for 2030, which seek to increase the share of clean sources within its electricity mix and strengthen the security of the national energy supply. Storage technology designed for extreme conditions Gotion Grid systems were developed to operate in environments with high temperatures, sandstorms and exposure to salt fog, common conditions in various regions of Egypt. The technology incorporates solutions aimed at ensuring operational safety, electrical stability and availability during extended operating cycles. The equipment offers millisecond response capability, allowing for compensation of rapid variations in electricity demand and improving network operation with greater participation of renewable generation. These features will allow for the optimization of the use of solar energy produced in Benban and provide flexibility to the electrical system to manage peak demand associated with the Zafarana wind farm. Gotion accelerates the delivery of large-scale energy storage The company completed the first shipment three months after the agreement was signed, a process that required coordination between the manufacturing, international transport and implementation stages of the project in Egypt. The start of the delivery represents a significant step forward for the development of energy storage infrastructure in the continent, where these technologies play a fundamental role in integrating larger volumes of renewable energy and improving the reliability of electricity grids. According to AMEA Power, this collaboration expands opportunities for energy cooperation between China, the Middle East, and Africa, as Gotion continues to expand its energy storage solutions beyond the Asian market. artigo.texto: A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed by NPR. Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators. In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts). The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands. The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state. "It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands. "The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it." In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company. "We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added. Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county. Small reactors, big plan Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build. Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft. The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive. At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip. "Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd. The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build. Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032. Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used." NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report. Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13 Copyright 2026 NPR Loading...

artigo.texto: Data center developers, investors, and communities across California face a changing development landscape as new requirements impact some of the industry’s most consequential land use and infrastructure issues. Governor Gavin Newsom signed a package of seven bills (AB 1577 – Bauer-Kahan; AB 2383 – Zbur; AB 2469 – Papan; AB 2619 – Papan; SB 886 – Padilla and McNerney; SB 887 – Padilla; SB 1168 – McNerney) on September 21 addressing the electricity, water, and environmental impacts of data centers. The new laws impose additional reporting requirements, address responsibility for electric grid and water infrastructure costs, and establish conditions data center projects must meet to qualify for streamlined judicial review under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). But the significance for developers extends beyond the individual requirements contained in the legislation. At the state level, California is establishing a framework seeking to address questions about power capacity, water supply, infrastructure, environmental review, and community impacts. At the same time, various cities and counties are taking their own approaches to data center development, creating a patchwork of local regulatory landscapes that can vary considerably from one jurisdiction to another. The result is an increasingly complicated development environment. While a site may appear suitable from a real estate or engineering perspective, depending on the local rules, the entitlement process can vary from straightforward to incredibly complex. Two near-identical sites in different locations may face entirely dissimilar entitlement paths depending on the jurisdiction’s rules, available infrastructure, and local response to data center development. Early diligence is thus key to a successful data center project. According to the state, the legislative package is intended to provide communities with more information about proposed projects while protecting utility customers from costs associated with data center growth. Specifically, the seven bills address data centers through three closely related areas: electricity, water, and environmental impacts. On electricity, the legislation addresses grid upgrade costs, energy procurement, and rate structures. The state says the new laws are intended to prevent costs associated with serving data centers from being shifted to other ratepayers, and the laws require projects to pay for necessary grid upgrades and comply with California energy procurement requirements. For water, proposed data centers must provide information to local governments and water suppliers about water use, supply, efficiency, and drought planning, and the projects will be responsible for upgrades needed to provide water service. Regarding environmental review, the legislation clarifies that data centers are not categorically exempt from CEQA. At the same time, the legislation also allows for expedited judicial review for qualifying data centers that meet certain environmental requirements. Projects must demonstrate that they meet state standards involving energy, water, and fuel consumption and will not shift costs to ratepayers before qualifying for that treatment. For developers, the new legislation means that infrastructure planning must become part of site selection and entitlement strategy early in the process. For example, data centers are energy-intensive, with the largest data centers typically including onsite power generation. However, proper energy planning also requires understanding available natural gas supplies, grid connectivity requirements with the local power provider, if desired, and a host of related regulatory requirements. California’s new framework is intended to prevent data center costs from being shifted to other ratepayers, meaning that when deciding whether a project is feasible, developers must consider all aspects of energy costs and availability early in the planning process. Water presents a similar issue. The new disclosure requirements mean that developers should be prepared to address anticipated water use and its relationship to local supply, efficiency, and drought planning. For developers evaluating competing sites, the relevant questions extend beyond whether water service exists. The availability and reliability of that supply, anticipated demand, and cost of necessary improvements may all affect project feasibility. CEQA adds another layer. The new legislation makes clear that developers should be prepared to engage in robust environmental review for virtually all data center projects, and that the potential for streamlined judicial review is deeply intertwined with questions about energy, water, fuel consumption, and infrastructure costs. Taken together, the laws reinforce a broader trend in data center development: data centers are no longer primarily a technology issue. They involve significant land use and infrastructure issues, with decisions about where and how facilities are developed increasingly tied to the capacity and priorities of the communities around them. Thus, California’s new laws make it clear that infrastructure and land use analysis should not be treated as separate tracks. They increasingly need to inform one another early in the strategy process. The new state laws establish a broader framework, but they do not create a uniform entitlement process across California. Developers must still navigate the land use requirements of the city or county in which a project is proposed. That local landscape is evolving rapidly. Some jurisdictions are reconsidering how, where, and even if data centers should be permitted, while others are continuing to process projects under existing rules. For a developer, that means statewide compliance is only one part of the regulatory analysis. artigo.texto: Sauk Rapids Reaches Agreement On NextEra Battery Facility, Accepts Limited Local Control SAUK RAPIDS (WJON News) -- The Sauk Rapids City Council has reluctantly approved a development agreement for a proposed battery storage facility. Monday night, the council voted 3-2 in favor of the agreement worked out between city staff and Mayhew Lake Energy Storage LLC, a NextEra Energy Resources company. All five council members are opposed to the project's location, but three members decided any agreement is better than no agreement at all. Under Minnesota law, the authority for the project rests solely with the Public Utilities Commission, and the city has limited authority over the project. Mayor Jason Ellering says the proposed battery energy storage facility would sit on prime land for city growth. It's smack dab in the middle of a significant development corridor for the city as we continue to grow. What the next 30 years look like for the city, I think that it is important to take that into consideration. What the property is going to look like, it'll be there indefinitely. The city council previously approved two objection letters to the PUC outlining the city's concerns with the proposed location. With the approval of the development agreement, the city will rescind the letter to the PUC citing its opposition to the project. Sauk Rapids City Attorney Adam Ripple says the agreement is an attempt to make lemonade out of lemons and to mitigate the impact on the city if the project moves forward. artigo.texto: Should Americans provide subsidies through the tax code for Meta’s creation of AI data centers and compensation paid to its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg? If you think the answer is yes, then you might believe that the Trump administration is doing an excellent job enforcing tax laws and that the two major pieces of tax legislation he and Congressional Republicans have enacted have left the revenue code in really good shape. On the other hand, if you think Meta should not be subsidized (through the tax code or in any other way) for building AI data centers and for compensating Mark Zuckerberg, then you should believe something is seriously wrong with our tax laws and how they are enforced. Earlier this year, ITEP described how Meta paid just 3.5 percent of its profits in federal corporate income taxes in 2025 – and why its effective tax rate for the year may turn out to be even lower than that. Today the New York Times explains part of how the company pulled that off, reporting that Meta is claiming the research tax credit — a tax break enacted decades ago to encourage innovation and experimentation — to pay for the equipment it uses in data centers to power its AI activities. The research credit is a tax subsidy that is supposed to encourage companies to conduct research and experiment to find answers, innovations, new processes, or approaches that are not already known. It is not supposed to simply subsidize whatever equipment a tech company needs to do its business. As the Times mentions, this is not Meta’s first R&D credit-abusing rodeo: the company is already embroiled in a longstanding dispute with the IRS over its claim that more than $4 billion in compensation paid to Mark Zuckerberg should count as eligible research expenses because he allegedly invented new features on Facebook. When most people hear the term “research”, they might think of people in lab coats trying to cure cancer or engineers searching for a way to make a more powerful engine. We do not think of Mark Zuckerberg figuring out how to use our personal data to help other companies tempt us to buy something when we are looking at Facebook to catch up on some relative or friend who we are too lazy to call. The research credit has long been used to subsidize things that normal people would not call “research.” Years ago, Congress had a chance to reform the credit before they made it a permanent part of the tax code and lawmakers passed up that opportunity. More recently, a study found that the research credit seems to subsidize many companies for doing things they would do anyway and encourages many to just recharacterize activities as research in order to obtain this tax break. When you give research credits to a company that is sitting on $43 billion of cash and cash equivalents, as Meta was at the beginning of 2025, it seems especially clear that the company involved already has the means to spend whatever it wants on whatever it wants and won’t be swayed by tax incentives into changing its plans. It is not surprising that a profit-seeking company will seek to lower its tax bill in whatever ways Congress and the IRS allow. What’s unusual about Meta is its willingness to identify the limits of what the law allows and then blow right past them. The company openly admits that over $2.6 billion of the tax breaks it claimed last year alone are “uncertain,” meaning they believe that tax authorities would likely disallow them if they were scrutinized. The budgetary stakes for the U.S. are potentially huge: the Times’ new revelations suggest that one of the most profitable corporations in American history is attempting to use the biggest capital-spending boom in the history of the world to reduce its already-low tax rates even more. In theory, it is up to the IRS and the Treasury Department to make it clear that equipment used in data centers is not “research.” Given that we have more than two more years of federal agencies serving under President Trump, the one American who fervently supports building more AI data centers, the only hope is that the next Congress begins to ask questions about Meta’s outlandish tax maneuvers.

artigo.texto: Round Up: commissioners back two school grant bids, set data center moratorium hearing Davidson County commissioners voted this week to support grant applications for new high school buildings in both Lexington and Thomasville, and agreed to schedule an Oct. 26 public hearing on a temporary moratorium on data centers, in a meeting that ran more than three hours and included heated public comment. Lexington High School The board's longest discussion centered on Lexington City Schools' application to the state's Needs-Based Public School Capital Fund for a new Lexington Senior High School. The application is due Oct. 2. Lexington City Schools Superintendent Dr. Ron Anthony told commissioners the school, described by speakers as 73 years old and the oldest school building in the county, has water intrusion, aging systems, structural settlement, and accessibility and life-safety deficiencies. He presented three options: limited repairs at $15.5 million, a $58 million renovation, or new construction that would use a county match of about $41 million to unlock roughly $62 million in state funding. Anthony said the school has the third-highest performance data in Davidson County and is rated a B school, arguing that students are succeeding despite the building. The district says Lexington Senior High earned its first B under the state's school performance grades in the latest results, with a graduation rate of 91.7%. Anthony did not specify which schools the county comparison covers, and the claim could not be independently verified. Outside rankings are less favorable: U.S. News ranks the school 410th among 604 ranked high schools in North Carolina, and the nonprofit GreatSchools gives it a 3 out of 10 rating. Anthony also noted that the school's auditorium serves as a community emergency shelter. Lexington City Board of Education Chair Angela Mcduffie told commissioners that renovation "band-aids" are no longer responsible. A commissioner who is a former teacher cited leaking ceilings, buckling floors and barriers under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Commissioners spent considerable time on how to pay for the local share. Commissioners discussed a worst-case scenario for a $104 million project, in which the county would need to borrow about $15 million after applying lottery funds, existing capital money and a possible $10 million transfer from dredging funds. They noted that upcoming debt relief from the Oak Grove project could help support that borrowing. One commissioner put the county's requested contribution at $41,255,567. The county attorney, Adam Jones, cautioned that approving the application "as written" effectively certifies that the county has the required local funding available, which could commit it to the full project cost and roughly $42 million in local money. Project architect Miki Keller said the state's main focus is the match tied to the $62 million grant, about $15.5 million in local funds, and that the firm would reduce scope if costs change. Anthony said he would work with the architect within 48 hours to propose cuts, and he was willing to negotiate on a reduced estimate of about $90 million to $95 million. Commissioners clarified that the vote authorizes applying for the grant rather than approving construction, and they voted to approve the application. Thomasville High School Commissioners then approved Thomasville City Schools' application in about six minutes. Rodney Shotwell said the building scope of the revised proposal is intact but planned athletic upgrades and some renovations were cut. The plan requests $15.5 million in local funds to complete a $77.5 million new school. Shotwell also described severe problems at a closed career-technical building and the need for a $1.2 million infrastructure project. Commissioners said that if neither district wins a grant, they would revert to existing allocations and revisit renovation funding for Thomasville High and other schools. Data center moratorium The board voted 4-2 to schedule an Oct. 26 public hearing on a temporary moratorium on data centers. The vote did not adopt the moratorium itself, Jones stressed. A four-month moratorium was discussed. Supporters said a pause would give time to study impacts, gather citizen input, and let planning staffer Lee Crook finish a zoning text amendment for data centers. One commissioner said the county has no specific data center regulations and argued a pause would also give state and federal officials a chance to explain policies they have promoted without answering local questions. Another commissioner said a moratorium would allow time to design plans in which large data center investments could fund schools and reduce property taxes for long-term residents and seniors. Shell said commissioners already have authority to scrutinize applications and worried a moratorium could delay an acceptable project midstream, "handcuffing" future boards. One commissioner initially described the moratorium as sending an anti-business signal before saying the commissioner supported it as a pause. Planning and Zoning Director Lee Crook said regulatory work can continue during a moratorium and that private land sales to data centers cannot be blocked but would be subject to any adopted regulations. Jones warned that adopting a moratorium and a new ordinance simultaneously would undermine the moratorium's purpose. Jones and Hiller said the county cannot offer targeted tax relief without state legislation, though Cabarrus County uses economic development incentives to fund such programs. During the discussion, Shell told a member of the audience to "shut up" after a tense exchange, and other officials called for decorum. Shell later apologized. artigo.texto: O Atlético-MG fechou uma parceria na área de data center com a Huawei. A empresa chinesa será fornecedora de servidores, soluções de armazenamento de dados e sistemas de backup para a Arena MRV, estádio do clube mineiro, em Belo Horizonte. O contrato é de cinco anos e a instalação da infraestrutura de dados está prevista para começar em novembro. A implantação e o acompanhamento da operação serão feitos pela SYX-AI, integradora parceira tecnológica da Huawei no Brasil. O clube informou que, a partir desse contrato, a Arena MRV passará a operar integralmente com tecnologia da Huawei na área de infraestrutura de dados. Como parte do acordo, o vice-presidente de Negócios do Atlético-MG, Márcio Freire, e o diretor de Tecnologia, Leandro Evangelista, visitaram instalações da fornecedora na China. Com base na experiência, os executivos indicam que, nos próximos anos, soluções de Inteligência Artificial (IA) podem ser incorporadas à operação do estádio, como para monitoramento do público que frequenta os jogos de futebol. Segundo o Atlético-MG, além da infraestrutura tecnológica, a parceria poderá ser estendida para atividades relacionadas ao futebol, como análise de desempenho, dados e scouting. "Estamos sempre nos atualizando, e a Huawei está muito à frente no que se refere à tecnologia. Ficamos muito satisfeitos com essa oportunidade. Foi um momento de conhecer as estruturas da Huawei, as cidades, entender o que eles estão realizando e avaliar como podemos agregar essas tecnologias ao futebol e à Arena MRV", afirma Evangelista, em nota.

artigo.texto: Com capacidade produtiva de 4 GWh por ano, a nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias da WEG, em construção em Itajaí (SC), receberá investimento total estimado de R$ 330 milhões, segundo ampliação do projeto anunciada pela companhia na última semana. De acordo com a empresa, o início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. A expansão faz parte da estratégia da WEG de acompanhar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil, em um momento de preparação para o primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento, previsto para dezembro de 2026. Com a atualização, o projeto passa a incorporar maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, que, segundo a companhia, permitirão ampliar a capacidade produtiva da unidade. A WEG aponta o avanço das fontes renováveis e a necessidade de maior flexibilidade e segurança para o sistema elétrico como fatores que vêm impulsionando a demanda por soluções de armazenamento no país. “O mercado de armazenamento de energia vive um momento de forte expansão, impulsionado pelo crescimento das fontes renováveis e pela necessidade crescente de maior flexibilidade e segurança para o sistema elétrico”, afirmou Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de Automação e Sistemas da WEG. “A ampliação deste projeto demonstra a capacidade da WEG de adaptar rapidamente seus investimentos para atender às necessidades do mercado e apoiar o desenvolvimento sustentável do setor energético brasileiro”, concluiu Johann. artigo.texto: A brief stop-work order was issued and then retracted for construction on the DC BLOX Thunderbird data center on Sept. 11 and 12. The order was issued after a nearby resident reported heavy machinery and work starting on the site without a posted permit. After an inspection, work was allowed to continue on the site under a drainage permit, which is required to be visibly posted on the site. While the construction continues, there are still concerns from some community members about the presence of private security and local police near the site. Frustrations have continued to rise after a lack of communication from DC BLOX. Megan Lapa is a member of Eastside Community Action (ECA), which has been organizing against the data center since it was proposed in July. “It’s the audacity of it,” Lapa said. “They want to come here and build this project, but they’re not telling us anything beyond what they’re required to. They’re not listening to our concerns or what we’re saying.” ECA has filed a petition for judicial review of the variance of use the Metropolitan Development Commission approved for development of the site. The petition says that the request did not adequately meet the requirements for a variance of use of a site zoned Industrial 3. “[The] goal is to get this [land] in the hands of the community,” Lapa said. “Whether that’s for a different industrial development or whatever it may be, we want to be able to have some [community input].” While the ECA has expressed its dislike of the project, some Butler students are experiencing the same issue in their own communities. Sophia McKinley, a sophomore philosophy and political science double major, is from Kokomo, Ind., a community an hour north of campus, which has also shown strong opposition to its own data center project. “Being at [Butler], so much of our curriculum is community-based,” McKinley said. “[Data centers] are an issue we’re seeing affect students in their hometown; we should carry that over [to] caring about it here.” McKinley sees the issue as an opportunity for students to get more involved in the local community. “This is the time you’re going to be most available to care, have the resources to [get involved] and be around people your age that care about similar things,” McKinley said. “If you’re seeing so many of your peers passionate about this, maybe it’s time to think about why that is.” While communities remain wary of data centers in their area, some involved are supportive of the initiatives, particularly the potential industrial and monetary benefits. Michael-Paul Hart is the city-county councilor for District 20, where the site is located. District 20 is also where Google withdrew a rezoning request for a data center last year after community disagreement and an expected no-vote from the City-County Council. “[Thunderbird Commerce Center] is a site that has power already,” Hart said. “It is surrounded by other industrial-type uses. If you were going to pick a site, [this] is a good site given its history of being a brownfield [and] being a manufacturing area.” Hart says that the development will provide benefits to District 20, allowing for further investment into the community as a result of potential tax abatements, commonly referred to as tax breaks, and community impact payments. “[The data center buildings] will be the smallest [ones] over there, but they will pay seven to 10 times more because of [the] equipment inside it, even under tax abatement,” Hart said. “In this case, the charity and community impact is between [$7 million] and $8 million. Without a tax abatement, I can’t get those checks.” While a vote for tax abatements for the DC BLOX site has not been scheduled, abatements were recently approved for the Sabey Decatur Township data center project and a vote on abatements for the Metrobloks site is scheduled for Oct. 21. DC BLOX could not be reached for comment at the time of publication.

artigo.texto: A Intel lançou a versão 26.3.5 (2026Q3) do seu Media Driver para Linux, adicionando suporte oficial à Crescent Island, sua próxima GPU voltada para acelerar cargas de trabalho em Data Centers. No novo driver, a placa é listada sob o código CRI, ao lado de outras plataformas da empresa como Panther Lake, Nova Lake e Battlemage. - ElmorLabs apresenta novo medidor de energia com recursos inéditos para placas de vídeo - Novo projeto homebrew leva streaming de jogos de PC a portátil clássico da Nintendo A implementação marca um passo fundamental no suporte de software de código aberto, ativando os motores dedicados à decodificação, codificação e processamento de vídeo do componente. Embora a empresa ainda não tenha publicado a tabela com os codecs e formatos suportados, a atualização sinaliza o avanço no desenvolvimento da infraestrutura para clientes corporativos. ESPECIFICAÇÕES E ARQUITETURA: Xe3P, não Xe3LP Diferente de relatórios anteriores que apontavam o uso da arquitetura Xe3LP, a Intel confirmou oficialmente que a Crescent Island é baseada na arquitetura Xe3P. Projetada principalmente para tarefas de inferência em Inteligência Artificial (IA), a placa combina capacidade computacional robusta com recursos dedicados de mídia: - Núcleos/Motores: 32 núcleos Xe e 256 motores XMX. - Memória: Capacidade expandida de até 480 GB de LPDDR5X (originalmente anunciada com 160 GB). - Consumo e Design: Formato PCIe resfriado a ar com consumo de 350W. ATUALIZAÇÕES NO ECOSSISTEMA LINUX Em paralelo ao driver de mídia, foi lançado o VPL GPU Runtime 26.3.5, que adiciona o suporte ao acelerador e organiza a família Wildcat Lake dentro do ecossistema Panther Lake no runtime. O pacote também inclui ajustes na estrutura de referência RAB para o codec HEVC, visando otimizar a qualidade das transmissões.

artigo.texto: Do you think Donald Trump is a secret R.E.M. fan? Trump was, wittingly or not, channeling “Shiny Happy People” when selling the virtues of data centers alongside some of Big Tech’s biggest names this week. They were gathered together to discuss how to win the global AI race without killing everyone. A noble mission. “This is a group that loves local communities,” Trump said, as the tech leaders around him stared like reluctant teenagers visiting an elderly relative, showing little enthusiasm for their supposed love of communities. These billionaire nerds are going to “work with local communities” on data centers to make them “very, very happy,” Trump said. How? By pumping them with enough money to buy off their concerns about these resource-devouring behemoths. Put another way, the tech brolionaires are going to throw their love around, take it into your town, and then put it in the ground as foundations for a data center. But don't worry, where the flowers used to grow, gold and silver will shine instead. And the local people will all be shiny happy people holding hands. No time to cry, happy, happy. You get the tedious drift. If you didn’t understand why a lot of R.E.M. fans kept it secret before, perhaps it’s a little clearer now. Trump reached into his own political lexicon for what to brand this inducement for reluctant residents: “you could call it a dividend because a dividend sounds right.” Ah yes, Trump’s solve-all “dividend,” currently going through a midterms test run. The trouble is, aren’t data centers just too unpopular for this form of legal-but-unsubtle bribery to work? In Congress, data centers are the AI issue scrambling the two main parties. Among voters, opposition crosses party lines, and the facilities have become attack-ad material before November’s midterms. The polling is grim reading for the likes of Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Pew found that 60 percent of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new data center nearby, including 54 percent of Republicans. Yet research on paying communities to accept other unwanted projects suggests Trump’s instinct is pretty sound. Money can buy goodwill, with caveats. The $10K Data Center Dividend In Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, NorthPoint Development has promised every eligible household $10,000 if it builds its Project Hazelnut campus, as part of a $165 million package that also pledges $7 million a year to the township for 15 years. That’s some dividend, but the offer hasn’t quieted the opposition to the data center at the heart of it all. Many local residents still oppose the data center, and city officials have previously rejected the development. “Ten-thousand dollars doesn’t match how much it’s going to tank my property value,” Jeff Fasnacht, a retired teacher who lives nearby, told The Wall Street Journal. Still, throwing money at your opponents isn’t futile in these fights. In a recent Boston experiment, doubling a developer’s offer from $1,500 to $3,000 per person raised support for nearby housing by 2.6 percentage points—modest, but meaningful when proposals averaged 49 percent support. Across Michigan wind-farm townships, surveyed landowners paid at least $1,000 a year were more supportive of additional turbines than those paid less or nothing. In Pennsylvania, a 2016 study linked more fracking “impact fee” revenue to greater support for a hypothetical gas project. Among residents already aware of fracking, the link was stronger when money went to municipalities rather than counties. Hazle Hits All the Tripwires The same literature helps explain what’s happening in Hazle. Among 520 Michigan landowners surveyed twice after a wind project opened, views diverged mainly on whether people judged the planning process fair, and only secondarily on whether they had a financial stake. A national survey of 1,705 wind-farm neighbors found compensation’s effect lost statistical significance once they accounted for broader attitudes. The authors called it “not a panacea.” In Boston, money stopped mattering once proposals included affordable housing, which the researchers argue triggers symbolic reasoning. And a classic Swiss study found that offering compensation roughly halved acceptance of a nuclear waste site. A civic duty became a transaction. Hazle’s offer trips nearly every wire. It came in June, seven months after township supervisors denied the project’s land-development plan and after a county judge turned down the developer’s appeal. It pays out only once the first building earns a certificate of occupancy. The fight has become symbolic, giving it coherence and a marker of local identity. At a township meeting in June, opponents wore “Project Hazlenot” T-shirts. What Trump’s Dividend Tells Us Trump’s own dividend is instructive. At the Republican National Convention in Dallas on September 9, he promised $5,000 to every adult citizen if, and only if, Republicans keep Congress. It is a temptingly juicy offer. More registered voters favor the idea than oppose it, 48 percent to 40 percent in an Economist/YouGov poll. But here’s the rub for Trump: 57 percent think he won’t deliver. His dividend has a credibility problem. The data center dividend has the opposite one. In Hazle, the worry isn’t that the developer won’t deliver. It’s that it will. The check arrives stapled to the building nobody really wants, even if anyone is tempted by the moolah. Alaskan Minerals Alaska shows a lucrative model. It has paid residents an annual dividend since 1982, paid for after the first year by earnings on a fund built with the state’s mineral royalties, communities rewarded for the resources around them. Nobody has to approve a project to receive it. The money arrives every year, a share of what the ground has already yielded. Interfering with it, a paper from the libertarian Cato Institute notes, risks political suicide. The same paper also argues, however, that AI’s proceeds don’t fit Alaska’s logic bec
