REUTERS/Annegret Hilse BERLIN, Sept 28 (Reuters) - China's Gotion will invest €1.1 billion ($1.25 billion) in Volkswagen's battery plant in Valencia under a broader plan to jointly develop a European battery supply chain. Chinese companies are boosting their presence in Europe ahead of expected moves by Brussels to shield EU industry from cheaper imports, including electric vehicles from China threatening to slash the market share of Volkswagen and other EU heavyweights. Gotion's investment allows it to take a 49% stake in the Valencia plant of Volkswagen's battery business PowerCo, which will remain the majority shareholder, VW said. The plant will become a European production hub for lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries. PowerCo, for its part, will invest €470 million in two Gotion sites – a cell factory in Šurany, Slovakia, and a new production facility for cathode material in Kenitra, Morocco – for a 49% stake in each. VW technology chief Thomas Schmall said the move "marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility".VW is Gotion's largest single shareholder, with 24%. It said it had agreed to sell a 5.3% stake - worth $373 million according to LSEG data - to an unnamed buyer. The German group is currently undergoing the most radical overhaul in its history, cutting 100,000 jobs, and also wants to drastically reduce its sprawling investment portfolio. ($1 = 0.8800 euros) ($1 = 6.7103 Chinese yuan) (Reporting by Rachel More; editing by Thomas Seythal and Kevin Liffey)

artigo.texto: Conversas da PF revelam diálogos de Hugo Motta com banqueiro sobre terreno e mercado de carbono Mensagens obtidas pela Polícia Federal (PF) trouxeram à tona uma série de diálogos entre o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), e o fundador do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro. As conversas, que agora são objeto de investigação, abordam temas sensíveis como uma possível “sociedade” para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) e discussões sobre um projeto de lei crucial para o mercado de carbono no Brasil. As revelações apontam para uma proximidade entre o parlamentar e o banqueiro, levantando questionamentos sobre a natureza desses contatos em meio a processos legislativos e transações financeiras. A apuração da PF sugere que a relação entre Motta e Vorcaro ia além de meros contatos institucionais. Os detalhes das mensagens indicam um envolvimento em negociações que podem ter implicações tanto no âmbito empresarial quanto no político, especialmente considerando o papel de Motta na Câmara dos Deputados e os interesses comerciais de Vorcaro. Diálogos sobre Negócio Imobiliário em João Pessoa Em 9 de março de 2024, Hugo Motta teria procurado Daniel Vorcaro para discutir a negociação de venda de um terreno situado na capital paraibana. Essa conversa ganha relevância ao ser contextualizada com um empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões, contraído no mesmo mês por Bianca Medeiros, cunhada do presidente da Câmara. O financiamento, concedido pelo Banco Master de Vorcaro, destinou-se justamente à aquisição de um terreno em João Pessoa, o que levanta suspeitas sobre a possível interligação dos eventos. A Polícia Federal investiga se houve algum tipo de facilitação ou influência indevida nas transações, dada a posição de Motta e a simultaneidade dos acontecimentos. A natureza da “sociedade” mencionada nas mensagens é um dos pontos centrais da investigação, buscando esclarecer os termos e os beneficiários de tal arranjo. O Projeto de Lei do Mercado de Carbono em Foco Além das questões imobiliárias, as mensagens revelam que Motta e Vorcaro também discutiram, em 19 de novembro de 2024, o projeto de lei que visa regulamentar o mercado de carbono no Brasil. Trata-se do substitutivo do Senado ao PL 182 de 2024, uma legislação de grande impacto econômico e ambiental. Em uma das mensagens, Motta faz menção a uma questão específica relacionada às seguradoras. A proposta em debate tratava da possibilidade de seguradoras, empresas de previdência e capitalização adquirirem “ativos ambientais” negociados no mercado de carbono para compor suas reservas técnicas e provisões. A versão aprovada pelo Senado previa um mínimo de 0,5% dos recursos para esses ativos, enquanto a Câmara retomou a redação anterior, que estabelecia um percentual de 1% ao ano. Essa alteração é significativa para o setor e para os negócios de Vorcaro. A investigação da PF já havia apontado, em junho de 2026, que Vorcaro teria enviado propostas legislativas diretamente ao gabinete do senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI), indicando uma “convergência de interesses ilícitos”. Uma dessas propostas, inclusive, tratava da regulamentação do mercado de carbono, reforçando o interesse do banqueiro na matéria. A Defesa de Hugo Motta e as Implicações Políticas Diante das revelações, a defesa de Daniel Vorcaro foi procurada, mas não se manifestou até o momento. Já Hugo Motta, em nota, defendeu-se afirmando que mantém diálogo com representantes do empresariado e de outros setores da sociedade, e que não há qualquer ilícito nos diálogos divulgados. O parlamentar alegou que as conversas foram descontextualizadas e negou ter atuado em benefício próprio ou de terceiros. Motta também anunciou que pretende apresentar queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rêgo (MDB-PB), acusando-o de calúnia, difamação e divulgação de fake news com finalidade eleitoral. O contexto político é relevante, uma vez que Veneziano concorre à reeleição e tem como adversário o pai de Motta, Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos-PB). Sobre o empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões contratado por sua cunhada com o Banco Master, Motta esclareceu que a operação ocorreu em um período anterior à divulgação das investigações sobre a instituição financeira e seu proprietário. O presidente da Câmara reiterou sua confiança nos órgãos responsáveis pelas investigações, afirmando que cabe a eles responder pelas apurações. artigo.texto: A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Centers (Redata) marca um novo momento para o país, com regras fiscais que devem apoiar a construção de novas estruturas de processamento de dados, algo que é estratégico para qualquer nação com visão de futuro. Mas, assim como outras infraestruturas críticas, os data centers precisam de energia segura e confiável. E, neste ponto, é preciso encarar as demandas do sistema elétrico com pragmatismo técnico, afastando-se de visões dogmáticas e sem considerar pressões externas que careçam de embasamento adequado. Um data center de grande porte exige suprimento ininterrupto de energia de alta densidade 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Cargas dessa magnitude não toleram oscilações de frequência ou tensão. O processamento de dados em nuvem e o treinamento de modelos complexos de inteligência artificial não podem ser paralisados ou desacelerados quando o vento cessa ou quando a noite cai. Uma carga dessa natureza exige um nível de confiabilidade acima de 99%, requerendo, portanto, a presença de fontes firmes de energia. A aprovação do Redata pelo Senado trouxe a flexibilização necessária ao estabelecer o uso de fontes de baixa emissão, abrindo um espaço legítimo para o gás natural no suporte a essas novas demandas. O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), por exemplo, já sinalizou que a regulamentação precisa contemplar múltiplas fontes de geração para dar viabilidade aos empreendimentos, mas as notícias que vêm de Brasília indicam que outras áreas não estão atentas o suficiente para os problemas que poderão ocorrer caso sejam banidas as fontes movidas a gás natural do suprimento a este tipo de demanda. Tal restrição traz um equívoco conceitual e um risco econômico. As fontes renováveis possuem uma limitação estrutural intrínseca, que é sua intermitência. Sem a presença de geração firme de base para regular o sistema, a conexão de gigawatts adicionais em cargas concentradas pode colocar riscos ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), uma vez que o encargo dessa confiabilidade especificamente recairá no próprio sistema interligado. A aposta em baterias para cobrir esse problema esbarra em limitações de custos, de tecnologias específicas e de maturidade comercial. É nesse cenário que o gás natural se afirma como o vetor indispensável para a transição. Tratando-se de uma fonte de baixa emissão, o gás provê a energia firme e despachável exigida pelos data centers. Países que lideram a corrida dos data centers, como os Estados Unidos, utilizam o gás natural como pilar central de segurança elétrica para viabilizar seus complexos de tecnologia. Impor sobrecustos, condicionalidades punitivas ou exigências de compensação ambiental de carbono trará um efeito adverso. O gás natural brasileiro se tornará menos competitivo, e os investimentos globais serão muito prejudicados em nosso país, e terminarão migrando para países como os Estados Unidos ou a Argentina, onde o suprimento firme a gás é garantido sem amarras regulatórias. O Congresso Nacional agiu com maturidade ao reconhecer a importância das fontes de baixa emissão no Redata. É preciso que o governo federal, respeitando a decisão dos parlamentares, siga pelo mesmo caminho. Xisto Vieira Filho é CEO na Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas (Abraget).

artigo.texto: The Pune battery technology centre planned by COEP Technological University and JSW Projects will receive an investment of more than Rs 800 crore and is expected to create over 1,000 jobs across the battery ecosystem, according to the memorandum of understanding signed by the two institutions. The centre will be established at COEP’s Chikhali Research Park in two phases. The partners describe it as India’s first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre, with work focused initially on lithium-ion battery cells and later expanding to sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. The first phase will cover battery-cell design, simulation and prototyping. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of manufacturing cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 Ah. The facility is intended to take technologies beyond laboratory research and towards testing and development at pilot scale. The partnership will bring COEP students and faculty into projects with industry engineers. It will support joint research, technology development, academic publications and intellectual property creation, while providing hands-on exposure to commercially relevant battery technologies. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud said the collaboration could help develop indigenous alternatives to imported batteries. The university said the centre would also create an institutional platform for training and research linked to the wider battery ecosystem. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said the partnership would focus on developing cells suited to Indian climatic conditions and applications. “Cells are the new fuel of this century,” he said, adding that India needed to build domestic capabilities to manufacture them. The proposed centre is expected to support applications in electric vehicles, grid storage and clean energy. Its planned research scope places Pune’s academic and industrial capabilities within a sector that requires cell design, validation and manufacturing expertise, rather than only battery assembly. The MoU does not specify an operational opening date in the information available. The project’s immediate milestones are the rollout of the first phase for design, simulation and prototyping, followed by the planned cell validation and pilot-scale manufacturing facility in the second phase.

artigo.texto: TerraFlow and DG Matrix Pair Flow Battery With Solid-State Transformer for Live AI Compute TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix plan to combine vanadium flow storage, a programmable solid-state transformer and Dell servers in a live U.S. AI-compute deployment designed to buffer fast-changing electrical loads. Published · 4 min read TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix announced on September 28 a commercial agreement to deploy a VRFB solid-state transformer system designed to power a live high-performance computing cluster in the United States. The initial installation will combine TerraFlow’s long-duration uninterruptible power system with DG Matrix’s programmable Interport solid-state transformer and Dell PowerEdge servers, creating a test of how long-duration storage and software-defined power conversion can buffer rapidly changing AI computing loads. The companies have not disclosed the deployment location, total megawatt load, battery energy capacity, project cost or commercial-operation date. That makes the announcement a technology-deployment milestone rather than evidence that the architecture has already proven performance at hyperscale. The central claim is narrower: the partners intend to put the combined system against live compute loads and use it to manage power flow between the grid, on-site generation, storage and servers in real time. VRFB solid-state transformer system targets fast-changing compute loads In their September 28 announcement, TerraFlow and DG Matrix said the architecture is intended to absorb rapid changes in computing demand before those changes propagate upstream into electrical infrastructure. TerraFlow’s LDUPS platform combines uninterruptible-power functionality with hours of energy storage, while DG Matrix’s Interport platform performs programmable power conversion and routing among sources, storage and compute loads. The approach addresses a problem that is becoming more important as AI data centers adopt denser computing hardware. Power demand inside an AI facility can change quickly as large GPU clusters move between workload states. Those variations do not automatically translate into a grid reliability event, but sufficiently large and synchronized load changes can complicate planning, protection and operational coordination. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation is already developing dedicated standards for computational loads. NERC’s Project 2026-02 identifies reduced visibility, system-instability risk during disturbances and planning uncertainty among the issues associated with rapidly growing data-center and other computational loads. Long-duration flow storage adds a different role than conventional UPS batteries TerraFlow describes its LDUPS architecture as a long-duration system rather than a conventional short-ride-through UPS. The company’s LDUPS platform supports vanadium or organic electrolyte chemistries and is designed in modular 1.25 MW building blocks with scalable energy duration. In the announced deployment, the vanadium redox flow battery is expected to provide both fast response and multi-hour energy capacity. That combination is important because data-center power systems normally separate several functions. UPS equipment handles very short interruptions and power-quality events, backup generators or other on-site generation provide longer-duration support, and grid-connected batteries may perform peak shaving or other energy-management tasks. TerraFlow and DG Matrix are proposing to coordinate several of those functions through a common power architecture. Microgrid Media has previously examined solid-state transformer testing at UC San Diego, where a California Energy Commission-funded demonstration is designed to connect a 2 MW AI computing load through medium-voltage power electronics and flexible-load controls. The TerraFlow-DG Matrix project is distinct, but both efforts reflect growing interest in replacing static data-center electrical architectures with systems that can actively control how computing loads interact with the grid. DG Matrix is also increasing the power density of its Interport platform DG Matrix said on September 25 that its Interport platform had increased output from 200 kW to 400 kW using silicon-carbide power electronics while maintaining essentially the same power-module footprint. That product update does not establish the size of the TerraFlow deployment, but it provides context for the platform being integrated with the flow-battery system. For the initial project, the companies have not disclosed how many Interport units will be deployed or the voltage architecture feeding the Dell servers. They also have not published a target for round-trip efficiency, load-ramp smoothing, outage duration, grid-services revenue or the amount of utility capacity the system could defer. Those omissions matter because claims about making data centers more flexible need operating evidence. Microgrid Media’s coverage of NERC’s computational-load reliability work has highlighted the need for better modeling, commissioning, telemetry and coordination as large computing facilities connect to the bulk power system. The commercial test will matter more than the first-of-a-kind label TerraFlow and DG Matrix describe the deployment as the first integrated U.S. architecture combining a vanadium redox flow battery with a solid-state transformer to directly power a live high-performance computing cluster. That characterization is a company claim and should be treated as such until independently established across the market. The more consequential question is whether the system can demonstrate measurable performance under real AI workloads. Useful results would include how quickly storage responds to workload transients, how much upstream load variability is reduced, how efficiently power moves through the architecture, and whether the battery can provide meaningful energy duration without compromising UPS-level respons

artigo.texto: As the artificial intelligence (AI) boom brings large data center proposals to small and rural communities across the United States and beyond, the most resounding story to emerge is one of mismatched agency. In journalist Jasmine Sun’s words, “big companies descend on a small town and run roughshod over small-d democracy.” Many people do not want data centers in their communities. And for good reasons: the costs are material, if still not fully understood, spanning noise and visual pollution, land-use change, and rising electricity demand with knock-on effects for water withdrawals and utility affordability. As with most large-scale developments, data centers also offer economic upsides—a surge of construction jobs, considerable tax revenue, and improvements in infrastructure. These can be significant but are not always guaranteed. Given the scale and impact of data centers, people should have a voice. However, decisionmaking about data center siting is often fragmented, noninclusive, and based on criteria other than their impact on communities. In many parts of the country, states set tax exemptions and approve utility contracts, while local officials, often working part-time, negotiate one siting approval at a time, up against experienced corporate counsel imposing time pressure and confidentiality agreements. Local citizens are rarely directly involved in these processes and, where confidentiality provisions apply, may learn the terms of a proposed deal only after negotiations are well advanced. The result is that residents feel sidelined, fueling skepticism as to whether data center proponents are sharing all relevant information and whether public officials are acting in the community’s best interests. Because data center developments are closely associated with the rapid diffusion of generative AI in the U.S. and elsewhere, uncertainty about the projects themselves can also become entangled with broader concerns about AI’s economic and social impacts, as well as its existential risks. Known remedies for these challenges exist—namely, community-led processes that surface varied priorities, align on a common vision, and help turn it into action. Historically, such processes have proven costly and complex, requiring time to build the trusting relationships on which collaboration depends—time that can be particularly scarce when communities are responding to fast-moving development proposals. Deliberative processes become more difficult to run when issues are emotionally and politically charged, as is increasingly the case with data center developments in the U.S. Given this context, we undertook to explore whether the same technological advances driving the need for large data centers—generative AI—could be leveraged as a community resource for problem-solving. We began with a simple question: What if communities could use AI to help reach better collective decisions about data center developments and other similarly complex local challenges? Those worried about AI’s impacts, or doubtful of its usefulness to society, may be skeptical. Our proposal may sound like a contradiction: If AI is seemingly—in contexts like the U.S. at least—being designed and deployed to replace people in work, how can it enhance people’s shared agency? We argue that it can. When designed to support, not replace, human-to-human collaboration, and deployed in ways that communities own, govern, and control, generative AI shows considerable potential for enhancing shared problem-solving and collective intelligence. AI can collapse the time and costs that have traditionally kept broad, sustained participation in such problem-solving out of reach. An AI facilitator, unlike a human, has no problem with everyone talking at the same time. The key question is how to design AI systems that support more inclusive decisionmaking and that communities will adopt and trust. Data centers are a test of community problem-solving For communities to answer an AI buildout with AI applications of their own may sound odd given the warranted skepticism of AI’s usefulness and the fact that the technology has not been designed or deployed on community terms. But the broader proposition of AI’s value to communities extends beyond data centers and the U.S. institutional context in which this work is situated. Communities across different national and development contexts regularly face complex decisions that cut across policy domains, institutions, and stakeholder interests while lacking the capacity to integrate what people know and value into a shared course of action. Managing the data center boom is a clear and relevant example of this type of community decisionmaking. Our motivating assumption was that communities can reach better decisions and better address shared challenges by transforming a complex issue (like whether to build a data center) from a discrete decision to an iterative process of community problem-solving that includes the perspectives, interests, and expertise of all stakeholders, not just elites and elected officials. Informed by existing literature, community problem-solving can be understood as including four phases that we summarize here as surface, align, implement, and learn, or “SAIL” (see Figure 1). The cycle synthesizes standard loops in adjacent literatures, including the policy cycle’s stages of agenda-setting, formulation, implementation, and evaluation; the plan-do-study-act loop from improvement science; the observe-orient-decide-act loop from strategy science; and the plan-act-monitor-adjust loop from adaptive ecological management. Where these cycles typically begin from observation or agenda-setting by a single actor or organization, these phases emphasize the need for surfacing values and perspectives across many stakeholders and issues and aligning them before decision and action across multiple domains. artigo.texto: Data centers are drawing protests and city hall spats across the country. You wouldn't have known it Saturday night in downtown Washington, DC. When I arrived at Data after Dark, a "pro-data center" party 10 minutes before it was scheduled to start, there were already a few dozen attendees waiting in the rain to get into Pubkey, a bitcoin-themed bar. I was led downstairs, into a VIP room sponsored by AI company Cognitio, where a live jazz trio was playing and drinks were flowing. White gift bags with a black server rack above the words "come and take it" were everywhere. The party hadn't officially started yet, but the room was already full of people. Guests in cocktail dresses and suits (a handful of whom donned the signature of a Hill employee — a pin on their lapel) bounced around the room, pitching themselves and networking. I surprisingly only saw two tech bro vests. The event brought together figures from a trio of tech and free-market organizations. Jonas Du, a journalist at Mike Solana's tech-and-politics media company, Pirate Wires, first posted it on X in August. He organized the event with Casey Given, CEO of Young Voices, a nonprofit talent agency for "classically liberal" writers and commentators, and Ed Tarnowski, a tech fellow at free-market think tank R Street Institute. They were expecting to throw a get-together at his rowhouse in DC, but after more than 300,000 views and hundreds of requests to attend, it became more serious. "We host parties every other month at my rowhouse — it's usually no more than 70 or 80 people, and that's what it was," Du told me. "But we hit 70 within a day." The final Partiful guest list was over 1,000 people, more than double Pubkey's 500-person maximum capacity. The venue was packed, and a security guard told me that if I left, I wouldn't be allowed back in. I wandered upstairs, where I was confronted by flashing lights and a DJ. Behind him, an LED screen showed stock assembly-line footage and the occasional video of Robert Downey Jr., presumably as Tony Stark. The music was loud, but so too were the conversations. The multiple bars never lacked patrons ordering one of the themed cocktails, like a Loudoun County Iced Tea — the county with the most data centers in the world — or an SMRtini, a play on small modular reactors. Around 10 p.m., the music was turned off, but the hum of the crowd stopped for no one. A few weeks before the event, a Partiful blast was sent asking for volunteers for the toast session: that time had come. At least three protesters jumped on the stage separately to hijack the pro-data-center toasts. I couldn't hear them, and the crowd couldn't either, but that didn't stop them from booing and chanting "USA" to get them off stage and out of the bar. "Who believes in freedom?" Adam Thierer, toast-giver and resident senior fellow at the think tank R Street Institute, asked the crowd. "Well, we know who doesn't believe in freedom, it's the kind of freaks that were just up here charging the stage." "All of us need to go out into the world and fight — not for AI, but for America," Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino told the crowd during his speech. What was a party quickly turned into a rally as the toasts turned more into battle cries. If you watched the crowd on hand, you'd think a ban on data centers had just been lifted, and a new version of America was on the horizon. The music came back on, and the dance floor was packed, with a few people dancing to the electronic music. Everyone seemed to be on the same page, but I did talk to a couple of guests who were hoping for a little more. One woman who came with her husband from Baltimore — about a 50-minute drive — said she was expecting more technical talk about data centers. She said her icebreaker for entering a conversation was, "Do you have a GPU?" She said only one person knew what that was. (A graphics processing unit is a piece of computing used for graphics and video rendering, a key tool for AI.) She said she'd be back if they hosted another party, though. Another guest didn't expect as many people as there were, and was excited to be among other pro-data-center people, but he didn't really get the chance to talk about them. One attendee, who works for a defense technology company, told me it was refreshing to be in an environment not ruled by "slopulism" (a term he explained to me as a sort of lazy populism). He said that people liked to hate data centers simply because it's popular to do so, but haven't bothered to explore the arguments for them. The audience was thunderous throughout, and the overall mood of the night was optimistic — celebratory even. What exactly they were celebrating is still unclear. They may have just been celebrating the fact that many people felt the same way they did. Du, one of the organizers, said the event wasn't planned to change people's minds — it was promoted widely as pro-data center — but he hopes they won over some skeptics. The main goal, though, was to party. "We want people to have a good time, and I don't know how much actual conversation and debate happens," he said. "I don't know how much appetite there was for that."

artigo.texto: TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix to Deploy First U.S. VRFB and Solid-State Transformer Architecture to Power Live High-Performance Compute Commercial agreement integrates TerraFlow's LDUPS™ with DG Matrix's Interport™ to create a new power architecture for AI data centers that manages compute loads while protecting the grid HOUSTON, Sept. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TerraFlow Energy and DG Matrix today announced a commercial agreement to deploy the first integrated vanadium redox flow battery (VRFB) and solid-state transformer (SST) architecture in the United States to directly power a live high-performance computing cluster. The initial deployment will integrate TerraFlow's LDUPS™ long-duration uninterruptible power system with DG Matrix's Interport™ solid-state transformer technology and Dell PowerEdge servers, putting a new data center power architecture into operation against real compute loads. The significance goes beyond combining two technologies. AI data centers are introducing enormous new loads to the power system, but the challenge is not only how much electricity they consume. High-performance compute can change power demand rapidly, pushing that volatility back through electrical infrastructure built for more predictable loads. The integrated architecture is designed to manage power between the grid, on-site generation, energy storage, and compute in real time. TerraFlow's LDUPS™ combines the millisecond response required for UPS functionality with hours of energy capacity, allowing it to continuously buffer changes in compute demand. DG Matrix's Interport™ provides programmable solid-state power conversion, routing, and control between power sources and the compute load. Together, the technologies are designed to absorb rapid changes in demand before they reach the grid and other upstream electrical infrastructure. "AI is changing the physics of the power system, and simply adding more generation doesn't solve that problem," said Jon Parrella, CEO of TerraFlow Energy. "We have to change how these enormous loads connect to and interact with the grid. By putting long-duration storage and intelligent power distribution between the grid and the compute, we can give data centers the power performance they need without asking the grid to absorb every movement in demand. That is how we start turning data centers from grid liabilities into grid assets." The commercial agreement establishes a framework for TerraFlow and DG Matrix to bring the integrated LDUPS™ and Interport™ architecture into data center projects beyond the initial deployment. The companies are targeting applications where AI and high-performance computing require greater control over how power is delivered, managed, and exchanged with the grid. "AI infrastructure requires us to rethink power distribution from the grid all the way to the compute," said Haroon Inam, CEO of DG Matrix. "Solid-state transformers allow us to control power dynamically rather than simply move it from one voltage to another. Combining that capability with TerraFlow's LDUPS™ technology creates an architecture that can respond to the compute load in real time while controlling how that load is presented to the grid. This is the direction data center power infrastructure needs to go." The architecture also addresses a growing issue facing utilities and data center developers: how to connect gigawatts of new compute demand without requiring the power system to respond instantaneously to every change occurring inside the data center. By controlling those changes behind the meter, integrated storage and power distribution can help make large loads more predictable, more flexible, and ultimately easier for the grid to serve. For TerraFlow and DG Matrix, the initial deployment is the starting point for a commercial architecture designed to scale with the rapidly growing power requirements of AI infrastructure. "We aren't building another layer of backup power," Parrella said. "We're building the infrastructure that sits between compute and the grid and allows both of them to perform better." About TerraFlow Energy TerraFlow Energy is transforming energy storage from backup equipment into critical power infrastructure. Built on long-duration, non-flammable vanadium flow battery technology, the company's battery-in-building architecture combines uninterrupted power, long-duration energy storage, and controllable load management in a single platform that simplifies electrical infrastructure for AI data centers and other energy-intensive facilities. By turning large electrical loads into flexible grid assets, TerraFlow helps customers improve resilience, reduce operating costs, accelerate deployment, and strengthen the electric grid. Learn more at www.terraflowenergy.com Advertisement About DG Matrix DG Matrix, the global leader in solid-state transformer solutions, is unlocking power as the binding constraint on AI. It is removing this critical bottleneck of stranded power by building the intelligent power fabric of the AI data center. Built on the world's first commercially available, programmable multi-port solid-state transformer, the company's AI-enabled Interport™ platform converts, routes and controls every electron, between the grid, on-site generation, storage and compute loads through a single, software-defined stage. DG Matrix delivers an integrated and simpler solution for faster deployment, lower energy costs, native 800 VDC readiness and protection from GPU pulse loads. Because speed to power is speed to inference, DG Matrix helps hyperscale, neocloud and colocation operators bring AI capacity online in months instead of years — at scale, anywhere in the world. Learn more at https://www.dgmatrix.com/. artigo.texto: A indústria de armazenamento de energia está entre as frentes consideradas estratégicas pela FIERN (Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte) para ampliar a participação do estado na cadeia de valor da transição energética. A proposta é atrair fábricas de baterias e sistemas de armazenamento, além de estimular projetos de grande porte, para isso, a agenda da FIERN prevê incentivos fiscais e de infraestrutura, tendo como uma das metas a atração de pelo menos um projeto-piloto em escala industrial. A estratégia integra a “Agenda Caminhos do RN 2027-2030”, desenvolvida pela FIERN por meio do Observatório da Indústria Mais RN. O documento foi entregue aos candidatos ao Governo do Estado e ao Senado pelo Rio Grande do Norte durante o Fórum Caminhos do RN. O movimento ocorre em um estado que possui 12,8 GW de capacidade instalada de energia eólica e 6 GW de energia solar fotovoltaica, segundo dados apresentados no material. Informações do Sistema de Informações de Geração da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), citadas no documento, mostram ainda que o Rio Grande do Norte possui 319 parques eólicos em operação e outros 17 em construção, além de 81 usinas solares fotovoltaicas em operação e cinco em construção. Apesar da capacidade de geração, a FIERN aponta que o aproveitamento desse potencial ainda esbarra em limitações para o escoamento da energia e na necessidade de atrair atividades econômicas capazes de consumir a produção dentro do próprio estado. Por isso, a agenda trata a energia como uma infraestrutura para o desenvolvimento de outros setores e reúne propostas para transmissão, geração solar, eólica offshore, hidrogênio e amônia verdes e armazenamento de energia. De acordo com a agenda , a produção de energia renovável no estado pode superar a capacidade de escoamento da rede de transmissão, com consequências econômicas para os investidores e dificuldades para a aprovação de novos empreendimentos. Para enfrentar o problema, a FIERN propõe a expansão coordenada das linhas de transmissão, de forma a acompanhar a geração dos parques eólicos, além de uma atuação mais ativa do poder público estadual no desbloqueio de licenças e autorizações necessárias às obras. O planejamento também prevê a elaboração e atualização das resoluções do CONEMA (Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente) relacionadas ao licenciamento para instalação de parques eólicos e solares. Para o segmento fotovoltaico, especificamente, a Federação defende o aprimoramento do marco legal para disciplinar e garantir segurança jurídica à produção centralizada de energia solar. Na energia eólica, a tabela de metas da FIERN considera uma capacidade instalada atual de 9,9 GW e um potencial superior a 30 GW. A expansão, entretanto, é condicionada à solução do gargalo de transmissão. A eólica offshore também aparece entre as prioridades. Segundo o documento, atualmente não existe um marco regulatório estadual para a atividade, e a direção estabelecida é aprovar essa regulamentação no curto prazo. Entre as propostas está o direcionamento do Porto Caiçara do Norte para atender prioritariamente às atividades de montagem, manutenção e logística da cadeia offshore. A agenda também prevê o estímulo à formação de um complexo industrial ligado ao mar e o aproveitamento dos ativos naturais do estado para oportunidades nos mercados voluntário e regulado de créditos de carbono. A combinação entre disponibilidade de energia renovável, potencial eólico offshore e infraestrutura portuária também é apontada pela FIERN como uma oportunidade para desenvolver a cadeia de hidrogênio verde. O segmento é classificado atualmente como inexistente no estado. Como meta, a agenda prevê a atração de projetos-âncora vinculados ao Porto Caiçara do Norte. Para isso, a Federação propõe a criação de um marco regulatório estadual específico, o desenvolvimento de cadeias industriais derivadas e a integração entre porto, energia e indústria como instrumento para atrair investimentos. Além das propostas, a agenda estabelece direções para o desenvolvimento das principais cadeias energéticas. Na eólica, o documento parte de 9,9 GW instalados e de um potencial superior a 30 GW, condicionando a expansão à solução das limitações de transmissão. Para a eólica offshore, a intenção é avançar da atual ausência de regulamentação estadual para a aprovação de um marco regulatório no curto prazo. No hidrogênio verde, a meta é desenvolver uma cadeia hoje considerada inexistente por meio da atração de projetos-âncora ligados ao Porto Caiçara do Norte. Todo o conteúdo do Canal Solar é resguardado pela lei de direitos autorais, e fica expressamente proibida a reprodução parcial ou total deste site em qualquer meio. Caso tenha interesse em colaborar ou reutilizar parte do nosso material, solicitamos que entre em contato através do e-mail: redacao@canalsolar.com.br.

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz has secured priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 solid-state battery cells, expanding a partnership that could help bring higher-energy, safer, and more efficient batteries to future electric vehicles. The companies signed a joint testing agreement on September 24, 2026. Mercedes-Benz will test ProLogium’s Gen4 cells for electrical, thermal, and safety performance at its own facilities and at specialist testing centers. One point is important: the official announcement describes “priority access,” not exclusive rights. The agreement gives Mercedes-Benz early access to test the technology, but it does not say that Mercedes has exclusive global rights to the cells. The deal builds on nearly 10 years of cooperation between the two companies. Mercedes-Benz invested in ProLogium in 2022 and joined its board as part of efforts to develop next-generation battery technology. Jörg Burzer, Mercedes‑Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, said: “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation. Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing, and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” More Energy, Less Weight: Gen4’s Big Battery Pitch Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The technology can allow manufacturers to use higher-capacity materials while reducing some fire and safety risks linked to liquid electrolytes. ProLogium’s Gen4 lithium ceramic battery uses a fully inorganic electrolyte and ceramic separator. The company says its anode-less version can reach 430–470 Wh/kg and 1,000–1,100 Wh/L at the cell level. These specifications come from the company. They show cell-level performance, not the energy density of a full vehicle battery pack. ProLogium states that Gen4 combines high energy density with fast charging. It also performs well in low temperatures and has better safety features. Its active safety system is intended to help prevent thermal runaway. The potential benefit for EVs is significant. Higher energy density means a battery can store more energy without adding as much weight. That could support longer driving range or allow automakers to use smaller battery packs for the same range. Mercedes Has Already Put Solid-State to the Road Test Mercedes-Benz has been testing solid-state batteries on public roads since 2025. In September 2025, the company reported that a modified EQS test vehicle traveled 1,205 kilometers on a single charge from Stuttgart to Malmö. The vehicle arrived with about 137 kilometers of remaining range. That vehicle used lithium-metal solid-state cells supplied by Factorial Energy, not ProLogium. Mercedes-Benz announced that the new battery boosts usable energy by 25%. It also maintains a weight and size similar to the standard EQS battery. The demonstration showed the potential of solid-state technology, but it was a test vehicle rather than a mass-produced model. The new ProLogium agreement gives Mercedes another route to develop the technology and compare different solid-state battery approaches. The EV Battery Market Is Getting Bigger—Fast The timing is important because global demand for EV batteries is growing rapidly. The International Energy Agency estimates that EV battery deployment hit 1.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This is nearly a 30% increase from 2024 and over seven times the level in 2020. EV batteries accounted for more than 70% of total battery deployment during the year. Global electric-car sales also exceeded 20 million units in 2025, up about 20% year over year. One in every four new cars sold worldwide was electric. That is creating strong demand for batteries that can deliver better range, faster charging, and improved safety without sharply increasing vehicle cost. But solid-state technology is entering a market already dominated by conventional lithium-ion batteries. The global battery industry remains heavily concentrated. The IEA says global lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 TWh at the end of 2025, up about 30% from 2024. China accounted for more than 80% of global manufacturing capacity and more than 80% of battery-cell production. Chinese battery makers also supplied almost 75% of global EV battery deployment in 2025. This creates a major challenge for European automakers seeking more control over their battery supply chains. Solid-state batteries could offer both a technology advantage and a chance to diversify supply. ProLogium is building its first overseas gigafactory in Dunkirk, France, giving Europe another potential source of advanced battery cells. ProLogium Is Moving Toward Mass Production ProLogium has already moved beyond the laboratory stage. The company began mass production of its Gen3.5 lithium ceramic battery in Taiwan in September 2026. A third-party TÜV test confirmed a 381 Wh/kg gravimetric energy density and 903 Wh/L volumetric energy density for its 185.4-Ah large-format cell. ProLogium says its Taiwan gigafactory had shipped more than 800,000 cells by 2026. It is now preparing to bring Gen4 production to Europe. The Dunkirk factory broke ground in February 2026. ProLogium’s current plan calls for 0.8 GWh of Gen4 production in 2028, with capacity rising to 4 GWh by 2030 and 12 GWh by 2032. The company has also reserved land that could allow the site to expand to as much as 48 GWh in the future. This planned expansion will be important if automakers want solid-state cells at meaningful scale. Europe Wants More Local Battery Production The European link is important for Mercedes-Benz. artigo.texto: With one foot in the Capitol and the other already on the campaign trail, the Senate is poised to consider a bill Wednesday that sounds, at least, like it would shield consumers from rising utility costs tied to data centers. The truth is far more complex — and a lot less consequential. Politically, Republicans are betting that the Ratepayer Protection Act will show voters they care about addressing the cost of living. Crucially, the legislation also would help one of the GOP’s own — Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio — who’s facing a tough re-election fight and has become a prime target for political attacks over data centers. Husted and the GOP claim that the legislation would protect consumers from paying more for electricity as a result of data centers. But, in practice, the legislation is little more than a recommendation. The measure would require state utility regulators to consider adopting new federal standards to ensure data center companies foot their own bill within two years. Because the legislation accomplishes about as much as a press release, Democrats appear poised to oppose it — or, at least, block it from advancing on an expedited timeline before the midterm elections. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the bill a “fraud, plain and simple.” Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., likened it to a “political act.” Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said that “it’s clearly designed to help them in campaigns” and not “actually solve any problems, because it does nothing.” And Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told MS NOW that it’s a “a political ploy to enable Husted to go home and boast about getting a bill done when it’s really a fraud on consumers.” While the bill received overwhelming bipartisan support in the House, passing earlier this month in a 417-3 vote, Senate Democrats are instead labeling it a “bait-and-switch.” And some Republicans acknowledge that the bill does more politically than it does practically. “Would I like to do more? Yeah,” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said. “But on the other hand, is it better than nothing? Yeah.” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., agreed that the bill doesn’t accomplish much, noting that most utilities are “managed through local and state decision making.” But he also agreed that it “probably would help” Husted in his re-election efforts. Ohio’s Senate seat — one of a growing number that Republicans are rushing to shore up ahead of November — could be instrumental in determining control of the Senate next year. Husted, who has routinely trailed in the polls in his bid for a full six-year term, has faced an onslaught of ads in Ohio — including from his Democratic rival, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown — casting him as the “face of data centers” that are contributing to higher energy bills. On Tuesday, Husted called his data center legislation “the only bill that has a chance to get to the president’s desk before we get to the election.” Asked why the bill does not make the regulations mandatory, Husted answered that it was because “the states run the grids, and so you have to work with the states to do that.” If Democrats block the bill during a procedural vote on Wednesday, Husted and other Republicans appear eager to cast Democrats as obstructionists. Husted told reporters that it’s up to Democrats “to determine whether or not they want to play politics or they want to solve affordability issues for the American people.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that voting against the bill “makes it pretty hard for Democrats” to attack Husted over data centers and the cost of living. “It’s a chance to actually make law. It’s not just making a point,” Thune said Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Bruce Lear lives in Sioux City and has been connected to Iowa’s public schools for 38 years. He taught for eleven years and represented educators as an Iowa State Education Association regional director for 27 years until retiring. He can be reached at BruceLear2419@gmail.com Growing up, organized sports consisted of little league, or high school baseball in the spring and summer. Fall and winter meant basketball, since our school was too tiny for football. No adult had yet figured out NBA, and MLB dreams were a sure money maker—so there were no sports academies or traveling leagues. But we did have the town basketball court. It was a kid sanctuary where kid law prevailed. No adult supervision, no minimum or maximum age, and both genders were welcome. The rules were simple and strictly enforced. If you cried, you left. We called our own fouls loosely. If you overshot, and the ball went into the crick, you retrieved it. There were arguments, and fights, but there was urgency to end conflict, because finishing the game was more important than the fight. We needed rules or our game would be swallowed by conflict. Now, like the basketball court, data centers need clear and enforceable rules, or Iowa small towns and rural life will be swallowed just like our basketball games. Currently, Congress seems to lack urgency and understanding on how to catch up to the data center invasion. That sounds like a bad movie, but it’s a serious threat. Even the creators of AI are warning there needs to be a slowdown. That means the urgency to govern is in the hands of local and state lawmakers. It’s time to play catch up. History tells us this happened before during the industrial revolution. As industry grew and became more powerful, there were no laws regulating child labor, worker safety, wages, and other general working conditions. Working class people suffered, while robber barons lived in gilded mansions. I fear the new crop of robber barons are tech billionaires who are quickly trying to build data centers before the laws catch up. They promise high paying jobs but offer no guarantees. They don’t acknowledge their huge consumption of electricity and water, and they ignore the impact these large structures will have on the community. The adage “History may not repeat itself, but it often rhymes” is on target—even if Mark Twain probably never said it. I can hear that haunting rhyme echoing across Iowa corn fields while politicians dither. President Donald Trump said, “Towns that reject data centers risk becoming backwards and poor.” But in a recent Emerson College poll, 60 percent of Iowans believe data centers will negatively impact the environment. Both candidates for governor have proposed new restrictions on data centers. The Iowa legislature needs to act quickly and decisively. Here are my suggestions for regulating data centers in Iowa. In 1991, Iowa lawmakers allowed gambling but also passed strict guidelines. For example, the Iowa Gaming Commission had to approve the location, communities had to vote to see if the majority supported the idea, and each casino was required to provide a percentage of revenue to a separate nonprofit organization for distribution to benefit the community and surrounding area. I’m on one of those boards now. I believe this model would work for data centers, along with five other requirements. 1. Billion-dollar tech companies don’t need tax breaks to locate in Iowa. 2. The tech company must strengthen the electrical grid and pay for its use. 3. The tech company must in writing assure the community there is sufficient water supply and pay for upgrades to the system and water used. 4. The tech company must reduce the noise pollution. 5. The tech company must guarantee the number of permanent jobs. Data centers may be an innovation revolution impossible to prevent, but it should be regulated. No one should ever threaten violence, but we should vote for politicians willing to seriously regulate data centers. Top photo is by Chad Davis, available via Wikimedia Commons.

artigo.texto: Scaling India’s BESS Electronics for Energy Transition ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: India’s energy storage requirement is projected to surge from 82 GWh in 2026-27 to 411.4 GWh by 2031-32, with BESS accounting for 236.22 GWh. - Why it matters: EPCs and developers must look beyond battery cells to the electronics layer—BMS, power conversion, and thermal controls—to ensure system reliability and grid performance. - Watch: The evolution of domestic manufacturing standards for BMS and power electronics as the industry shifts toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale storage. Background and Context As India accelerates its renewable energy transition, the focus on energy storage has intensified. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) National Electricity Plan, the nation’s total energy-storage requirement is projected to rise from approximately 82 GWh in 2026-27 to a massive 411.4 GWh by 2031-32. Within this framework, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are expected to contribute 236.22 GWh. To support this trajectory, the government has introduced viability-gap funding mechanisms, incentivizing developers to integrate storage with renewable projects. Key Details While procurement trends show a shift toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale applications, the industry must pivot its focus toward the electronics layer. A modern BESS is a complex integration of cells, battery-management systems (BMS), power-conversion equipment, sensors, and thermal-management systems. The BMS, in particular, is critical; as systems move toward higher voltages and longer durations, the BMS architecture must manage complex parameters including voltage monitoring, cell balancing, and fault detection. The localization conversation in India is expanding beyond simple battery-pack assembly. There is a growing need to domesticate printed circuit board assemblies, control boards, communication modules, and power-management systems. This shift is not merely for import substitution but is essential to customize systems for India’s unique operating conditions, such as extreme temperatures and grid fluctuations. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, reliability is the new benchmark for project success. As BESS installations scale, an electronics failure can compromise system availability and grid performance. Consequently, manufacturing and procurement processes must prioritize inspection, functional testing, and traceability. The ability to track the production history and test results of critical electronic assemblies is becoming a vital component of the broader reliability architecture required for long-term project viability. What Happens Next India’s standards ecosystem is currently evolving to match this market growth. New regulatory frameworks covering electrical energy-storage systems and safety requirements are expected to create greater consistency in system design and performance. As the nation continues to integrate massive amounts of variable renewable energy, the development of a robust domestic electronics supply chain will be the cornerstone of India’s energy security. This transition reflects the broader maturity of the India renewable energy sector as it moves from pilot projects to a sophisticated, grid-integrated ecosystem.

artigo.texto: A Kyivstar, que lidera o mercado de telefonia celular ucraniano, foi atingida por um bombardeio russo no domingo (27), segundo o TecMundo. A companhia informou à agência Interfax que ninguém se feriu. Na mesma ofensiva, um data center da Vodafone teria sido atingido, de acordo com o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. A Vodafone, dona da segunda maior rede celular da região, não quis se pronunciar. Outro data center na capital ucraniana também foi alvo da ofensiva de domingo, que feriu um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky. Conforme a Reuters, estruturas do tipo usadas por operadoras locais estão entre os alvos prioritários. Em um dos episódios, explosões cortaram a conexão de aproximadamente 100 mil residências ao longo da semana, principalmente em Kiev e cidades vizinhas, segundo o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia. Autoridades ucranianas afirmam que os bombardeios comprometeram sistemas críticos de segurança, elevando o risco de mortes durante ataques. O ministro das Relações Exteriores, Andrii Sybha, declarou no X que a Rússia mira centros de dados para interromper o fluxo de informações. Ele também mencionou drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, variante capaz de voar acima de 600 km/h e em altitudes maiores, o que dificulta a defesa aérea. No mês passado, um drone guiado por IA matou três civis no país. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and China’s Gotion have agreed plans for three battery joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, involving combined estimated investment of approximately €3.22bn ($3.65bn). Gotion is expected to invest about €1.59bn, while PowerCo – Volkswagen’s battery manufacturing subsidiary – will contribute approximately €1.62bn. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. The ventures are planned to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells and cathode materials in Valencia, Šurany and Kenitra. Volkswagen Group technology management board member and PowerCo supervisory board chairman Thomas Schmall said: “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. “Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.” In Valencia, PowerCo’s under-construction gigafactory is expected to transfer into a joint venture producing LFP cells, with an annual capacity of 29.1GWh. PowerCo will hold 51% and Gotion 49%, making the venture a controlled PowerCo subsidiary. Gotion is expected to invest about €1.1bn for its stake. The Valencia facility is intended to serve as a European production hub for Volkswagen’s LFP-based Unified Cells. Gotion’s planned cell factory in Šurany will also transfer into a joint venture. The facility will have an annual capacity of 8.4GWh and produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Gotion will own 51%, with PowerCo holding 49%. In Kenitra, the companies plan to establish a facility producing 100,000t of LFP cathode material annually. Gotion will retain a 51% stake, while PowerCo will own 49%. The project is intended to diversify supply sources for key cathode active materials. PowerCo is expected to contribute approximately €470m to the Šurany and Kenitra projects by 2030 for its 49% stake in each project. The agreement extends a partnership that began in 2020 and covers joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The transactions remain subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, including approval from Gotion shareholders and governmental approvals in China and overseas. Gotion said implementation would take place in phases. Volkswagen Group, through its subsidiary Volkswagen (China) Investment, has also entered definitive agreements to sell a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion. The company said its voting rights, board representation, nomination rights and position as a strategic investor would remain unchanged after completion. Gotion chairman Li Zhen added: “Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry.”

artigo.texto: Data center company stays silent at public meeting Central City residents question a proposed data center as city leaders work on ordinance CENTRAL CITY, Iowa (KCRG) - Central City residents packed the Falcon Civic Center Wednesday night looking for answers about a proposed data center, but the company behind the project did not speak. The facility would be 18,000 square feet and within city limits near the Linn County Fairgrounds. City leaders emphasize smaller size The city council says the data center would be much smaller than hyperscale facilities being built near the airport in Cedar Rapids. It is about the size of four basketball courts. The proposed data center would sit on about 3 acres, use 4 megawatts of electricity. It would use a closed-loop cooling system with no water needed for cooling. The city says the project would create up to 10 full-time jobs. The developer estimates nearly $986,000 a year in public revenue from taxes and fees. City Council member Dustin Moyer said the council is in the early stages of plans for the data center and is working on drafting an ordinance. “The moment this was brought to our attention it was something at a scale beyond a little shed in a backyard, we said, ‘No, we are putting a moratorium in place, we need time to collect public input,” Moyer said. Residents question company’s silence At the meeting, people said they expected to hear from Charlie White, a representative of the project, but did not. “How come we didn’t hear from him? We are not understanding the attraction to this one company,” one resident said. White did not speak to TV9 on the record, saying he is not authorized to speak to the media and that he is concerned about his safety. Company gives statement Aurum’s CEO JohnPaul Baric provided a statement that reads in part: “It is our desire for the Elk Data Center Project to bring skilled jobs, work for local contractors, and tax revenue to Central City. We’re working to show how smaller data centers can fit into communities through careful planning and cooperation with residents.” Moyer said the council will continue to work on the ordinance, and hearing from the public. Wednesday night was part of that process. Copyright 2026 KCRG. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A carbon credit may be traded as a single unit, but its value is shaped long before it reaches a buyer. Decisions about project ownership, finance, data, verification and benefit-sharing determine who participates, who carries the risk and who ultimately benefits. As new regulations and international partnerships expand market access, these questions are becoming increasingly important across Africa. They will be central to the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026, taking place from 13 to 15 October at the Kigali Convention Centre in Rwanda. The summit will convene African governments, project developers, investors, buyers and technical experts involved in decisions across the carbon-market value chain. Countries are approaching these decisions from different regulatory, economic and environmental positions. While recent developments in East Africa demonstrate growing market activity, questions concerning international requirements, technical capacity, investment and benefit-sharing are relevant across Africa. Ousmane Fall SARR, Coordinator of the West African Alliance on Carbon Markets and Climate Finance, says: “African countries are developing carbon markets from different starting points. Stronger African expertise and regional cooperation will be important if the continent is to contribute to the standards and market practices that determine how its projects compete, attract investment and create value.” Against this continental backdrop, East Africa provides a timely example of how the market is developing. In January 2026, Rwanda and Singapore invited applications for carbon-credit projects under their bilateral Implementation Agreement, aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Credits from authorised projects may be used by eligible Singapore-based carbon tax-liable companies to offset up to 5% of their taxable emissions, subject to both governments’ requirements. Across the continent, carbon market frameworks are rapidly taking shape. Kenya and Uganda are strengthening regulatory oversight, regional partnerships are helping governments build market capacity and infrastructure, and South Africa is advancing reforms to modernise its carbon-credit ecosystem and attract investment. Together, these developments are bringing greater focus to questions of authorisation, project ownership, verification, pricing and access to international buyers, while also raising expectations that carbon finance should deliver sustainable economic and development value beyond the credit itself. Emmanuelle Nicholls, Portfolio Director for CMAS, says: “A carbon credit may be the final product, but behind it are decisions about ownership, data, risk, pricing and who ultimately benefits. The conversations in Kigali will examine what credible participation looks like across the full carbon-market value chain.” These decisions have consequences beyond individual transactions. Carbon finance is increasingly connected to conservation, agriculture, soil restoration, food security, clean energy and waste management. Its success will therefore also be judged by whether projects produce credible environmental outcomes and lasting benefits for African economies and communities. A practical example comes from the Chinko Conservation Area in the Central African Republic, where revenue from the Chinko Carbon Project is channelled through a community fund that supports locally selected initiatives, including the expansion of a medical centre in Agoumar. At CMAS 2026, African Parks and Welthungerhilfe, both Bronze Sponsors, will share perspectives on how carbon finance can support conservation, climate resilience, food systems and community development, while highlighting broader questions around project governance, impact and the distribution of value. From project-level impact to market-wide structures, these questions will underpin discussions at CMAS 2026. The programme will address government authorisation, buyer requirements, pricing and offtake, investment risk, early-stage finance, registries and African measurement, reporting and verification capacity. It will connect the question of who sets the terms with the practical requirements for building credible, investment-ready projects and transactions. CMAS 2026 is hosted by the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda, with UNDP and the African Development Bank as host organisations, the Development Bank of Southern Africa as host partner and AUDA-NEPAD as strategic institutional partner. Taking place ahead of COP31, CMAS will focus attention on the decisions behind every carbon credit and what they mean for African governments, projects, investors and communities.

artigo.texto: This Albertan trades in a murky carbon market crucial to Carney's pipeline deal When Ana Avramovic was young, art school was her plan. She landed a job trading power instead, and 20 years later runs her own Calgary firm, dealing in something you can’t see or touch. And the stakes are enormous Article content Everything Ana Avramovic sells sits as numbered entries in a government registry, and none of them are hers. She trades carbon credits, a job so unusual even her mother doesn’t fully understand what she does for a living. She came to carbon from power trading, having cut her teeth at Calgary-based TransAlta Corp. Ask her whether leaving a traditional paycheque to build a firm of her own was brave or reckless. The answer depends on the day. “Overall, excited,” she says. “And then sometimes like, oh my God, what am I doing? What have I done?” When she traded power, explaining her job took one gesture toward a window. “You see that hotel?” she says. “Somebody has to sell them electricity.” Carbon is trickier. You can’t see electricity either, but everyone knows what it’s for. She founded Carbon Merchant in July 2026 to trade industrial carbon and clean fuel credits. Every big emitter in Alberta, from oilsands operators to power producers and miners, has a limit on what it can release into the atmosphere. Beat the limit and you earn credits for cutting emissions. Miss the benchmark and you buy them from somebody who did. Avramovic is the broker in the middle, helping buyers and sellers find each other. The 42-year-old works in a market so opaque that outsiders can’t make sense of it. And, yet the stakes are enormous. The market is one of Canada’s biggest levers against climate change. Its design is a signature priority in Ottawa and lies at the centre of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s deal with Alberta on a possible West Coast pipeline for oil. But there are flaws, too. Critics worry the market is falling short and flooded with cheap credits, which means that meeting the rules is far less expensive for industry. For Avramovic, it is personal. She has two young children, and they will inherit whatever this market does or fails to do. She chose the work because it was the one place her own effort might count. “I’m just one person. It’s not like I can fix it all,” she says, “but I can at least do a little part.” Location, location, emissions Avramovic rents an office at Pavilion, a coworking space in downtown Calgary. She starts around 7 a.m., and her day is nonstop: ICE chat, where energy traders connect on the Intercontinental Exchange, plus texts, calls, Teams meetings, in-person meetings and coffee, lots of it. “A lot of my day is just communicating with different people and figuring out what are they doing, what are they looking to do,” she says. Most of her deals are spot work: one buyer, one seller, done in days. The deal she is building now is slower — a multi-year clean fuel arrangement. She is not matching a buyer to a seller on something that already exists; she is building the deal itself, putting sides together for years rather than for a week. Those are the harder matches. “It’s the challenge, the hunt. That’s what makes it fun,” she says. Avramovic’s work is similar to what a real estate agent does, minus the house. A company calls knowing what it needs but not who has it. Avramovic knows who does, and who needs to sell before its deadline. The property just happens to be carbon, so there is nothing to walk through and no keys to hand over, just a line in a registry that moves out of one account and into another. She takes a fee when the deal closes, or a monthly retainer from clients who want to know where prices are heading. Alberta’s industrial carbon market is the biggest in Canada, and it exists because the province requires it, and has since 2007, when Ed Stelmach’s government put a price on industrial carbon. No one in North America had priced industrial carbon before Alberta did. The European Union got there first. The regulation is meant to be the stick. “But then, within that regulation,” Avramovic says, “there’s also a carrot that if you do those actions, you can then create credits and monetize them.” The actions are emissions cuts. One credit is not the same as another. Each one carries a vintage, like wine, the year it was created. One made in 2024 is good until 2029, then it expires. On the open market, these credits trade for less than $30 a tonne. The alternative is paying $95 a tonne into a government fund. In recent years, big emitters have used as many credits as the rules allow, Avramovic says. Those prices are about to go up. Sarajevo to power trading Avramovic was born in Sarajevo. The family escaped in the early 1990s, when a war started, and moved to the coast of Croatia, where her mother is from, and lived with her maternal grandparents. Her father escaped in the summer of 1994. Her parents applied to immigrate to Canada, and they arrived in June 1995, two weeks after her 11th birthday. She wanted art school. Her parents had crossed an ocean to start over in a new country, and they wanted their daughter to have a profession. She went to the Haskayne School of Business at the University of Calgary, and after graduation took a creative job at Critical Mass, a Calgary agency that was doing some of the first advertising on the internet. On a whim she answered an ad for a real-time power trader at TransAlta. The desk was hiring four new traders for Alberta, she says, two women and two men. “I just put my hand up,” she says. She got one of the four. Power is a 24-hour commodity, so the desk ran 12-hour shifts, two days, two nights, then days off, moving power between regions to capture the gap between what it cost to send and what it fetched at the other end. “I was lucky at TransAlta because they were trying to prioritize hiring more women onto a trade floor,” she says. “And so, I got my chance that way.” Trading is still a man’s business, she says, and whi

artigo.texto: A controversial data center proposal cleared another hurdle this week in Inver Grove Heights after the developer filed a lawsuit against the city. The Inver Grove Heights City Council approved a major site plan Monday that calls for a nearly 55,000-square-foot data center to be constructed at the former Travel Tags site. Monday’s decision comes two weeks after the council voted to amend its yearlong data center moratorium after the developer, Florida-based QLevr, filed a lawsuit against the city challenging the validity of the moratorium. In a letter to the city council, attorneys for Larkin Hoffman, who represent the developer, called the city’s moratorium decision “arbitrary” and “capricious.” The lawsuit, which was filed in Dakota County District Court, could have cost the city at least $20 million. As for the city’s liability insurance, that maxes out at $1 million, meaning any amount over that threshold would have fallen to the city’s taxpayers. With the city voting to amend the moratorium, the developer agreed to dismiss the case. Controversial decision The recent decision to amend the moratorium was not a unanimous one. At the Sept. 14 meeting, several council members expressed frustration about the city’s lack of options given the lawsuit. Council member Mary T’Kach, who cast the sole vote against the amendment, said, “I think our litigating attorneys should be litigating this.” This week, again, council members appeared to struggle to lend their support to the project. When Mayor Brenda Dietrich asked for a motion to approve the site plan, silence followed until she herself made the motion. “Is there a second?” Dietrich asked. Another pregnant pause followed until council member John Murphy spoke up. “Hilarious,” he said. “I’ll second it.” T’Kach, again, was the sole vote against. Site plan QLevr, a real estate company that specializes in data centers, intends to build a new 54,000-square-foot data center on a 13.9-acre property at 5890 Carmen Ave. As proposed, the data center will be a 3-megawatt facility in its initial phase and a 5-megawatt facility at full buildout, which is considered to be smaller than most hyperscale data centers in Minnesota. For context, Meta’s data center campus in Rosemount has a capacity of approximately 308 megawatts. QLver’s site plan also calls for a closed-loop water system for cooling data center equipment and a screened mechanical equipment area. The proposed 23-foot-tall screening wall for the equipment is an acoustic sound wall, which provides noise dampening, according to the site plan. The property, located just west of the South St. Paul Municipal Airport, is zoned as Limited Industrial, which permits data centers, said Kevin Shay, the city’s planning manager. Next steps for QLver include an approved development contract and a building permit from the city. Inver Grove Heights initially approved the interim moratorium on June 26 with the intent of giving the city time to study the potential impacts of data centers. The city’s moratorium is still in place until next June.

artigo.texto: A NorthPoint Development fez uma proposta indecente aos moradores de Hazle Township, uma pequena cidade de 10 mil habitantes no interior da Pensilvânia: US$ 10 mil por residência para aceitar a instalação de um grande data center na cidade. Hazle Township tem 4,5 mil residências, e se todo mundo topar, a conta ficaria em US$ 45 milhões, uma gota de água num projeto de data center, cuja conta total fica na casa dos bilhões de dólares. O problema, sintomático de como está a coisa nos Estados Unidos com o boom dos data centers no momento, é que quase ninguém topou. Segundo reporta o Wall Street Journal, só 100 moradores aceitaram o pagamento. A conta dos moradores é simples: a instalação de um data center pode causar uma desvalorização dos seus imóveis muito maior do que os US$ 10 mil, por conta de problemas como aumento do barulho, das contas de energia e o temor de redução da oferta de água. Nos seus comunicados, a NorthPoint Development até disse que não vai usar água potável para resfriar os equipamentos e diz que o barulho ouvido nos arredores será equivalente a uma máquina de lavar louça, mas não colou. A empresa também patrocinou um festival local e prometeu mais US$ 120 milhões em investimentos ao longo de 15 anos. A oferta de dinheiro foi feita em junho, após a Prefeitura negar a autorização para a construção do data center e ainda impor uma moratória a esse tipo de projeto, por 180 dias. O número de cidades e estados que adotaram moratórias a novos projetos como esses já soma 294, segundo o Bitcoin Policy Institute. Em 2024, eram 6. Os estados de Nova York e Texas anunciaram pausas na aprovação de novos centros de dados. Na Pensilvânia, o governador Josh Shapiro vetou NDAs entre governos locais e empresas, para evitar acordos secretos. Uma pesquisa do Gallup, do começo do ano, apontou que mais americanos (71%) são contra ter centros de dados na vizinhança do que uma usina nuclear (51%). Parte do problema é que as grandes empresas de tecnologia não querem colocar um data center em qualquer lugar. Empresas como a NorthPoint Development correm atrás de grandes extensões de terra com acesso a redes elétricas de alta capacidade e infraestrutura de água. Hazle Township fica numa dessas áreas, a cerca de 400 quilômetros do grande hub de data centers no chamado Data Center Alley da Virgínia, onde fica a famosa região AWS us-east-1 e circulam nada menos de 70% do tráfego de internet do mundo.
