artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Submer Group lança Corenix, empresa de data center modular para IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Submer Group anunciou em 28 de setembro de 2026 o lançamento da Corenix, uma empresa de infraestrutura de data center modular que atende neoclouds, hyperscalers e operadores de IA, e nomeou o ex‑executivo da Johnson Controls, Martin Renkis, como seu diretor executivo. A Corenix oferece plataformas de data center modular projetadas sob medida, baseadas em designs de referência da NVIDIA, que o Submer Group descreve como industrializados para IA em escala e entregues desde a construção e teste em fábrica até o comissionamento no local. A nova empresa tem sede em Houston, Texas, e foca na camada de implantação da infraestrutura de IA, reunindo energia de rack, refrigeração, rede e TI em um único sistema integrado, testado em fábrica, destinado a colocar capacidade de IA em operação em uma data fixa. Modelo de entrega fábrica‑para‑site De acordo com o modelo de entrega descrito pela empresa, a Corenix projeta, constrói, integra e testa em fábrica módulos completos e funcionais de data center — abrangendo TI, energia, refrigeração e rede — nas instalações de produção antes de entregá‑los aos locais dos projetos. A instalação, conexão à infraestrutura do site, teste de aceitação no local, comissionamento e preparação operacional ocorrem então no site do cliente. A Corenix gerencia o escopo do projeto acordado em ambas as etapas, combinando engenharia, manufatura, coordenação da cadeia de suprimentos e implantação no local em um único modelo de entrega. O Submer Group afirmou que as construções tradicionais de data center não conseguem acompanhar as demandas de energia, rede, refrigeração e capacidade de serviço da computação acelerada, nem a necessidade de suportar gerações sucessivas de computação de alta densidade, e que a Corenix foi criada para fechar essa lacuna. O grupo descreve a abordagem modular como oferecendo aos clientes um caminho repetível de uma arquitetura técnica aprovada até a capacidade operacional no local necessário, com cada plataforma baseada em um design de referência da NVIDIA e projetada sob medida para os requisitos específicos do cliente. Renkis afirmou que os clientes precisam de clareza antes de se comprometerem sobre o que deve ser construído, como será testado, quem é responsável e quando entrará em operação. “A Corenix coloca um programa datado e uma data de início em produção na mesa antes mesmo de existir um contrato”, disse ele. Ele acrescentou que uma equipe permanece responsável desde a integração e teste na fábrica até o comissionamento no local e a preparação operacional, com flexibilidade para suportar sistemas de computação acelerada atuais e futuros. Liderança Renkis chega à Corenix vindo da Johnson Controls, onde atuou como diretor executivo de Serviços de Infraestrutura de Data Center e desenvolveu ofertas de infraestrutura de IA que abrangem energia, refrigeração, recuperação de calor, operações e financiamento. Anteriormente, foi fundador e CEO da Smartvue, uma empresa de plataforma de hardware e software IoT adquirida pela Johnson Controls, e da Trainersoft, uma empresa de software corporativo de e‑learning adquirida pela OutStart, agora IBM. Patrick Smets, CEO do Submer Group, afirmou que as fábricas de IA estão gerando uma demanda sem precedentes por nova capacidade de data center e que o mercado precisa de uma forma mais rápida e previsível de construí‑la. “Estamos trazendo essa experiência para um negócio dedicado, criado para fornecer infraestrutura de IA em escala”, disse Smets, referindo‑se ao histórico do grupo na entrega modular de data centers e à expertise em engenharia, térmica e de infraestrutura que desenvolveu ao resolver desafios de computação de alta densidade. Estrutura e escala do Submer Group A Corenix baseia‑-se na experiência do Submer Group em engenharia térmica de alta densidade, implantação global de infraestrutura e operações. O grupo afirma que essa experiência foi comprovada em escala por um campus com centenas de megawatts de capacidade entregue como uma construção totalmente modular de computação em nove meses, desde o pedido até a entrega, juntamente com mais de uma década de engenharia de refrigeração líquida. A Corenix trabalha ao lado de duas empresas irmãs cujas capacidades apoiam os requisitos de implantação de infraestrutura de IA de ponta a ponta de um cliente: Rubix Data Centers, que desenvolve e opera campuses de data center de IA, e Radian Arc, que oferece GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service. O Submer Group, que se descreve como uma empresa de infraestrutura de IA de pilha completa, reúne empresas operacionais especializadas ao longo da pilha de infraestrutura de IA, abrangendo terra e energia até nuvem e edge. O grupo afirma ter implantado mais de 500 MW de infraestrutura refrigerada a líquido e possuir mais de 8 GW de terreno energizado nas Américas, EMEA e APAC. Fundado em Barcelona em 2015, o grupo opera globalmente com centros em Houston e Taipei. O site do grupo apresenta quatro camadas de capacidade: GPU‑as‑a‑Service e AI‑as‑a‑Service, alimentados pela Radian Arc; desenvolvimento e operações de data center, alimentados pela Rubix; soluções de data center modular; e arquitetura térmica. O site também cita três laboratórios globais de P&D e mais de 90 redes de parceiros de telecomunicações em todo o mundo.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Facilities seeking backup power will help boost annual installations in the commercial-sector energy storage market 27% in megawatt terms through 2031, according to an estimate by the American Clean Power Association and renewable power data firm Wood MacKenzie. - Data centers facing grid-connection bottlenecks are a big driver of the growth. “Storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone," Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie, says in a summary of the U.S. Energy Storage Monitor that the firm puts out with ACP, released this week for the third quarter of 2026. - When utility-scale and residential sectors are factored in, annual installations of energy storage are expected to grow more than 50% in megawatt terms through 2031. Utility-scale storage will see 8% average annual growth, and residential storage 9% average annual growth, over the next five years, the report says. Dive Insight: Energy storage encompasses several technologies, but most commercial applications are battery systems, and about 90% of those are lithium-ion, the International Energy Agency says based on 2025 data. Hydroelectric, thermal and compressed air are among the other types of systems. Those are generally utility-scale applications, EIA says. Innovation in the battery space is giving facilities options in addition to lithium-ion. Google, for instance, closed a deal earlier this year with Form Energy and utility Xcel Energy to install 30 GWh of battery storage at one of its data centers in the form of iron-air batteries, which engineers tout for their duration. “By … pioneering long-duration storage … we are helping to build a more resilient system,” Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s head of data center energy, said when the deal was announced. Form Energy says on its website that its batteries can release energy for up to 100 hours, delivering power “for multiple days at a time.” In the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis, improving durations, particularly in utility-scale and residential applications, is one reason the sector saw an increase in megawatt hours even though the number of installations dipped in the second quarter. “Longer duration … systems drove MWh growth,” the report said. The average duration of U.S. energy storage systems increased from 2.8 hours to 3.5 hours, the report said. Changes in public policy priorities are supporting storage growth, too. In addition to states and municipalities requiring data centers and other large load users to bring their own power, which in many cases include a storage component, public entities at local, state and federal levels are pushing virtual power plants. VPPs are programs in which utilities leverage excess capacity in commercial facilities, homes and other sources to support grid power. Storage is a frequent component of VPPs. “Distributed storage's value proposition is broadening beyond customer-centric benefits to include grid services, as the industry seeks to position virtual power plants … as a key enabler of load growth,” the report says. Looking at second-quarter data, the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis says 48 MW of energy storage was installed in the commercial property segment. That’s down from the first quarter, which was unusually high, it says, because of a rush in California by facilities and households installing storage before state tax incentives dropped. Although the reduced incentives took effect in 2023, the state’s top court didn’t settle questions about their legality until June, spurring the rush. As a result, while the storage installed in the second quarter is lower than in the first quarter, it’s in line with historic norms, the report says. Utility-scale deployments for the quarter totaled 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh, down 8% year-over-year in MW terms, which the report attributes to market saturation. Residential deployments also declined, falling 15%, to 676 MW, which the report attributes in part to the federal clean energy and energy efficiency tax credits eliminated in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Despite the quarterly drop among the segments, the outlook is bright for the next five years because of the broader trends favoring energy storage, the report says. “With a strong pipeline and continued technology improvements, the outlook for storage remains exceptionally strong,” John Hensley, ACP’s senior vice president of markets and policy analysis, said in a statement.

artigo.texto: The investment was financed through EU-funds available during the previous government.Continue reading SolServices Kft. and Huawei Technologies Hungary are developing one of the region’s largest battery energy storage systems (BESS), with a power capacity of 150 megawatts (MW) and a storage capacity of 300 megawatt-hours (MWh). The companies announced at a press conference in Budapest on Wednesday that construction of the full portfolio is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027. Representatives of the companies signed an agreement on Wednesday to implement the energy storage project at Huawei’s annual renewable energy conference, the Digital Power Summit 2026. Róbert Szabó, director of the Digital Power business at Huawei Technologies Hungary, emphasized that commissioning the 150 MW/300 MWh energy storage facility planned for early 2027 will make state-of-the-art smart technology an integral part of Hungary’s energy system. The system will provide the grid with the flexibility that is essential for the continued expansion of renewable energy sources. He added that hybridization is a key strategic priority for both companies: coordinated operation of different generation and storage technologies enables more efficient use of the grid and greater system-wide flexibility. The total cost of implementing the project is approximately €50 million, and the entire investment will be financed on a commercial basis, Gábor Juhász-Farkas, managing director of SolServices Kft., told MTI. Citing data from holadelej.hu, he said that during the summer, on one of the most critical days of the energy crisis, solar generation accounted for 85% of the country’s electricity consumption. At the same time, this has created new challenges: the most important questions now are when energy is generated, when it is used, and how the entire energy system can be made more resilient and flexible. He stressed that hybridization provides the best answer to these challenges. Grid capacity is currently one of the scarcest resources in Hungary’s electricity system, Juhász-Farkas noted. When a solar power plant’s connection point is considered on an annual average, it is utilized only 16% of the time, leaving 84% of the infrastructure unused. As an example of hybridization, he noted that combining solar and wind power with battery energy storage can increase grid utilization to more than 40%. Juhász-Farkas explained that the companies are working together to develop an integrated energy platform in which solar power, energy storage, wind power, and geothermal energy do not operate in isolation, but instead complement and reinforce one another as part of an interconnected system. He said that the project’s commercial financing demonstrates that storage is no longer a technology of the future, but a commercially viable solution that can be built on a market basis.” He said the scale of the cooperation can be illustrated by the fact that a fully charged energy storage system would be capable of compensating for the loss of peak-generation output from an entire unit of the Paks nuclear power plant for more than half an hour. If this storage capacity had entered the market with its surplus supply, it would have had the effect of reducing prices by 40%, he indicated. SolServices operates solar power facilities with a combined capacity of approximately 380 MW across Hungary, making it the country’s third-largest operating investment of this type. Under the new agreement, the company will build energy storage capacity alongside its existing solar parks. The first storage units have already been commissioned in Mezőtúr and Mezőberény, and commercial operation of the full storage portfolio is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, he said. Huawei Technologies, the largest Chinese privately owned company, operates in more than 170 countries, and its products and services are used by nearly one-third of the world’s population. All five of Huawei’s business groups—telecommunications, enterprise, cloud, digital power, and consumer—generated more than $120 billion in revenue globally last year. SolServices Kft. is one of Hungary’s leading renewable energy companies. Since 2017, the company has participated in the development of more than 1 gigawatt of large-scale solar power generation capacity. Via MTI, Featured image: Pexels

artigo.texto: East Hampton wants 2 battery plants shut down pending new fire systems East Hampton Town is demanding that the owners of two East-End battery-energy storage plants, including one impacted by forever chemicals, cease operations of LIPA-contracted facilities in East Hampton and Montauk by Friday until new fire suppression systems are in place. The demand follows a meeting between town officials and co-battery owner NextEra earlier this week, and revelations by the state earlier this month that a fire-suppression system was responsible for toxic contamination discovered at one of the sites earlier this year. In a letter to battery owner NextEra on Tuesday, a copy of which was obtained by Newsday, East Hampton Town supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez wrote that the town remains "deeply concerned" about the "pace and scope" of actions being taken by the owners to "protect the health and safety" of town residents and the environment. Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen have previously called for the East Hampton facility on Cove Hollow Road to cease operations, Newsday reported. NextEra spokesman Chris Curtland at the time said NextEra remains "committed to working with local and state officials on the investigation. The project is operating safely." NextEra and East Hampton didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Newsday reported in May that the plant was the subject of a federal lawsuit by the Suffolk County Water Authority concerning forever chemicals from the East Hampton plant that affected drinking water wells. New York State has since determined that the toxins known as PFPrA were the result of a fire suppression system used during a May 2023 thermal runaway fire at the facility that took 30 hours to get under control. No agency, state or local, or NextEra has released information about the cause of the fire. Earlier this week, the state Department of Environmental Conservation in an email told Newsday it "does not have the authority to regulate the design or operations at the [East Hampton] facility, nor does DEC have the authority to investigate causes of a fire beyond the environmental impacts it may have caused." In her letter to NextEra, Burke-Gonzalez referenced a Sept. 25 meeting she had with battery-plant officials, noting that the company said it could remove all "Novec 1230" fire suppression equipment from both the East Hampton and Montauk battery plants in two weeks, and to take the system’s automatic fire-suppression system offline even sooner. But Burke-Gonzalez said the town would not approve that modification to the fire suppression systems "without a detailed report from a qualified engineer confirming that water alone is sufficient to extinguish any fire at the facility. East Hampton also requested that the company take "immediate" interim remedial measures to ensure the safety of residents around the plant, including excavation and off-site disposal of "all impacted soil," demanding that the soil be removed to a licensed facility outside of East Hampton Town. East Hampton also is demanding that soil and groundwater sampling be done at five-foot intervals around the plant "to determine whether additional remedial measures are necessary," including remediating groundwater. Tests by the state and Suffolk County have shown PFPrA at upward of 10,000 parts per billion, well above a site-specific screening level set by the state Department of Health of 3 parts per billion, Newsday has reported. "In the interim," Burke Gonzalez wrote, "and until Novec 1230 [fire suppression system] has been taken offline under an approved alternative fire-suppression plan and the required remediation at the 3 Cove Hollow Road facility has been completed, the affected facilities should cease operations by Friday, Oct. 2, 2026." The town, she wrote, "does not believe continued operation is appropriate while these unresolved risks remain." Up close with Gilgo killer's court officer ... Deadly North Bellport shooting ... artigo.texto: The backlash against data centers is growing, driven by concerns about their environmental impact, effects on local communities, and demands on public infrastructure. But the backlash is also developing a partisan dimension. Recent polling shows that Democrats are substantially more likely than Republicans to oppose data centers and that support has fallen sharply over the past year, particularly among Democrats. Much of that shift reflects growing concerns about the resources data centers consume. The risk is that legitimate concerns about particular projects become absorbed into a broader partisan narrative in which data centers are treated as inherently harmful. Those concerns deserve serious attention, but Democrats should be wary of allowing opposition to data centers to become an ideological reflex. The campaign against data centers increasingly resembles the opposition that wind and solar projects have faced for years. Large infrastructure projects create real local impacts, but those impacts can often be managed without abandoning investments that serve broader economic and environmental goals. Democrats once made that case in support of clean energy. They should be careful not to abandon it now that the infrastructure in question is data centers. Indeed, many objections to data centers closely resemble objections to clean energy projects. Some residents simply do not want large industrial facilities in their communities, whether that means wind turbines altering the landscape, solar farms replacing open land, or massive data centers appearing in rural areas. Others object to noise, whether from wind turbines or the backup generators and cooling equipment associated with data centers. Similar disputes arise over who bears the costs and who receives the benefits. Private landowners may profit directly by selling or leasing their property, while neighboring residents worry about effects on property values or quality of life. Infrastructure presents another source of tension. Both clean energy projects and data centers require substantial investments in transmission lines, substations, roads, and other supporting infrastructure. Residents understandably worry that public resources or utility customers will ultimately bear costs associated with a private company’s investment, particularly if a developer abandons a project. The concerns about data centers are not frivolous, but neither were the concerns raised about wind and solar development. The appropriate response was not to halt clean energy construction altogether. Policymakers instead sought ways to reduce conflicts and distribute benefits more broadly. Developers and communities experimented with approaches such as agrivoltaics, which allows solar generation and agricultural production to coexist on the same land. The broader lesson is not that every concern about new infrastructure proves unfounded. Some problems are real and require meaningful safeguards, while others reflect uncertainty, exaggerated claims, or resistance to development itself. Policymakers should distinguish among them rather than treating every objection as equally persuasive. The same approach should guide data center development, with practical solutions to genuine concerns about water use, electricity costs, noise, land use, and community impacts. For years, Democrats were among the strongest advocates for deploying clean energy despite local opposition. They correctly recognized that building wind and solar capacity could create jobs, generate local tax revenue, and help build the industries that would underpin the future American economy. That basic judgment remains sound. Clean energy projects are worth pursuing even when individual projects generate controversy and when some of the companies developing them are large, profitable corporations. The same principle should apply to data centers. The United States is in the midst of a major technological transformation driven by artificial intelligence. Data centers are the physical infrastructure supporting that transformation. They also represent a significant source of construction and investment, often in communities seeking new economic opportunities. Data center growth can also support clean energy expansion. Major technology companies have made substantial commitments to reduce the carbon intensity of their operations and are investing in new sources of electricity, including wind, solar, and nuclear power. Microsoft’s agreement to support the restart of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant illustrates the scale of investment that growing demand for computing is helping mobilize. Some communities will reasonably decide that a particular data center proposal is not appropriate for a particular location. Others may demand changes to address concerns about water, electricity, noise, or local infrastructure. Policymakers should take those concerns seriously and ensure that their communities benefit from these infrastructure investments. But blanket moratoriums and reflexive opposition to data center development treat complex and often addressable challenges as reasons to stop building altogether. The United States does not need to choose between technological progress and protecting communities. Policymakers can establish rules that mitigate genuine harms and fairly allocate costs while allowing investment to proceed. Democrats understood that approach when the infrastructure at issue was wind turbines and solar panels. They should apply the same judgment to the infrastructure powering the next generation of the American economy. Image credit: Chad Davis/Flickr

artigo.texto: As the entire tech industry shifts its focus to the development of artificial intelligence, there are almost 3,000 planned or ongoing data center projects across the country. At the same time, numerous tech executives and members of President Donald Trump’s administration continue to champion data centers and AI as the next boon of economic progress. Yet, the discontent seen in communities nationwide has made it clear: Data centers are not working for Americans. While politicians across the political spectrum promise local economic benefits, many data centers receive obscure tax breaks and lackluster environmental regulations that encourage development to the detriment of local communities. Furthermore, these massive facilities often leech off of local public utilities, skyrocketing energy bills for households and weighing down local infrastructure. Apart from these immediate impacts, the construction, cooling and powering of these data centers can devastate local environments and watersheds. This stimulates immense distrust and frustration with pro-data center politicians and has unified bipartisan sentiment against data center construction throughout the country — almost three-quarters of Americans now oppose data center projects in their area. Data centers look to create incredibly large returns for their owners and partners, but those returns are currently happening at the expense of the local communities they reside in. If data centers are going to be significantly involved in our future, the communities they impact need a share in the profits they create. Instead of prolonging the ongoing cycle of deception and discontent, citizens, corporations and governments can work together and leverage data center development to invest in infrastructure, community sustainability and environmental resilience. First, private interests should be responsible for internalizing the external costs of data center construction and operation. Data centers are driving a substantial revitalization of fossil fuel electricity generation to accommodate their immense energy needs. Beyond releasing high carbon emissions, it is estimated that the air pollution from these sources can create annual localized public health costs as high as $20 billion by 2028. They also tap into local water resources for cooling, threatening the integrity of piped water sources. Accordingly, the baseline for a data center to be built must include commitments to fulfill energy needs with strictly clean, renewable sources and investments in environmentally friendly cooling methods. Second, stakeholders also have to resolve the financial issues that data centers create. In many cases, state and local governments create tax breaks and other incentives to encourage developers to build data centers. These incentives are generating hundreds of millions — and in a few cases, billions — of dollars in lost annual revenue for state governments across the country. If data centers are to support the local communities they inhabit, all levels of government across the country must be aligned on holding them accountable for their full share of development costs, operational expenses and taxes. Furthermore, data centers that are integrated into local utilities strain infrastructure through their huge water and energy demands. This rising demand risks rate hikes for nearby households and businesses. To compensate for this, governments must require that data center developers invest in expanding generation capacity to the required level and building efficient water use systems, instead of leaving the costs to consumers. Across the country, most of the communities rallying against data center proposals are demanding moratoriums on data center construction or the blocking of permits. Right now, data centers are built and operated at the expense of the public and should be opposed. In this effort, many communities have been successful: Local opposition led to project cancellations worth $68 billion over April, May and June of this year alone. In a modern data center, every 100 megawatts of capacity generates more than $340 million per year in revenue. For perspective, the data center currently under construction in Saline Township has a capacity of almost 1,383 megawatts. While we must respect the will of local constituencies in demanding moratoriums — like those in Ypsilanti — the value created by these facilities presents an opportunity we should consider. Communities, aligned with local, state and national governments, should force developers and tech companies to redistribute shares of their profits to infrastructure projects or other investments through intentional, intelligent policy decisions. The best way to accomplish this is to mandate extensive and complete investment in sustainable infrastructure from data center developers. This should first include responsible construction practices, like dust suppression and pollutant monitoring to minimize air pollution, hazardous runoff and waste. Next, data centers should invest in a sufficient capacity of clean energy that is situated to the local geography. Alongside this, they must also invest in facilities that are efficient and implement sustainable engineering in order to minimize environmental costs during the following decades of operation. The true list of responsible investments extends far beyond this, but these are some of the most important and neglected across the sector today. While a moratorium can keep a community safe, it is a neutral outcome. If we allow data centers while prioritizing community investment, more jobs will be created and sustained, and more tangible, shared value will be added to local communities. Facilitating investment in sustainability can aid communities in becoming more resilient to climate and environmental crises while also driving the energy transition. artigo.texto: BYD said the flagship sedan will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology” and will reportedly be the first EV to use its solid-state batteries. BYD takes on ultra-luxe brands with Yangwang EV sedan Yangwang is BYD’s highest-end brand with ultra-luxury models ranging from electric hypercars to extreme off-road SUVs. BYD also uses Yangwang to showcase its breakthrough technologies. In the past, Yangwang vehicles have debuted with disruptive new tech, including BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its Disus Intelligent Body Control System. A new Yangwang model was recently spotted testing in China that, according to local reports, will push the brand further into the elite segment. New images of the vehicle surfaced online, revealing a nearly identical design to the Rolls-Royce Phantom. It will even be BYD’s first vehicle with rear-hinged coach doors. Hu Xiaoqing, Yangwang’s general manager, shared a few images of the flagship sedan on Weibo and confirmed that the car’s name has yet to be finalized. Internally, BYD is calling it “HU” for now. The new model is “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” No other details were revealed, but one image shows the vehicle at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it can support megawatt fast charging. According to China’s Autohome, Yangwang’s executive-class EV sedan will be BYD’s first EV to use solid-state batteries among other new technologies. Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, confirmed the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics. The sedan measures about 5.5 meters in length, or about the size of the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class. BYD executive vice president Stella Li confirmed in an exclusive interview with Carwow.es earlier this month that the company is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery tech and its commercialization. Li said that BYD will “prove it” with its first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries set to debut in 2027. BYD’s battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying the battery chemistry as well as the manufacturing and equipment needed for mass production. FinDreams, BYD’s battery business, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, scaling up to mass production by 2030. Will Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan be the first to showcase BYD’s solid-state batteries? If it does, it will likely be offered on higher-priced variants, while standard models could still use BYD’s latest Blade LFP batteries. Top comment by Blake I expect this will have sold state batteries. The huge sales price means they can afford to ‘hand make’ the batteries and have a high failure rate. Solid state batteries will matter more when it comes to the inherent complexities of mass production Outside of that, the flagship model is expected to feature BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering over 1,000 hp combined. BYD has yet to announce prices or any details, but reports estimate the Yangwang sedan will cost over 2 million yuan, or nearly $300,000. The Yangwang U7, the brand’s current luxury electric sedan, starts at just 658,000 yuan ($98,000). According to Autohome, the new executive-class sedan is expected to make its official debut in October, so we should learn more shortly. Check back soon. We’ll keep you updated. artigo.texto: A Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, informou que sua sede em Kiev foi atingida por um ataque russo no domingo (27), sem vítimas no local. A Rússia afirmou ter atingido também um data center da Vodafone, que não comentou o caso. Outros centros de dados da capital foram alvo de bombardeios. Segundo autoridades ucranianas, uma dessas ações feriu um adulto e duas crianças; interrupções ao longo da semana teriam deixado cerca de 100 mil residências sem conexão. O governo ucraniano alerta que os ataques à infraestrutura de comunicação podem prejudicar a distribuição de avisos sobre mísseis e drones. Kiev e cidades próximas estão entre as áreas afetadas pela perda de acesso à internet. O ex-procurador especial Jack Smith defendeu nesta terça-feira (29), no Senado americano, os processos contra Donald Trump. Afirmou que reuniu provas de “crimes graves contra a nação” e negou motivação política. As acusações envolviam tentativas de reverter a eleição de 2020 e retenção de documentos confidenciais. Os casos foram arquivados após a vitória de Trump em 2024, diante da regra contra indiciar presidentes em exercício. Foto: Sargento Nathan Mitchell/Marinha dos Estados Unidos A Marinha autorizou o navio Atlantic Explorer, dos Estados Unidos, a realizar pesquisas na Plataforma Amazônica entre 3 e 13 de outubro. A portaria foi publicada no Diário Oficial da União nesta terça-feira (29). A embarcação pertence ao Instituto de Ciências Oceânicas das Bermudas, ligado à Universidade Estadual do Arizona. Os estudos serão realizados em parceria com a Universidade de São Paulo. Donald Trump afirmou nesta terça-feira (29) que teria feito um “trabalho de merda como presidente” se o America.gov fosse a maior realização de sua gestão. Apesar da declaração, ele elogiou o novo portal de serviços do governo americano. A plataforma usa inteligência artificial para responder a perguntas e facilitar o acesso a informações oficiais. Segundo o site, conversas e dados de localização serão apagados automaticamente após cada consulta. A Suprema Corte dos Estados Unidos autorizou nesta terça-feira (29) a retomada das deportações de imigrantes para países diferentes dos de origem. A decisão é provisória e permite ao governo Trump continuar o programa enquanto sua legalidade é analisada. O tribunal ouvirá os argumentos em dezembro, com decisão final prevista para o próximo ano. A discussão envolve a possibilidade de os imigrantes contestarem o envio e apresentarem riscos de perseguição ou tortura no destino. Três senadores democratas enviaram nesta terça-feira (29) uma carta a Marco Rubio cobrando o reconhecimento do resultado das eleições brasileiras e relações diplomáticas normais com qualquer candidato eleito. Os parlamentares acusam o governo Trump de interferência e dizem que pressões diplomáticas, econômicas e políticas ameaçam as instituições brasileiras. artigo.texto: COEP Technological University and JSW Projects have signed an agreement to establish an indigenous lithium-ion battery technology centre at the university’s research facility in Chikhali, Pune district, in a project estimated to cost ₹800 crore. The centre will be developed in two phases and is planned to include battery prototyping, pilot-scale research and development facilities. According to the report by Loksatta, the project will support the development of lithium-ion battery cell technology within Pune’s academic and engineering ecosystem. The agreement was signed by COEP registrar Dr D. N. Sonawane and JSW Group executive vice-president Naresh Lalwani. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud, Dr S. P. Mahajan, dean Prof P. A. Sadgir, Dr Ranjit Date, professor of practice Dr Sarika Kelkar and other university officials attended the signing. JSW senior vice-president Amitabh Singh, associate vice-president Chandrakant Mahalingam and deputy general managers Vijay Chaudhary and Sudeep Sarkar were also present. Bhirud said the centre could help develop an indigenous alternative to imported batteries and contribute to India’s effort to build domestic capability. He said students would receive opportunities to learn advanced battery technology and work on practical applications, while the facility would provide a wider platform for research, innovation and technology development. The project places an engineering university at the centre of a technology area that has implications for electric mobility, energy storage and industrial manufacturing. However, the supplied report does not specify the proposed capacity of the facility, the exact timeline for either phase, the technologies to be developed, or whether the centre will manufacture commercial battery cells. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said India had spent substantial foreign exchange on crude oil imports over several decades and needed to develop advanced skills and capabilities to manufacture batteries domestically. He described the partnership with COEP, which has a 172-year engineering history, as a collaboration that could create new opportunities across industry, research and education. The agreement marks a new industry-academia initiative for Pune’s research landscape. Its eventual impact will depend on the execution of the two phases, the research infrastructure established at Chikhali, and the translation of laboratory and pilot-scale work into deployable battery technologies. The next milestones will be the detailed implementation of the project and the development of the proposed centre.

artigo.texto: COEP Technological University (COEP Tech), Pune, and JSW Projects, a JSW Group company, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to establish an Advanced Battery Research & Development Centre at COEP Tech’s Chikhali Research Park. The Centre marks India’s first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale R&D platform, bringing lithium-ion cell technology development onto an academic campus in Pune for the first time. The collaboration positions COEP and Maharashtra as India’s battery-technology hub, with the potential to catalyse over 1,000 battery ecosystem-related jobs. It is a step towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s Net Zero 2070 ambition, anchoring the electric vehicle, grid storage and clean-energy future in Indian innovation. The partnership addresses one of the most persistent gaps in India’s innovation ecosystem: the distance between university research and industrial application. Under the MoU, COEP Tech’s faculty and students will work alongside JSW’s engineers on live, commercially critical technology, in an industry-academia collaboration model at the scale India needs. Prof. Sunil Bhirud, Hon’ble Vice Chancellor, COEP Technological University said, “This collaboration has the potential to create a strong indigenous alternative to imported batteries and make a significant contribution to India’s journey towards self-reliance. For students, it will provide a unique opportunity to learn and work on cutting-edge battery technologies. The scale and scope of the Phase I and Phase II collaboration between COEP Technological University and JSW make it a landmark industry-academia initiative. At a time when next-generation battery technologies are receiving significant research attention across the country, the partnership places research, innovation and technology development on a much larger platform. The collaboration has the potential to develop technologies that can reduce dependence on imported batteries and contribute to the vision of a self-reliant and developed India. The scale of this initiative makes it a significant step forward in strengthening India’s battery technology ecosystem. We are grateful for the valuable support extended by the Government of Maharashtra and the Board of Governors of COEP Technological University in enabling this important initiative.” Mr. Sajjan Jindal, Chairman, JSW Group, said, “Cell is the new oil. Just as oil powered the last century, battery cells will power this one, from electric vehicles to the grid. For decades, India has spent precious forex importing oil. This time, we must build the cutting-edge skills and capabilities to make these cells right here, for a new India. Our partnership with COEP Tech, with its 170-year legacy of engineering excellence, will bring industry and academia together to design, test and validate cells built for Indian conditions, and help shape India’s clean energy future.” A Shared Ambition Across the JSW Group The initiative draws on ambitions across the JSW Group, one of India’s most diversified industrial conglomerates. JSW Energy is aggressively building out grid-scale battery energy storage (BESS) alongside its renewable power business, while JSW Motors is expanding rapidly into electric mobility across every vehicle segment. Batteries sit at the heart of both ambitions, and JSW Group has committed to lead the indigenous value chain in this domain. Talent development, R&D capability, and a battery ecosystem at home are foundational to both the Group’s and India’s future. About the Engagement The project will be built in two phases, with a combined investment of more than ₹800 crore. Phase 1 will establish a Cell Research & Development Centre to design, simulate and prototype indigenous Li-ion and other advanced chemistry cells, including Sodium-ion. Phase 2 will scale this into a Cell Validation Centre capable of producing cells from 100-600 Ah. The batteries developed at the Centre are targeted to perform at par with the best in the world, while being built for India-centric climatic conditions and applications. The facility will serve as a foundation for joint research, publications, projects and IP development, taking India’s battery technology from lab to industry, on campus. Why This Matters - Pilot lines are what separate success from failure at giga-scale. The Centre allows JSW to de-risk the foundation before committing to giga-scale manufacturing. - It fulfils the Government of Maharashtra’s vision for COEP’s Chikhali Research Park as a hub for automotive and allied technology development. - It addresses India’s biggest structural gap in clean energy—with over 90% of the global Li-ion supply chain controlled by China—by building indigenous capability. - It positions COEP and Maharashtra as India’s battery-technology hub, with the potential to catalyse over 1,000 battery ecosystem-related jobs. - It is a step towards Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s Net Zero 2070 ambition, anchoring the EV, grid storage and clean-energy future in Indian innovation. This partnership between one of India’s most dynamic industrial groups and one of India’s most historic technical institutions marks the beginning of a journey that will shape the nation’s energy independence for decades to come.

artigo.texto: A public records request regarding a July 27 meeting between one of the main companies behind Project Jupiter and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham provided virtually no information on its content. The meeting with Oracle occurred as the timeline around an important permitting process for the massive and controversial data center in Santa Teresa was accelerated seemingly out of the blue in late July. The New Mexico Environment Department hearing officer Max Shepherd initially favored a later October date for an air quality permit hearing given its “highly technical” nature, doubling down at a July 27 scheduling conference even after being pushed by the developers to move it up. Officials with Oracle met with the governor that same day. Two days later, Shepherd advanced the hearing to Sept. 14, leading some to speculate there was a connection. “This proceeding is becoming more focused on reaching a result favorable to the governor’s economic development agenda than ensuring a fair process and protecting the due process rights of the parties and the public,” said Mariel Nanasi, executive director and attorney for New Energy Economy, at the time. Leah March, a spokesperson for the governor, wrote in an email Aug. 12 that "the governor routinely takes meetings with companies like Oracle to stay informed, as she did in July for a general update.” “The governor does not interfere in state agencies' regulatory decisions and has made no effort to influence the outcome of Project Jupiter’s air permit application,” March wrote. “Instead, it is her responsibility to ensure that state agencies meet their statutory obligations for a fair, transparent and independent process." The data center's regulatory proceedings have shaped up to be a bitter battle. Shepherd recused himself from the hearing on Aug. 23 and the state Supreme Court placed proceedings for Project Jupiter's air quality permit and water use on pause before allowing them to continue in a Sept. 17 decision. The New Mexican requested on Aug. 13 any notes, agenda, emails or other correspondence regarding the July 27 meeting between the governor and Oracle. On Aug. 18, the Governor’s Office acknowledged the request and said it would respond on or before Aug. 28. On Aug. 28, the request was deemed “excessively burdensome or broad due to the large volume of potentially responsive records and the time required to review those records for redactions or withholding required or permitted by law.” The new deadline was set as Sept. 14, on which day the materials were made available. The Governor’s Office closed the request, marking it as complete. However, the only material included was a photo of an iMessage exchange with the governor’s schedule for the day. The Oracle meeting took up one line. The completed request did not include the governor’s official schedule for the week, which was sent to the The New Mexican Aug. 10 by an environmental advocacy group. In a phone call Tuesday, Donicia Herrera, a records custodian at the Office of the Governor, said that after conducting a full search of records to fulfill the request, that was “all that came up.” Julia Gentin is a reporter for The Las Cruces New Mexican, The Santa Fe New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico through a partnership with Report for America, a national service program that places journalists into local newsrooms. artigo.texto: News Mercedes-Benz Secures Deal To Advance Solid-State Battery Technology Mercedes-Benz has strengthened its decade-long partnership with ProLogium to gain priority access to its fourth-generation solid-state battery cells, marking a significant advancement in EV technology. Solid-state batteries offer higher energy density, faster charging, and increased safety compared to traditional lithium-ion cells. Mercedes-Benz is partnering with ProLogium to test these Gen4 lithium ceramic batteries, aiming to integrate the technology into its next-generation electric vehicles within the coming year. “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility,” said Jörg Burzer, Board of Management member. “Our partnership with ProLogium helps us advance next-generation battery technology. By combining ProLogium’s solid-state expertise with our development capabilities, we are reaching a milestone in evolving our future electric vehicle fleet.” ProLogium currently operates a significant battery manufacturing facility in Taiwan and is planning a new site in Dunkirk, France, with a projected capacity of up to 44 GWh. This facility is expected to facilitate the supply of cells to European customers, including Mercedes-Benz. Beyond its collaboration with ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz is actively diversifying its solid-state battery initiatives by testing lithium-metal battery cells from the American firm Factorial Energy. In a notable development last year, a Mercedes-Benz EQS equipped with a Factorial solid-state battery pack successfully achieved a range of 748.8 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge. artigo.texto: Processing and storing data is now pushing the frontier of economic development around the world, and huge amounts of capital are flowing into building out the infrastructure to support this big bet on cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence. The race to establish an advantageous position on the digital frontier is driving a major capex boom in the United States and elsewhere, and this wave has now fully arrived in Southeast Asia. Data centers require substantial land and resources, like electricity and water, and they need reliable connectivity such as access to subsea cable networks. Countries that have land, reasonably well-developed energy and telecommunications infrastructure and friendly regulatory environments are attracting investors and developers looking to ride the data center wave. Affordable inputs, like electricity, can sweeten the deal. It just so happens that many countries in Southeast Asia fit this bill. Malaysia is leading the pack. Clear policy guidance, well-developed infrastructure and close proximity to land-constrained Singapore are helping fuel a boom in data centers. The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone has seen a flurry of activity, but it is part of a broader phenomenon. In the first quarter of 2023, the Department of Statistics recorded a cumulative $11 billion of foreign investment in the information and communication sector, accounting for 5 percent of total foreign investment. By first quarter of 2026, this figure had risen to $32.5 billion, equal to 12 percent of total inbound investment. And there is no sign of slowing. According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the body that reviews and approves investment projects, between 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, $96 billion worth of data center and cloud computing projects were approved, including $24 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. These are project approvals rather than realized investment, but it gives a sense of the speed and scale at which the data center boom is unfolding across Malaysia. Indonesia is also seeing an uptick in data center investment. Like Malaysia, some of this is driven by demand from Singapore, particularly in and around the island of Batam. Nongsa Digital Park is a Special Economic Zone that offers eligible projects tax and other fiscal incentives. Combined with Batam’s strong subsea cable connectivity, this has fueled a wave of new data center construction in the area. There is also a lot of investment activity in and around Jakarta where a number of large industrial scale data centers are being developed by state-backed players such as Telkom, as well as private sector firms and investors. As reported by Antara News, Indonesia’s current data center capacity sits around 580 MW and the plan is to grow it to 1.3 GW in the near-term. Government data shows that investment in information services jumped from $967 million in 2023 to $3.4 billion in 2025 and it looks set to keep climbing. Thailand is also now rushing to add more data centers, with several large industrial-scale projects in the pipeline. According to the Board of Investment, in 2025 they received $24 billion worth of applications across 151 projects in the digital industry, mainly data centers. Not all of these projects will be approved and become operational, but it again gives a sense of the speed and scale with which this industry is moving. Vietnam is following suit, with local media reporting that the government plans to reach 870 MW of data center capacity by 2030. The trend is clear: data centers are beginning to pop up all around Southeast Asia, attracting billions of dollars in investment and uncorking a major construction boom. But a bigger, perhaps more fundamental, question is whether demand for digital services can justify these enormous outlays and the resources they will absorb. Investment is pouring into Southeast Asian digital infrastructure, with the expectation that businesses and consumers will spend billions of dollars on cloud computing, AI and other digital services in the years ahead. This is not unique to Southeast Asia, of course. The same assumption about future demand has been driving eye-popping capex investment in data centers and cloud computing all around the world, raising similar questions. What we can say for sure is that the data center boom has reached the major economies of Southeast Asia. Whether these massive bets on future demand for digital services pays off is anybody’s guess. But considering the amounts of money involved, how this plays out is something we should all be watching very, very closely in the months and years ahead.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Dados da empresa norte-americana Cushman & Wakefield apontam crescimento de 91% na capacidade operacional de data centers em São Paulo em um ano. No primeiro semestre deste ano, a capacidade chegou a 661 MW (megawatts), ante 346 MW no mesmo período de 2025. Com o avanço, São Paulo se tornou o terceiro maior mercado primário das Américas, atrás apenas de Atlanta e Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos. A empresa lembra que o desempenho do setor ocorre em meio à criação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), sancionado em 15 de setembro, que prevê a suspensão de tributos federais, como Imposto de Importação, PIS/Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação e IPI (Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados), sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização de empreendimentos de data centers. No eixo São Paulo-Campinas, a capacidade dos empreendimentos em construção cresceu de 148 MW para 250 MW. Além disso, há 2.066 MW em projetos planejados para a região. Esse volume equivale a mais de três vezes a capacidade atualmente em operação, mas não significa que toda essa capacidade será efetivamente construída. A concretização dos projetos depende de fatores como disponibilidade de energia e acesso à rede de transmissão, equipamentos, conectividade, licenciamento e existência de clientes interessados em contratar a capacidade. Apesar da expansão da oferta, a vacância permaneceu baixa, em 4,1%, o que significa que cerca de 96% da capacidade de colocation estava ocupada. Nesse contexto, segundo a Cushman & Wakefield, o Redata pode contribuir para a viabilização dos projetos planejados ao reduzir os custos de aquisição de equipamentos destinados aos empreendimentos elegíveis. A empresa projeta que esse crescimento deve se estender para além de São Paulo. Regiões do país com oferta de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, conexão de alta capacidade e terrenos preparados poderão disputar os próximos investimentos em data centers.

("Kandi” or the "Company”) (NASDAQ GS: KNDI), a global innovator in intelligent equipment and a technology-driven platform company, today announced that its wholly-owned subsidiary, China Battery Exchange (Zhejiang) Technology Co., Ltd. ("China Battery Exchange”), has secured a second batch procurement order for heavy-truck battery swap station equipment from QIJI Energy, a subsidiary of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited ("CATL”). The order follows just two months after the initial batch order placed in July 2026, highlighting the continued commercial development of the Company’s relationship with CATL. China Battery Exchange’s cooperation with CATL began in August 2025, when the two companies signed a Framework Procurement Contract under which China Battery Exchange became part of CATL’s global supplier network and began coordinating CATL’s first order for a heavy-truck battery swap station, which was secured later that month. In January 2026, China Battery Exchange entered into a three-year strategic cooperation agreement to serve as a designated equipment supplier for QIJI Energy’s heavy-truck battery-swapping program. In July 2026, QIJI Energy placed its first batch procurement order under the strategic cooperation agreement, marking China Battery Exchange’s transition from product validation to commercial deployment. With its supplier relationship with CATL and approved-supplier status with QIJI Energy, China Battery Exchange is positioned to pursue additional equipment orders in connection with CATL’s heavy-truck battery-swapping program . China Battery Exchange’s Lin’an intelligent manufacturing facility commenced production in July 2026. With an expected annual production capacity of up to 200 battery swap stations, the facility is intended to support China Battery Exchange’s ability to fulfill existing and potential future orders from CATL and serve additional battery swap equipment customers. Feng Chen, CEO of Kandi, commented, "We have received two batch orders within eight months of signing the QIJI Energy agreement, reflecting CATL’s continued confidence in our products and delivery capabilities as well as the commercial potential of this partnership. artigo.texto: By Brian Kennedy Pew Research Center Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year. And a majority say they’d be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area, according to a new Pew Research Center survey. The survey comes as protests against new data center construction have spread and as some state and local politicians have spoken out against data centers. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers. More than half of Americans (54%) now say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half say they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38%. And 49% say they are mostly bad for people’s quality of life nearby, up from 30%. The new survey was conducted from July 20 to Aug. 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Just 4% of Americans think data centers have a mostly good impact in each of these areas. Similar shares (between 21% and 24%) say data centers are mostly good and mostly bad for these things. Since January, there have been increases of 9 percentage points in the shares of Americans who say data centers are mostly bad for local jobs (from 15% to 24%) and local tax revenue (from 12% to 21%). Many Americans are still unsure or unfamiliar with data centers altogether. Shares ranging from 18% to 32% say they are not sure how data centers impact the five things the survey asked about. And overall, 12% say they haven’t heard of data centers. Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers. Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things the survey asked about. For example, rural Americans have become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for the environment (from 32% in January to 50% in August), home energy costs (32% to 46%) and the quality of people living nearby (28% to 45%). Most data centers currently being planned or under development will be in rural areas. Americans in urban and suburban areas have also become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for these things. As was the case earlier this year, Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents are more likely than Republicans and Republican leaners to view the impacts of data centers negatively. Still, Republicans’ views have also turned more negative: In the new survey, for example, 42% say the facilities are mostly bad for the quality of life of people nearby, up from 24% in January. Republican elected officials have staked out varying positions on data centers. While Trump has consistently supported their construction in his second term, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott previously supported expansion but issued a statewide moratorium on new data centers in August. Some Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, have also recently shifted their positions to support additional rules and oversight on data center construction and operation. Among Democrats and Republicans alike, views on the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are somewhat more negative than they were at the start of the year. But many people in both partisan groups either say that they’re not sure or that the effects are neither good nor bad. More Democrats now say the effects of data centers in these two areas are mostly bad than mostly good. Liberal Democrats have primarily driven this shift: For example, 34% of liberals now say data centers are mostly bad for local tax revenue, up from 19% in January. More Republicans continue to say the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are mostly good than mostly bad. Still, Republicans are now 7 percentage points more likely than in January to say the effects in both areas are mostly bad. The new survey also finds that 60% of Americans say they would be not too or at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Much smaller shares say they would be somewhat comfortable (19%) or extremely or very comfortable (7%) with this. Just over half of Republicans (54%) and about two-thirds of Democrats (68%) say they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new local data center. Liberal Democrats stand out, with 81% saying they’d be uncomfortable. Majorities of urban, suburban and rural Americans say they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area. Americans are more aware of data centers than they were earlier in the year. The share of Americans who say they have heard or read a lot about them has increased from 25% in January to 35% today. About 9 in 10 adults (88%) have now heard at least a little about data centers.

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Wisconsin voters continue to believe the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits and also said data centers were the least desirable of five development options and that state tax incentives reward companies that don’t pay their fair share in a new poll of registered voters in the state. The poll showed 54% of voters believe state incentives reward companies that don’t pay their fair share while 45% believe that the economic benefits of state incentives for business are worth the cost. When it comes to data centers specifically, however, 74% of Wisconsin voters said that the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits, down from 78% who said the same last month in the Marquette Law School Poll. The Marquette Poll was conducted Sept. 16-23, interviewing 843 Wisconsin registered voters, with margin of error of +/-4.3 percentage points. For likely voters, the sample size is 692 with a margin of error of +/-4.8 percentage points. The September poll expanded what it asked about data centers and development in September, with just 9% of voters saying data centers were the most desirable of large-scale developments they would like to see in their area with none of the five (44%), a semiconductor fabrication plant (33%), an e-commerce fulfillment center (27%), an automobile manufacturing plant (24%) and a steel or aluminum mill (14%) all more desirable. Respondents could choose more than one option on what they would like to see. The poll showed 49% of registered voters felt that new manufacturing and commerce developments were very important for jobs while 43% said they were somewhat important while 61% felt that unfairness favoring the wealthy was a larger problem than over-regulation.

artigo.texto: Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD has confirmed plans to introduce its first electric vehicle equipped with a solid-state battery in 2027. The company says it is in a leading position in the development and commercialisation of the technology. Solid-state batteries could offer higher energy density, lower weight, longer driving ranges and improved safety compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Key Overview - Company: BYD - Technology: Solid-state batteries - First model: Planned for 2027 - Initial application: Higher-end electric vehicles - Battery development: BYD’s FinDreams battery division - Expected mass production: Around 2030 - Existing batteries: Lithium iron phosphate batteries will continue across other vehicle segments BYD Confirms 2027 Solid-State Battery Plans BYD has confirmed that it plans to introduce its first electric vehicle using solid-state battery technology in 2027. BYD Executive Vice-President Stella Li said the company is in a leading position in both the technology and its commercialisation. The announcement follows plans previously outlined by BYD’s battery division, FinDreams, which indicated in 2025 that the company intended to demonstrate and install solid-state batteries in vehicles from 2027. Solid-State Batteries Could Improve EV Performance Solid-state batteries differ from conventional lithium-ion batteries primarily through the use of a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. The technology has the potential to provide higher energy density, which could allow electric vehicles to use smaller and lighter battery packs while maintaining or increasing driving range. Solid-state batteries are also expected to offer safety advantages because solid electrolytes are less prone to the thermal runaway associated with some conventional lithium-ion battery systems. The technology could also provide improved performance under certain temperature conditions. BYD Previously Targeted 2027 for Demonstration The 2027 timeline is consistent with plans announced by BYD in February 2025. At the time, Sun Huajun, technical director of BYD’s FinDreams battery division, said the company planned to begin demonstrating and installing solid-state batteries in vehicles in 2027. Mass production was expected to follow around 2030. BYD’s latest comments therefore reinforce the company’s previously stated development timeline rather than introducing a completely new target. Higher-End Models Expected to Use the Technology First The high cost of producing solid-state batteries remains one of the challenges facing wider adoption. Because of this, BYD is expected to initially use the technology in higher-end models. BYD Chief Scientist Lian Yubo previously said solid-state batteries would mainly be used in high-end models while lithium iron phosphate batteries continue to serve vehicles across different segments. This means the introduction of solid-state technology is not expected to replace BYD’s existing battery technologies across its entire vehicle range. Context is everything. Lithium Iron Phosphate Batteries to Continue BYD will continue using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries across different vehicle segments. The company’s approach is to use different battery technologies according to the requirements and positioning of individual vehicles. Solid-state batteries could therefore initially serve vehicles where their higher energy density and potential range benefits can justify higher production costs. As production technology develops, costs could become an important factor in determining how widely solid-state batteries are adopted. Other Automakers Are Developing Solid-State Batteries BYD is among several major automotive companies working on solid-state battery technology. Toyota has previously targeted 2027–2028 for vehicles using solid-state batteries. Mercedes-Benz has also been testing solid-state battery technology, while Stellantis has been conducting road testing involving a solid-state battery-powered electric vehicle. Honda has also been working with QuantumScape on solid-state battery development. The activity across several automakers reflects continued investment in battery technologies that could increase electric vehicle range and improve battery performance. Cost Remains a Major Challenge Despite the potential advantages, solid-state batteries remain more expensive to produce than established lithium-ion battery technologies. Manufacturers must also develop production processes capable of producing the batteries at automotive scale. For BYD, the initial use of solid-state batteries in higher-end vehicles could allow the company to introduce the technology while continuing to use established battery systems across its broader vehicle lineup. The company has not indicated that traditional lithium-based batteries will be phased out following the introduction of solid-state technology. Outlook BYD’s planned 2027 introduction will mark an important step in the company’s solid-state battery development programme. The technology is expected to initially appear in higher-end vehicles because of current production costs, while LFP batteries continue to be used across other segments. BYD’s longer-term plan points toward broader commercialisation, with mass production previously targeted for around 2030. artigo.texto: GMP grows battery storage program aimed at preventing outages COLCHESTER, Vt. (WCAX) - Green Mountain Power is working to make sure customers’ lights never go out through what it calls a “virtual power plant.” GMP’s shared battery storage system takes energy from the grid and stores it away to be used later. Then, when there’s a severe storm or another extreme weather event that knocks out power, people who have the batteries in their home are able to keep their lights on. This energy stored in the batteries flows back into the grid during peak periods when demand is high. GMP says it’s now Vermont’s biggest energy source, made up of clean energy. “Energy storage is seamless and simple backup power. So it connects into your home; a lot of our customers tell us they don’t even know they have an outage because it’s so seamless, and so they can last for days and days with this energy storage,” said Kristin Carlson of Green Mountain Power. The system is growing; GMP says it has approximately 5,600 customers, up from around 5,000 in July. The batteries cost about $55 a month, or $5,500 outright. Copyright 2026 WCAX. artigo.texto: The Pegasus long endurance drone, developed by Li-S Energy, V-TOL Aerospace and Halocell Energy, completes a successful series of test flights over Queensland Key Highlights: - The EATP Pegasus long endurance drone completed several successful test flights in Queensland, culminating in an endurance flight of almost 2 hours covering more than 75 kilometres, on a single Li-S Energy battery pack. - The endurance flight met expected flight performance and landed safely with battery capacity to spare. - On a same cell weight basis, the Li-S Energy cells delivered 80% more range and flight time than would have been achieved by an equivalent high-performance professional lithium polymer UAV battery pack # - The Pegasus drone comprises V-TOL Aerospace's airframe, Li-S Energy's lithium sulfur battery system, and Halocell Energy's perovskite solar array. - Designed to accommodate two Li-S Energy battery packs, in due course Pegasus is expected to deliver flight durations of 5-8 hours, and 250 kilometres, ideal for long endurance mapping, surveillance, and agricultural, utilities and environmental monitoring missions. - Demand for drones is growing exponentially across commercial and defence markets, with proposed US and Australian government investment in drone and counter-drone technologies now exceeding A$100 billion[1]. - Following this success, the collaboration partners intend to assess further commercial development, targeting future platform sales. - See a one-minute video of the flight here: https://lis.plus/EATP BRISBANE, Australia , Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Li-S Energy Limited (ASX: LIS) ("Li-S Energy", "LIS" or "the Company") is pleased to announce that Pegasus, the long endurance drone developed under the Emerging Aviation Technology Partnership (EATP) programme, has completed a series of successful test flights in Queensland, culminating in endurance flight of almost 2 hours, powered by a single Li-S Energy lithium sulfur battery pack. The twin motor, five-metre wingspan Pegasus was designed and built from the ground up through the collaboration of three innovative Australian companies. It combines an airframe and power systems designed and developed by V-TOL Aerospace (V-TOL), the 382 Wh lithium sulfur battery packs and battery management system designed and built by Li-S Energy, and a perovskite solar cell array fabricated by Halocell Energy (Halocell). As announced in June 2024, the project is supported by a grant of just over $1.35 million from the Commonwealth Government under the EATP programme, matched by the collaboration partners. The collaboration is targeting the development of a family of long endurance surveillance drones powered by Li-S Energy batteries. This flight marks the culmination of the EATP project and the successful completion of its practical development and flight test work. Milestone flight testing The flight test programme comprised several flights, culminating in an endurance flight of almost 2 hours on a single Li-S Energy battery pack. The aircraft met its expected flight performance throughout and landed safely with battery capacity to spare. The Li-S Energy battery system enabled sustained cruise flight of more than 75 kilometres, with the Company's battery management system integrated with V-TOL's power management system controlling the battery power for the twin motors and control systems, while being capable of simultaneously managing the feed-in from the solar array. The Pegasus was designed to accommodate two Li-S Energy battery packs, and with the latest improvements to Halocell's solar array performance beyond those fitted to the current airframe, we expect the platform to be capable of flight missions of five to eight hours and 250 kilometres, ideal for long endurance mapping and surveillance, and for agricultural, utilities and environmental monitoring missions. The flight data will now be analysed by the partners to characterise platform performance and inform the assessment of the platform's commercial potential. Toward commercial development Demand for long endurance uncrewed aircraft continues to grow rapidly across commercial and defence markets, and both endurance and sovereign supply are decisive competitive strengths. With their integrated technologies now proven in flight, the collaboration partners intend to capitalise on this market potential. Li-S Energy filed two patent applications to protect innovative developments during the project relating to the battery management system and battery pack design. Quotes Dr Lee Finniear, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of Li-S Energy, said: "With the exponential growth of drones and uncrewed systems in both commercial and military applications, flight endurance and sovereign capability are critical to Australia's future in this sector. Today, with our partners, we have shown what Australian innovation and collaboration is capable of. The EATP Pegasus drone is the result of two years of work by the teams from V-TOL Aerospace, Halocell and Li-S Energy, proving that Australia has the sovereign capability and the unique technology to be leaders in this field." Mark Xavier, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of V-TOL Aerospace, said: "The Pegasus flew exactly as our team designed it to. Our airframe and power systems performed faultlessly throughout the flight, and pairing them with Li-S Energy's new lightweight pouch cell battery system gives the platform an endurance advantage operators will immediately recognise. I am proud of what our engineers have delivered, and our focus now turns to the pathway from successful trials to commercial platform sales." Paul Moonie, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Halocell Energy, said: "Seeing our ultra-lightweight perovskite cells take to the air on the Pegasus is a proud moment for the Halocell Energy team, whose skill in fabricating flexible solar modules for such a demanding application has been outstanding.
