artigo.texto: LG Electronics apresenta soluções “Chip-to-Chiller” para resfriamento de data centers de IA na Data Center World Asia 2026 AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 29 de setembro de 2026 Empresa destaca infraestrutura integrada para fábricas de IA e portfólio completo de soluções de resfriamento para data centers de IA Resumo da notícia - A LG Electronics apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” na Data Center World Asia 2026, ao mesmo tempo em que demonstra sua abordagem “One LG” para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA, em conjunto com a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution. - O portfólio da LG inclui soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas, chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar, Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs) qualificadas pela NVIDIA, resfriamento por imersão, Fan Wall Units (FWUs) e o Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), apoiando uma implementação mais rápida, operação confiável e expansão eficiente da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. - As soluções modulares de resfriamento da LG são projetadas para reduzir o tempo de construção no local, diminuir o investimento inicial e apoiar os operadores de data centers na expansão eficiente de seus ambientes de servidores de IA. - A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias otimizadas para data centers de IA, incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). - A LG CNS apresenta o “Prefabricated Modular Data Center”, com módulos padronizados e pré-fabricados de GPUs, servidores e energia. SÃO PAULO, 29 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A LG Electronics (LG) apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” para servidores de Inteligência Artificial (IA) na Data Center World Asia 2026 (DCWA 2026), realizada de 29 a 30 de setembro no Marina Bay Sands Expo & Convention Center, em Singapura. A exposição destaca a abordagem integrada da LG para atender às crescentes demandas de gerenciamento térmico e energia do setor de data centers de IA. Uma parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA com o “One LG” Participando da DCWA pelo segundo ano consecutivo, a LG demonstra suas capacidades como parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA em um espaço de exposição com mais de três vezes o tamanho de seu estande de 2025. A empresa apresenta uma solução integrada de infraestrutura baseada na estratégia “One LG”, que reúne as tecnologias de climatização/HVAC da LG com a expertise da LG CNS em projeto, construção e operação (DBO) de data centers e os equipamentos de energia da LG Energy Solution. A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias desenvolvidas para apoiar o fornecimento confiável de energia para data centers de IA incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). Implementação acelerada com soluções modulares pré-fabricadas As soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas e os chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar da LG contribuem para uma implementação e expansão mais rápidas da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. A solução hidrônica incorpora equipamentos de resfriamento, equipamentos de energia e sistemas de controle em um único módulo pré-fabricado, reduzindo o trabalho de engenharia no local e encurtando o tempo de implementação. O chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar da LG incorpora um compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético sem óleo, que minimiza as perdas por atrito mecânico e melhora a eficiência energética. Além disso, o chiller utiliza a tecnologia free-cooling por refrigerante da empresa, que aproveita as baixas temperaturas externas para reduzir a carga sobre o compressor e ajudar a diminuir o consumo de energia do data center. Tecnologias especializadas de resfriamento para servidores de IA de alta densidade A exposição também apresenta as mais recentes soluções de resfriamento líquido da LG para servidores de IA, incluindo suas avançadas Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs). Uma CDU é um componente essencial de um sistema de resfriamento líquido direto para o chip (DTC), que fornece e circula o líquido refrigerante para placas frias (cold plates), instaladas diretamente sobre CPUs e GPUs para absorver seu calor. As CDUs de 1 megawatt (MW), 2,6 megawatts (MW) e 600 quilowatts (kW) da LG concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura da NVIDIA neste ano, atendendo a critérios técnicos que abrangem desempenho de resfriamento, capacidades de failover e confiabilidade do sistema. Além disso, a CDU de 2,6 megawatts (MW) da LG foi qualificada como NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU, atendendo aos requisitos aplicáveis do projeto de referência NVIDIA DSX para soluções de resfriamento líquido da AI Factory Platform. Na DCWA 2026, a LG demonstra uma solução de resfriamento por imersão que remove o calor de forma eficiente ao submergir os servidores em um fluido de resfriamento não condutivo. Paralelamente, a empresa apresenta sua Fan Wall Unit (FWU), uma solução de resfriamento a ar que incorpora ventiladores EC de alta eficiência e serpentinas ovais de baixa perda de pressão para fornecer um fluxo de ar energeticamente eficiente e estável aos racks de servidores. Soluções integradas de gerenciamento e energia A LG apresenta seu Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), que permite o gerenciamento integrado dos principais equipamentos de resfriamento, incluindo CDUs, FWUs e chillers. Utilizando tecnologia de IA, o DCCM pode prever a carga de resfriamento e otimizar os sistemas de resfriamento para possibilitar uma operação mais eficiente do data center. Como parte da oferta “One LG”, a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution também apresentam suas soluções para data centers na DCWA deste ano. artigo.texto: The CEO of T5 , a development company set to build what could eventually become the second largest data center in Illinois by square footage, spoke exclusively to NBC 5 Monday amid an outcry of opposition from local residents. "We haven't hidden behind anything," Peter Marin said. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. A group of residents called the Lake County Data Center Opposition Coalition has sued to block the project, claiming the village wasn't transparent about the project during public meetings. "it wasn't out in public. It wasn't open," said coalition leader Morgan Coghill. "It wasn't on the agenda of the Grayslake like town meeting. And because they knew it was going to be a problem." In a statement, Grayslake mayor Elizabeth Davies says there were 18 public meetings and “Every one of those meetings and hearings was open to the public, publicly noticed, and on the record.” The village has put out a fact sheet online assuring residents the project won’t increase power bills, and will bring in $1.4 billion in tax revenue over the next 20 years. Martin says the company has communicated directly with residents through public meetings, as well as pamphlets and billboards. Local "We did everything by the book," he says. The Grayslake facility will be large enough to house companies that build generative AI, but activists opposed to the project say there has been a lack of specifics. "Who's the tenant? Is it Anthropic? Is it OpenAI? Is it going to be a swarm of AI agents pouring out from this data center to attack our government websites?" Coghill asked NBC 5. Martin says the Grayslake data center will operate on a closed-loop system, which means it will rely more on power than water to cool the computer servers inside. The project is slated to consume up to 1.2 gigawatts of energy once all phases are complete, which is the equivalent to powering a city of about one million residents. Marin says T5 has a separate rate agreement with ComEd, and will be effectively paying for all the power it consumes, but coalition members say they aren't buying that argument. "All they do is tap into the same grid we're all using, and they're getting their electricity," said Coalition member Michael Smith. "And we're being told, 'hey, throttle down your electricity use during hot summers because we're taxing the grids.'" Martin says the Chicago region is attractive because Illinois is a high power-producing state and he believes the grid can easily handle the influx of data centers. And he says if communities here say no, data centers will just go somewhere else. "Data centers are in every part of your life from, you know, from 911 to the grocery store to shopping online, whatever you interact with, everybody touches a data center every day," he said. The two sides are set to meet in court in November, but preliminary site-evaluation has already begun on the land. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has urged Illinois lawmakers to pass the so-called "POWER Act" when they return for their fall veto session that month. The legislation would put strict new limits on a data center's water and power usage. The coalition members were unswayed by Marin's explanations, but told NBC 5 they had one remaining question for him: would he personally want a data center of this size in his community? "Yeah I'd be fine with it," he said. "You're not going to see the building. You're not going to hear anything that's going on."

artigo.texto: Volkswagen AG VWAGY is strengthening its position in the European electric vehicle (EV) battery market through a partnership with China-based Gotion High-Tech. The companies plan to expand regional production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and cathode materials, supporting Volkswagen's strategy to establish a competitive and more secure European battery supply chain. LFP batteries offer competitive costs, long service life and strong durability, making them increasingly important for affordable EVs in the volume segment. Their share of the European battery market is expected to increase from around 10% currently to 40-60% by 2030. Volkswagen Expands LFP Production With Gotion Under the agreement, Gotion will invest around €1.1 billion (about $1.25 billion) for a 49% stake in the Valencia site, with PowerCo retaining a 51% majority. The Valencia plant is expected to become a European production hub for LFP battery cells and Unified Cells. PowerCo is expected to contribute around €470 million in total by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake in the Šurany cell factory in Slovakia and a new cathode-material facility in Kenitra, Morocco. Gotion will hold the 51% majority in both. The deal remains subject to regulatory approvals and Gotion shareholder approval. VWAGY Strengthens European Battery Supply Security The agreement builds on a partnership between Volkswagen and Gotion that dates back to 2020. Gotion already supplies cells to Volkswagen and works with its battery arm, PowerCo, as a strategic partner. Volkswagen is currently Gotion's largest single shareholder, holding about 24%. Separately, it has agreed to sell a 5.3% stake, while keeping its board representation and voting rights, pending regulatory clearances. The joint ventures are expected to strengthen regional battery production, reduce supply-chain concentration and improve access to key cathode materials. The agreement marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings them closer to the forefront of electric mobility. artigo.texto: Kozlowski and Savela discuss data centers, mining at forum Incumbent Liish Kozlowski and challenger Shawn Savela addressed the Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth and mining DULUTH, Minn. (Northern News Now) - District 8B incumbent Liish Kozlowski and Republican candidate Shawn Savela took the stage Tuesday for a candidate forum hosted by the Duluth News Tribune and Duluth Area Chamber of Commerce, the second of a two-day series of forums. The candidates addressed the proposed Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth, and the economy and mining. Savela said the Hermantown data center project is “a blueprint for how to do things wrong.” He said public officials signing non-disclosure agreements have caused chaos and mistrust for the project. Kozlowski called for more research. “We’re asking for a pause; we’re asking for a comprehensive regulatory framework to look at air, noise, groundwater,” Kozlowski said. Savela said increasing county jails and services would help clean up the streets and increase public safety. “Fund our jails and make them bigger so that we can take people in who are violent offenders, people that need to get off the street,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they want to see Duluth residents receive basic necessities to afford to live. “Basic needs, thrivable wage, access to childcare, good education, housing, all of it to live your best life,” Kozlowski said. Savela spoke about his desire to see copper-nickel mining in Minnesota. “We need these resources, copper and nickel. We need it for your phones, we need it for your cars, we need it for everything,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they are against copper-nickel mining. “We are now in what the international climate community has identified as a water bankruptcy,” Kozlowski said. Kozlowski also brought up the need for the top 1% to be taxed at a higher rate, while Savela called for more republican representation in the state. The two-day forum series also included debates between Sen. Grant Hauschild and challenger Andrea Zupancich, Rep. Pete Johnson and Allan Kehr, and Rep. Natalie Zeleznikar and Aaron Schweiger. artigo.texto: AI data centers erupt as major battleground in Florida governor’s race The three alarms of the AI boom Big picture view: TAMPA, Fla. - The nationwide boom in artificial intelligence is raising three distinct levels of concern among policymakers and the public: - Existential risk: Warnings from tech leaders that advanced AI could eventually escape human control. - Workforce disruption: The potential for rapid automation to eliminate millions of traditional jobs. - Physical infrastructure demands: The immediate environmental, energy and land-use impacts of industrial-scale data centers. While the first two alarms involve national and global debates, the third alarm has arrived directly in Florida, making the state's election a key factor in where these massive facilities go—or don't go. Loudoun County’s $1.2 billion trade-off The backstory: To examine what a data center boom looks like on the ground, Democratic candidate David Jolly traveled to Loudoun County, Virginia—commonly known as "Data Center Alley." While Loudoun County has been a tech hub since the late 1990s, rapid expansion over the past decade has steadily converted open land and wooded parcels near residential neighborhoods into industrial campuses. Today, Loudoun County hosts roughly 230 existing data center buildings, with another 100 facilities in the pipeline. The Virginia experience highlights the trade-offs facing local communities: - Community strain: Residents express concerns about noise and air pollution, industrial views replacing natural woods, and concerns over declining property values. - Massive tax revenue: Loudoun County Economic Development Director Buddy Rizer notes that data centers deliver approximately $1.2 billion in annual local tax revenue—an asset class unmatched by any other industry. That tax base funds local public schools, roads, and community projects, including a local recreation center featuring pools, weightlifting rooms and amenities built largely from data center revenue. Whether Florida should embrace Virginia's high-revenue, high-density model or block it at the state line, has become a core issue between the candidates. Jolly’s plan: A statewide pause, environmental review, and potential ban Democrat David Jolly argues that the state must step in to protect communities, public health, and natural resources before data centers proliferate across Florida. Jolly proposes a one-year statewide moratorium on new data center construction to study their impacts on Florida's air, water systems, energy grid, real estate values, and overall economy. Key pillars of Jolly's position include: - State jurisdiction & permanent ban potential: Jolly asserts that the state has a clear duty to intervene on environmental and health grounds. If research shows severe negative impacts, Jolly says he would extend the temporary moratorium into a permanent statewide ban. - Economic skepticism: While acknowledging short-term construction jobs, Jolly questions the long-term economic value of data centers relative to their resource consumption, raising concerns about the "functional obsolescence" of these massive structures 5 to 10 years down the road. - Quality of life and AI anxieties: Beyond noise pollution and real estate devaluation, Jolly notes that data centers have become a physical symbol of broader public anxieties regarding job loss, wage disruption, privacy, and security. - Clean energy contrast: Jolly strongly supports expanding solar, wind, and renewable technologies, stating that clean energy can lower utility bills, create jobs, and protect Florida's natural environment. Donalds’ plan: Local control, ratepayer safeguards Republican Byron Donalds strongly opposes a statewide pause, arguing that banning or stalling data center construction sends a dangerous signal to the business community that Florida is closed to capital investment. Donalds' strategy relies on local government authority and legislative ratepayer protections: - A departure on local preemption: In recent years, Florida's Republican-led state government has preempted local municipalities on a range of issues. However, on data centers, Donalds explicitly opposes state preemption, arguing that cities and counties should retain full authority to decide whether a facility belongs in their community. - Current ratepayer protection law & caveats: Donalds points to current state law—enacted through legislation sponsored by his running mate, Representative Bryan Avila—which requires large data centers to pay their full energy and water infrastructure costs, so traditional utility bills do not increase. However, that law applies specifically to Florida's four major investor-owned utilities (leaving municipal utilities and rural electric co-ops exempt) and relies on the Public Service Commission (PSC) for enforcement. - Transparency vs. past legislation: Donalds calls for full transparency for local data center proposals, stating there should be "no more NDAs" (non-disclosure agreements). Earlier legislative efforts sponsored by Avila sought to exempt data center plans from public records laws, but that transparency exemption failed to pass. Donalds emphasizes the consumer-protection provisions that did become law. - Replacing solar arrays with nuclear reactors: Skeptical of solar power—which he argues takes large tracts of land out of productive use for relatively low power output—Donalds states he is "dovish on solar and wind power." Instead, Donalds proposes placing four data centers on the footprint of a single solar array and powering them with an SMR (Small Modular Reactor)—a small nuclear fission reactor. Any excess electricity generated by the SMR would be fed back into the public power grid. - Protecting pristine land and tourism: Donalds argues Florida has available interior land to accommodate high-tech development without building next to residential homes or harming core tourism hubs like Disney, Universal, and state beaches. artigo.texto: Georgetown council votes to draft ordinance banning data centers Council members raise concerns over water, land and infrastructure GEORGETOWN, Ky. (WKYT) - The Georgetown City Council voted Tuesday night unanimously to ask legal counsel to prepare an ordinance banning data centers. The ordinance would also define what a hyperscale data center is. The action comes as council members shared their concerns about the possibility of a data center in Georgetown. Council members said they also want to be cautious of the impact a ban could have. “I think most of us are talking about the mega ones is what the issue and just making sure that were not trying to take out somebody who has a small one that needs for processing for the facility,” said Mayor Burney Jenkins. Councilmember Karen Tingle-Sames said that the city can’t support a data center. “If you look at the things as we know about data centers as of today, the city of Georgetown can’t handle a data center. We don’t have the water for it, we don’t have the land for it, we don’t have the infrastructure for it,” she said. Jenkins said he also wants to be prepared if a total ban faces legal challenges. The ordinance to completely ban data centers would also need approval from the Planning and Zoning Commission. The Scott County Fiscal Court extended its data center moratorium last week. artigo.texto: Nigeria has moved to its next implementation stage for its carbon market framework by establishing specific criteria to determine which carbon projects the government will approve. The National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) held a National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations in Abuja. NCCC Director-General Omotenioye Majekodunmi told the workshop that Nigeria had secured approval for the carbon market framework. The task now facing stakeholders is establishing approval criteria that protect national interests while giving credible investors and project developers certainty, she added. University of Nigeria, Nsukka Vice-Chancellor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, represented by university Professor Nnaemeka Chukwuone, said the approval criteria would provide guidance on the eligibility, screening, and assessment of carbon market projects, describing their development as guided by sound research. The workshop marks a further step in a process that began nearly a year earlier, following President Bola Tinubu’s approval of the National Carbon Market Framework in late October 2025 ahead of COP30 in Belém, Brazil. Tinubu signed off on the framework’s full implementation in January 2026, with oversight resting with the NCCC, chaired by the President and supported by a dedicated carbon market office. Financial projections and international compliance The government has projected the framework could unlock between $2.5 billion and $3 billion annually in carbon finance over the next decade, positioning carbon trading as a significant driver of non-oil revenue. The framework spans forestry, energy, and agriculture, aligning Nigeria’s carbon market activities with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which governs international cooperation on emissions trading and carbon credits between countries. Read also: Stakeholders advocate domestic financing for Nigeria’s carbon market The host country approval criteria under review are a practical mechanism to determine which offset or reduction projects the government will formally authorise to sell credits internationally. Getting this stage right is designed to prevent problems that have undermined voluntary carbon markets elsewhere, such as projects of questionable integrity, double-counting of credits, and weak enforcement that erodes investor confidence. Whether Nigeria’s final approval criteria succeed in attracting projected investment while avoiding international credibility pitfalls will determine how much of that projected $2.5 billion to $3 billion actually materialises.

artigo.texto: Battery maker Eve Energy says it signed deals covering more than 30 GW/h at IAA Transportation 2026, where it showed its Open Source Battery 4.0: AI Battery in Europe for the first time. Named buyers include WEG, BMZ, Sunswap, Janus Electric and Morris Commercial, though Eve gave no split by customer or delivery date. Its pitch rests on LMX, a cell chemistry it says keeps the safety and stability of lithium iron phosphate while raising energy density and cold-weather output. Cells on show included the LM815, LM285 and V63. Eve paired those cells with two packs: an LM815-641kWh underfloor pack for heavy trucks and a B3E-LF206S system for buses. It says both meet European market access rules and suit harsh operating conditions. The AI Battery adds a custom AI chip that, according to Eve, enables cell-level sensing and real-time diagnostics. That would shift battery management from passive monitoring towards active control, although the release offered no test data. Commercial vehicle OEMs including BAIC, Sany and Nivalis visited the stand, the company said. Eve argues that tough regulation and extreme conditions are raising the bar for traction batteries in Europe, a market where the IAA deals give it a firmer foothold. Source: Eve Energy

artigo.texto: Buffalo, NY (WBEN) The Buffalo Common Council will vote Tuesday on whether to impose a two year moratorium on data centers in the city. Mayor Sean Ryan says the city previously looked at a moratorium. "We had been working on a one-year moratorium as an executive order, and then we kept in close contact with the state legislature and the governor, and so the state came in with a one-year moratorium. So we pulled back our executive order; it wasn't necessary anymore. Now the council has a two-year moratorium that differs significantly from the states, so we're going to take a look at that," says Ryan. But while the concern is companies coming in and buying land, he has a caveat. "We have to make sure that we don't inadvertently sweep up Roswell Park's computers, M&T Banks computers, Kaleida's computers, so we're going to be checking with all the University of Buffalo. So we're going to be checking with all these institutions that have rather large computer storage facilities to make sure that this somehow doesn't affect them," warns Ryan. Count Councilmember Mitch Nowakowski among those willing to vote for the moratorium. "I believe that a moratorium will allow the city of Buffalo to get in conjunction with the state of New York, with an ability to be able to better get ahead of data centers that are being proposed through you know the region, but also the country," says Nowakowski, who would like to take it from an urban planning standpoint. "I believe that a moratorium would allow the city of Buffalo planners to get ahead of if a data center was proposed in the city, where would it be most applicable or not? What environmental impacts would transpire if this happened? So we really have to take this from a planning perspective, but ultimately from an environment standpoint as well, to because of the the amount of water and electricity, and can the grid handle this? And ultimately, where would this, you know, where would a proposal go? I mean, we're we're a city of a quarter of a million people, and you know, we we hit with the vacant land that we do have. We would like it to be used for housing, and and and where in this city would this even be proposed? And even if it was appropriate, where where would this be? So taking this from a municipal planning perspective is not only the right thing to do, but it's it's the appropriate thing to also do for our city, our built environment, and for our residents." Leah Halton-Pope says she wants to make sure the city has the right infrastructure when it's ready. "A lot of people have an issue with environmental hazards and what it does to communities around it," she says. She notes underprivileged communities tend to be most affected. She says a moratorium allows to make sure the Green Code is up to date. The Council votes this afternoon at 2pm. Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium Lawmakers to decide on two year moratorium

artigo.texto: Capacidade de data centers em São Paulo cresce 91% em um ano Região do entorno da capital já é o principal parque de dados da América Latina, de acordo com levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield A capacidade operacional de data centers no eixo São Paulo–Campinas cresceu 91% em um ano, passando de 346 megawatts no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 661 megawatts no mesmo período de 2026, segundo levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield, empresa global especializada em serviços imobiliários corporativos. O resultado consolida a região como o principal mercado de data centers da América Latina. Além da capacidade já em operação, o eixo composto pelas duas cidades paulistas possui 250 megawatts em projetos em construção e outros 2.066 megawatts planejados. O volume planejado equivale a mais de três vezes a capacidade operacional atual e supera, somados, os projetos previstos em Querétaro, no México, Santiago, no Chile, e Bogotá, na Colômbia, que totalizam cerca de 1.47o megawatts. Apesar da expansão da oferta, a consultoria destaca que a vacância dos projetos que já estão em operação permaneceu baixa, ficando 4,1% no primeiro semestre no eixo de São Paulo, indicando a alta demanda por esse tipo de infraestrutura. A Cushman & Wakefield também destaca os novos impulsos que o Brasil deve receber com o Redata, novo regime de incentivos tributários aprovado em setembro. O Redata prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização desses empreendimentos. “O mercado brasileiro já vinha apresentando crescimento consistente antes da sanção do Redata”, disse Dennys Andrade, chefe de pesquisa e intligência de mercado da Cushman & Wakefield no Brasil. “A redução dos custos de implantação pode favorecer o avanço dos projetos, mas sua viabilidade continuará dependendo de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, terrenos adequados, licenciamento e segurança regulatória.” Com 661 megawatts em operação, o hub de São Paulo tem quase o dobro da capacidade de Querétaro, que registra 336 megawatts, e supera Santiago, com 272 megawatts, e Bogotá, com 58 megawatts. Consideradas todas as Américas, contudo, os Estados Unidos continuam sendo o principal centro deste mercado: o estado da Virgínia, por exemplo, seu maior parque, tem 12.338 megawatts em operação, enquanto a cidade de Atlanta possui 3.488 megawatts. Além disso, dos 38 gigawatts que já estão em construção em todo o continente (equivalente a 38.000 megawatts), 92% estão nos Estados Unidos.

artigo.texto: A restauração florestal após a exploração mineral abre oportunidades no mercado de carbono. A extração mineral contribui significativamente para o desenvolvimento econômico, mas também exerce pressão sobre os recursos florestais, a terra e os ecossistemas. Com a demanda por minerais para impulsionar a transição energética projetada para continuar aumentando acentuadamente, o controle do desmatamento e a restauração de ecossistemas após a mineração estão se tornando uma necessidade urgente. Especialistas acreditam que, se feita corretamente, a restauração florestal pós-mineração não só ajudará a restaurar as funções ecológicas, como também abrirá oportunidades para gerar financiamento adicional a partir de projetos de carbono. Na manhã de 29 de setembro, em Hanói, o Centro de Certificação de Florestas Sustentáveis da Academia Vietnamita de Ciências Florestais, em colaboração com a organização Forest Trends, realizou um workshop de consulta sobre "Soluções baseadas na natureza para a restauração florestal após a exploração mineral e oportunidades de participação no futuro mercado de carbono". Segundo To Xuan Phuc, Diretor do Programa de Política Florestal, Comércio e Finanças da Forest Trends, a mineração é a quarta maior causa de desmatamento no mundo, sendo responsável por aproximadamente 7% do desmatamento em regiões tropicais. Ao mesmo tempo, a demanda por minerais poderá quintuplicar até 2050 devido ao desenvolvimento de tecnologias de transição energética, como painéis solares, energia eólica, veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Isso exige um equilíbrio entre o desenvolvimento econômico e a proteção das florestas e dos ecossistemas. Sem um controle adequado desde as fases de planejamento, licenciamento e operação, o impacto sobre as florestas pode persistir mesmo após o fechamento da mina. No Vietnã, segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, Diretor do Escritório de Certificação de Gestão Florestal do Vietnã (VFCO), o país possui mais de 5.000 áreas de mineração com cerca de 60 tipos de minerais, incluindo bauxita, apatita, titânio, carvão, elementos de terras raras e granito. A exploração mineral (excluindo petróleo e gás) contribui com cerca de 4 a 5% do PIB anualmente, impulsionando o desenvolvimento econômico local. No entanto, a mineração a céu aberto pode fragmentar a paisagem, destruir a vegetação florestal, perturbar as camadas do solo, poluir as fontes de água e degradar a qualidade do solo. Esses impactos dificultam a restauração da floresta após a exploração madeireira, especialmente em áreas de rejeitos. Você também pode gostar Segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, a mineração a céu aberto de carvão, apatita e bauxita tem um forte impacto na cobertura vegetal, na topografia e nas camadas do solo. As condições do solo e do local nas áreas de rejeitos de carvão e apatita representam muitos desafios para a restauração florestal. Portanto, a restauração não pode se limitar ao simples plantio de árvores para arborizar a área, mas precisa ser realizada de forma contínua, formando gradualmente um ecossistema florestal estável. As soluções baseadas na natureza devem ser escolhidas de acordo com as condições específicas de cada área após a mineração. A restauração deve ser baseada nas características do local para determinar as espécies de árvores apropriadas, a densidade e os métodos de intervenção. Para depósitos de rejeitos de carvão e apatita, o objetivo principal é restaurar a função ambiental, estabilizar o solo, limitar a erosão e estabelecer gradualmente um ecossistema florestal, gerando simultaneamente benefícios de carbono. Em áreas com condições mais favoráveis após a extração de bauxita, a regeneração florestal pode ser orientada para objetivos econômicos, combinada com a geração de créditos de carbono. Essa abordagem contribui para a restauração da terra e da paisagem, além de criar valor econômico adicional a partir da área florestal após a mineração. No entanto, para traduzir esse potencial em resultados tangíveis, especialistas acreditam ser necessário abordar as lacunas na gestão da extração mineral e da conversão florestal. De acordo com o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long, membro da equipe de pesquisa apoiada pelo projeto "Apoio Técnico para Atividades no Vietnã com o Apoio do Programa de Governança Florestal, de Mercado e Climática (FGMC)", as lacunas existem desde as fases de planejamento e licenciamento. O planejamento de recursos minerais e o planejamento florestal são desenvolvidos dentro de sistemas de gestão diferentes, o que pode levar a sobreposições entre áreas com potencial mineral e áreas florestais. Outra questão é a avaliação do impacto ambiental de projetos de mineração. Os relatórios precisam considerar de forma mais completa os impactos cumulativos, a fragmentação de habitats, a perda de biodiversidade e os efeitos de instalações auxiliares, como depósitos de rejeitos, rotas de transporte e plantas de processamento. Além disso, a gestão pós-licenciamento precisa ser fortalecida. O monitoramento dos limites da mineração, a expansão dos depósitos de rejeitos, a restauração ambiental e o reflorestamento após a mineração não foram implementados de forma sincronizada em todos os setores, o que dificulta a inspeção, a supervisão e a determinação da responsabilidade pelas áreas florestais após o encerramento do projeto. O Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long sugeriu que os critérios de proteção florestal sejam integrados desde a fase de planejamento da exploração mineral; que a qualidade das avaliações de impacto ambiental para projetos que se sobrepõem ou são adjacentes a áreas florestais seja aprimorada; que o monitoramento pós-licenciamento seja fortalecido; e que a coordenação entre as agências de gestão mineral, fundiária e florestal seja reforçada. artigo.texto: Brasil deve dobrar capacidade de data centers até 2030, diz Kanamaru Em entrevista, Senior advisor do BCG relaciona expansão da infraestrutura ao ReData, à soberania digital e demanda por processamento no País. O Brasil deve duplicar sua capacidade instalada de data centers até 2030, na avaliação de Márcio Kanamaru, senior advisor do Boston Consulting Group (BCG) para telecomunicações, mídia e tecnologia (TMT). Em entrevista ao Tele.Síntese, ele associou a expansão aos investimentos em infraestrutura digital e às políticas voltadas ao setor, entre elas o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (ReData). “Então o Brasil deve, até 2030, duplicar a sua capacidade em data center”, afirmou Kanamaru. Segundo ele, grandes projetos de investimento em andamento no País estão relacionados à construção dessa infraestrutura. O executivo também relacionou o cenário à aprovação do ReData e a outros estímulos tributários. Para ele, essas medidas deverão acelerar investimentos e projetos de data centers no mercado brasileiro. Acompanhe a entrevista: Soberania passa pela infraestrutura instalada no Brasil A disponibilidade de capacidade computacional no território nacional também aparece, na avaliação de Kanamaru, como parte da discussão sobre soberania digital. Ele citou empresas interessadas em manter no País dados de clientes e parceiros e o treinamento de modelos. “É importante a gente ter uma capacidade instalada aqui de data centers para que isso possa ser feito”, afirmou. Para Kanamaru, porém, a instalação de data centers não encerra a discussão. Ele defendeu que as políticas públicas considerem uma cadeia tecnológica mais ampla, chegando à capacidade nacional relacionada aos semicondutores. “O Brasil tem que buscar, através dessas políticas públicas, a construção de uma soberania mais verticalizada”, disse. Como horizonte para os próximos anos, ele cita “inclusive a construção e desenho de semicondutores no país”. Futurecom terá casos de uso com retorno sobre investimento Kanamaru também antecipou alguns dos temas que estarão em discussão na Futurecom 2026. A 31ª edição terá cinco eixos: inteligência artificial e economia de dados; infraestrutura digital; regulação e soberania; indústrias digitais; e uma arena dedicada a entretenimento e esportes. Na área de IA, a mudança apontada pelo executivo é a passagem da discussão sobre possibilidades da tecnologia para aplicações empresariais já implementadas. “Nas últimas edições a gente estava falando muito sobre perspectivas, oportunidades que a IA poderia propiciar. Nós veremos aqui casos de uso já materializados, com retorno sobre investimento”, afirmou. Segundo Kanamaru, a programação deverá apresentar business cases já construídos pelas empresas. Ele também destacou a evolução dos modelos generativos em áreas como ciência, matemática, física e saúde, além do avanço dos modelos abertos. Empresas poderão desenvolver modelos próprios baseados em open source, tema que também deverá aparecer nos debates do evento. BCG discutirá agentes e integração com redes orbitais O BCG participará de dois painéis na Futurecom, nos dias 6 e 7 de outubro. O primeiro tratará da utilização de agentes de IA no Brasil, com foco nos casos de uso e em como essas aplicações estão sendo implementadas. No segundo, o debate avançará sobre a integração das redes terrestres com redes orbitais. Kanamaru citou o uso dessas redes para ampliar a conectividade em áreas de difícil atendimento e em situações de missão crítica, onde a disponibilidade de infraestrutura por cabo, fibra ou redes móveis é mais limitada. Segundo ele, a discussão contará com a Anatel e outros participantes do ecossistema e abordará a integração entre diferentes infraestruturas de conectividade.

artigo.texto: Google aims to answer questions on Pine Island Data Center project (ABC 6 News) — Pine Island residents are still pushing back against the prospect of a Google-based data center project. Google and partner companies attempted to address some of the main concerns expressed to the residents. One of the main concerns surrounded Google’s water use, with residents expressing worries about discharge and usage. Presenters at the webinar attempted to assure that the center would not overuse water at a more-than-necessary level. “Overall, the water strategy is focused on safe and sustainable construction process, reducing ongoing demand and relying on public infrastructure in a planned and regulated way,” Dave Meadows of Kimley-Horn said. “ Some residents were skeptical about the center’s plan, wondering if they will commit to their goal of limiting water usage. “My biggest concern is the water,” resident Lee Ondler said. “They won’t tell you how they’re going to dispose of it.” Another major concern for residents surrounded the rural land that would be repurposed for the center. “What makes me worry about the idea is it’s taking up farmland,” resident Calob Darci said. The webinar presenters spent time focused on the water conversation, as it is a common concern among communities in the early stages of data center development. “People care deeply, deeply about the quality of water in this state,” said John Wade of Rochester Area Economic Development, Inc. Construction is currently halted on this project as it navigates a temporary restraining order and court proceedings. Other data centers The city of Harmony is continuing progress on the creation of a new ordinance related to data centers. The ordinance draft will now go to the Planning and Zoning Commission on Oct. 14. They will determine whether it will go to the council for approval. In Hancock County, the board discussed a resolution that could have put a moratorium on data centers for six months. However, the motion died from the board’s desire to study the public health effects and concerns, along with building an ordinance to create guidelines for prospective companies.

artigo.texto: Data centers não podem virar mais um encargo na conta de luz Em artigo à CNN Infra, Lino Cançado argumenta que restringir o Redata às energias renováveis pode gerar encargos bilionários aos consumidores O Brasil encontra-se diante de uma oportunidade histórica com o avanço da demanda global por novos data centers, impulsionada sobretudo pelas soluções de inteligência artificial. A atração desses investimentos trará inovação, geração de empregos e desenvolvimento tecnológico para quem souber aproveitar essa janela. Nesse sentido, o Redata (Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento de Infraestrutura de Data Centers) é uma oportunidade fundamental para garantir que não fiquemos para trás nessa corrida. No entanto, o debate atual sobre a regulamentação desses incentivos fiscais tem girado em torno das fontes de energia que irão abastecer as estruturas de processamento de dados, em especial na questão de incluir apenas fontes intermitentes para atender à grande demanda energética dos data centers. A consequência direta de preterir fontes seguras e de baixa emissão pode ter um impacto preocupante: o aumento da conta de luz do consumidor comum. Data centers são instalações que funcionam sem parar. Por isso exigem energia contínua, estável e segura, 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana. Embora o Brasil tenha uma matriz elétrica invejável e predominantemente renovável, sabemos que as fontes eólica e solar são intermitentes. Quando o sol se põe e os ventos cessam, coincidindo com o horário de ponta de consumo, eles não são capazes de sustentar o fornecimento constante que esses centros de processamento exigem. Se o modelo não for bem estruturado, a expansão acelerada sobrecarregará o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) na ponta, exigindo uma contratação massiva de reserva de capacidade. Esse encargo de potência tem um alto custo, que acaba sendo rateado e repassado para a conta de luz de todos os brasileiros. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) já realizou uma segunda revisão do plano de carga para o horizonte 2026-2030, saltando a previsão da carga de data centers de 2.157 MW para alarmantes 5.653 MW. É uma diferença repentina de 3.496 MW. Para garantir que essa demanda seja atendida com segurança dia a dia no horário de pico, o sistema terá um custo de capacidade adicional de R$ 7 bilhões ao ano. Isso equivale a 13,35% de todo o orçamento previsto para a Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético (CDE) em 2026 (orçada em R$ 52,7 bilhões) e a 17,95% do LRCAP. Em outras palavras, seria um encargo severo imposto à tarifa de cidadãos e indústrias, que não têm relação nenhuma com a operação desses centros de dados. A saída para evitar essa penalização social não é frear o desenvolvimento, mas adotar uma política pragmática. O ideal é condicionar a instalação de novos data centers à autoprodução de energia. Esse é um modelo internacional já testado, que vem sendo aplicado de maneira eficiente nos Estados Unidos. Na definição do conteúdo do decreto do Redata, o poder público deve focar em estabelecer as regras de atendimento e deixar que o próprio empreendedor decida como supri-las da forma mais competitiva e eficiente. A melhor equação para esses complexos é a combinação inteligente de matrizes: aliar a energia limpa das renováveis ao atributo da confiabilidade e firmeza do gás natural. Dessa forma, os data centers não demandam do grid na hora da ponta, o que evita a criação de custos adicionais para o restante dos consumidores. O gás natural, como combustível da transição energética, viabiliza uma solução de baixíssima emissão para suprir essa intermitência, garantindo a resiliência operacional do investidor sem onerar os demais usuários da rede. A transição energética e a digitalização não podem ser desenhadas de costas para a realidade sistêmica do país. Restringir o Redata exclusivamente à energia renovável forçará o sistema a prover uma reserva artificial bilionária paga pela sociedade. Precisamos criar um marco legal que incentive a autoprodução e reconheça a importância da flexibilidade do gás natural, assegurando que o Brasil avance rumo à liderança digital sem transferir o custo dessa modernização para o bolso do cidadão. * Lino Cançado é CEO da Eneva

artigo.texto: DE PERE, Wis. — De Pere, Wis., and Milwaukee are moving toward one-year moratoriums on large-scale data center development, as Wisconsin communities consider how to address potential impacts on land use, utilities and local infrastructure. Planning bodies in both communities approved proposed moratoriums Monday night. Both measures still need final approval from their respective common councils. De Pere Mayor James Boyd said the moratorium would give the city time to review its local rules. “The City of De Pere doesn’t have any of them in the works. We don’t have the land for it, most likely. That said, you just never know,” Boyd said. “The moratorium gives you a chance to pause and get your code up to date regarding the hyper-scale centers.” Boyd said local officials are seeking more direction as data center proposals become a larger issue across Wisconsin. “What’s most likely going to happen is you’re going to see legislation at the state and federal level that will give us guidance,” Boyd said. “That’s really what we’re hoping for. I don’t know of any municipality that cherishes this moment where they’re handling this by themselves.” The issue has drawn attention from residents concerned about how large developments could change the landscape. Lauren French lives in Denmark, Wis., and drives through rural Brown County to her downtown De Pere business: Idolscape. “Driving here, there’s so much open space,” she said. “I don’t want that leveled. I don’t want to look and see this big, huge building and big, huge parking lot, and it’s just another concrete thing. We don’t need that.” Concerns about data center development also extend to utility costs and infrastructure needs. Tom Content, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, said part of the organization’s work is making sure data centers pay their own way for needed infrastructure. “Communities want to be ready,” Content said. “If a data center comes, they want to be ready to make sure the community impacts are talked about. The energy costs are talked about. The water issues are addressed, and the community needs are part of the conversation.” Boyd said the scale of large data centers became clearer to him after seeing one of them near Port Washington, Wis. “I didn’t really realize the size and scope of it until you drive down 43 and go toward Milwaukee and back,” Boyd said. “Then you really get a handle on what you’re looking at. The magnitude. The size. And the usage those things need to survive.”

artigo.texto: Talbot County considers zoning rules for battery storage facilities Planning commission holds first public hearing on proposed regulations TALBOT COUNTY, Ga. (WTVM) - Talbot County leaders are looking at new rules to prepare for large battery storage facilities, the kind often used to power heavy developments like data centers. The planning commission held its first public hearing Monday on how to zone for them. County says current rules don’t cover private systems County leaders say their rules currently don’t cover private battery systems, which store extra electricity and pump it back out when the grid is strained. No developer has applied to build one yet, but neighbors and local planners are already weighing in. Clarence Napier said he believes more work needs to be done on the plan. “I think more work needs to be done with developing the plan,” Napier said. “Like I asked the question this plan came from a template and maybe the plan needs to be designed or scaled down or maybe even elevated for just this town.” Allison Slocum, assistant planning director for the River Valley Regional Commission, said the facilities could benefit the grid. “This is really going to help make our energy grid more resilient by taking power off the grid when it’s not being used, storing it and then releasing it when it’s most needed,” Slocum said. Existing facility not subject to local zoning Talbot County already has one battery storage facility, built by Georgia Power in North Talbot. Because Georgia Power operates as a utility, it was not required to follow local zoning rules. A private developer would be. The Board of Commissioners will hold a second public hearing next Monday at 6 p.m. Copyright 2026 WTVM. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media On a sunny September day in New York City, I followed a throng of people off the subway and into Queens’ Flushing Meadows Corona Park. The crowds were there for the U.S. Open tennis tournament, but I wasn’t — I’d come to see a novel experiment to wean the city’s iconic food carts off dirty generators. Street vendors in NYC and around the world use fossil-fueled generators that contribute to climate change, can sicken workers, and are just plain noisy. Batteries are a silent, emissions-free alternative, but they represent an upfront cost and introduce logistical challenges around when and where to charge. So Brooklyn-based startup PopWheels is testing a model that doesn’t require vendors to buy their own batteries, allowing them to instead access swappable batteries throughout the day at nearby charging cabinets. In July, the firm launched a six-month pilot in the Flushing Meadows Corona Park area, installing two black-and-yellow cabinets where the 10 participating vendors can exchange their dead batteries for fresh ones. Right now, the vendors can access these batteries for free, thanks to $46,000 in grant funding from the City Parks Foundation and another $30,900 from the nonprofit Resilient Cities Catalyst. But PopWheels’ vision is that vendors would eventually pay a monthly subscription fee to use the battery-swapping infrastructure, plus a fee to buy or lease the inverter that houses the batteries in the food cart itself. The firm aims to make the setup price-competitive with the cost of buying and fueling a generator. “We understand that this only works if we meet not just our green needs but also the economic needs and the logistic needs of these vendors,” said Ben Rosenn, PopWheels’ director of deployments. “They’re not going to want to switch if it’s more expensive.” Scaling the battery-swapping model is not far-fetched. The company already runs a similar program for New York’s delivery workers, charging them between $65 and $95 a month to access batteries for their e-bikes from over 45 cabinets scattered across the city. “We know that this technology is safe, and it has been used before,” said Isabelle Thomas, policy adviser for living streets and public spaces at the NYC Mayor’s Office of Climate and Environmental Justice, a partner on the PopWheels pilot. “It’s just that it hasn’t necessarily been used in this way” for food vendors. And get this: The batteries used for the e-bikes are the same exact ones that are used for the food carts, meaning that delivery workers and street vendors could eventually take advantage of the same infrastructure. PopWheels has also identified another neat symbiosis in its food-cart pilot, paying some of the delivery workers who already rely on the service to shuttle batteries to street vendors that are farther away from the charging cabinets. William Arevalo, the owner of the food cart I toured, said that his batteries have worked well so far and that he’d be willing to pay for a subscription to keep using the service. It would likely cost far less than the roughly $500 to $600 a month he pays to fuel his generator, which also requires regular maintenance and repairs. Finances aside, the generator’s noise sometimes makes it hard for customers and workers to hear each other, Arevalo said, and he’s acutely aware of the smoke’s insidious effects. “Little by little, there can be damage to the lungs,” he said. “I have a lot of friends who have this problem.” Though the electrical equipment in Arevalo’s cart now runs on batteries, the grill still uses propane gas. And, within eyeshot of his battery-powered food cart, which fries up empanadas and other savory dishes, Arevalo operates an ice cream truck that still relies on a diesel-fueled generator. PopWheels’ batteries are not capable of providing enough power for that operation. “To be honest, right now the technology can’t serve ice cream trucks,” said Rosenn. “I don’t think it’s feasible, and you would have to be constantly swapping it.” Electrifying super-energy-intensive vendors would likely require a substantially different battery type and cabinet fleet, according to PopWheels. PopWheels’ model isn’t the only option for electrifying food carts. Vendors can purchase their own batteries and charge them up at home or in the commissaries and depots where they park overnight. Arevalo said a friend with a food truck in Brooklyn did that after receiving lots of noise and pollution complaints, switching his generator for a battery he charges at a depot. But it’s not a given that vendors have access to a space with the electric infrastructure needed to safely charge. “Every commissary really is different, and some of them have the capacity for there to be charging happening there,” Thomas said. “But then there are others that would need electrical upgrades or don’t have enough outlets.” Batteries also tend to cost more upfront than generators, and vendors must be able to afford a system big enough to get them through the entire day. The nonprofit Street Vendor Project — a partner on the PopWheels effort in Queens — ran a pilot a couple of years ago in which it provided NYC vendors with batteries they were responsible for charging themselves. Given the rules around cart footprints, the organization offered batteries that were around the same physical size as generators, but that capacity was sufficient for fewer vendors than expected, said Andrew Conca-Cheng, programs manager at the Street Vendor Project. Then there’s the somewhat obvious choice of just letting vendors plug into outlets on the street. Some cities around the world do that, Conca-Cheng said, and a 2013 pilot let a vendor in New York’s Union Square electrify with grid power from a pedestal installed by the startup Simply Grid, but the approach never got much traction. “I’ve had people emailing me from Europe saying, ‘Why isn’t New York doing this yet?’” Conca-Cheng said. “And you know, thos

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority on Wednesday selected eight bulk energy storage and 13 large-scale renewable projects to receive financial support, totaling almost 1.7 GW of clean energy resources expected to be online by the end of 2030. - The state’s first bulk energy storage awards went to 950 MW of lithium batteries ranging from four to eight hours in duration. Renewables awards will go to solar, wind and hydroelectric projects totaling 719 MW of capacity. - The state has fallen behind its clean energy goals and earlier this year made changes to the greenhouse gas reduction targets laid out in its Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act. “This announcement couldn’t come at a better time,” Amisha Rai, Advanced Energy United’s senior vice president of advocacy, said in a statement. Dive Insight: New York pushed back its emissions targets this year, but officials say the state remains committed to clean energy and has not adjusted its procurement goals. The state’s target of 70% renewable energy by 2030, set when the CLCPA was passed in 2019, is unchanged. New York doubled its storage target in 2022 to have 6 GW of storage online by 2030. NYSERDA plans to issue a second annual bulk energy storage request for proposals by the end of this year and said it intends to select 3 GW of energy storage procurement over its first three solicitations. The newly contracted large-scale energy projects “not only further the growth of clean energy and more than double the utility-scale energy storage that exists currently statewide – but they contribute to New York’s comprehensive, all of the above energy strategy,” NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris said in a statement. The selected projects in New York range in size from a 4-hour, 94-MW facility being developed by Key Capture Energy in Ulster County; to a similar 150-MW facility in Suffolk County, also developed by KCE; to the 8-hour, 140-MW Lighthouse Energy Storage project in Chautauqua County, proposed by Grid Connected Infrastructure LLC and Neoen US. The projects will more than double the utility-scale energy storage that has been awarded, contracted, and installed in New York to date, “making meaningful progress toward 6 gigawatts by 2030,” NYSERDA said. “Bringing new renewable energy and storage projects online means more homegrown power, more flexibility for the grid, and more investment in communities across the state,” AEU’s Rai said. The projects announced last week are expected to support 1,000 jobs and generate over $3.7 billion in private investment, NYSERDA said. Payments to the contracted projects will only begin once projects are operational.

artigo.texto: Nebraska data center growth raises questions for host counties NORTH PLATTE, Neb. (KNOP) - Nebraska’s push to attract data centers is facing questions from the counties that would host them. Lincoln County commissioners met last Tuesday in Grand Island with power companies, water districts and Gov. Pillen for the first meeting of Nebraska’s Data Center Task Force. Task force reviews power, water strain The group is looking at how the state should handle the rapid growth of data centers and the strain they could put on power and water supplies. Lincoln County Commissioner Kent Weems said the county is not against the idea but wants any deal to come with benefits for taxpayers. “If we’re going to be the ones taking the heat for these, whatever they evolve into, if they evolve at all, which apparently there’s something and it works locally. It’s my hope and prayer that this community can, in fact, have substantial beneficial results and be mandated in the agreement so that the county can see property tax relief,” Weems said. Not all data centers are the same, commissioner says Lincoln County Commissioner Micaela Wuehler said data centers vary in scale and impact. “It’s important for people to remember: not all data centers are created equal. They’re not all hyperscale... they may not all be appropriate for Lincoln County. That’s where our good planning and zoning regulations come in,” Wuehler said. The task force meets again in Columbus on October 20th. Click here to subscribe to our KNOP News 2 daily digest and breaking news alerts delivered straight to your email inbox. Copyright 2026 KNOP. artigo.texto: Trending PARKERSBURG, W.Va. -- The Democratic challenger for one of West Virginia's congressional seats pitched legislation Friday to place a two-year moratorium on new, large data centers and to give local communities a say in whether they're built. Ace Parsi, a Morgantown community organizer running for U.S. House of Representatives 2nd District seat occupied by Rep. Riley Moore, said the proposed "Neighbors, Not Servers Act" would be "the very first piece of legislation that I would introduce as a member of Congress." Moore said Friday, "West Virginians need a voice in this important debate," and he has co-sponsored legislation to that effect. Parsi said the impact of data centers on the environment, communities and utility costs is an issue he's heard about from Democratic, Republican and independent voters alike. "Our communities do not have a say in whether these things go in our backyards," he said, referencing transmission lines as well. The legislation would pause new construction of data centers using 20 megawatts or more of power, according to a news release from Parsi. During that time, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine would conduct studies into the effects of such facilities on public health, water, jobs, utility bills, property values and the power grid. It proposes a fine of up to $1 million a day for developers who break the pause. The bill also would ban nondisclosure agreements between developers and public officials, including those already in place. NDAs signed by Washington County, Ohio, officials for a proposed data center in the Waterford area have ignited debate. Commissioners have said such agreements are standard for preliminary conversations about potential development and signing allowed them to enter into conversations with the developers. Parsi's proposed bill also would establish a referendum process so community members could seek a vote on approving construction of a data center. Before a vote, developers would be required to disclose information such as who is behind the project, who will use it, how much power and water it will use, noise levels, tax breaks sought and number of jobs it will create, the release states. Parsi said during an online news conference Friday that a public vote would not be mandatory, as local bodies like county commissions could make the call as representatives of residents. "We would direct those (federal) agencies to not give those permits (for data center construction) until they made sure the community" had a voice in the process through one of those mechanisms, he said. "The local people need to be able to determine this," Parsi said. "This bill is not about big government." Moore said "it is critical that America wins the AI race against countries like China, but we must do so responsibly. "I'm for local control. Local communities need to have a say about whether to build data centers in their backyard, and we need to ensure that Americans are not being forced to foot the bill for increased energy demands and water usage," he said. "That's why I proudly cosponsored and voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act in the House to ensure that local communities have a voice in these important decisions and ensure that West Virginians are not being forced to foot the bill for data center development." Moore announced in an Aug. 31 news release he was co-sponsoring that bill, which would "require state public utility commissions to consider standards ensuring that large data centers pay the full incremental costs associated with generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve their electricity demand." It adds that the bill would protect ratepayers while preserving the authority of state regulators to determine how its standards were implemented. OHIO ELECTION TOPIC Data centers are also a topic of interest in Ohio's gubernatorial election. Democratic nominee Dr. Amy Acton this week called for the state Legislature to enact a conditional moratorium on data centers, including prohibiting data centers and investors from passing along costs to ratepayers, banning their use of NDAs and requiring them to be built with union labor, maintain zero environmental impact and prioritize the use of brownfield sites. In the release, she also criticized Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's investments in data centers. "I am calling on lawmakers from across the aisle to come together and fight against the unchecked development of data centers driving up costs in our communities," Acton said. "I will always put the needs of working families over the wants of billionaires, corporations and special interests." Ramaswamy's campaign website lists three "non-negotiable" requirements for companies wanting to build data centers in Ohio: Ensure nearby families receive free electricity by providing power or compensation, pay their full property taxes so revenue can be used to provide relief for homeowners, and comply with strict air and water quality standards while minimizing water use and prioritizing brownfield and industrial sites over farmland.

artigo.texto: Sept. 30 (UPI) -- Democrats in the U.S. Senate on Wednesday blocked a bill that would have made states consider adopting ways to make data center developers pay for water and energy costs, calling the legislation "toothless." The Ratepayer Protection Act, which was led by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, would not force states to adopt these standards. Democrats said they sought legislation to mandate that developers cover the costs, The Hill reported. The act, which would set a federal standard on the issue, passed the House by a vote of 417-3 earlier this month. The procedural vote Wednesday was 57-43, short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster. Data centers, which use huge amounts of energy, are increasingly unpopular among voters, an NBC News poll earlier this month said. By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they'd be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community, the poll said. Some Democratic senators, including Sens. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, joined Republicans to vote for the bill. However, Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said that the act was "optional" for states and "a fraud." "It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said Tuesday. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers." Husted said Tuesday that the act could be a "bipartisan win." "I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices," he said of Democrats. "All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president's desk." Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, who is running against Husted, has criticized him as "the point man to bring these data centers to Ohio" when Husted was Ohio's lieutenant governor.

artigo.texto: Exide Tops ₹5,200 Crore in EV Battery Bet as Bengaluru Plant Goes Live Key Takeaways - Exide Industries has committed ₹5,202.23 crore to EESL as of 29 September 2026, a cumulative figure equivalent to nearly 30% of the parent's FY26 annual revenue, all directed into a subsidiary yet to generate meaningful commercial revenue. - Phase I of EESL's 6 GWh Bengaluru gigafactory was commissioned on 23 September 2026, making it one of the only operational domestic lithium-ion cell manufacturing facilities in India, where total commissioned PLI-ACC capacity stood at just 1.4 GWh out of a 50 GWh target as of October 2025. - First revenue from LFP cells is targeted for Q3 FY27, with break-even projected at late FY27 or early FY28 only if utilisation exceeds 40-50% of Phase I capacity, a threshold that remains unproven at this stage. - EESL's loss after tax widened from ₹209.12 crore in FY25 to ₹248.16 crore in FY26, a pattern consistent with the depreciation and interest burden of heavy capital expenditure overwhelming nascent revenue during a ramp-up phase. - Zero PLI-ACC incentives have been disbursed to any beneficiary as of September 2026, meaning the investment economics that underpin EESL's case rest on government payments that have not yet materialised, representing the single most consequential structural risk to watch over the next four to six quarters. Exide Industries has now committed ₹5,202.23 crore to a single battery subsidiary, closed the latest ₹99.99 crore tranche of that commitment just yesterday, and switched on the plant it has been funding less than a week ago. That is a landmark figure for the Indian energy storage sector, and the timing is what makes it worth reading closely. Exide Energy Solutions Limited (EESL) has crossed a threshold. It is no longer a construction project on a balance sheet; it is an operating facility chasing its first commercial revenues. To reach this point, the parent has poured in more than five thousand crore rupees, and the next phase, where revenue arrives from Q3 FY27 and break-even hinges on how fast the plant fills up, is where an ambition of this size either proves out or strains. Here is what the ₹5,200 crore commitment actually tells you about Exide’s strategic direction, what the commissioning of Phase I means in practical terms, and the specific variables that will decide whether this concentrated bet was correctly sized. Exide closes ₹100 crore rights issue in EESL as cumulative bet crosses ₹5,200 crore The mechanics of the latest transaction are straightforward. Exide subscribed to a fresh rights issue of equity in EESL, its wholly owned cell manufacturing arm, on a cash consideration basis at arm’s length. No ownership percentage changed; Exide already held 100% of the subsidiary and still does. Here is what the tranche involved: - 2,85,71,428 equity shares allotted - Face value of ₹10 per share, issued at a premium of ₹25 per share - Total raised: ₹99.99 crore - Allotment completed on 29 September 2026 This tranche did not arrive in isolation. In January 2026, Exide’s board approved up to ₹1,400 crore in additional infusions to keep the project moving, and management has executed that approval across multiple tranches through the year. Yesterday’s rights issue is simply the latest instalment in a steady, deliberate drip of capital. Add it all up and the number lands with real weight. ₹5,202.23 crore invested in EESL as of 29 September 2026 That figure only becomes fully legible against the parent’s own scale. Standalone Exide Industries reported revenue of roughly ₹17,269 crore in FY26. So the cumulative commitment to EESL now equals close to 30% of the parent’s annual turnover, all directed into a subsidiary whose net worth stood at ₹3,991.06 crore as of 31 March 2026 and which has yet to generate meaningful revenue. For anyone tracking Exide’s balance sheet and capital allocation, the message is unambiguous. This is not a paper reorganisation or an accounting entry. It is a genuine cash commitment at commercial terms, and both the size of the total and the pace at which it has grown deserve scrutiny. When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first Phase I of Exide’s 6 GWh Bengaluru gigafactory enters commercial operations The capital has been buying something concrete, and six days before the latest tranche, that something switched on. EESL commissioned Phase I of its lithium-ion cell manufacturing facility on 23 September 2026 at the Hi-Tech Defense and Aerospace Park in Devanahalli, Bengaluru. Phase I carries a 6 GWh design capacity built on two chemistries, a configuration that hedges the plant against shifts in demand across different end-markets. The commercial sequencing follows demand readiness. Initial revenue will come from LFP cells serving three-wheelers, telecom, and battery energy storage systems (BESS), stationary units that store power for later use. NMC cells for two-wheelers follow once that line ramps. Global BESS demand is one of the key demand drivers underpinning the LFP line at Devanahalli, with grid-scale stationary storage contracts offering longer-term, higher-volume offtake compared to the more cyclical two-wheeler segment. A few facts anchor the facility: - Total design capacity of 12 GWh across two phases, with Phase II timing dependent on demand signals - Phase I capital expenditure estimated at approximately ₹6,000 crore through FY28 - Cell manufacturing technology underpinned by a technical collaboration with SVOLT The six-day gap between commissioning the plant and injecting fresh capital was not coincidental. Exide is funding the ramp-up phase, the stretch that converts a commissioned facility into a revenue-generating one. That distinction matters for how you read the risk. artigo.texto: As elétricas que podem lucrar com o medida tributária Redata, segundo o Safra O presidente Luis Inácio Lula da Silva aprovou, neste mês, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, mais conhecido como Redata. A medida envolve incentivos fiscais para centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. Com o Redata, o Safra enxerga uma oportunidade para as companhias do setor elétrico. O relatório do banco cita a estimativa que a demanda de eletricidade dos data centers deve crescer 15% ao ano até 2030, dado da Agência Internacional de Energia – IEA. Além disso, o Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), projeta que o Brasil pode alcançar 20 GW de capacidade instalada de data centers até 2035. O Safra ainda diz que esse número pode ser ainda maior com o Redata. Nesse contexto, o banco acredita que sete companhias do setor elétrico podem se beneficiar desse cenário. As ações que podem se beneficiar com o Redata O Safra utiliza a experiência dos Estados Unidos como referência. Por isso, eles enxergam um potencial para um aumento de 2,7% na demanda, caso a participação dos data centers passe de 5% para 8% da demanda total de energia. Esse cenário beneficiaria distribuidoras como ENEL, CPFL (CPFE3), Light (LIGT3), Equatorial (EQTL3) e Energisa (ENGI3). Além disso, o banco cita a alta de preços de energia em regiões dos EUA, que aumentaram aproximadamente 30% entre 2020 e 2025 tanto por uma maior demanda dos data centers, quanto possivelmente por condições climáticas e custos de combustíveis. Nesse contexto, maiores pagamentos por capacidade podem beneficiar Axia (AXIA3) e Copel (CPLE3), segundo os analistas. *Sob supervisão de Renan Dantas

artigo.texto: CATL, the world’s largest EV battery and energy storage manufacturer, began trial production at its newly built cell manufacturing gigafactory in Debrecen, Hungary, towards the end of September, 2026. This means the Chinese manufacturing giant has met all necessary preconditions and regulatory requirements for what is essentially a trial period, where equipment is optimised and validated ahead of full-scale series production. The €7.3 billion facility’s first two production lines are now operational for testing and are operating at a capacity of 34 GWh. As of autumn 2024, CATL’s Debrecen site has built over 537,000 battery modules. Since the firm’s foundation in 2011, CATL batteries have been fitted to more than 17 million vehicles globally. CATL-using manufacturers include Tesla, Volkswagen, Porsche, Audi, Kia, Changan, and Stellantis. With a 100 gigawatt-hour (GWh) capacity, the Debrecen plant will be CATL’s largest outside China. For context, a 1 GWh capacity factory can make enough batteries for some 17,000 vehicles. Earlier this year, local authorities from Debrecen’s surrounding Hajdu-Bihar county ordered a temporary shutdown of certain zones of the factory due to safety concerns when nine employees were exposed to nickel. CATL then implemented several health and safety changes, which the authorities confirmed met the correct regulatory frameworks. CATL is the latest EV player to join what appears to be a gold rush for manufacturing and production space in the Central and Eastern European (CEE) region. Also in Debrecen, Chinese battery specialists, EVE, have confirmed it will build a 30GWh factory next to the BMW plant where the new BMW iX3 is built. By the end of this year, BYD has promised to open a production site in the Hungarian town of Szeged to circumnavigate European Union tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles. Meanwhile, Toyota promises to build its next EV at its Kolín factory in the Czech Republic. In 2008, Ford built a factory in Craiova, Romania. At present, the facility manufactures the all-electric Puma Gen-E, E-Tourneo Courier, and E-Transit Courier. The Mercedes-Benz GLC’s electric drive system is also Romanian-made.
