artigo.texto: Medford council, planning commission to discuss data centers Published 4:26 pm Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Medford man launches online petition urging city officials to prohibit the facilities, which have been a subject of extensive environmental concerns A Medford man is urging residents to tune in for a planned discussion of data centers by Medford city officials on Wednesday night. The joint study session, which will include Medford City Council and the city’s Planning Commission, is set for 6 p.m. Sept. 30 in the Medford Police Department’s Prescott Room. The agenda for the meeting — residents can attend in person or via Zoom — is posted to the city website. Discussion of data centers comes amid ongoing conversations around the state and nation as community leaders grapple with how to navigate a growing number of the facilities. While data centers provide technology for artificial intelligence, data storage and other online services, concerns range from heavy electricity usage, large consumption of water for equipment cooling purposes and environmental impacts. Land use considerations range from the amount and cost of available land to demands on water, sewer, transportation and stormwater infrastructure. Large facilities may require 50 to 150 acres. City and county municipalities tout economic development, with the facilities projected to create millions in tax revenues and thousands of jobs. Medford city officials report no existing applications have been submitted and no decisions will be made during the study session. Online petition Medford resident Matthew Damigos expressed concern that consideration of data centers by city officials could mean proposed data centers could soon be under consideration. Damigos has launched an online petition on Change.Org titled, “Prevent the construction of an AI data center in Medford, Oregon.” Damigos told the Rogue Valley Times he was “deeply concerned about the potential implications for our city and our way of life” if a data center should be constructed, and he said he felt the topic warranted a community conversation “and not just a discussion between the council and planning commission.” Damigos expressed concern about the council’s “willingness to take citizen input,” pointing to a recent back-and-forth involving changes to downtown Main Street, where traffic pattern changes were made and then changed again. Damigos said he hoped citizens would weigh in on the topic of data centers. “Public comment is absolutely necessary regarding an AI data center. AI data centers simply have shown negative effects on communities, and (there are) long-term effects that are unknown,” he told the Times. “This is not a political matter. This is a public health matter, and the Medford and nearby communities in Jackson County should be heard,” Damigos said. Damigos said notice of the study session posted Friday did not allow for enough time for residents to plan to attend. “I just think it’s odd to announce they’re having this discussion and then, ‘Oh, by the way, you have only two business days for the public to even see it.’ Everything the city of Medford does is quite questionable in my opinion. This is an important issue for our community,” he said. “I was concerned they were entertaining the discussion, and I wanted to make sure people were aware because not everyone is going to go to the city of Medford website to see that this discussion is happening.” Currently, Medford Land Development Code Section 10.337 allows data centers in all commercial zones as well as the Light Industrial zone. They are not permitted in the General or Heavy Industrial zones, and the city has no special design or location standards established for data centers. Council and planning commission members will discuss whether to make changes to city land-use regulations pbefore any future proposals for data centers. State and national date center headlines Following concerns raised by a large coalition of environmental, farm and social advocacy groups, and the urging of a moratorium of data centers, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek earlier this month ordered a pause on data centers on state lands, effective through July 2027. A report this week by the Oregon Capital Chronicle detailed plans for a data center proposed on 100 acres of BLM land near Hermiston — the project would be the first on federal public land in Oregon and one of a dozen proposed in six western states. Reach reporter Buffy Pollock at 458-488-2029 or buffy.pollock@rv-times.com. Follow her on Twitter @orwritergal.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) propôs à ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) que o encargo para custear a contratação de baterias seja reduzido para as fontes que entregam mais potência na ponta de carga – janela em que a geração solar cai e o consumo aumenta, exigindo resposta rápida do sistema. A proposta introduz um novo conceito, batizado de “ICP-JC”, que mede a contribuição de cada usina para adequar a potência no período mais crítico do dia, entre 18h e 22h. Segundo o ONS, o indicador deveria ser usado para graduar o rateio do encargo entre os geradores. O ONS disse que essa metodologia para verificar a contribuição de potência de cada fonte já está em desenvolvimento para subsidiar o montante a ser contratado no leilão de baterias, em dezembro. Para isso, solicitou à ANEEL que incorpore a variável de potência verificada em um intervalo de tempo à consulta pública em andamento. A sugestão foi apresentada em reunião com o gabinete do diretor Gentil Nogueira, no último dia 14, e disponibilizada na terça-feira (29). O operador frisou que a definição sobre o critério de rateio deve ser conhecido pelos agentes antes do leilão.

artigo.texto: Battery storage (BESS) financing in the Netherlands In the Netherlands, several reports were published in 2026 predicting growth of battery energy storage systems (BESS) located in the Netherlands in terms of both Dutch GWh capacity and Dutch market share in Europe. For lenders, investors and developers, this expansion presents opportunities. However, financing, regulatory and business-case challenges require careful navigation. In this blog, we highlight some key developments and considerations for the financing of BESS projects. The Dutch BESS market The Netherlands is fast developing into a more attractive jurisdiction for BESS projects. Whereas other countries took an early lead in BESS project development, the Dutch market was behind the curve due to limitations in supporting legal infrastructure for BESS development, grid capacity and connection issues, high grid fees and limited bankability of the business case. However, this has changed as a result of various initiatives yielding results starting from 2025. In various market reports published in 2026, the Dutch BESS market is predicted to grow into a major European BESS jurisdiction. Opportunities for BESS in the Netherlands - Dutch government priorities for BESS In the Dutch state budget for 2027, published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government announced further support for energy storage, in the form of enhanced tax advantages for companies investing in innovative energy storage systems. In the updated National Energy System Plan, also published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government acknowledged the need for risk-sharing to facilitate the scale-up of energy infrastructure and storage.From 2027, the Netherlands must establish goals for non-fossil flexibility to stabilise the electricity grid pursuant to the EU Electricity Regulation, on the basis of assessments determining how much clean flexibility electricity systems require and identifying existing barriers. Although the outcomes of the Dutch assessment and the Dutch goals are not yet known, these may encourage BESS projects further. These developments follow earlier initiatives that have mitigated and supported the business case for Dutch BESS projects. - The Dutch grid operator reduced grid rates The Dutch grid operator TenneT published a position paper on BESS in 2024 to clarify its position regarding the application of large batteries (>70MW) by market parties to the grid, which served as guidance to the market and public authorities. TenneT also started offering new flexible contract forms with lower transport rates for batteries and other flexible capacity: TenneT now offers time-based transmission rights for high-voltage grids and transmission rights of at least 85% availability. By leveraging time-based rights, flexible grid users like batteries can achieve significant discounts. - Improved bankability for debt and equity funding The willingness of debt and equity investors and financiers to fund BESS projects in the Netherlands has traditionally been undermined by uncertainty around cash flows and floor prices of BESS projects. These days, the Dutch government’s subsidies mitigate the floor price risk and the measures taken by TenneT help reduce the cost and risk elements, improving the cash flows in relation to BESS projects. The new developments described above may improve the bankability of BESS projects further.The bankability of a BESS project could require both debt and equity funding, with alternative lenders and investors providing a mix of both. The Netherlands is known for its flexible legal framework in respect of corporate and finance laws. This effectively provides access to corporate and project-based debt and equity funding solutions, allowing capital flows into and within the Netherlands. BESS projects in the Netherlands have been financed through corporate financings or project financings. Other forms of BESS financing – already applied internationally and depending on the BESS project involved – could also include innovative forms of securitisation, green bonds, possibly in combination with corporate or project financing. Legal expertise of the Stibbe team We are a multidisciplinary team of professionals who are top-ranked practitioners in projects, energy, administrative law, corporate law and debt finance, with expertise in BESS projects. The Stibbe team has market-leading expertise in the Benelux in respect of the full development and financing life-cycle of utility-scale BESS projects, from advising on site acquisition, zoning & permitting, energy regulatory matters, procurement structure and supplier contracts, to FDI, competition, corporate and project financing expertise. We have been involved in various roles (as developers’, equity investors’ and lenders’ counsel) in many of the utility-scale projects to have achieved financial close in the Benelux to date. Through our experience in working with investors, lenders, developers, contractors and other key players in these areas, we have an excellent understanding of the objectives and challenges facing this fast-developing critical segment of the energy industry. If you have any questions, please contact Marieke Driessen or Ellen Vintges from Stibbe’s Financial Markets team.

artigo.texto: Six major financiers signed on to fund Nvidia's AI build-out. Buried in the deal: Nvidia's promise to cover up to 25% of losses if the hardware loses value, a guarantee that could hit $125 billion, with much of that risk headed for insurers' balance sheets. On August 10, Nvidia announced memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to build financing platforms meant to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure, according to Axios. The pitch to these firms was straightforward: raise money from pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and insurers, use it to buy Nvidia chips and build data centers, then lease the capacity to AI companies for years of steady payments. To make that pitch land with investors who don't normally gamble on chip depreciation, Nvidia added a sweetener. It said it "may provide a residual-value support mechanism for up to 25% of an opportunity, assessed carefully on a project-by-project basis." That covers part of the gap if hardware turns out to be worth less than expected when a lease ends. Do the math across every deal Nvidia is courting, and that backstop could total $125 billion in exposure, per Axios's reporting on the plan. That's Nvidia, the company selling the shovels in this gold rush, agreeing to personally guarantee that the shovels won't rust. Here's the part that should catch your attention: none of that $500 billion sits on Nvidia's own balance sheet, and neither does most of the credit risk behind it. The GPUs get bought by special purpose vehicles. The vehicles issue debt. And increasingly, according to CNBC's reporting from April 2026, that debt gets placed with insurance and retirement capital managed by firms like Apollo and KKR. Data centers are expensive, decades-spanning projects, and they happen to match the long-dated liabilities insurers already carry - things like annuities and pension obligations. The risk doesn't disappear. It just changes owners, and it arrives on an insurer's books relabeled as investment-grade fixed income. CNBC's April reporting quotes the phrase "GPU debt treadmill," coined by AI commentator Dave Friedman, to describe the core mismatch driving this whole structure. GPUs have a useful life of roughly seven years. The data centers housing them are built to last 20 to 30. Lenders and insurers underwriting a 20-year facility are implicitly betting that today's Nvidia chips, or their replacements, will still be worth something in year fifteen, even though the hardware itself will have been swapped out two or three times by then. Nvidia's $108 billion fiscal third-quarter forecast assumes it sells zero AI data center chips to China, even though analysts peg potential Chinese demand at $30 billion. Trump hosts Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24, with Jensen Huang expected at the state dinner and chip access on the agenda. - Nvidia China AI chip sales forecast outlook - state dinner Xi Jinping impact on Nvidia revenue Capacity is also a live problem. One insurance executive told CNBC that insuring a single $20 billion data center campus was nearly impossible to price in 2023. By 2026, it's become, in that executive's words, a weekly conversation. Insurers have responded with new products built for this exposure: cover for credit losses, cover for declines in chip resale value, and cover for contract breaches tied to power outages or cooling failures at the facilities themselves, according to the same CNBC report. The scale of the debt underneath all of this has grown fast. Incremental borrowing funded about 9% of hyperscaler capital spending in fiscal 2024. By mid-2026 that figure had climbed to roughly 32% on a trailing basis, and U.S. data-center debt issuance roughly doubled to about $182 billion in 2025, per the reporting Axios cited in its financing coverage. Frankly, that's the kind of growth curve that makes credit analysts nervous even when the underlying business is healthy. Why the timing matters Nvidia isn't doing this in a vacuum. Bain & Company said this week that the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion a year in new revenue by 2031 just to justify the data center spending already committed. Existing AI services might cover $1.8 trillion of that, leaving a $4.2 trillion gap to fill from businesses that barely exist yet, like autonomous robotics and AI-driven drug discovery. Bain separately projects $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion in data center spending through 2030. Those are the numbers Wall Street is holding up against Nvidia's financing push. They explain why insurers are being asked to carry so much of the weight: the traditional lenders and Nvidia's own balance sheet can't absorb spending at that scale alone. Nvidia's arrangement doesn't eliminate risk. It reroutes it, from Nvidia's income statement and from the banks that might otherwise hold this debt, into the reserves of companies whose entire business model depends on correctly pricing tail risk decades in advance. If AI demand keeps compounding the way Nvidia's revenue guidance assumes, the residual-value guarantee mostly sits unused, a marketing device that made institutional capital comfortable enough to write the check. But if a major AI lab pulls back capacity, or a cheaper chip generation arrives faster than expected and strands the current fleet, the 25% backstop gets tested for real. Insurers holding the debt behind it find out how much of that "investment-grade fixed income" was actually GPU depreciation risk wearing a different label. None of the six firms named in the MOUs have disclosed how much capital they've actually committed, or whether the residual-value terms are even finalized. Nvidia's own release says the partnerships remain subject to final agreements. That's worth sitting with: the market has already reacted to $500 billion in financing infrastructure and a $125 billion guarantee ceiling, and so far, not a single dollar of it is conf

artigo.texto: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed by NPR. Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators. In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts). The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. Loading... Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands. The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state. "It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands. "The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it." In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company. "We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added. Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county. Small reactors, big plan Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build. Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft. The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive. At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip. "Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd. The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build. Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032. Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used." NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report. Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13

artigo.texto: Abraget estima impacto de R$ 7 bi com gás natural fora do Redata Associação diz que exclusão do combustível pode elevar custos do sistema elétrico e gerar insegurança jurídica A Abraget (Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas) estima que a exclusão do gás natural das fontes elegíveis ao Redata pode gerar um impacto de cerca de R$ 7 bilhões na conta de luz dos consumidores. Segundo nota da entidade, data centers precisam de fornecimento contínuo de energia e, sem o gás natural entre as fontes contempladas, o sistema teria de recorrer a outras formas de geração nos períodos de baixa produção renovável. A associação também afirma que o modelo pode exigir novos investimentos em transmissão, principalmente para levar energia renovável do Nordeste a projetos instalados no Sul e Sudeste. A Abraget alerta, ainda, para risco de insegurança jurídica e sustenta que excluir o gás da regulamentação do Redata "vai na contramão do que foi aprovado pelo Congresso Nacional". *Sob supervisão de Daniel Rittner

artigo.texto: The construction industry accounted for around half of the non-farm job growth in Wisconsin over the last year, as a few high-profile data center projects moved forward in the state. Wisconsin added 10,500 construction jobs from August 2025 to August 2026, more than half of the 19,400 total non-farm jobs added over that period, according to data from the state Department of Workforce Development. The industry accounted for 156,500 jobs as of August, the most recent month with available data. That growth has come in a year in which Microsoft completed the first phase of its data center campus in Mount Pleasant, while construction continued on other campuses in Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Scott Hodek, an economist at the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development, said there’s a variety of factors contributing to the sector’s growth statewide and the agency did not have the “specificity of data” to break out construction jobs tied to data centers. Hodek said there was demand coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and — as inflation has remained high — more companies are deciding to move forward with building projects in hopes of beating future cost increases. “We’re seeing a lot of growth in construction in general, and that’s all across the board,” he said. “Honestly, that’s generally a good sign when you’re still seeing construction, even though materials and labor costs are up.” Data center development is widely unpopular with the public in Wisconsin. In a Marquette Law School Poll of Wisconsin residents released in August, 67 percent of respondents said they would like to ban data center development for at least a year. For voters questioned for the poll, data centers were a bigger issue than abortion policy, public schools and crime in their communities. Despite pushback from the public, the industry has been growing fast in the state. Especially in southeast Wisconsin — home to two of the three major data center projects under construction in the state — business and labor leaders say data centers are driving growth in both the construction and manufacturing industries, though manufacturing job growth has been weaker statewide. Union construction industry views data centers as ‘decade-long runway’ for growth Chris Mambu Rasch is the executive director of Building Advantage, a labor management association for the union construction industry in southeast Wisconsin. He said both data center campuses being developed in southeast Wisconsin “are essentially 100 percent union construction” projects. The Microsoft development in Mount Pleasant completed its first phase earlier this year. Mambu Rasch said the phase had around 3,000 union construction workers at peak construction, while roughly 10,000 workers cycled through the site over a two-year period. He said phase two is expected to “see similar numbers” and is already “pretty heavy” into construction, with one union sending 600 workers to that project alone. In Port Washington, he said there are between 2,500 and 2,800 union construction workers at the data center site. He said he expects “well over 4,000” union jobs on that project during peak construction. “Data centers have created an extraordinary amount of work related to the projects in Mount Pleasant and in Port Washington,” he said. Meanwhile, social media giant Meta, the company behind the data center being developed in Beaver Dam, has said its project would support “approximately 1,000 construction jobs.” Mambu Rasch said he believes there’s a “decade-long runway” where union construction could see strong growth tied to data centers. He said Microsoft plans to build 15 more in Mount Pleasant, while the Port Washington project is in the first phase of development. He said data center developers are interested in other sites in Wisconsin. “This is sustained, long-term employment,” Mambu Rasch said. “We have the utmost confidence that this work is going to be there for the next decade, and that shows because our contractors are bringing on a record number of apprentices.” Data centers help spur construction of power facilities Aside from building data centers themselves, the projects are also spurring construction of new power plants and electric infrastructure to help meet an expected spike in power demands. Mambu Rasch said union workers generally build Wisconsin’s power infrastructure, from natural gas power plants to solar and wind farms. “The energy infrastructure buildout to supply the energy for the data centers is certainly having a positive impact on our industry,” he said. A recent draft report from state regulators found peak electricity demand in Wisconsin could increase by more than 40 percent by 2032, with more than 70 percent of that increase tied to data centers. The Port Washington and Mount Pleasant data centers are in We Energies’ service territory. artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O Copergs (Comitê de Planejamento Energético do Rio Grande do Sul) defendeu que a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) permita o uso de gás natural em projetos de data centers no estado como fonte para “soluções eficientes de geração dedicada, potência firme, flexibilidade operativa e segurança de suprimento”. Em manifestação institucional enviada ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nesta terça-feira (29), o comitê, vinculado à Sema (Secretaria do Meio Ambiente e Infraestrutura), afirma que a elegibilidade dos projetos deve ser definida por critérios de desempenho, como eficiência energética e hídrica, intensidade de emissões, confiabilidade, rastreabilidade dos combustíveis e trajetória de descarbonização. O Copergs argumenta que “a exclusão prévia do gás natural reduziria as alternativas de engenharia disponíveis e poderia impedir que os estados transformem vantagens concretas de energia e conectividade em investimento produtivo” e afirma que conectividade e energia precisam avançar de forma integrada. Segundo o documento, data centers operam de forma contínua e exigem estabilidade, redundância e potência firme, condições que não seriam garantidas apenas por contratos de energia renovável ou por baterias. “Contratos de energia renovável são fundamentais para reduzir emissões e assegurar lastro comercial, mas não garantem, isoladamente, que a potência estará fisicamente disponível no local e no instante da necessidade. Sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta e baterias respondem por milissegundos, minutos ou poucas horas. Contingências prolongadas, restrições de rede e recomposição do sistema exigem recursos controláveis de maior duração.” O comitê destaca que a matriz gaúcha tem elevada participação de fontes renováveis, mas sustenta que isso não elimina a necessidade de recursos despacháveis. Nesse contexto, o gás natural é apontado como alternativa para reserva, ponta, acompanhamento de carga ou operação contínua, conforme os critérios técnicos e ambientais de cada projeto. Para o Copergs, excluir previamente o gás natural do Redata poderia reduzir a capacidade do Rio Grande do Sul de transformar conectividade internacional e infraestrutura energética em desenvolvimento econômico. “O gás natural não substitui a vocação renovável local. Ele assegura que ela possa sustentar cargas digitais críticas sem comprometer confiabilidade, resiliência e competitividade. Excluí-lo previamente do Redata significaria reduzir a capacidade de converter infraestrutura energética e conectividade internacional em desenvolvimento econômico”, afirma o posicionamento.

artigo.texto: S.C. Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews calls for moratorium on data centers WALTERBORO, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT) - South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews is calling for a two-year moratorium on new data center projects in the state. Andrews said large data centers are receiving billions of dollars in tax breaks while local families deal with high gas, diesel and living costs. She said local officials are outmatched by the corporations building the projects. “We have incredibly wealthy, powerful companies coming into these rural communities in South Carolina, dangling a few carrots, and then the communities are getting steamrolled,” Andrews said. “I’ve been really heartened to see people from both sides of the political spectrum joined together to fight back against these large corporation.” Andrews said the proposed moratorium would give communities more protection from the projects. She said the race is tightening and said she will continue to make data centers and family budgets central issues on the campaign trail. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

The financing will support floating solar, ground-mounted solar, rooftop solar and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects, while contributing to the growing clean energy requirements of the railway ecosystem, stated IRFC. Commenting on the development, Manoj Kumar Dubey, CMD, IRFC said, “With Indian Railways targeting Net Zero Carbon Emissions by 2030, investments in renewable energy and energy storage will play an increasingly important role in building a sustainable infrastructure ecosystem.” Indian Railway Finance Corporation (IRFC) has announced that it has signed an INR 4,200 crore Term Loan Agreement with Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) to finance renewable energy projects across Jharkhand and West Bengal. The financing will support DVC's portfolio of floating solar, ground-mounted solar, rooftop solar and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects, leveraging its existing land, reservoirs and transmission infrastructure, while contributing to the growing clean energy requirements of the railway ecosystem, stated IRFC. Commenting on the development, Manoj Kumar Dubey, CMD, IRFC said, “Renewable energy is no longer peripheral to the Railways; it is at the core of Indian Railways' journey towards Net Zero Carbon Emissions by 2030. artigo.texto: Minister Lecce, IESO and more recognized at 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards Awards presented Sept. 22-23 at ESC Conference in Toronto. Talking Points Energy Storage Canada (ESC) honoured leaders in the energy storage sector at its 2026 Awards, held September 22-23 in Toronto. The awards recognized achievements across seven categories, including the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which went to Lesley Gallinger for his role in advancing utility-scale storage in Ontario. - Gallinger emphasized the importance of energy storage for Ontario’s electricity future. - The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was awarded to Jim Fonger, a former ESC chair. - Stephen Lecce, Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award for his support of energy storage initiatives. This recognition highlights the critical role of energy storage in enhancing grid reliability and supporting Canada’s transition to sustainable energy solutions. Energy Storage Canada (ESC) recognized outstanding examples of leadership, innovation, and research at its 2026 Energy Storage Canada Awards, taking place September 22 and 23 at the Energy Storage Canada Conference in Toronto. The awards program is a technology-agnostic showcase of accomplishments from across the sector, recognizing generators, developers, utilities, regulators, researchers, manufacturers, and service providers across seven categories. Categories include the Grid Management Storage Award, the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award, the Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, the Energy Storage Milestone Award, the Friend of Energy Storage Award, and the Energy Storage Trailblazer Award, which is presented both as a standard award to an active member of the industry and as an “In Memoriam” tribute to a recently deceased industry leader. The Energy Storage Trailblazer Award is presented to individuals selected by the ESC’s board of directors who has demonstrated exceptional leadership and contributed to the development of energy storage that serves the overall needs of the industry at large. Lesley Gallinger, past president and CEO of the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO), received the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award for his contributions toward the procurement of more than three gigawatts of utility-scale storage projects in the province during his tenure with the IESO. “I am honoured to receive the 2026 Energy Storage Trailblazer Award. Energy storage has moved from the technology of tomorrow to an essential part of Ontario’s grid and Canada’s electricity future. I am grateful to have contributed to this remarkable journey,” Gallinger said. The In Memoriam Trailblazer Award was presented to Jim Fonger, who once served as chair of ESC and held roles with Rodan Energy Solutions and Ameresco. Fonger passed away in July 2026. “Jim Fonger was a true trailblazer whose vision and leadership helped lay the foundation for Energy Storage Canada and the growth of the sector nationwide,” said Justin Rangooni, president and CEO of ESC. “His legacy lives on in the momentum he helped create and in all of us who continue advancing the storage advantage.” Ontario’s Minister of Energy and Mines, Stephen Lecce, received the Friend of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes individuals from outside of the energy storage sector selected by ESC’s board of directors as a supporter of the industry. Minster Lecce was recognized for his continued commitment to the role of energy storage through the launch of initiatives such as Long Lead-Time Procurement and the modernization of the province’s electricity system. “From nuclear and hydro to battery storage, we are harnessing every resource to keep the lights on and our economy moving. This work has seen over 1,200 MW of battery storage capacity come online to help offset peak demand times, and I am proud to champion the technologies that continue to deliver reliable, affordable electricity to Ontario,” said Minister Lecce. BluWave-ai became the ESC Awards’ first consecutive winner after being recognized with the Grid Management Storage Award for the second year in a row. The award recognized a project that leveraged BluWave-ai’s artificial intelligence-driven platforms to coordinate stationary energy storage and electric vehicles as a single, grid-aware flexible resource. IESO’s Mohamad Shamelstein was presented with the Foundational Research in Energy Storage Award for his demonstration of how energy storage assets supporting large data centres can provide services to the broader electricity system without compromising essential IT infrastructure. The Landmark Application of Energy Storage Award, which recognizes new energy storage technologies or innovations in existing technology, was presented to AlumaPower Corporation. AlumaPower was recognized for its off-grid microgrid demonstration that showed solutions beyond the traditional single-use model of aluminum-air energy storage through its usage of solid recycled aluminum. The Energy Milestone Award was presented to NextStar Energy in honour of the grand opening of its battery manufacturing facility in Windsor, Ont., and the benefits this development is set to bring to Canada’s domestic battery supply chain and the North American energy ecosystem at large.

artigo.texto: 29 de set, 2026 A descarbonização da economia brasileira pode ser não apenas uma resposta às mudanças climáticas, mas também uma estratégia para reduzir custos e aumentar a competitividade das empresas. “Usar formas de energia mais limpa, renovável, já é uma estratégia de negócio,” Grazielle Parenti, vice-presidente de Sustentabilidade da Vale, disse em um debate promovido pelo Brazil Journal durante a Climate Week, em Nova York. A executiva destacou ainda que o Brasil tem alternativas próprias para a transição, como a biomassa, e que grandes empresas precisam trabalhar em conjunto com fornecedores e outras companhias para desenvolver tecnologias em escala. Já Paulo Skaf Filho, CEO da ComBio, empresa de energia térmica renovável para a indústria, lembrou que o custo de capital influencia muito nos projetos de transição energética. “Não é um problema de tecnologia, é um problema de capital e de demanda.” Como os projetos de transição são intensivos em capital e exigem investimentos altos e compromissos de longo prazo, disse Skaf Filho, a incerteza sobre o custo de capital e a falta de previsibilidade regulatória podem dificultar a tomada de decisão das empresas. Roberto Waack, presidente do Comitê de Sustentabilidade da MBRF, chamou atenção para outro desafio: adaptar as metodologias internacionais de mensuração de carbono à realidade brasileira. “Nós estamos num ambiente tropical e a maior parte das metodologias de mensuração de carbono não capturam as características da agricultura e dos ecossistemas brasileiros.” Waack também defendeu o reconhecimento econômico do capital natural brasileiro e afirmou que o mercado de carbono será um dos temas centrais para a transição no país. Para os três executivos, a agenda de descarbonização avançará apenas se o Brasil conseguir transformar soluções que miram uma economia de baixo carbono em negócios.

artigo.texto: Tecnologia: novo plano divulgado na China prevê baterias de estado sólido em larga escala até 2030 e modelos com vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos (Imagem gerada por IA) Agência Publicado em 28 de setembro de 2026 às 15h45. A China quer levar as baterias totalmente de estado sólido a uma fase inicial de aplicação em larga escala até 2030. O país também estabeleceu como meta que baterias de lítio de longa duração cheguem a uma vida útil de até 15 mil ciclos. As metas fazem parte de um novo plano para a indústria de baterias divulgado nesta segunda-feira (28) pelo Ministério da Indústria e Tecnologia da Informação e outros seis órgãos do governo chinês. O documento prevê avanços em diferentes tecnologias, incluindo baterias de lítio, sódio e fluxo. A estratégia também envolve o desenvolvimento de novos materiais para eletrodos, eletrólitos e outros componentes usados na fabricação. Uma das prioridades será ampliar o uso dessas baterias para além dos veículos elétricos e produtos eletrônicos. O plano prevê aplicações em embarcações, aviação, robôs inteligentes, máquinas de engenharia e equipamentos agrícolas. A expansão também deve alcançar sistemas de armazenamento de energia. As novas baterias poderão ser utilizadas junto à geração de energia, em redes elétricas, parques industriais e data centers. Outros formatos também aparecem no planejamento. Baterias flexíveis e de formatos especiais deverão ter aplicações ampliadas em dispositivos vestíveis, casas inteligentes e equipamentos médicos móveis. O plano inclui ainda medidas para aumentar a coleta, reciclagem e reutilização de baterias usadas. As empresas deverão participar da estruturação desses sistemas, diretamente ou por meio de terceiros, de acordo com o volume de produtos colocados no mercado. Fonte: China news

artigo.texto: Lynus AG, a subsidiary of Enerfin AG, starts manufacturing large-scale battery storage systems in Dillingen an der Donau, Bavaria. With the Lynus BESS Cube 2.0, the company produces a modular storage system with a usable battery capacity of around 800 kWh. The system is scaled by cascading, can be integrated into energy projects on both the DC and AC sides, and can also be used as a gray current storage system. Lynus has developed the BESS Cube 2.0 specifically for the requirements of the German market and can flexibly adapt the configuration to project-specific grid connection conditions. The storage system is supplemented by an energy management system (EMS), also developed by Lynus, as well as the multi-market marketing of electricity and storage flexibility. Lynus thus offers hardware, control and marketing as an integrated, European overall solution. The machine learning-based multi-use EMS is already in use in more than 1,500 plants in Germany and Switzerland. Developed for the requirements of the German market One focus in the development of the BESS Cube 2.0 was on flexible integration into PV systems. This is especially true for co-location projects in which existing photovoltaic parks are subsequently expanded to include battery storage systems. Here, storage systems must fit into existing plant layouts and grid connection concepts. With a footprint of just over 5 m2 and a weight of around 7.5 tons per cube, the system is compactly designed and thus facilitates transport and positioning on existing plant areas. Another basis for development was the different technical grid connection conditions in Germany: Depending on the grid operator, voltage level and existing infrastructure, the requirements for a storage project can differ considerably. “EPC companies and operators are regularly faced with the challenge of adapting storage systems to the specific grid and plant situation on site. Since we develop and manufacture the BESS Cube 2.0 ourselves in Germany, we can react quickly to project-specific requirements and significantly accelerate adjustments,” says Paul Hauser, CEO of Lynus. DC and AC coupling for new and existing systems In new photovoltaic systems, the BESS Cube 2.0 can be connected directly to the DC side via MPPT modules. This saves additional AC components such as inverters and reduces conversion losses. AC coupling, on the other hand, is particularly suitable for retrofitting existing systems. LFP technology, liquid cooling and multi-stage safety concept Technologically, the BESS Cube 2.0 relies on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells. The battery cells are designed for more than 8,000 full cycles with 80 percent residual capacity. The rack system achieves DC round-trip efficiency (RTE) of at least 94 percent at 0.5 C. The storage system is available with the voltage levels 400 volts, 690 volts and 800 volts. The charging and discharging capacity is up to 500 kW, depending on the version. An integrated liquid cooling and heating system keeps the battery cells within as homogeneous a temperature range as possible, thus supporting performance and service life. The multi-level safety concept includes smoke, gas and temperature sensors, an automatic aerosol extinguishing system and mechanical pressure relief.

artigo.texto: CATL Leading global battery maker, launched first-gen sodium-ion battery in 2021 A new life cycle assessment from China, drawing on factory data, has concluded that layered-oxide sodium-ion battery packs carry a lower production footprint than lithium iron phosphate packs, even as recent European research points the other way for cells. The findings, reported by ESS News, indicate that making a one kilowatt-hour sodium-ion pack in China emits 56.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent, which is 24.9 percent below the 75.5 kilograms attributed to an LFP pack. The researchers gathered inventory data directly from Chinese battery manufacturers operating at gigawatt-hour scale. For both chemistries, the assessment attributes the bulk of emissions to the electricity used in manufacturing, a pattern the authors link to China's coal-heavy grid. They suggest sodium-ion's footprint could decline further through process optimization and cleaner power supplies, while LFP producers would need to pursue raw-material substitution and reduce material intensity. The study's authors note that earlier work, including research by Peters and colleagues in 2016 and by Guo and colleagues in 2023, placed sodium-ion's footprint slightly above that of lithium-ion, a result they attribute to reliance on lab-scale data and default European databases. A 2025 study by researchers at Fraunhofer and RWTH Aachen University, also built on primary factory data, reached the opposite conclusion. That work put cradle-to-gate emissions for layered-oxide sodium-ion cells at 75 to 87 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, compared with 59 to 70 kilograms for LFP cells. Because the European study measured cells rather than packs, the two sets of figures are not directly comparable. Both assessments stop at the factory gate, so neither incorporates cycle life, meaning they compare manufacturing impacts rather than emissions per unit of lifetime energy delivered. Both also cover only layered-oxide cathodes. HiNa Battery, for instance, uses layered oxides, while Hithium's 785 Ah storage cell relies on a sodium iron pyrophosphate cathode. The Chinese researchers additionally modeled a scenario in which broader sodium-ion adoption avoids 147 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2035. Using a cradle-to-gate boundary spanning raw materials through manufacturing, they determined that the total environmental impact of sodium-ion packs is 27.3 percent lower than that of LFP packs. The scientists set out their findings in a paper titled Comparative life cycle assessment and carbon footprint of sodium-ion and Lithium Iron phosphate batteries, recently published in Environmental Impact Assessment Review. artigo.texto: Governo fará 3 leilões incluindo baterias de 2027 a 2029 Ministério de Minas e Energia projeta 11 certames para o setor elétrico nos próximos 3 anos O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) publicou nesta 4ª feira (30.set.2026) o cronograma de leilões do setor de energia elétrica para o triênio 2027-2029. Serão ao menos 11 certames nos próximos 3 anos, dos quais 3 vão permitir soluções de armazenamento de energia, as chamadas baterias. O calendário também inclui outras modalidades inéditas para os leilões do setor, como usinas reversíveis nas disputas de Reserva de Capacidade e inclusão de usinas térmicas com resíduos, além de diretrizes para certames de energia nova e existente. Leia a íntegra da portaria do MME com o cronograma (PDF – 189 kB). No 1º semestre de cada ano, serão realizados leilões para contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. O cronograma também estabelece, em 2027 e 2029, leilões para assegurar suprimento de Sistemas Isolados –instalações ou redes de distribuição que não têm conexão com a rede elétrica principal do país. A maior parte está nos Estados de Rondônia, Acre, Amazonas, Roraima, Amapá e Pará. Nessas disputas, o atendimento será condicionado ao planejamento de expansão feito pela EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) ou ao direcionamento estratégico de substituição de geração térmica com combustível fóssil por fontes renováveis. Com essa regra, o governo assegura que a realização de novos leilões só ocorra quando houver necessidade real de carga ou quando houver uma diretriz para descarbonizar a matriz dessas regiões, substituindo fontes poluentes por soluções limpas. Já os LRCap (Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência), que contratam potência elétrica disponível para assegurar a segurança do abastecimento de energia do país, dependerão de estudo técnico conjunto da EPE e do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) sobre a necessidade sistêmica. Os dados devem ser encaminhados ao MME até 30 de abril de cada ano. Assim como nos Sistemas Isolados, a inclusão desses leilões no calendário do MME funciona como uma previsão, mas a sua efetivação prática depende de aprovação prévia. À princípio, haverá um LRCap por ano até 2029, sempre no 2º semestre. Se os estudos do ONS e da EPE demonstrarem que o sistema elétrico precisa de reforço de potência de reserva para garantir a segurança do abastecimento na época da respectiva disputa, o leilão será confirmado. Caso contrário, o certame pode não ser realizado naquele ano. A medida busca evitar contratações desnecessárias e questionamentos como os do último leilão de reserva, de março deste ano, quando foram contratados cerca de 20 GW a R$ 515 bilhões. Ao longo do 1º semestre, as contratações foram amplamente criticadas, inclusiva no Congresso, e resultaram em processos na Justiça Federal, TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) e no Cade (Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica). Os resultados acabaram sendo mantidos pelo Judiciário e pela Corte de Contas. Leia o cronograma de leilões do setor elétrico para 2027, 2028 e 2029: 2027 - 1º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW (megawatt); – Leilão para Suprimento aos Sistemas Isolados. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência, podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos; – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos de Geração e de Empreendimentos de Geração Existentes. 2028 - 1º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência,podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos; – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos e de Empreendimentos Existentes. 2029 - 1º Semestre – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência, podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos. – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos de Geração e de Empreendimentos de Geração Existentes; – Leilão para Suprimento aos Sistemas Isolados.

artigo.texto: KP Group Unveils KP 3.0 with 10 GWh Battery Manufacturing Goal KP Group to develop cell manufacturing and BESS assembly capabilities while targeting 10 GW each in IPP capacity and third-party EPC execution by FY32. October 01, 2026. By News Bureau KP Group has unveiled KP 3.0 at its Investor Day and announced revised commitments for FY32. The Group is targeting 10 GW of IPP (Independent Power Producer) through KPI Green Energy, 10 GW of third-party EPC execution, excluding related-party projects and 10 GWh of integrated battery manufacturing capability spanning cell production and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly. KP Group’s renewable energy portfolio including operational and under construction projects is on track and is expected to achieve the goal of 10 GW in next few quarters. KP Group’s total portfolio stands at 9.21 GW. This progress has prompted the KP Group to set higher ambitions and a more focused roadmap for its next phase. The new targets cover three distinct businesses: power assets the Group will own, renewable projects it will execute for external customers and storage systems and cells it plans to manufacture. KP 3.0 marks the induction of a group team of highly experienced professionals in leadership roles across renewable energy, emerging renewable opportunities, international business, green hydrogen, investor relations and governance. This team will also strengthen engineering and manufacturing execution as KP Group scales its businesses. KP Group is expanding into several emerging clean-energy segments. Sundrops Energia serves as the Group’s dedicated Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) platform, with activities spanning BESS IPP, group captive and C&I projects, as well as assembly and cell manufacturing. The Group is also developing a floating solar platform, including the 110 MW AC/142 MW DC Kadana Dam project in Gujarat. In energy trading, KP Group has obtained CERC and GERC licences and is developing capabilities across power exchanges and bilateral markets. In addition, the Group is building capabilities in green hydrogen and green ammonia, covering hydrogen production, mobility, logistics and utilisation. Its Matar facility currently operates a 1 MW electrolysis-based green hydrogen plant with an output of 432 kg per day. As on Q1 FY27, KP Group’s reported renewable energy portfolio stood at more than 9.2 GW across solar, wind and hybrid. Its operating platform includes approximately 12,104 acres of land footprint, 5.10 GW of power evacuation capacity, 400,500 MTPA of manufacturing capacity, a 6.4 GW EPC portfolio and a 2.8 GW IPP portfolio. In the renewable energy sector, KP Group's rapidly expanding footprint now extends across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Furthermore, international opportunities presented span Botswana, Zambia and Tanzania in Africa, as well as Saudi Arabia in the GCC. In Botswana, the Group is pursuing a proposed 5 GW renewable power and associated infrastructure development, with an initial phase planned at 500 MW. In the manufacturing sector the group continues to secure diverse order from pan India. The Group’s revised targets are supported by a clearer business structure and an emphasis on disciplined execution and governance as the next generation assumes wider responsibilities. Dr. Faruk G. Patel, Founder and Chairman, KP Group, said, “Looking our orderbook to grow nearly to 10GW. It shows commitment of our people and the trust of our customers, partners and investors. We have always delivered and will be delivering what we commit. Hence at KP 3.0 we are updating our commitment: to expand owned renewable generation, deliver more projects for customers and build battery manufacturing capability in India. Known for our faster execution, we are committed to achieving these new targets ahead of schedule as well. I am proud to see the next generation take on greater responsibility alongside our experienced professional team. As our ambitions grow, we will remain guided by the principle on which this Group was built: what we commit, we deliver.” please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Macurco Introduces 10-Year Hydrogen Detector for BESS and Data Center Applications UL 2075-Listed HD-6 offers early fault detection with minimal maintenance SIOUX FALLS, S.D., September 29, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Macurco Inc., a DwyerOmega brand and a leader in fixed gas detection solutions, announces the launch of the new HD-6 Hydrogen Gas Detector, designed specifically for continuous hydrogen monitoring in Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) applications and other critical environments where hydrogen detection is essential. Hydrogen detection in BESS applications is vital for safety and monitoring normal equipment operation. When a battery begins to malfunction, it can emit hydrogen gas, which may create explosive and dangerous conditions. Early detection can help identify fault events, prevent further equipment damage, and keep personnel informed of potentially hazardous environments. The new HD-6 provides reliable, continuous hydrogen monitoring and early warning to help protect personnel, equipment, and facilities. The detector features two configurable alarm levels with relay activation, allowing facilities to automate responses such as activating fans, valves, louvers, horns, and strobes. Standard features also include local audible alarms, bright visual indicators, and analog communication for seamless integration with Building Management Systems (BMS). The HD-6 is UL Listed to UL 2075 and CAN/ULC 588 and is CE marked. These listings and the CE marking reflect rigorous electrical safety, performance, and gas detection requirements, demonstrating the detector's electrical integrity, accurate response to hydrogen gas, and reliable operation. CE marking supports the HD-6's availability in the European market. The detector is engineered for long-term performance with a robust, low-maintenance design ideal for demanding applications, including data centers, BESS facilities, and industrial hydrogen monitoring "The Macurco HD-6 is an iteration and upgrade of our current flagship hydrogen detector, the GD-6," said Jonathon DeKam, Macurco Line Product Manager for DwyerOmega. "The new HD-6 includes many significant upgrades - minimal maintenance, resistance to silicone poisoning, additional alarm setpoints, and a generous 10-year lifespan. Macurco developed the HD-6 to address ongoing customer requests for a hydrogen detector that is more robust, more reliable, and lasts longer in the field. "With a UL 2075 listing for hydrogen gas detection, customers can be confident in relying on the HD-6 to monitor their data centers, BESS facilities, or any application where hydrogen detection is imperative. We are eager to get the HD-6 into our customers' hands and begin collecting feedback for future product improvements." Key Features and Benefits of the HD-6: - 10-year sensor life - UL 2075 & CAN/ULC 588 Listed - Minimal maintenance requirements - Resistance to silicone poisoning - Two configurable alarm levels - Sensor range: 0-50% LEL Hydrogen - 5A SPDT fan relay and 0.5A alarm relay - LED display for easy gas concentration monitoring - 4-20mA output for VFD control and BMS integration - End-of-life notification - Compatible with Macurco digital control panels - Easy installation to standard 4×4 electrical boxes - Operates on 12 to 24 VAC or 12 to 32 VDC power Availability & Contact To learn more about the HD-6, visit www.macurco.com or contact Macurco_info@dwyeromega.com. About DwyerOmega DwyerOmega is a leading global manufacturer of precision measurement and control solutions, trusted across a diverse range of industrial and controlled environment applications to monitor, manage, and optimize critical processes with confidence. Serving customers worldwide with a portfolio of industry-leading brands, including Macurco, DwyerOmega has a legacy of, and ongoing commitment to, innovation and quality. The Macurco product line designs, develops, and manufactures a full set of fixed and portable gas detection monitors for the protection of workers, responders, and the community. Macurco has 50 years of proven gas detection experience in residential, commercial, and industrial gas monitoring. Macurco gas detection systems (HVAC, Fire & Security, AimSafety, and TracXP) are widely recognized by distributors and users for their high performance and consistent reliability. For more information, visit www.dwyeromega.com. Contact: Tim Howlett Chief Marketing Officer thowlett@omega.com SOURCE: DwyerOmega Source: DwyerOmega

artigo.texto: CHEYENNE — City officials are considering leasing a portion of Belvoir Ranch for a proposed 140-megawatt solar project and battery storage facility. Representatives from Hanwha Renewables, a Korean utility-scale solar and energy storage developer, presented a preliminary proposal, called Project Wrangler, to members of the Cheyenne City Council at a work session Friday. The company is seeking to lease approximately 3,300 acres of the 18,800-acre ranch while it conducts environmental, engineering and other feasibility studies. The project is expected to eventually occupy 1,200 to 1,400 acres. Councilman Tom Segrave said the city has been exploring ways to generate additional revenue from portions of Belvoir Ranch that aren’t reserved for the city’s planned landfill and water development. “(Hanwha has) been working with the city and me, specifically, on a proposed solar development on the Belvoir Ranch,” Segrave said. “This has been a council goal for, I don’t know, four or five years. … We have areas that we’ve been leasing for grazing, and we’ve been looking for opportunities to increase the revenue off of those lands that are not set aside for the original purposes.” Tyler Nokleby, Hanwha project developer, said the company isn’t looking to gain formal project approval yet. Instead, he wants to enter an option-to-lease agreement that would allow it to conduct necessary studies. “We’re not asking for a permit, we’re not asking to annex,” Nokleby said. “We are hoping to engage with the city, to be the land owner in this process, so that we can kick off everything.” The agreement would last up to four years, although Nokleby said the company hopes to complete its studies within two. During that period, Hanwha would conduct environmental and wildlife studies, geotechnical work, topographical surveys and other assessments. Existing uses of the land, including grazing, would not be affected, Nokleby said. Lida Jauregui-Rivera, Hanwha project engineer, said the solar panels would be around 4 to 5 feet above the ground, but the final design is subject to change based on study results. The battery storage facility would be located near the project’s substation and would occupy around five acres of large, container-like battery units, Jauregui-Rivera said. Hanwha is considering connecting the project to Black Hills Energy’s West Cheyenne substation, which is located a mile from the proposed project area. Council members questioned how the facility would withstand severe weather conditions like hail, and Jauregui-Rivera said the company would consider thicker-glass solar panels and tracking systems that would automatically reposition panels during hailstorms. She estimated crews could inspect the facility and return it to operational condition within four to eight hours after a significant storm, if panels become damaged. The proposed agreement also includes a $50,000 one-time payment to the city for future development at Belvoir Ranch. Payment would occur within 30 days of signing the option-to-lease. “If the project falls through, that $50,000 is the city’s to keep,” Nokleby said. “So that’s kind of a no-strings-attached payment there, as well — a good-faith payment, we’ll say.” Additionally, if the project falls through after the four-year agreement period, Nokleby said the city would also receive $912,160 in option payments, which includes the $50,000. But the larger financial benefit would come if the project becomes operational. Nokleby said projected lease revenue could range from $30 million to $60 million, depending on the project’s final size and how long the lease remains in effect. The currently proposed lease has a 30-year operating term with four potential five-year extensions. While Hanwha is the proposed developer of the project, Nokleby said it would not own or operate the solar farm long term. Southern Power, which owns South Cheyenne Solar, could potentially become the owner. Hanwha developed the 150 megawatt South Cheyenne Solar project off South Greeley Highway in unincorporated Laramie County under its former name, Qcells Development. Black Hills Energy is also interested in purchasing the electricity, he said, but neither arrangement has been finalized. Because the land is widely known for its wildlife inhabitants, Nokleby said the proposed agreement also includes protections similar to those used at South Cheyenne Solar, including dividing the solar facility into separately fenced sections to preserve wildlife migration corridors. “We did not get into the sustainable energy industry to destroy the environment,” Nokleby said. “These projects are obviously very large and impactful, so we do everything we can to mitigate those impacts.” Nokleby further clarified that signing the option agreement is not a guarantee that the project will be constructed. “Not every lease or option-to-lease turns into a project,” Nokleby said. “If we run our studies and they come back with a very rare type of butterfly that only lives in this one specific spot on Earth, we’re not in the business of putting solar over that. … We won’t be cutting corners. We’re not asking for rubber stamps on any approvals.” The developer’s option-to-lease agreement is planned to be introduced at the City Council meeting for consideration Oct. 12.

artigo.texto: Os Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência por meio de Sistemas de Armazenamento de 2026 (LRCAP Armazenamento) serão os primeiros certames de reserva de capacidade voltados exclusivamente a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Brasil. Até aqui, o país contratava potência de reserva majoritariamente de grandes hidrelétricas e termelétricas. Na prática, os novos leilões buscam contribuir para suprir o déficit de potência do sistema, especialmente nos horários de pico, e ampliar sua flexibilidade operativa. As baterias poderão absorver excedentes de geração e devolvê-los à rede quando necessário, sob comando do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). O desenho adotado prevê dois certames. O Leilão de Armazenamento Nacional será realizado primeiro, em 2 de dezembro, seguido pelo Leilão de Armazenamento Aberto, em 4 de dezembro. A divisão busca conciliar dois objetivos: contratar potência e, ao mesmo tempo, fomentar uma cadeia nacional de baterias. O desafio é que ainda não se sabe quanto a indústria brasileira consegue entregar no curto prazo. Por outro lado, sem essa exigência, a indústria local, ainda incipiente, teria de competir com equipamentos importados provenientes de cadeias já consolidadas. A solução adotada foi realizar primeiro o leilão nacional, com a contratação de volume compatível com a capacidade da indústria local. O leilão aberto completará a necessidade do sistema, descontada a capacidade contratada no primeiro certame. Um mesmo projeto vencedor no primeiro leilão não poderá disputar o segundo. Para os empreendedores, porém, um dos principais desafios está na estrutura contratual necessária para cumprir as obrigações assumidas no Contrato de Potência de Reserva de Capacidade (CRCAP). A Portaria nº 136/2026 já determina que o CRCAP preveja penalidades ao empreendedor por indisponibilidade e pelo descumprimento do despacho centralizado, conforme definido pelo ONS, além da extinção do contrato em caso de não atendimento aos requisitos mínimos de nacionalização. Embora responda por essas obrigações, o empreendedor depende de terceiros para cumpri-las. Por isso, será necessário alinhar os diferentes contratos envolvidos na viabilização do CRCAP, como os de fornecimento, execução das obras e operação durante os 15 anos de vigência. O ponto central é garantir que os riscos sejam adequadamente alocados entre esses instrumentos. E essa estruturação precisa ocorrer antes da apresentação do lance, porque o preço ofertado depende das responsabilidades assumidas e das garantias efetivamente obtidas pelo empreendedor. Um risco que não possa ser transferido ou mitigado contratualmente precisa, em última análise, ser considerado na formação do preço. Outro ponto de atenção está na habilitação dos projetos. O cadastramento na Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) foi encerrado em 31 de julho, mas o simples registro não significa que os empreendimentos estejam aptos a participar dos leilões. Os projetos cadastrados passarão pelas etapas de análise e habilitação técnica na EPE. Somente depois será conhecida a quantidade de empreendimentos e, consequentemente, a potência efetivamente apta a participar das fases subsequentes dos certames. Entre os projetos com maior risco estão aqueles concentrados em pontos da rede sem capacidade de escoamento suficiente para todos os interessados e os que não atingirem a capacidade de recarga. No Leilão de Armazenamento Nacional, há ainda os projetos que declararam conteúdo local sem fornecedor credenciado: eles podem vencer o certame e, posteriormente, não conseguir assinar o contrato. A quantidade de projetos cadastrados também indica que a disputa pode ser elevada. Foram 6.091 projetos, somando quase 297 GW de potência. Mesmo que apenas uma parcela chegue à fase de lances, a relação entre oferta e demanda tende a ser alta. A experiência internacional aponta na mesma direção. Na Itália, cujo leilão de 2025 tem parâmetros semelhantes aos dos certames brasileiros, com contratos de 15 anos e entrega em 2028, as ofertas superaram a demanda e o preço médio ficou abaixo do esperado. Esse cenário exige cautela. Uma competição agressiva pode levar a lances muito baixos e a projetos com margem insuficiente para absorver riscos como atrasos, variação cambial ou penalidades contratuais. O desafio, portanto, começa antes do lance e não termina com o resultado do leilão. Para os empreendedores, será necessário estruturar previamente contratos, responsabilidades e garantias que sustentem o preço ofertado e, uma vez contratados, assegurar o cumprimento das obrigações assumidas durante os 15 anos de vigência do CRCAP. Ana Luisa Dala Déa é advogada da área de desenvolvimento de projetos e contratos complexos do Toledo Marchetti Advogados.

artigo.texto: A second Alachua City Commission meeting confused residents Monday after the meeting was abruptly cancelled because three commission members, including Mayor Walter Welch, weren’t present. Vice Mayor Jennifer Ringersen and Commissioner Shirley Green Brown were also absent, while commissioners Jacob Fletcher and Jackson Youmas attended. The city’s ordinance doesn’t allow business to be conducted at commission meetings without at least three commissioners present. The no-shows come just two weeks after a Sept. 14 city commission meeting in which Welch abruptly killed Fletcher’s motion to revisit a moratorium, or pause, on data center development. The pause was proposed by Ringersen earlier that night, and Fletcher was unable to get specifics from the rest of the commission. He moved for the board to further hash them out at Monday’s meeting. However, when Fletcher reminded Welch a few minutes later that he had to second the motion to delay the vote to Monday’s meeting, Welch replied with, “It died.” Welch’s response garnered reactions from residents and Fletcher because the mayor doesn’t have the power to deny a motion before it’s seconded and voted on. During an interview Sept. 15, Commissioner Jacob Fletcher said many Alachua residents have called moratoriums “a good step to figuring out the next step.” The Sept. 14 data center discussion resembled one step in a long process requiring community participation, he said. “I think there [are] more conversations to be had,” Fletcher said. “A moratorium, again, is only a Band-Aid.” He said the next step will require the commission to listen to Alachua residents and ensure the city’s regulations align with their concerns. Following the Sept. 14 meeting, attendees expressed confusion over whether the data center moratorium would be further discussed at Monday’s meeting. It was on the agenda leading up to the meeting. Zoe King, a transit maintenance manager for Gainesville’s Regional Transit System, stayed over an hour after the meeting’s cancellation Monday to speak with Fletcher, Youmas and fellow residents. More than 70 people attended the meeting, and King said most had come to comment on data centers. “We were told that the draft for the moratorium would be presented today to the commissioners,” King said. Following its cancelation, the meeting was rescheduled to Oct. 5, when the commission plans to discuss and vote on the meeting’s agenda items. The city’s budget, a data center moratorium and a contract between the city and Duke Energy were among items on the agenda. “This is becoming a game,” she said. To King, it feels like every time an important topic is scheduled to be discussed, something pushes it back. It’s caused residents to lose faith in the city, she added. On Sept. 8, a planning and zoning board committee meeting, during which data centers were set to be discussed, was canceled for the same reason: a lack of board attendance. Fletcher and Youmas met with citizens outside Alachua City Hall on Monday to discuss the meeting's cancellation, its rescheduling and to catch up with supporters. Deborah Bagley, a 60-year-old Alachua resident, questioned the qualifications of some of Alachua’s public officials, including Matthew Webster, who was appointed to the planning and zoning board in August. Webster is the son-in-law of Virginia Johns, a former planning and zoning board member whose term expired a month before Webster assumed the role, according to Bagley and a Facebook post by Our Alachua Water. “[Webster] has monetary gain, so they knew that he would vote yes on things related to development,” said Bagley, adding that Webster’s construction company, Sterling Builders Group, would benefit from more development. A special planning and zoning board meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at 6 p.m., where the board is scheduled to discuss permits, site plan proposals and the city’s comprehensive plan. Contact Christian Haas at chaas@alligator.org. Follow him on X @ChristianH58745. Christian is an environmental reporter with The Alligator, and studies journalism at the University of Florida. He is a fourth-year student who prefers to spend his free time trying new and random things, cooking, reading, watching TV, or hiking.

artigo.texto: Spring Hill, Tennessee is blazing a new trail in battery technology, as Ultium Cells LLC â a joint venture between General Motors and LG Energy Solution â just announced plans to produce lithium manganese rich (LMR) prismatic battery cells at its plant just outside Nashville. This is expected to make Ultium Cells the first manufacturer globally to commercially produce this next-generation technology, positioning GM at the forefront of bringing the technology to market in future electric vehicles. LMR prismatic battery cells mark a major step forward for GMâs future EVs. The technology is designed to offer energy density 33% greater than lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry â todayâs leading, low-cost battery technology â but at a comparable cost. Establishing LMR prismatic cell production at Ultium Cells in Spring Hill is a key step in our strategy to match the right battery technology to customer needs and strengthen our leadership in domestic battery manufacturing and innovation. High-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in our portfolio, while adding LMR positions us to leapfrog today's more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance. This flexibility allows us to scale efficiently, reach more customers, and support our long-term EV strategy and profitability journey. Adding LMR to the Ultium Cells portfolio also demonstrates the flexibility of its manufacturing capabilities. Ultium Cells will be able to produce battery cells in multiple chemistries and form factors, helping tailor battery technology to the needs of different vehicles and applications. Beyond flexing manufacturing might, bringing this new battery cell to market first is a milestone moment for keeping America competitive globally in EV and battery technology leadership. Construction and facility upgrades at Ultium Cells Spring Hill will begin later this year and are expected to be completed in 2028. This expansion is projected to create 500 new jobs, in addition to the facilityâs total current workforce of 1,200 employees.
