artigo.texto: Nova Gales do Sul aprova projeto de armazenamento por bateria Deniliquin East de 100MW/200MWh O governo de Nova Gales do Sul deu sinal verde para o sistema de armazenamento de energia por bateria de Deniliquin East, um empreendimento de 100MW/200MWh na região australiana de Riverina apresentado pela BESS Arctic Pty Ltd. A BESS Arctic está levando o projeto adiante por meio da Gransolar Development Australia, subsidiária local do grupo espanhol Gransolar Group. A instalação está prevista para a Riverina Highway, na área do governo local de Edward River, situada a cerca de 7km a sudeste de Deniliquin. Depois de construída, a instalação será conectada ao Mercado Nacional de Eletricidade e ocupará um terreno de 3,53 hectares que historicamente serviu para pastoreio de ovelhas. O consentimento foi emitido pelo Diretor Executivo Interino de Avaliações de Energia, Recursos e Indústria, no exercício de autoridade delegada pelo Ministro de Planejamento e Espaços Públicos. Durante a avaliação, foram apresentadas 71 objeções públicas, além de uma única manifestação de apoio. Pela aprovação, o sistema de baterias fica limitado a uma potência máxima de 100MW e a uma capacidade máxima de armazenamento de energia de 240MWh no local. As condicionantes exigem um Estudo de Segurança contra Incêndio antes da construção, um Plano de Emergência antes do comissionamento e uma faixa corta-fogo trafegável de pelo menos 10 metros ao redor da área de armazenamento de baterias. O Departamento de Planejamento, Habitação e Infraestrutura concluiu que as vantagens do projeto superavam seus efeitos adversos, destacando sua capacidade de armazenar energia renovável para despacho nos picos de demanda e sua consonância com o Marco de Política de Mudança Climática de Nova Gales do Sul, a Estratégia de Eletricidade de Nova Gales do Sul e o Roteiro de Infraestrutura Elétrica de Nova Gales do Sul. Segundo o departamento, o risco de contaminação no local era baixo, conforme estabelecido por uma Investigação Preliminar e Detalhada do Local, e a perda de área agrícola seria insignificante, afetando menos de 0,0004% das terras agrícolas da área do governo local de Edward River. Risco de incêndio e perigos, os méritos da energia renovável e a compatibilidade do uso do solo formaram o núcleo das 71 objeções, enquanto várias manifestações também apontaram preocupações com o abastecimento de água para combate a incêndios, a garantia de descomissionamento e a contaminação por PFAS. O departamento determinou que essas questões poderiam ser adequadamente tratadas pelas condicionantes do consentimento, observando que nem o órgão do governo de Nova Gales do Sul nem o Conselho de Edward River apresentaram objeções ao projeto. O aviso de decisão avalia o investimento de capital do projeto em cerca de AU$ 118 milhões, ou US$ 82,6 milhões, e projeta até 52 empregos na construção e dois cargos operacionais. A BESS Arctic também se comprometeu com um Acordo Voluntário de Planejamento com o Conselho de Edward River que prevê AU$ 600.000 em contribuições de benefício comunitário. Essa aprovação insere um projeto regional em um pipeline estadual que vem se expandindo muito além da escala de qualquer empreendimento isolado. A AEMO registrou que 9,1GW de nova capacidade de geração e armazenamento atingiram plena produção no NEM durante o ano fiscal de 2026, um número recorde que mais que dobrou o volume do ano anterior, enquanto o pipeline mais amplo de conexões cresceu 42%, para 75,4GW. Outros projetos em estágio comparável ao de Deniliquin East estão avançando pelo processo de registro da AEMO. Vena Energy, o Tailem Bend BESS 3, na Austrália do Sul, e o Wooreen BESS, em Victoria, desenvolvido pela EnergyAustralia e pela Banpu Energy Australia, ambos entraram no Sistema de Gestão de Mercado da AEMO no início deste mês, contribuindo com 554MW de capacidade combinada enquanto avançam rumo à operação comercial. O próprio histórico de contratações de Nova Gales do Sul ilustra como um projeto como o de Deniliquin East poderia, em última análise, obter certeza de receita. Todos os projetos de armazenamento por bateria e resposta à demanda selecionados no leilão de firming de 2023 do estado já estão operacionais, proporcionando cerca de 1GW/3GWh de capacidade despachável e mais de AU$ 1,8 bilhão em investimento por meio de Acordos de Serviço de Energia de Longo Prazo concedidos à AGL Energy, à Akaysha Energy, à Iberdrola Australia e à Enel X. O órgão responsável pelos leilões do estado indicou que pretende continuar usando essa abordagem de contratação para ajudar projetos de alto valor a alcançar o fechamento financeiro mais rapidamente. artigo.texto: Saginaw approves new rules for future data centers as moratorium nears end The ordinance sets rules for water and energy use, noise, residential buffers and neighborhood meetings before any data center can set up shop in the city. SAGINAW, Mich. (WNEM) - Saginaw now has a rule book in place for data centers before any come to town. The Saginaw City Council approved a new ordinance Monday night setting regulations for any future data center development in the city. The ordinance comes ahead of Saginaw’s data center moratorium ending at the close of 2026. There are currently no data centers in development in the city. Under the new rules, data centers would only be allowed as special land uses in light industrial and general industrial districts. Developers would have to provide information on expected water and energy use, wastewater and noise. Data centers and most related equipment would generally have to stay at least 500 feet from homes and residential districts, with noise near residential areas capped at 55 decibels. Developers would also have to hold at least two neighborhood meetings before moving forward with a project. The moratorium remains in place through the end of the year. The new ordinance is expected to be added to Saginaw’s code of ordinances Oct. 9. Subscribe to the WNEM TV5 newsletter and receive the latest local news and weather straight to your email every day. artigo.texto: Vaisala Indigo Supervisor Vaisala Indigo Supervisor helps data centers scale environmental monitoring by enabling up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system. As monitoring requirements grow, the challenge is shifting from measurement coverage to operational scalability. Environmental monitoring must scale with AI infrastructure As data centers scale to support growing AI workloads, environmental monitoring infrastructure must keep pace. Higher computing densities and accelerated construction schedules are increasing the need for environmental measurements throughout data centers, including data halls, technical spaces, support areas, and other critical locations, while leaving less time for installation, commissioning, and maintenance. As monitoring requirements grow and measurement networks expand, operators need ways to deploy, standardize, and maintain environmental monitoring across facilities without adding complexity or slowing project timelines. From sensors to systems: a new approach to environmental monitoring To address this need, Vaisala today introduced the Vaisala Indigo Supervisor, a solution designed to simplify environmental monitoring in data centers by shifting from managing individual sensors to managing measurement networks as a unified system. The solution enables up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system through a local touchscreen interface and integrated into a building management system (BMS) through a single standardized connection. The Indigo Supervisor reflects a broader industry shift toward modularity and system-level environmental monitoring. As data center infrastructure expands, operators increasingly need solutions that can be deployed consistently across sites, scaled over time, integrated into building management systems, and managed efficiently throughout their lifecycle. Designing infrastructure for the next generation of data centers "AI is accelerating data center growth at a pace that is changing how supporting infrastructure is deployed, managed, and scaled," said Anu Kätkä, Product Line Manager for HVAC and Critical Buildings at Vaisala. "When a facility contains dozens or hundreds of measurement points, environmental monitoring can no longer be managed one sensor at a time. Operators need a system-level approach to environmental monitoring that can be commissioned efficiently, maintained without disrupting operations, and scaled consistently as capacity expands." artigo.texto: Loudoun County hosts open house as debate over data center growth continues ASHBURN, Va. - Loudoun County held the first in a series of community open houses in Ashburn Monday to give residents a chance to weigh in on the future of data center development in the community. What we know: The event, held at Broad Run High School, allowed community members to speak directly with county staff, take surveys and view noise-monitoring demonstrations. Similar open houses for tech infrastructure have taken place in Loudoun County and across the region, including in Prince William County. The feedback gathered from the sessions will help shape recommendations that are expected to go before the planning commission in 2027. The open house comes amid public debates and community pushback over rapid infrastructure expansion. Neighbors have expressed concerns over noise levels, power consumption, power substations and the proximity of data centers to surrounding neighborhoods. "I think they need some guidelines, especially for controlling some emissions and the noise. And too close to where people live... yeah, they need some standards," said Loudoun County residents Kathy and Paul Wagner, who noted they live just 500 feet away from existing infrastructure. In response to growing community concerns, Loudoun County supervisors recently approved a one-year pause on certain new AI data centers and substation applications, giving officials time to review standards for future projects. However, supporters of data center infrastructure emphasize the economic benefits, pointing to substantial local revenue and employment opportunities for workers like contractors and electricians. Don Slaiman, political coordinator for the IBW Local 26 electricians union, highlighted the financial and labor impact of the industry in the region. "That is a lot of revenue coming to this state, that is a lot of great jobs," Slaiman said. "I have 1,018 members who live in the richest county in the country right here in Loudoun... we have 17,500 members... we have doubled our membership in the last 9 years." The Source: information in this article is from a Loudoun County open house and previous FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: Gov. Abigail Spanberger dropped a few hints Tuesday about what will be in the energy plan she’s releasing on Thursday. She said she backs more on-site electricity generation for data centers so they’re not pulling power from the grid. She also said her energy plan will lay out multiple options for Virginia to meet its power needs in the years ahead. “What are the gives and takes?” Spanberger asked. “What are you sacrificing? What are you getting from the different energy mix choices? And so we modeled out and actually pushed out a variety of different examples where we show these different types of plants have various different localized pollutant risks with these types of energy generation. We have this amount of CO2 emissions. And what is the ultimate cost to the user? So that really anyone who chooses to read a 100-page report on Virginia’s energy plan has a good sense of what all the options are. “And importantly, I think as you’ll see when we release it, there’s not one single right path because there’s something you give up with every choice that you make. When you forego one option, you’re giving something up even when you’re gaining something. And so, making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future is something that very intentionally will be including in the plan we’re going to be releasing later this week.” She said one goal of the energy plan is “making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future.” Spanberger’s hints about the energy plan came at an event in Danville sponsored by Cardinal News and the Institute for Advanced Learning and Research where the governor was invited to speak about economic development and then took questions from the audience. I served as moderator to read those audience questions. (Cardinal sponsored a similar event during then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s first year in office; the event was held in Bristol.) Those remarks came in the context of a question about data centers and their energy requirements. While data centers have become pariahs in many localities, political and business leaders in Danville and Pittsylvania County have embraced a large-scale data center coming to the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill. The developer, Stack Infrastructure, has signed a performance agreement that calls for creating 2,500 permanent jobs over the next 20 years at the site. The Stack project prompted several questions from the audience about how Virginia can guarantee that localities that want data centers can still host them — and about on-site power generation. The governor said her chief of staff had spoken recently with Stack representatives to make sure that the project is a go; she also noted that the company had spoken favorably of her recent executive order — and related legislative proposals — on data centers. “This is a project that, importantly,” she said, “is a project that is wanted by the local community. And when I’m looking at how it is that we handle data center investment, or frankly, any type of investment into the future, it is a question of what do communities want.” She was asked specifically about whether data centers could use natural gas to generate power on site. She enthusiastically backed on-site power — “It’s incredibly important that we have on-site generation” — but did not specifically address natural gas, something that environmental groups oppose. “This is a place where I’ll go back to the word that I mentioned before, innovation,” she said. “Here is a lot of work being done as it relates to fuel cell, other types of noncombustion natural gas types of energy generation, where we can really ensure that we are meeting long-term the Virginia Clean Economy Act goals into the future, and also ensuring that we’re adding greater stability and reliability to the grid by having a behind-the-meter work, the bring-your-own generation.” She also mentioned the prospect of small nuclear reactors and fusion technology, the latter of which is being developed by Commonwealth Fusion Technology in Chesterfield County. “There are, on the path outside of Richmond, the potential, there are deals in place with data centers to develop small modular reactors,” the governor said. Her staff later said Spanberger was referring to previously announced plans by Amazon to work with Dominion Energy on a small nuclear reactor at Dominion’s North Anna nuclear station in Louisa County. (Disclosure: Dominion is one of our donors but donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy.) Separately, Appalachian Power has announced plans to explore a small nuclear reactor at its Joshua Falls substation in Campbell County. Last year, the Goochland County Board of Supervisors voted to adopt a Technology Overlay District designed to attract data centers; it specifically allows small modular reactors. Among other things the governor said Tuesday at the Danville event: She acknowledged ‘solar fatigue’ in some rural counties One questioner told the governor that Pittsylvania County, and other rural counties, “have complete solar fatigue” by the number of solar facilities in those communities. artigo.texto: Can Supercapacitors Smooth AI’s Power Swings? Supercapacitors promise millisecond response for AI-induced power transients, but most experts see them complementing, not replacing, UPS systems and batteries. AI workloads can create load swings far sharper than steady-state compute, producing hard power spikes that conventional architectures struggle to absorb. Supercapacitors, also called ultracapacitors, sit between conventional capacitors and batteries. They store energy as a surface charge rather than through a battery’s chemical reaction, which gives them higher power density than batteries but lower energy density. That trade-off suits short, frequent bursts rather than sustained runtime. Operators are testing supercapacitors alongside batteries and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems rather than replacing them. Batteries and UPS systems still support the sustained load and provide a longer backup window. A September 2026 report from IDTechEx identifies three roles for supercapacitors in data centers: voltage stabilization, peak shaving, and short-term backup power. Supercapacitors charge and discharge in milliseconds to seconds – fast enough to track AI training cycles and recharge before the next spike. Market Outlook: Small Today, Growing Fast IDTechEx projects the data center supercapacitor market will reach $950 million by 2037, a 40.9% compound annual growth rate from 2026. That growth rate stands out against the wider category. A separate IDTechEx report from August 2025 puts total global supercapacitor revenue across automotive, grid, and industrial uses at $4.86 billion by 2036, growing 15.3% annually. Three Designs Vying for the Rack Slot IDTechEx groups data center supercapacitors into three categories, based on how they store charge and where they fit: - EDLCs (electric double-layer capacitors). The most commercially mature of the three, EDLCs store charge electrostatically at the electrode surface, much like a conventional capacitor. - Hybrid capacitors. These are usually lithium-ion (Li-ion) hybrids, combining an EDLC’s surface charge storage with the “rocking chair” lithium-ion chemistry in which ions shuttle back and forth between electrodes during charge and discharge. - Pseudocapacitors. These store charge through fast, reversible chemical reactions at the electrode surface rather than purely by electrostatic storage, delivering higher energy density than an EDLC but lower power density. Backup power is the narrowest application across all three. Typical EDLC deployments sustain output for approximately 2 minutes, while some hybrids can last up to 10 minutes – enough to prevent data corruption during brief outages but not enough to replace a UPS system. IDTechEx frames supercapacitors as a complement to backup infrastructure, not a substitute. From Pilots to Deployment: Pace and Roadblocks The market for supercapacitors in data centers is still in its early stages, but growing. “The market is transitioning from early evaluation to meaningful deployment, although adoption rates vary by technology type and supply chain maturity,” said Chris Butler, president of embedded and critical power at Flex, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “Instantaneous load transients can reach more than 150% of a power shelf’s rated capacity during certain AI compute events.” Rack designers are building in flexibility rather than committing to one architecture. “Rack designs typically include dedicated slots that can accommodate BBUs (battery backup units), CBUs (capacitor backup units), or mixed configurations, providing deployment flexibility,” Butler said. “Supply chain concerns remain a major hurdle, particularly for newer hybrid supercapacitor technologies with limited qualified suppliers.” Parag Nathaney, principal quantitative engineer for energy policy and power markets at Exelon, tied the pace of adoption to the reliability bar data centers operate under. He told Data Center Knowledge that the technology must meet 99.999% reliability for the power supply, which is why he sees the market as in its early stages. “Supercapacitors are advancing toward greater deployment, but the current state is characterized by pilot and early commercialization,” Nathaney said. Ian Wright, chief technology officer at DIMAAG, which builds battery systems designed to avoid supercapacitors, argued that the DC-to-DC conversion stage determines the response time, not the device alone. “The response speed to load changes is then determined by the DC/DC, which will be slower than either caps or batteries,” Wright told Data Center Knowledge. “If supercaps have been tried and not observed to get hot, that’s probably because they are not actually absorbing the cyclic loads.” What’s Next and How Operators Decide Whether IDTechEx’s forecast for supercapacitors plays out remains to be seen. Wright expects directly connected batteries, not supercapacitors, to become the primary tool for smoothing AI power swings. Nathaney reached a different conclusion, tied to reliability rather than economics. “I think the application of supercapacitors for data centers is novel, but the long track record of the technology in other applications could lower the barrier for adoption by data centers,” he said. Butler is somewhat more optimistic. As rack power levels scale from hundreds of kilowatts toward multi-megawatt designs, he expects CBUs to see growing use in managing transient peak demands. Over time, he anticipates workload-driven optimization will determine the mix of batteries and capacitors, with supercapacitors playing an increasingly important role in handling high-cycle, peak-power events. “I expect capacitor-based energy storage to become a mainstream element of next-generation AI power architectures,” Butler said.

artigo.texto: Jesup advances data center regulations despite pushback from packed crowd SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Following hours of fierce public debate inside a packed Cracker Williams Recreation Center, Jesup city officials voted Tuesday night to advance proposed regulations governing data centers. In a 4-2 vote, commissioners approved the first reading of an ordinance that formally defines data centers and permits them as a “conditional use” in light industrial zoning districts. Because Tuesday’s vote was only a preliminary step, the measure must pass additional readings before taking final effect. Dozens of residents lined up at the microphone to voice concern, urging leaders to enact a complete moratorium rather than moving ahead with regulations. Opponents argued a temporary freeze on new applications would allow the city adequate time to study potential impacts on local water resources and the power grid. “My concern is that commissioners are talking about — we need the ordinance because if the moratorium doesn’t go through, then we’re not protected,” said Jesup resident Erin Wallace. “But then the others are saying they don’t want the ordinance because the moratorium will give us time to make the ordinance stronger. It just seems disingenuous to me that we don’t do both.” City officials have not yet announced the date for the ordinance’s second reading. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Dixon City Council approves 45-day ban for data center development Dixon's City Council unanimously voted Wednesday night to impose a 45-day moratorium on data center developments, allowing city staff to evaluate their potential impacts on the community. "It's a national conversation right now about data centers and battery storage," said Vice Mayor Jim Ernest. The special meeting comes in response to recent council discussions about Dixon's regulations and its ability to manage this type of development. City officials said they need to prioritize evaluating potential strains on local infrastructure and environmental impacts associated with these facilities. "I'm not for or against it at this point, but I think it's very obvious our citizens want to know what's going on," Ernest said. "They don't want to be surprised by a project moving into town without them knowing." During the meeting, a member of the public asked, "What the hell is a data center for?" The moratorium gives city staff time to investigate the potential effects of data centers, including their impact on water, air, noise, and the local tax base. "There are things that could happen with our water, our air, our tax base, noise. A lot of things," Ernest said. "The transparency, I think, is what we're looking for." Dixon High School seniors Nick Albertazzi and Christian Morelos attended the meeting as part of a school assignment and expressed their support for the moratorium. "Data centers have a lot of downside, such as material consumption, water usage which could be a concern," Albertazzi said. Morelos added, "Put the pause so they can actually talk over it, think about it more clearly, than just rushing through something. Because if you rush it and you don't get the votes or talk to the people before building something, then the residents of Dixon are not gonna like it." The moratorium could be extended twice, for up to two years at a time, with a four-fifths council vote required for each extension. "Get ahead of this to get a planning process in place, so when one does come, which I'm sure it will, we're ready for it," Ernest said. Dixon also pointed to a statewide increase in the development of data centers and battery energy storage systems, known as BESS facilities. Dixon joins other cities in addressing the rapid growth of data centers. Earlier this month, the city of Riverbank approved a 45-day moratorium on data centers. Last week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed seven bills into law to strengthen California's approach to data centers. The Dixon City Council would also have the authority to extend the moratorium, twice for up to two years, if needed. artigo.texto: Q3 Executive Roundtable Recap For Data Center Frontier’s Q3 2026 Executive Roundtable, three industry leaders examined a question increasingly central to the AI infrastructure buildout: What happens when data centers are asked to become larger, denser and faster at the same time? Across three discussions, a consistent theme emerged. AI is not simply increasing the amount of infrastructure required to support the modern data center. It is exposing assumptions that were easier to tolerate at lower densities, expanding the boundaries of what operators must consider mission-critical, and making the interaction between systems increasingly important to overall resilience. That begins with density. As the value and power concentrated in individual racks rises, traditional approaches to redundancy, monitoring and risk mitigation can leave less room for error. Resilience can no longer be measured simply by installed capacity or the presence of backup equipment. Operators increasingly need to understand how electrical, thermal and control systems behave together under dynamic AI workloads — and how quickly the facility can respond and recover when something goes wrong. The same shift is broadening the definition of critical infrastructure. Power generation, UPS systems and network connectivity remain fundamental, but energy storage, liquid cooling, leak detection, controls, monitoring and the interfaces connecting them are becoming part of the same reliability equation. A component can perform exactly as designed while the larger system still fails if coordination, communications or control logic break down. And all of this is happening while the market is demanding faster deployment. Standardization, modular construction, factory integration and earlier modeling can legitimately compress project schedules. But the Q3 panelists drew a clear distinction between eliminating unnecessary time and eliminating rigor. As infrastructure becomes more tightly coupled, commissioning, integrated systems testing, operational visibility and system-level validation may need to become more thorough precisely because projects are moving faster. Taken together, the Q3 discussion points toward a broader change in how AI data center resilience must be understood. The challenge is no longer simply designing enough redundancy, specifying reliable equipment or reaching first power quickly. It is building an increasingly complex infrastructure system whose components, controls and operators can perform together — under load, under stress and at the speed the AI market now demands. Here's the full question-and-answer session, organized by topic: - Roundtable: AI Infrastructure Under Pressure - Roundtable: Redefining Critical Infrastructure - Roundtable: Speed Without Compromise Here are links to the individual Q&A summaries for each of our panelists: - Chrissy Olsen, Vice President of Critical Power Solutions, MPI Energy - David Shepard, Global Head of Data Center Business, Chemelex-Raychem - Pierre-Adrien Bel, Product Manager, EMEA, Rehlko The conversation is moderated by Data Center Frontier Editor in Chief Matt Vincent. Thanks to all of our executive participants for sharing their time and insights! About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Data centers in Alaska: Fairbanks leaders weigh in on controversial issue FAIRBANKS, Alaska (KTUU/KTVF) - Candidates running for seats on the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly have weighed in on whether they support the building of data centers in the borough. The issue garnered attention earlier this year, when the U.S. Department of Defense announced potential data centers housing artificial intelligence servers to be constructed near three installations in Alaska, including Eielson Air Force Base. On Aug. 27, the Assembly voted 6-1 in favor of adopting a set of legislative priorities for 2027 which includes a moratorium on commercial data centers on municipal or state-owned lands in Alaska, pending the creation of standards for addressing community concerns. Alexis Howell, who is running for the open Assembly seat D, agreed with the idea of a moratorium in the borough. “There is a lot of interest and excitement in this idea that we’re going to move these data centers forward, that they’re going to create jobs. I think they might do that for a month or two while they’re being built,” she said. Arguing that the borough’s grid is currently struggling, Howell said, “I would hate to see us dump a data center on top of that.” “I think that at the end of the day, a lot more analysis needs to go into that. A lot more processes should be in place before a data center just gets built,” she said. Her opponent Miguel Ramirez said there should be a study on these centers’ environmental impact before they are built. “I think we should, you know, do a study where we can all agree and see the, work with the environmental folks and find out where the goods are, where the pros are, where the cons are, if it’s good, if it’s not, but I can’t really say ‘yay’ or ‘nay’ because I think there need to be more studies done,” he explained. Nick LaJiness, running for reelection to seat E, didn’t mince words on his opinion on data centers. “I don’t think that data centers are good for any community, to be honest with you,” LaJinness said. Shelly Shupe, meanwhile, who is running for the same seat, divided public opinion on data centers into three groups: those who are concerned about environmental impacts from data centers, those who support them, and those who are not discounting them but need more information. “I’m somewhere in between the ‘I’m worried about what it might bring’ and ‘I don’t want to discount it’ groups,” she said. Scott Crass, who is running to retain seat H on the Assembly, defended his vote in favor of the moratorium. “I think that’s important that we understand the potential impacts that come from these large data centers,” Crass said. “Energy costs in our community have skyrocketed. They’re incredibly high, some of the highest in the nation, and grappling with that while thinking about a project that would consume more energy than our entire town is absolutely terrifying at first blush.” Adding that a data center which supplied its own power might be a different conversation, Crass discussed the advantages to data centers of Fairbanks’ cold climate. “That moratorium would allow us to find some time to figure out if our community is ready to accommodate those sorts of large-scale projects,” he said. Joshua Leaders, who hopes to unseat Crass from seat H, said he likes the idea of data centers as long as their presence benefits the community. “We need to take a serious look at the impact on the infrastructure, the power grid, the water and how that’s affected, and we need to see if that benefit outweighs the cost,” Leaders explained, adding that he supports a temporary moratorium while data is collected. Election Day in Fairbanks is Oct. 6, and early voting has already begun. See a spelling or grammar error? Report it to web@ktuu.com Copyright 2026 KTUU. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen and Gotion expand partnership in LFP batteries — InsideEVs Volkswagen is expanding its partnership with Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion through three joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. As InsideEVs reports, the agreements are intended to develop a manufacturing base for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for the mass-market electric vehicle segment. Investment in Valencia Gotion will pay $1.25 billion for a 49% stake in PowerCo's plant in Valencia, Spain. The facility will be jointly managed by PowerCo and Gotion. Volkswagen said the plant is to become a European production hub for unified LFP cells. According to financial documents, its production capacity will amount to 29.1 GWh. The unified prismatic battery cell is being developed by Volkswagen subsidiary PowerCo. The group plans to use this platform for different battery chemistries, including potentially solid-state batteries, in models of various brands, from Volkswagen to Porsche. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Projects in Slovakia and Morocco Volkswagen also plans to spend about $535 million by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake in a Gotion plant in Slovakia and establish a facility in Morocco. The Slovak plant, with a capacity of 8.4 GWh, is expected to produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems. The Moroccan facility will manufacture cathode materials for such batteries. Volkswagen called LFP batteries a key technology for affordable electric mobility in the mass-market segment. The company expects their share of the European market to increase from the current 10% to 40–60% by 2030. At the same time, the automaker noted that Europe currently lacks significant LFP battery production capacity.

artigo.texto: As battery energy storage systems move into larger and denser configurations, fire and explosion risk has become one of the industry’s most closely scrutinized engineering challenges. At Wärtsilä Energy Storage, Mishaal SyedNaveed has focused his work on that challenge. That combination of utility experience, product engineering, testing, and standards work has made SyedNaveed a finalist for POWER’s 2026 Rising Star Award. SyedNaveed is product manager for fire protection at Wärtsilä Energy Storage, where he focuses on product development, compliance, verification, and risk assessment for the company’s GridSolve battery energy storage system portfolio. A licensed Professional Engineer in fire protection, he has experience in risk engineering, design, loss prevention, and code consulting across the energy industry. His work at Wärtsilä has centered on translating battery fire and explosion hazards into engineering requirements, test programs, and product design. According to his Rising Star nomination, SyedNaveed played a central technical role in the company’s 2025 fire safety testing for the 5-MWh GridSolve Quantum3 system, including UL 9540A unit-level testing, large-scale fire testing, and testing of Wärtsilä’s Active Ignition Mitigation System, or AIMS. The large-scale fire test intentionally ignited a fire and allowed it to burn for more than 22 hours. Wärtsilä reported that the event remained contained within the initiating unit and did not propagate to adjacent units, without suppression or intervention. AIMS testing evaluated a different hazard: the accumulation of flammable gases during a thermal event. The system is designed to ignite those gases early, before they can produce an uncontrolled deflagration. According to the nomination, CSA Group witnessed the tests for third-party verification. SyedNaveed also supported large-scale and full-system testing of Wärtsilä’s GridSolve Quantum2 platform. Testing included U.S.-based AIMS validation under worst-case gas-release scenarios, as well as large-scale fire testing that showed no unit-to-unit propagation. Wärtsilä said those results have also helped inform evolving industry guidance, including future editions of NFPA 855. His work extends beyond Wärtsilä’s own products. SyedNaveed participates in CSA and UL technical committees related to energy storage and works with customers, authorities having jurisdiction, fire protection engineers, insurers, and first responders. Wärtsilä credits his ability to translate test data into design guidance and permitting support with reducing project risk and improving permitting outcomes. Before joining Wärtsilä, SyedNaveed worked as a fire protection engineer at Dominion Energy, where he served as subject matter expert for more than 64 MWh of installed and 284 MWh of planned energy storage projects. He holds a master’s degree in Energy Systems Engineering from Northeastern University and a bachelor’s degree in Fire Protection Engineering from the University of Maryland, College Park. —POWER

artigo.texto: Lowndes County residents continue to oppose proposed data center project LOWNDES COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA) -Lowndes County residents continue their fight against the so-called red clay project as they packed out another county commission meeting. “The truth does not fear light or hard questions,” said Lowndes County resident Dennis Blair. Opponents of a proposed data center in Lowndes County say a majority of residents have been against the project for months. What’s unclear to some, like Marie Barnes, is the current status of the project, known as “red clay.” “We live here. This is our world, this is our property, this is our land, and we don’t want a data center here because we don’t want to look like a Silicon Valley,” said Barnes. So far, residents say they only know the name of the developer, Cloverleaf Infrastructure, and the proposed site, a piece of farmland along Highway 80 near Highway 21. This is about 6 miles southwest of Montgomery. “I think anyone with common sense would say this is not a part of the county that’s economically distressed, so why here? It looks like they gerrymandered pretty good to get enough undeserved people in it to qualify for an opportunity zone,” said Blair. “It’s not in the right place. Within 2 and a half miles of this data center, there are 276-something families right around it,” said Elder Tom Gardner III of Beulah Primitive Baptist Church. “It shouldn’t be that these residents have to show up week after week after week after week and not get answers, said Alabama state Rep. Phillip Ensler. This is the third commission meeting Ensler attended. He says he’s not against data centers as a rule, but says transparency is key. “We have to do it in a way that is smart and responsible. We have to do it in a way that if the community really doesn’t want it or it’s going to hurt the community, we shouldn’t have it. And this here in Lowndes County, it feels like and seems like to a lot of residents that it’s being forced on them. And we first need answers before it goes to those.” “No matter what they do, how they do it, when they do it. We’re still going to be here until this is done,” said Barnes. artigo.texto: Data centers powering AI have rapidly become a new layer of critical infrastructure worldwide that are central to technology innovation, economic growth, and national sovereignty. US capital investment in data centers as a share of GDP now rivals what it spent building its railroads, telecom networks, and electrical grid: generational projects. The data center boom is moving faster. Five years ago, a 50-megawatt (MW) facility was considered large. Now, hyperscalers are planning to build data center campuses 100 times bigger: 5 gigawatts (GW) or more, costing $150 billion to $200 billion each. AI compute demand is already outrunning supply, and the shortage is intensifying. To overcome it, the tech industry is planning investments at unprecedented scale and speed. In a base case, Bain’s Data Center Model projects approximately $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of spending to build nearly 150 GW of new compute capacity by 2030 (see Figure 1), almost tripling global capacity in just five years. Most of the growth will come from the US, but compute capacity will grow by double digits across regions. What many business leaders are missing is that the AI compute shortage is unlikely to resolve on its own. The usual assumption that supply chains respond to demand and that they’ll eventually balance doesn’t hold here. Power, hardware, and skilled labor are simultaneously constrained (see Figure 2), and public approvals are increasingly difficult to secure. Lead times are long enough that decisions made today determine capacity several years from now. - Power: Grid connection is delaying and freezing projects. Adding grid capacity takes four-plus years, and critical equipment inventory (e.g., transformers, etc.) is scarce. Onsite, behind-the-meter power relieves some of the bottleneck, but it adds regulatory exposure, longer equipment lead times, and more project complexity. - Semiconductors: GPUs, memory, optical networking, and other components are being locked in years ahead. Operators without long-term supply agreements are effectively out of the queue. - Labor: Skilled trades are the human version of the same problem, with too few electrical workers, mechanical tradespeople, and cooling specialists. Meeting demand means recruiting, training, and retaining talent far above historical rates. - Regulations and public opinion: Complex permitting rules across local, state, and national levels add time and uncertainty, even when primary inputs are secured. Citizens and politicians are increasingly pushing back regarding water use, energy prices, and noise. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 projects worth $130 billion in the first quarter of this year alone, nearly matching the $156 billion worth of projects disrupted in all of 2025. In July, New York became the first US state to pause construction of the largest data centers; 14 others have introduced similar legislation. Countries including Ireland, the Netherlands, and Denmark have restricted or paused new grid connections, at least temporarily. Structural solutions are required Individual projects are finding workarounds, but they can’t be replicated at scale, and some are controversial. Colossus (from xAI, now part of SpaceXAI) was built in under a year by repurposing a factory and leasing dozens of gas turbines without federal clean air permits, drawing a lawsuit. Constructing a 1 GW data center typically takes one to four years, even on sites with existing power (see Figure 3), and it can take longer when new generation and transmission infrastructure is needed. Meeting the global ambition instead will require system-level fixes outside the usual free-market playbook. A grand challenge on this scale demands grand solutions, and executives planning on business as usual will get blindsided. The forces below are deliberately provocative and mostly long term, and some will create new challenges, even as they mitigate others. But overcoming the shortage will take at least one of the following forces: consolidation, new power at scale, orbital data centers, government investment, and social license. Consolidation: Consolidation could occur as capital requirements grow so large that only a handful of companies survive. Hyperscalers’ data center capex could top $1 trillion by 2028. Semiconductors provide a useful corollary. Staying at the leading edge grew so costly (tens of billions of dollars per generation) that missing one generation made catching up effectively impossible. Companies exited, were acquired, or retreated to older nodes (see Figure 4). Facing unsustainable costs, data center providers may also turn to once-unthinkable solutions: shared power procurement, colocated servers, and jointly funded grid upgrades. New power at scale: Power is one of the most challenging, multidimensional bottlenecks, and no single source solves it. The realistic path combines near-term options that could come online this decade with long-term ones that are scheduled to pay off in the 2030s. Near term, behind-the-meter generation (mostly natural gas today) is one of the few ways to add large blocks of power on data center timelines. Pairing it with carbon capture, utilization, and storage could make it cleaner, but that’s unproven at scale. Tech companies are also turning to renewables, storage, and virtual power plants (VPPs) that use software to aggregate and redirect power in real time from distributed sources such as batteries and smart thermostats. Google, for instance, is funding 1.6 GW of renewables (mostly wind) and 300 MW of storage alongside a new Minnesota data center. North America’s VPP market grew by 13.7% last year, to 37.5 GW, per Wood Mackenzie. Novel VPP agreements are emerging, such as the Google-Voltus deal that would aggregate up to 100 MW annually over three years in the PJM grid. Nuclear is another clean source that could eventually help, but new, large-scale capacity realistically won’t arrive until the mid-2030s. Recommissi

artigo.texto: Das ‘baterias de água’ às novas soluções de armazenamento de energia Em artigo à CNN Infra, Fernanda Genova Martins, da CTG, afirma que o leilão de baterias dará mais flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico, mas será apenas parte da solução Antes das baterias de lítio, o Brasil já contava com armazenamento de energia em larga escala. Por décadas, os reservatórios das usinas hidrelétricas funcionaram como “baterias de água”: deslocaram a disponibilidade hídrica entre períodos chuvosos e secos e ofereceram flexibilidade para atender às variações sazonais da demanda. Essa capacidade foi um diferencial estratégico da matriz elétrica brasileira. O país construiu um sistema renovável, integrado e capaz de aproveitar a complementaridade entre regiões. Mas essa característica já não responde sozinha à complexidade da operação. A expansão hidrelétrica ocorreu com maior participação de empreendimentos a fio d’água, com menor capacidade de regularização, enquanto a geração eólica e solar avançou rapidamente. Em 2025, as fontes renováveis responderam por 86,8% da oferta interna de eletricidade. Eólica e solar, somadas, já representam 26,4%, ante 10,9% em 2020, segundo a EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética). Esses resultados ampliam a necessidade de recursos capazes de oferecer flexibilidade, potência, controle e deslocamento temporal de energia. Mais renováveis exigem novas formas de flexibilidade Solar e eólica apresentam perfis variáveis de geração: a produção solar se altera ao longo do dia, enquanto a eólica depende dos ventos. Em determinados momentos, restrições elétricas, energéticas ou operativas exigem reduzir parte da produção renovável porque o sistema não consegue absorvê-la ou transportá-la. Em 2025, o corte de geração eólica e solar (curtailment) chegou a 20,6%, mais que o dobro de 2024, com prejuízo estimado acima de R$ 6 bilhões, segundo a Volt Robotics. O desafio é ajustar oferta e demanda, armazenando o excedente e disponibilizando energia quando ela gera mais valor ao sistema. Essa flexibilidade pode vir de baterias, reservatórios, usinas reversíveis, transmissão, resposta da demanda e gestão inteligente da geração distribuída. As usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis merecem atenção especial. Ao combinar armazenamento em grande escala e maior duração com resposta às necessidades de potência e flexibilidade, elas podem aproveitar a experiência hidrelétrica do Brasil e complementar as baterias em serviços de maior duração. O debate deve incluir soluções capazes de sustentar a expansão renovável nas próximas décadas. Já as baterias ganharam protagonismo pela rapidez de implantação, capacidade de resposta e queda de custos. Em 2025, foram instalados 108 GW de novos sistemas no mundo, avanço de 40%, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia. Já não é uma tecnologia experimental. No Brasil, o ambiente econômico e regulatório precisa direcioná-la aos pontos e serviços em que o benefício para o sistema seja maior. Leilão será um teste para o desenho do mercado Os primeiros leilões no Brasil voltados ao armazenamento em baterias, previstos para dezembro, marcam a passagem dos projetos-piloto para uma nova escala. O desenho prevê contratos de 15 anos, início do fornecimento em 2028 e entrega de energia por pelo menos quatro horas. O interesse foi imediato: a EPE recebeu 6.091 projetos, que somam 296.807 MW. O número é expressivo, mas o cadastro não equivale a projeto habilitado, investimento contratado ou necessidade do sistema. Avaliação técnica, capacidade de conexão e volume demandado ainda funcionarão como filtros. Essa diferença entre intenção e execução é central. Para atrair capital de longo prazo, o marco regulatório deverá oferecer previsibilidade sobre remuneração, alocação de riscos, medição do desempenho e tratamento das limitações da rede. Será preciso, ainda, evitar que a competição pelo menor preço produza ativos incapazes de sustentar o desempenho por 15 anos. Baterias perdem capacidade com o tempo, e conexão, software, manutenção e destinação final fazem parte da conta. Escala depende de uma combinação de soluções O primeiro leilão é voltado a baterias com ciclos de quatro horas de duração. Esse produto pode contribuir para o deslocamento intradiário de energia, a gestão de rampas e a resposta rápida a necessidades operativas. Sua contribuição, contudo, deve ser avaliada com outros recursos de flexibilidade, porque nenhuma tecnologia de armazenamento atende isoladamente a todos os requisitos do sistema elétrico brasileiro, por isso a importância da diversificação e complementariedade. Nesse contexto, as usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis podem ocupar posição estratégica. Esses empreendimentos utilizam energia para bombear água a um reservatório superior e voltam a gerar quando o sistema requer energia, potência ou outros serviços de flexibilidade. O Brasil reúne experiência hidrelétrica e condições naturais favoráveis; sua inserção dependerá de inventários, licenciamento, conexão e mecanismos de remuneração compatíveis com os serviços prestados. As tecnologias devem ser comparadas conforme o serviço requerido. Duração, tempo de resposta, localização, disponibilidade, prazo de implantação, conexão, impacto ambiental, usos múltiplos do reservatório e custo total são atributos relevantes. Conforme a necessidade, a alternativa poderá ser bateria, usina reversível, transmissão, participação da demanda ou uma combinação desses recursos. Projetos-piloto ajudam a converter hipóteses em evidências. Em janeiro, a CTG Brasil inaugurou, na Usina Hidrelétrica Ilha Solteira (SP), o FlexBess, laboratório que combina geração solar e baterias para avaliar desempenho, segurança e modelos de operação. A experiência reforça que armazenar energia exige inteligência operacional, qualificação técnica e regras que reconheçam o valor entregue ao sistema. artigo.texto: A inclusão dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento da Infraestrutura (Reidi) foi um avanço para o setor elétrico, mas ainda não eliminou as incertezas tributárias que podem afetar a estruturação dos projetos de BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems) no Brasil. Para Breno Sarpi, sócio da área tributária do Lefosse Advogados, o principal ponto de atenção está no desenho do incentivo criado pela Lei nº 15.269/2025, que incluiu os sistemas de armazenamento no Reidi e estabeleceu limite de R$ 1 bilhão por exercício para a renúncia fiscal, condicionado à previsão na Lei Orçamentária Anual. Segundo ele, esse teto pode limitar a vantagem para projetos de maior porte, principalmente diante da concentração dos investimentos em determinados períodos de construção. Em um empreendimento com capacidade entre 2 GW e 6 GW, por exemplo, a necessidade de incentivo em um único exercício pode superar o espaço disponível dentro do limite anual. A preocupação ganha peso diante do cronograma dos projetos que podem disputar os leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) exclusivo para baterias no Brasil, que estão marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Caso a construção e a entrada em operação comercial estejam concentradas em uma janela relativamente curta, os empreendedores podem precisar disputar uma parcela limitada do benefício tributário. “Apesar de ter sido publicado no ano passado, o Reidi para sistemas de armazenamento ainda não foi regulamentado e, até o momento, carece de regras que permitam sua aplicação efetiva”, afirmou, durante participação em painel do Storage Leaders, evento promovido pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar) nesta quarta-feira, 30 de setembro, em São Paulo. O advogado destacou que o benefício foi estruturado com base no PIS/Cofins, tributos que serão substituídos a partir de 2027, o que também gera incertezas sobre sua aplicação aos projetos de BESS. Ainda não se sabe se o regime poderá ser aproveitado no novo ambiente tributário ou se será necessária uma nova regulamentação para contemplar os tributos introduzidos pela reforma. Essas definições são relevantes para a modelagem financeira dos projetos porque o tratamento tributário influencia diretamente o custo de implantação, a estrutura de capital e o preço que os empreendedores conseguem oferecer no leilão. Ele ainda comentou que a estrutura atual do incentivo cria uma restrição de prazo. Para aproveitar a desoneração nos moldes conhecidos até o fim deste ano, seria necessário concentrar as compras nesse período, o que não seria factível para projetos de BESS cujas obras estão previstas para começar apenas em 2027. Outros impostos não serão desonerados Outro ponto destacado por Sarpi na discussão é que o Reidi não representa uma desoneração integral do investimento em baterias. Pela legislação, o regime prevê a suspensão da cobrança de PIS/Pasep e Cofins sobre determinadas operações de aquisição, no mercado interno ou por importação, de máquinas, equipamentos e materiais destinados a projetos de infraestrutura. Com a Lei nº 15.269/2025, o benefício passou a contemplar projetos de investimento em sistemas de armazenamento de energia voltados à transição energética, modernização e estabilidade do setor elétrico. Outros tributos continuam fora do alcance direto do Reidi, entre eles IPI e ICMS. No caso do IPI, há dúvidas especialmente diante das diferenças que podem surgir entre fabricantes instalados na Zona Franca de Manaus e produtores localizados em outras regiões. A reforma tributária prevê regras específicas relacionadas à manutenção de incentivos para a industrialização na Zona Franca. Como há empresas avaliando a instalação de fábricas de baterias na região, o tratamento do IPI pode afetar a estrutura de custos e a competitividade dos fornecedores de sistemas de armazenamento. Já o ICMS permanece relevante durante o período de transição. A substituição dos tributos atuais pelo novo modelo será gradual, com efeitos que se estendem até 2033. Até lá, os projetos de BESS ainda precisarão considerar a incidência e os diferentes tratamentos estaduais do imposto. Legislação ainda precisa acompanhar o modelo de negócio do BESS A discussão tributária também expõe um outro ponto da legislação brasileira, que foi estruturada para modelos tradicionais de infraestrutura de energia, enquanto os sistemas de armazenamento introduzem uma atividade com características diferentes. No caso do BESS contratado em um leilão de reserva de capacidade, por exemplo, o projeto não se limita à geração de energia. O empreendimento presta um serviço associado à disponibilidade de capacidade e potência, o que gera dúvidas sobre o enquadramento tributário da atividade e sobre a forma de aplicação de incentivos originalmente desenhados para outros segmentos do setor elétrico. Essa diferença pode ter impacto inclusive na escolha do regime tributário das empresas que participarão do leilão. Entre os pontos que precisam ser avaliados está a opção pelo lucro presumido ou pelo lucro real, além da definição da natureza da receita obtida pelo empreendimento. No lucro presumido, outro ponto de discussão é o percentual de presunção aplicável à atividade. A definição entre 8% e 32%, por exemplo, pode alterar significativamente a carga tributária e, consequentemente, a margem projetada para o empreendimento. A preocupação com os tributos não está restrita ao investimento inicial. O tratamento tributário da receita futura também precisa entrar na modelagem econômica dos projetos que disputarão o leilão de armazenamento, já que a carga tributária projetada afeta a margem do empreendimento e, consequentemente, o preço que o empreendedor consegue oferecer no lance.

artigo.texto: UL Solutions Launches Certification for Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling Equipment Used in AI Data Centers Certification evaluates liquid cooling subassemblies for safety, performance, leak integrity and interoperability, helping support reliable AI infrastructure. - AI chips generate intense heat, making effective cooling essential to data center performance and reliability. - The certification provides a consistent way to assess critical cooling components before deployment in AI data centers. - Certification can help manufacturers demonstrate product readiness and help data center customers make informed purchasing and integration decisions. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260929465054/en/ UL Solutions today launched a certification program for liquid cooling subassemblies that target powerful chips directly, providing more effective cooling in AI data centers and other high-density computing systems. AI computers use chips that produce a large amount of heat. If that heat is not removed, equipment may slow down, shut off or become damaged, but traditional air cooling, such as fans or chilled air, may not be enough for today’s most powerful computing systems. With direct-to-chip liquid cooling, coolant flows through a cold plate that is attached to the chip. The coolant absorbs heat from the chip and carries it away, much like water flowing through a radiator. “As AI data centers handle more powerful computing, they depend on even more advanced cooling systems to operate safely and reliably,” said AI and other high-performance computing systems are increasing energy use and heat in data centers. Global data center electricity use is expected to more than double between 2024 and 2030. Cooling can account for up to 40% of a data center’s energy use. Liquid cooling can improve heat control, but it also brings risks. Leaks, corrosion, contamination or parts that do not work well together can affect system safety, performance and reliability. Connecting parts from different suppliers can also be a challenge. Parts may fit together but require different coolants, pressure levels or operating conditions. Industry observers have identified integration problems and limited standards as barriers to wider use of liquid cooling. The UL Solutions certification program covers eligible liquid-filled parts and subassemblies that move coolant through information and communication technology equipment. These may include: - Cold plates, which absorb heat directly from computer chips - Manifolds, which send coolant to servers and equipment racks - Quick disconnects, which allow equipment to be serviced without draining the full cooling system UL Solutions uses UL 4501, the Outline of Investigation for Safety, Performance and Interoperability of Liquid-Filled Components and Assemblies Used in Liquid Cooling Systems, to evaluate eligible liquid cooling subassemblies. The evaluation covers coolant compatibility, pressure and leak integrity, durability, liquid flow, interoperability, production controls and installation requirements. Evaluating these parts before adding them to a complete cooling system can help identify problems earlier and reduce the need for repeated testing. Independent certification demonstrates that an eligible product meets applicable requirements. This helps manufacturers support their product claims and helps data center customers make informed buying and integration decisions. “AI infrastructure must scale without sacrificing safety or reliability,” said UL Solutions can also evaluate other data center cooling equipment under applicable UL Standards. This equipment includes coolant distribution units, self-contained liquid-filled systems, liquid-cooled busways, cables, connectors, power whips, gaskets, O-rings and hoses. Requirements depend on each product’s design, function and intended use. Learn more about UL Solutions services that support data center development and operations. About UL Solutions A global leader in applied safety science, UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS) transforms safety, security and sustainability challenges into opportunities for customers in more than 110 countries. UL Solutions delivers testing, inspection and certification services, advisory offerings and software solutions that support our customers’ product innovation and business growth. The UL Mark serves as a recognized symbol of trust in our customers’ products and reflects an unwavering commitment to advancing our safety mission. We help our customers innovate, launch new products and services, navigate global markets and complex supply chains, and grow sustainably and responsibly into the future. Our science is your advantage. Learn more about UL Solutions. artigo.texto: Business Follow Us on Google September 29, 2026 by Franca Ochigbo, Abuja FG approves carbon market framework, moves to establish approval criteria The Federal Government has taken steps to institutionalise Nigeria’s carbon market by approving a framework for its operation, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Nigeria, Prof. Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, has said. Ortuanya, represented by Prof. Nnaemeka Chukwuone, spoke at the National Stakeholders Review and Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations, organised by the National Council on Climate Change in Abuja. He said the global carbon market offered countries opportunities to mobilise climate finance for greenhouse gas emission reduction and removal while supporting the transition to a low-carbon economy. According to him, the opportunities are particularly important for Nigeria as the country seeks to pursue economic growth, industrial development, energy access and poverty reduction while responding to climate change. “The approval represents an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations in the country. The next critical task is the reason why we are in this meeting, which is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent host country approval criteria,” he said. Ortuanya said the criteria would guide the eligibility and assessment of carbon market projects while clarifying institutional responsibilities, measurement and reporting procedures, verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards, alignment with Nigeria’s nationally determined contributions, registry and transparency arrangements, and carbon accounting. He stressed the need for the criteria to protect Nigeria’s interests while remaining practical and predictable within the country’s regulatory environment. He said the proposed criteria were developed with research input from the University of Nigeria, adding that effective public policy should be based on credible research, evidence and stakeholder engagement. The Vice Chancellor said the participatory approach adopted for the workshop included technical sessions, stakeholder group discussions and plenary deliberations aimed at generating recommendations for refining and finalising the Host Country Approval criteria. He urged participants to examine the proposed project eligibility and assessment requirements and determine whether institutional roles and coordination arrangements were sufficiently clear. He also called for an assessment of whether the proposed approval and authorisation procedures could operate effectively within Nigeria’s institutional and regulatory framework. 📢 ADVERTISEMENT DISCLAIMER: Links above are sponsored posts. artigo.texto: PJM to Data Centers: Stop Bailing on the Grid Every Time It Blips Remember that July morning when 4,000 megawatts (MW) of Northern Virginia data centers yanked themselves off the PJM grid because of a routine, properly cleared fault on a single transmission line (see PJM: Data Centers Panicked, Nearly Crashed the Grid on Purpose)? PJM hasn't forgotten either. On Sept. 8, PJM's Planning Committee got its first look at proposed "ride-through" standards that would require big data centers and crypto mines to stay connected and keep drawing power when the grid wobbles — instead of hitting the eject button and running for their diesel generators. And PJM isn't easing into it: new facilities entering the study process would have to demonstrate compliance starting Nov. 1, 2026 — about five weeks from now. By accepting direct 800 VDC input, power conversion losses are reduced and overall efficiency is improved. For gigawatt-scale AI data centers, even modest efficiency gains can translate into meaningful power capacity to support additional server racks and compute workloads, improving performance per megawatt. In a typical 200 MW data center, this efficiency gain could unlock up to 1.8 MW of additional compute capacity, enough to support up to fifteen 120 kW racks or up to three 600 kW racks. artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, its battery subsidiary PowerCo SE and Gotion High-tech have expanded their battery production partnership, with an agreement to establish joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco. The agreement will see facilities covering lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery-cell production developed in Valencia, Spain and Šurany, Slovakia, while Kenitra, Morocco will house a cathode-material operation. It also includes joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The moves form part of a wider strategy by the groups to ‘jointly accelerate the development of a regional battery supply chain for Europe’. ‘Major breakthrough’ “I am delighted that we are expanding our long-standing partnership with Gotion into the joint industrial production of LFP batteries to strengthen Europe’s battery industry,” commented Thomas Schmall, member of the board of management of Volkswagen Group for technology and chairman of the supervisory board of PowerCo SE. “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production.” As the groups noted, the market share of LFP batteries is expected to rise from around 10% today to between 40% and 60% by 2030, with Europe currently lacking LFP battery production capacity. Project structure The largest project under the partnership, in Valencia, is being positioned as a future ‘European production hub for unified LFP battery cells’, and will be 51% owned by PowerCo and 49% by Gotion. The companies also plan a joint venture around Gotion’s battery project in Šurany, Slovakia, with Gotion holding a 51% majority stake, to PowerCo’s 49%, while a similar structure will be maintained at Kentira. The Morocco project will supply cathode material to the two European battery operations. Li Zhen, chairman of Gotion Hith-tech said that the latest announcement follows “six years of close collaboration” between Volkswagen and Gotion. “Through cross-shareholdings and three joint sites, we are anchoring our shared strategy to localise battery production in Europe, racing to seize the opportunities of global electric mobility, and jointly forging a new paradigm of world-class, win-win cooperation in the lithium battery industry,” he commented. artigo.texto: Renesas Unveils Industry's First 650V GaN in Dual-Side Cooled 8x8mm Package for Megawatt-Scale AI Data Centers - Dual-side cooling (DSC) shrinks package footprint by 57% compared with TOLT, packing more power into space-constrained megawatt-scale racks. - One of the lowest on resistances in the 650V class, at 20 mΩ in an 8x8 mm package. - Single-source path to 800V designs with industry-standard PQFN footprint plus full controller, driver and MCU lineup. These solutions will be on display at OCP Global Summit in San Jose, CA ,October 12-15 . This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260930184285/en/ Built on its Gen IV Plus GaN architecture, the device is purpose-built for the megawatt-scale demands driving next-generation AI data centers supporting up to 700V operation. It targets the 800V DC/DC intermediate bus converter (IBC) stage that steps down to 48V, 12V or 6V, along with the battery backup (BBU) and capacitor bank (CBU) stages of the sidecar power rack. As rack power climbs from roughly 120 kW toward megawatt scale, space and heat have become critical factors in sustaining the power level. Unlike conventional top-side-cooled packages, the new device dissipates heat from both top and bottom, lowering top-side thermal impedance by 10%. Its 8 x 8mm PQFN footprint is also 57% smaller than the existing 10 x 15mm TOLT package. The device incorporates the full strength of Renesas Gen IV Plus 650V GaN technology: low gate charge and output capacitance, a built-in freewheeling diode with minimal reverse recovery and a high threshold voltage that runs without a negative gate bias. Engineers can drive it with a standard silicon gate driver, switch into the MHz frequency range to minimize passive components and cut overall BOM cost without requiring a specialized E-mode driver. "Customers building megawatt-scale AI data centers are running out of board space and thermal headroom before they hit their power limits," said The new dual-side-cooled (DSC) PQFN package is defined in collaboration with major AI infrastructure customers, enabling an industry-standard footprint for sourcing flexibility. When paired with Renesas AUX controllers, gate drivers and MCUs, the GaN device creates a one-stop-shop power solution for OEMs, ODMs and hyperscalers moving to 800V architectures. Renesas has already validated the approach in silicon. A 6kW, 800V-to-48V LLC DC transformer (DCX) reference design built on the new device and controlled by a Renesas RA6T3 MCU reaches a power density of 2.6 kW/in³ with per-module testing measuring full-load efficiency 0.21% higher than an equivalent TOLT-based board. The smaller package also saves PCB space and enables a better-matched layout across the FETs. 800V-to-12V and 6V DC/DC IBC reference designs also leverage the new DSC 8x8 platform, delivering similar enhanced performance, scalability and power density levels. Renesas will showcase the new TP65H020G4PLSGBD GaN device as part of its 800V power solutions at OCP Global Summit, Availability The TP65H020G4PLSGBD is sampling today. Mass production is planned for mid-2027. More information about Renesas GaN solutions is available at: renesas.com/gan-fets. Get Powered by Renesas Driven by innovation, quality and reliability, Renesas leads the way in power electronics, shipping more than four billion parts per year from our portfolio of power management ICs, discrete and wide-bandgap GaN products, computing power devices and many more. These products span all major segments including automotive, IoT, infrastructure and industrial applications. Our power portfolio seamlessly attaches to our leading MCU, MPU, SoC and analog solutions, simplifying and accelerating the design process with hundreds of engineering-vetted Winning Combinations and innovative tools such as PowerCompass™ and PowerNavigator™ design software. Find out more at renesas.com/power. artigo.texto: O workshop contou com a presença de especialistas, palestrantes, parceiros nas áreas de energia solar e armazenamento de energia, bem como empresas e investidores atuantes no setor. Soluções integradas de energia solar e armazenamento para uso comercial e industrial. No dia 29 de setembro, em Dak Lak, a Unitek, a Uhome e a Usolution organizaram em conjunto o seminário ALL-IN-ONE ENERGY TOUR 2026 com o tema "Soluções Integradas de Energia Solar + Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias - Liderando o Mercado". Segundo avaliações, o mercado de energia do Vietnã está entrando em um período de transformação significativa, o que impõe novas exigências em termos de gestão e otimização dos custos de eletricidade. Juntamente com as regulamentações do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio sobre horários de pico, o Decreto nº 243/2026/ND-CP, de 26 de junho de 2026, do Governo, ampliou o mecanismo de venda do excedente de energia elétrica proveniente de sistemas solares fotovoltaicos instalados em telhados. Essas mudanças criaram novas exigências, que incluem não apenas a geração de energia, mas também a otimização do fornecimento no momento adequado. Segundo os organizadores, a energia solar gera a maior parte da eletricidade durante o dia, enquanto a demanda e os custos de energia elétrica podem aumentar à noite. Portanto, a combinação de energia solar com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) é considerada uma solução para armazenar o excedente de eletricidade, utilizando-o em momentos oportunos, otimizando custos e melhorando a eficiência do investimento. O mercado atual oferece diversas tendências, tecnologias de armazenamento e soluções Solar + BESS para atender a diferentes necessidades. Para que um sistema seja eficaz, a questão reside não apenas na seleção de dispositivos individuais, mas também na capacidade de conectar, sincronizar e otimizar os componentes em uma solução completa que atenda às reais necessidades do negócio. No workshop, o Comitê Organizador atualizou os participantes sobre as mudanças do mercado e apresentou soluções práticas, tais como: sincronização e otimização da eficiência do investimento; modelos e soluções adaptados às necessidades de negócios; operação, manutenção, teste e melhoria do desempenho e estabilidade do sistema… fornecidas pela Pylontech, Fox Ess, Fluke e Goneo. Durante o programa, palestrantes e parceiros também discutiram diretamente e responderam a perguntas de empresas e investidores sobre a implementação de sistemas de energia solar combinados com armazenamento de energia. O conteúdo focou na seleção da capacidade adequada, na capacidade de suprir a demanda, nas opções de armazenamento e na utilização eficiente da eletricidade em diferentes momentos. Portanto, o workshop contribuiu para fornecer mais informações e soluções tecnológicas para empresas em processo de transição para modelos de uso de energia mais eficientes, tornando-se mais proativas no fornecimento de eletricidade e reduzindo gradualmente os custos operacionais.
