artigo.texto: Gotion High-Tech has secured 6 GWh of battery energy storage capacity under Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) procurement program, representing around 75% of the total capacity awarded in the first phase. The award was made by Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) as part of the Kingdom’s efforts to expand energy storage alongside renewable energy deployment. The G1 project has a total capacity of 2 GW/8 GWh and an estimated value of $1.16 billion. Gotion has been selected for three sites: Al Muwayah, Haden, and Al Kahafa. Each site will have a capacity of 500 MW/2 GWh. The award makes Gotion the largest single technology supplier in the first phase of Saudi Arabia’s utility-scale storage program. The projects will deploy Gotion Grid, marking the first international large-scale deployment of the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. According to Gotion, the system is designed for harsh desert conditions and can operate between -30°C and 55°C. The company said its thermal management system is optimized for high-temperature and dusty environments, allowing the batteries to maintain output during sandstorms and reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The system has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. Gotion Grid also incorporates an artificial intelligence-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, safety monitoring, and lifecycle diagnostics. The three projects will be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380 kV transmission network. The award strengthens Gotion’s presence in the Middle East and North Africa energy storage market. The company said its regional pipeline and projects total around 9 GWh, including a 1.5 GWh BESS project in Egypt and a 1.2 GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. In Egypt, Gotion is also planning a 3 GWh local manufacturing facility. Globally, the company said its cumulative system-level energy storage projects have exceeded 10 GWh. Its international portfolio includes a 281 MW/843 MWh solar-plus-storage project in Australia, which is under construction and expected to achieve commercial operation in the first half of 2027. Saudi Arabia has already started the next stage of its storage procurement program, with G2 underway. The G1 award is therefore expected to provide an important reference for future utility-scale BESS tenders as the Kingdom increases renewable energy capacity and strengthens grid flexibility. artigo.texto: Data centers may provide a major economic development opportunity for local communities in Wisconsin, but concerns around water and energy use and potential costs to residents have made them increasingly controversial. A new report from the Wisconsin Policy Forum aims to put those issues — and Wisconsin’s data center debate — into context. Researchers examined tax incentives supporting those projects as well as their energy and water use. Three major data center projects are in varying stages of development in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Others have been proposed but canceled in DeForest, Greenleaf and Janesville as polling has shown the issue to be unpopular with the public. Communities have ‘significant protections’ under data center incentive deals State law allows qualified developers to avoid paying sales and use tax on most purchases supporting the construction and operation of a data center. The Legislative Fiscal Bureau estimates Wisconsin will lose out on $1.5 billion in sales tax revenues related to data center construction between 2024 and 2028, as well as forgo $369 million annually in sales tax revenue related to data center operations. Wisconsin is one of 38 states that offer tax incentives to data centers. Jason Stein, one of the report’s authors, said without its sales tax exemption, Wisconsin might not have attracted the prominent developments. “I think it’s reasonable to think that a lot of this investment — maybe most of this investment — would not have occurred without the incentive,” he said. The report says the state could “recoup a significant portion of the forgone sales tax revenues” if the sales tax exemption helped attract a significant share of data center investment to Wisconsin. That’s through income and sales taxes paid by construction workers and corporate income taxes paid by construction companies, as well as additional taxes paid by utilities serving data centers. Data centers are also expected to generate increased property tax revenues in the communities hosting them. Researchers reviewed local development agreements in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington and Beaver Dam, as well as proposed deals in communities where developments fell through. They found that, in general, local communities were striking “reasonable deals” that included financial safeguards. Those safeguards often included limits on municipal borrowing, guaranteed property values and incentives tied to project performance, the report said. “If the developer and the community follow through on their agreement and it moves forward as laid out, then those agreements offer substantial protections for the communities,” Stein said. “There are significant protections in each of these deals.” Data centers use water, but Wisconsin water use has declined While much of the public debate around data centers in Wisconsin has centered around water use, policy forum researchers found the bigger challenge is meeting the large electricity demands of those projects while protecting existing ratepayers. That’s because water use in Wisconsin has declined over the past generation as some heavy industry left the state, industrial and residential users became more efficient and electric utilities shifted some energy generation from “water-intensive” coal plants to natural gas and renewable energy, the report said. From 2011 to 2024, water withdrawals in the state fell by more than 500 billion gallons, or almost 24%, according to the report. The three main data center projects in Wisconsin are projected to use less water than the decline in water withdrawals over that period, the report states. “We were on this track to use less and less water because of changes in our society, and maybe this will slow that down somewhat,” Stein said. “But that is a different thing than saying, ‘Oh my gosh, we’re using more water than ever before.’” For example, Racine Water Works, the utility providing water for Microsoft’s data center campus in Mount Pleasant, saw its annual water sales decline by 2.3 billion gallons from 2000 to 2025, according to the report. That’s “more than 250 times” as much water as the 8.4 million gallons annually Microsoft’s data center will use when fully operational, the report states. Electricity demand expected to rise significantly While long-term declines in water use are expected to help offset demand from data centers, Wisconsin’s electricity demand is expected to grow, in large part driven by demand from data centers. Peak demand from all customers on the grid is expected to rise from 14.6 gigawatts in 2024 to 19.9 gigawatts by 2030, the report states. A recent report from state utility regulators found data centers were driving that projected peak demand growth. The report found that the state Public Service Commission modified proposals from We Energies and Alliant Energy establishing rates for data center-scale customers to shield existing residential customers from costs associated with data centers. But it remains to be seen how data centers will affect transmission rates, which are set at the federal level, said Tyler Byrnes, one of the report’s authors. “It’s a little bit easier to do the math on one power plant for one data center, whereas you’re starting to divide up electrons moving across power lines (and) across state lines, so it’s more complicated,” he said. He also said there is not currently an approved data center rate framework for developments of that scale outside the service territories of Alliant Energy and We Energies. He said policymakers may want to consider adopting a statewide framework for electric rates tied to data centers. The report also notes that there are unresolved questions about whether utilities will be able to bring new energy generation and transmission lines online quickly enough to meet the growing demand. This story was originally published by WPR. Originally published by Wisconsin Watch.

artigo.texto: Motta conversou com Vorcaro sobre “sociedade” e PL sobre carbono Presidente da Câmara diz que não há ilícito nas conversas e que os diálogos foram descontextualizados Mensagens obtidas pela Polícia Federal mostram que o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), manteve conversas com o fundador do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro, sobre uma “sociedade” relacionada à compra de um terreno em João Pessoa (PB) e sobre um projeto de lei que trata do mercado de carbono. Em 9 de março de 2024, Motta procurou Vorcaro para tratar da negociação de venda de um terreno na capital paraibana. A conversa se deu no mesmo mês em que Bianca Medeiros, cunhada do presidente da Câmara, contraiu um empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões com o Banco Master para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa. Mercado de carbono Motta e Vorcaro também conversaram em 19 de novembro de 2024 sobre o projeto de lei que regulamenta o mercado de carbono no Brasil. Trata-se do substitutivo do Senado ao PL 182 de 2024. Na mensagem, Motta menciona uma questão relacionada às seguradoras. A alteração feita pelo Senado e posteriormente modificada na Câmara tratava da possibilidade de seguradoras, além de algumas empresas de previdência e capitalização, comprarem “ativos ambientais” negociados no mercado para compor suas reservas técnicas e provisões. A versão aprovada pelo Senado estipulava que essas empresas destinassem, no mínimo, 0,5% dos recursos a esses ativos. A Câmara retomou a redação anterior, que estabelecia percentual de 1% ao ano. O tema interessava aos negócios de Vorcaro. Em junho de 2026, a PF afirmou que o então banqueiro havia enviado textos de propostas legislativas diretamente ao gabinete do senador Ciro Nogueira (PP-PI). Segundo a investigação, os 2 tinham uma “convergência de interesses ilícitos”. Uma das propostas encaminhadas por Vorcaro ao gabinete do senador tratava justamente da regulamentação do mercado de carbono no país. Outro lado O Poder360 entrou em contato com a defesa de Daniel Vorcaro para saber se gostaria de se manifestar sobre o assunto, mas não teve resposta. A reportagem será atualizada caso a parte envie manifestações a este jornal digital. Procurado pelo Poder360, Motta afirmou, em nota, que mantém diálogo com representantes do empresariado e de outros setores da sociedade e disse não haver ilícito nos diálogos divulgados. O presidente da Câmara também afirmou que as conversas foram descontextualizadas e negou ter atuado em benefício próprio ou de terceiros. Motta informou que pretende apresentar queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rêgo (MDB-PB). Disse que Veneziano promove calúnia, difamação e divulgação de fake news com finalidade eleitoral. O senador concorre à reeleição e tem como adversário na disputa o pai de Motta, Nabor Wanderley (Republicanos-PB). Sobre o empréstimo contratado com o Banco Master, Motta afirmou que a operação ocorreu quando ainda não eram conhecidas as investigações posteriormente divulgadas sobre a instituição financeira e seu proprietário. Leia a nota de Hugo Motta na íntegra: “Enquanto parlamentar em meu quarto mandato na Câmara dos Deputados, sempre mantive diálogo com os diversos segmentos do empresariado e representantes da sociedade brasileira. Enfatizo que não há nenhum ilícito retratado nos diálogos publicados e repudio a tentativa de atribuir conversas descontextualizadas a qualquer relação de interesse espúrio ou de favorecimento por minha parte. Tenho uma vida limpa, assim como é limpa a minha atuação política nesses 15 anos de vida pública. Informo que estou protocolando queixa-crime contra o senador Veneziano Vital do Rego, diante da série de calúnias, de difamação e produção de fake news que ele tem efetivado contra mim neste período eleitoral. Não permitirei a suspeição de ilícitos promovidos por ele, especialmente com fins eleitoreiros. Como já explicitei anteriormente, o contrato de empréstimo realizado por empresa privada com um banco privado se deu quando não se tinha conhecimento dos fatos e investigações que posteriormente vieram a público sobre o Master e o seu dono. Reitero que confio nos órgãos responsáveis pelas investigações, a quem cabe responder pelas apurações.”

artigo.texto: Data centers vivem "boom" no Brasil e podem dobrar capacidade até 2030 Novas instalações já têm ocupação pré-locada; apesar de crescimento acelerado, setor debate fornecimento de energia Com alta demanda, o Brasil deve dobrar a capacidade de seu mercado de data centers até 2030, com boa parte da nova capacidade já contratada antes mesmo de ficar pronta. Ao todo, dos 660 MW (megawatts) que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. A ocupação dos data centers chegou a 96% no primeiro semestre, deixando uma taxa de 4% para novos clientes. De acordo com o relatório, a baixa disponibilidade deve continuar até 2030, mesmo com a chegada de novos projetos. Desde 2012, a capacidade instalada aumentou mais de seis vezes, com crescimento médio anual de 15%. No primeiro semestre deste ano, o país recebeu 106 MW de nova capacidade, sendo o maior volume registrado. Outros 134 MW estão previstos para entrar em operação ainda no segundo semestre deste ano. Com isso, as entregas de novos data centers devem terminar o ano em níveis recordes, segundo a consultoria. Mesmo com o crescimento constante, o setor ainda enfrenta desafios significativos de infraestrutura, regulação e impacto ambiental. O Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center), nova lei que prevê um programa de incentivos para o setor no país, foi sancionado no dia 15 pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e deve estimular a instalação e ampliação dos centros de dados no país. Em entrevista à CNN, Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, prevê que o Brasil dobre a capacidade até o fim de 2027. E que, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplique o volume. Atualmente a empresa tem sete data centers em operação, sendo três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro e três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Outros dois centros estão em construção: um em Porto Alegre e outro de 200 MW (cerca de 20% da capacidade brasileira) em Santana de Parnaíba, na Grande São Paulo. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. "Eu tenho bastante segurança hoje de que é bem provável que a gente, já no ano que vem, dobre a capacidade. E, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplicar é bastante razoável", afirma Costa. Para o executivo, o "segredo" do aumento na capacidade está na energia que poderia ser gerada, mas cuja produção é restringida, principalmente em usinas eólicas e solares, por meio dos cortes de geração, conhecidos como curtailment, que são impostos pelo ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico). De acordo com Costa, seriam 4 GW (gigawatts) em curtailment no país, diante de uma capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil de cerca de 1 GW. Os cortes de energia impostos pelo ONS ocorrem para preservar a segurança e a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico. Entre os motivos estão: a falta de infraestrutura de transmissão, como linhas danificadas ou atrasadas; quando as linhas de transmissão atingem o limite de capacidade e a energia não pode ser escoada; e o excesso de oferta em relação à demanda. Nos dois últimos casos, não há direito a compensação. Para Joísa Dutra, diretora do Ceri-FGV (Centro de Regulação em Infraestrutura) e colunista da CNN Infra, a flexibilidade energética pode ser uma solução, com os data centers sendo projetados para modular seu consumo em até 100 horas por ano — menos de 1% das 8.760 horas anuais — e podendo gerar reduções de tarifas de até 2%. Isso diminuiria a necessidade de investimentos em geração a partir de gás natural. Ela defende que a adoção antecipada de boas práticas e protocolos é essencial para que esses investimentos sejam vistos não como problemas, mas como parte da solução — tanto para o setor elétrico quanto para os demais sistemas de recursos com os quais se relacionam. "Flexibilidade é tudo que a gente quer neste momento, onde o setor elétrico navega para essa descentralização, para essa produção de mais eletricidade a partir de solar e eólica", destaca a colunista. Além do consumo de energia, Joísa chama a atenção para o impacto desses projetos sobre outros recursos naturais, como água, minerais e terra, citando o projeto de data center na região de Pecém, no Ceará, que tem o TikTok como um dos membros da parceria e está localizado em uma área com estresse hídrico. Para ela, a adoção antecipada de boas práticas e protocolos é essencial para que esses investimentos sejam vistos não como problemas, mas como parte da solução — tanto para o setor elétrico quanto para os demais sistemas de recursos relacionados. Ainda segundo o executivo, o Brasil está super bem posicionado e está muito perto de explodir o mercado, tendo a IA como uma outra frente de expansão. Na avaliação dele, assim como a demanda americana, que tem superado as projeções nos últimos, o movimento também deve chegar ao Brasil em breve. Para atrair a demanda que está fora do país, Costa defende a redução no custo dos data centers e dos serviços de nuvem. "Cerca de 40% do workload brasileiro roda nos Estados Unidos, [o crescimento] depende de eu fazer o datacenter mais barato para a cloud no Brasil ficar mais barata, ou tão barata quanto a lá de fora, para o usuário usar aqui", pondera. Em relação ao Redata, Costa afirma que o projeto reduz a barreira tributária sobre equipamentos e aproxima o Brasil dos custos internacionais, mas ainda assim estima que construir e implantar um data center em solo nacional custa entre 15% e 20% mais, além de defender a discussão do ICMS no setor. “A gente deve estar 15% a 20% acima. artigo.texto: BYD says it will have an electric vehicle with a solid-state battery in 2027 — InsideEVs Chinese company BYD plans to have its first electric vehicle model with a solid-state battery in 2027. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said this in an interview with Carwow.es, InsideEVs reports. First model with the new technology According to Li, the company will “have one model” with this technology next year. She also said that BYD holds a leading position in the development of solid-state batteries. At the same time, the top manager did not specify which model would be equipped with the new battery or when it would appear. It is also unclear whether this refers to a full market launch of the vehicle or a demonstration prototype. The publication notes that Chinese automakers, including BYD, are rapidly introducing new technologies into production models. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Possible Yangwang flagship CarNewsChina sources claim that the solid-state battery may be used in the recently teased flagship sedan of the Yangwang brand. BYD has not confirmed this information. The InsideEVs author suggests that the expensive technology at an early stage could first be used in a premium model, such as the Denza Z9 or BYD Great Tang. Solid-state batteries are considered a promising technology for electric vehicles: they may be lighter and safer, have higher energy density, and support faster charging. At the same time, automakers are still working to resolve technological issues and establish mass production of such batteries. Toyota plans to launch an electric vehicle with this technology in 2027 or 2028, while Honda and Mercedes are targeting a period closer to 2030.

artigo.texto: The Elements of Innovation Discovered Metal Tech News - September 29, 2026 An up to $75 million Pentagon grant awarded to Amprius Technologies to reconfigure an electric vehicle battery production line to one that produces high-energy-density silicon-anode lithium-ion cells for drones highlights an emerging shift in the battery market. Since the introduction of the Nissan LEAF and Chevrolet Volt in 2010, electric vehicles have increasingly driven lithium-ion battery demand. Automakers have shifted among cathode chemistries to balance cost, range, safety, and performance, including the growing use of lower-cost but less energy-dense lithium iron phosphate. Graphite, however, has remained the predominant material on the anode side of both battery types. Drones, robotics, and more compact transportation such as e-bikes are changing the battery equation. Unlike passenger EVs, where cost per kilowatt-hour is a major consideration, drones and other weight-sensitive technologies place a premium on packing more energy into every kilogram and cubic inch of battery. Amprius Technologies is targeting that market with lithium-ion batteries that replace much of the graphite traditionally used on the anode side with silicon, an abundant element capable of storing substantially more lithium than graphite. The challenge is that silicon expands dramatically as it absorbs lithium during charging, which can cause conventional silicon particles to crack and degrade after repeated cycles. Amprius has developed two primary battery platforms to overcome this problem. Designed to deliver maximum energy density, its SiMaxx technology uses a high-purity silicon nanowire anode that provides room for the silicon to expand and contract during charging and discharging while maintaining electrical contact. The company's SiCore platform uses a proprietary silicon-carbon anode material designed to balance high energy density with power, cycle life, manufacturability, and cost. Amprius introduced a second-generation SiCore cell in September capable of being manufactured on conventional lithium-ion battery production equipment. This ability to produce high-energy silicon-anode batteries on existing equipment is central to the Pentagon-backed project. To explain the energy-density advantage in an easy-to-visualize way, Amprius CEO Tom Stepien compares conventional graphite batteries with drip coffee and the company's silicon-anode batteries with espresso. Both can provide roughly the same caffeine, but espresso fits that dose into a much smaller volume. Likewise, an Amprius battery can provide a similar amount of energy in a smaller and lighter package, or significantly more energy within the same weight and space constraints. For a drone, that can mean longer flight time, greater range, or room for additional payload. The U.S. Department of War's Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program has awarded Amprius up to $75 million to bring that technology into high-volume domestic production. Under what the company calls Project acCELLerate, Amprius plans to reconfigure an existing U.S.-based EV battery production line operated by an unnamed major South Korean battery manufacturer to produce advanced silicon-anode pouch cells for unmanned aerial systems. The converted line is expected to be operating by early 2028 with capacity to produce 12 million Amprius cells annually. Amprius estimates the conversion will cost roughly $100 million, including in-kind investments from the company and its South Korean manufacturing partner. "Our technology, combined with the U.S. manufacturing prowess of our South Korean manufacturing partner, positions us to accelerate adoption of standardized, high-performance pouch cells in a fast-growing market," said Stepien. The decision to convert an EV battery production line to manufacture cells for military drones also underscores a changing lithium-ion battery market. EVs created enormous demand for batteries that balance range, longevity, safety, and affordability. Drones, advanced aviation, robotics, light electric vehicles, and other mobile technologies are creating markets where reducing battery weight and volume can be worth paying a premium. This is particularly true for aircraft, where every pound devoted to batteries is a pound that cannot be used for payload, and every improvement in energy density can translate directly into longer flight times. The Pentagon-backed production line could also provide Amprius with the manufacturing scale needed to expand further into commercial drones, robots, e-bikes, electric aviation, and other applications where packing more energy into a smaller space carries a premium. And if higher production volumes and manufacturing efficiencies lower the cost of silicon-anode batteries, the market for the technology could broaden further. That could eventually open the door for EVs and other transportation systems capable of carrying drip-coffee-sized energy in an espresso-sized package.

artigo.texto: World’s largest single-location battery energy storage system (BESS) Ahmedabad, 01 October 2026: Adani Green Energy Ltd (AGEL), India’s largest renewable energy company, has expanded its operational Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity to 6.63 gigawatt-hours (GWh) at Khavda, Gujarat, from 3.55 GWh in June 2026. AGEL now accounts for more than 50% of India’s operational BESS capacity of about 12.6 GWh. This milestone consolidates Khavda’s position as the world’s largest operational battery energy storage installation at a single location, with 6.63 GWh of operational capacity. AGEL achieved the 6.63 GWh milestone within 14 months of commencing on-site BESS construction at Khavda, Gujarat with this latest capacity addition being commissioned in just 10 months from the start of its construction. The BESS is integrated with AGEL’s renewable energy (RE) development at Khavda, where the company is developing a 30 GW RE plant across 538 square kilometers of barren land. The AGEL 6.63 GWh BESS can store enough clean energy to power around two million homes a day, and support peak electricity demand of cities like Nagpur, Patna or Vizag for several hours. This BESS capacity at Khavda is equivalent to battery storage capacity of more than 150,000 mid-sized EVs and can store enough energy daily to meet almost twice the Delhi Metro's estimated daily electricity requirement, underscoring the unprecedented scale of the installation. The scale-up to 6.63 GWh strengthens the integration of renewable energy into the grid by enabling clean power to be stored and dispatched when required. Mr Sagar Adani, Executive Director, Adani Green Energy, said, “Reaching 6.63 GWh of operational battery storage in just 14 months is a significant milestone for AGEL and India’s clean energy transition. At this scale, storage can make renewable power firmer, more reliable and dispatchable when the grid needs it. As India’s power demand grows, we will continue to scale energy storage solutions, both, battery and pumped storage to support a more resilient, lower-carbon grid.” Photo: World’s largest Battery Energy Storage at Khavda, Gujarat where Adani Green Energy is also developing the World’s largest RE plant Advanced project controls, digital monitoring systems, agile construction management practices, and strategic partnerships with leading global BESS OEMs enabled adherence to aggressive project timelines while maintaining stringent quality and safety standards. The deployment serves as a benchmark for large-scale energy storage execution and operations, supporting India's energy transition through reliable and scalable storage infrastructure. The BESS uses lithium-ion battery technology, integrated with an Energy Management Systems (EMS) and automated telemetry to manage charging and discharging, optimise system performance and support grid services. Battery storage can improve grid stability, manage peak demand, reduce energy curtailment and enable renewable power to be delivered when required. AGEL is on track to add over 10 GWh of BESS capacity in FY 2026-27 and is targeting 50 GWh of storage capacity over the next 5 years. The company is also pursuing pumped storage projects (PSPs) as part of its broader strategy to build large-scale, firm and dispatchable renewable power capacity. About Adani Green Energy Limited: Adani Green Energy Ltd (AGEL) is India’s largest and one of the leading renewable energy companies in the world enabling the clean energy transition. AGEL develops, owns, and operates utility scale grid-connected solar, wind, hybrid and energy storage solutions. AGEL currently has an operating renewable portfolio of 20.76 GW and 6.63 GWh of battery energy storage, the largest in India, spread across 12 states. The company has set a target of achieving 50 GW by 2030 aligned to India’s decarbonization goals. AGEL is focused on leveraging technology to reduce the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) in pursuit of enabling large-scale adoption of affordable clean energy. AGEL is developing the world’s largest renewable energy plant (30 GW) on barren land at Khavda, Gujarat, covering 538 square kilometers, an area five times larger than Paris. AGEL’s operating portfolio is certified as water positive, single-use plastic free and zero waste-to-landfill, a testament to the company’s commitment to power sustainable growth. artigo.texto: Redata aproxima o Brasil da soberania na infraestrutura digital A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, criou condições para acelerar projetos represados e ampliar a capacidade brasileira de processamento. Essa medida gerou uma oportunidade industrial de alcance. Chegou no momento em que a inteligência artificial exige mais servidores, memória, energia e capacidade de rede. O novo modelo tributário destrava bilhões em aportes paralisados diante da corrida pela computação de alto desempenho. Mais de 106 megawatts foram entregues no primeiro semestre de 2026 e outros 134 megawatts estão previstos até dezembro. Cerca de 56% do estoque de data centers em construção no país já apresentava contratos de pré-locação consolidados antes mesmo da aprovação parlamentar e da sanção presidencial. Havia uma demanda latente. O Redata catalisou um mercado preexistente ao eliminar a trava tributária que adiava decisões urgentes. O marco regulatório canaliza e multiplica essa força. A norma alcança dois atores fundamentais. Um deles é a empresa habilitada, responsável por operar o data center. O outro é a coabilitada, que fabrica os equipamentos para essa infraestrutura de TI. Em troca das isenções federais, o operador reserva ao menos 10% da capacidade instalada ao mercado interno e aplica 2% do valor dos equipamentos adquiridos em inovação. O formato operacional dessas contrapartidas, os critérios de sustentabilidade e os trâmites de coabilitação ainda dependem de regulamentação complementar do Executivo. A direção estratégica, contudo, já está dada. Esse percentual ganha corpo ao lado dos 5% injetados compulsoriamente pelas fabricantes de servidores por meio da Lei de Informática. Essa união de cifras constrói a maior transferência de recursos já destinada à pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país. O ponto central do marco legal, previsto no artigo 11-C da Lei 11.196/2005, com redação dada pela Lei nº 15.504/2026 e que instituiu o Redata, revela uma engenharia regulatória inteligentíssima. A desoneração da contribuição ao PIS-Pasep e da Cofins alcança de forma horizontal toda cadeia produtiva. A manutenção da cobrança do Imposto de Importação para equipamentos com produção nacional equivalente e do IPI para os equipamentos produzidos na Zona Franca de Manaus, cria as travas de proteção essenciais. Incentivo fiscal para tecnologias inexistentes no país constitui política industrial coerente e responsável. Desonerar importações predatórias de máquinas já fabricadas internamente causa desindustrialização subsidiada. A regra atual protege quem produz no Brasil, seja qual for a origem do capital investido. Empresas globais de hardware mantêm fábricas aqui ao lado de companhias brasileiras, sob o mesmo rigoroso critério. O mercado nacional de servidores ganha uma expansão sem precedentes com essa barreira inteligente. Permitir a importação isenta de um equipamento pronto anularia a competitividade das operações industriais instaladas no país e destruiria cadeias inteiras de fornecedores. O Redata evitou essa armadilha. A legislação assegura a previsibilidade necessária para as fábricas investirem pesado em novas linhas de produção e contratarem mais talentos para a engenharia local. O parque fabril no nosso país superou, definitivamente, a fase de mera linha de montagem. A realidade das fábricas expõe uma maturidade densa e o domínio prático de uma etapa decisiva. Engenharia de ponta, arquitetura térmica, integração complexa, testes exaustivos e suporte contínuo ocorrem no território nacional. Fabricar a infraestrutura da inteligência artificial exige calibração milimétrica de energia e certificações rigorosas que consomem meses de dedicação exclusiva de times altamente especializados. Nos últimos anos, a título de exemplo, entregamos sucessivos sistemas de supercomputação para o setor de óleo e gás, com integração nacional completa. Construímos sólida tradição tecnológica nesse segmento, e essas máquinas operam hoje entre as maiores do mundo em capacidade de processamento de dados. As placas aceleradoras vêm de fora, mas toda a inteligência da integração ganha forma, escala e excelência aqui. A repatriação veloz de cargas de trabalho tem impulsionado a demanda por hardware local. Em paralelo, os custos financeiros para treinar modelos computacionais aumentaram exponencialmente. Faturas forçam as organizações a transferir operações complexas das nuvens públicas para ambientes locais blindados. Diretores de tecnologia encontram na escolha de um servidor nacional a convergência exata entre eficiência de custos e segurança de dados. Esses líderes corporativos valorizam a vantagem estratégica de ter o fabricante do hardware fisicamente próximo. Essa proximidade garante a customização ágil da arquitetura, viabiliza manutenções críticas em tempo recorde e assegura a continuidade das operações sem o risco atrelado à dependência de um suporte técnico estrangeiro distante. A soberania digital do Brasil ganha uma dimensão muito concreta com o Redata. O país dispensa a fantasia da autossuficiência em semicondutores para desenvolver uma indústria real de inteligência artificial. Nós podemos importar GPUs e processadores e, ainda assim, dominar a engenharia que transforma esses componentes isolados em sistemas capazes de processar dados, sustentar aplicações críticas e receber suporte local. Os próximos cinco anos serão decisivos para essa estratégia. O Brasil reúne mercado vigoroso, matriz elétrica favorável, conectividade internacional e uma indústria de servidores totalmente preparada para acompanhar o aumento expressivo da demanda. O avanço dependerá, essencialmente, da coordenação entre política tributária, energia, infraestrutura, ciência e regulamentação tecnicamente precisa. O Redata cria oportunidade rara de converter novos investimentos estrangeiros em produção fabril, engenharia aplicada e capacidade computacional instalada no país. artigo.texto: Oklahoma lawmakers hold interim study on benefits, costs of data center growth OKLAHOMA CITY (KOKH) — As residents across the state deal with the possibility of data centers coming to their communities, Oklahoma lawmakers held an interim study to determine the benefits and impacts of data center development in the Sooner State. This week, Rep. Mark Chapman, R-Broken Arrow, led an interim study examining the benefits, costs, and long-term impacts of data center developments in Oklahoma. Chapman said he wanted give lawmakers an opportunity to look at the issue from multiple perspectives. "For the past year, I've heard a lot of discussions and concerns about data centers, and I felt it was time to lay the cards on the table and look at this issue as objectively as we can," Chapman said. "There are potential opportunities, but there are also legitimate questions about infrastructure, resources and the effects on communities. We need to understand what communities may be saying yes to, what they may be saying no to and what safeguards need to be in place." Much of the study focused on how data centers affect utility planning and local resources. Experts discussed the large power needs of newer facilities, safeguards intended to keep project costs with the customers creating them and how water use can vary. They also discussed ways to better connect existing resources so communities can more easily evaluate proposed projects and understand potential impacts. Chapman said he will continue reviewing information gathered during the study to determine whether additional legislative action is warranted.

artigo.texto: Can Data Center Design Choices Change Public Acceptance? Operators use biomimicry, community co-design, and brownfield redevelopment to reduce the visual impact of data centers and improve local acceptance. Beauty may be in the eye of the beholder, but it’s unlikely that the recent rash of data centers popping up across the US and globally is winning many people over on looks alone. To ease community concerns about noise, energy, and water use – and especially their visual impact – some operators are rethinking how facilities look, how they sit within landscapes, and even where they’re built. Anti-data center sentiment often goes beyond complaints about water, energy, and noise pollution to include criticism of a facility’s appearance and its aesthetic impact on nearby neighborhoods. A description from the Virginia-based Piedmont Environmental Council captures a common view: “The data center developments proposed in the County are hyperscale facilities, which are massive, windowless concrete buildings that can bring potential noise and electrical infrastructure such as substations and transmission lines. They are also often out of scale with existing communities and fenced with cameras, security guards, and guard gates.” Designing to Disappear: Biomimicry and Landscape Strategies Some operators are taking steps to make facilities a bit easier on the eyes. One approach is to use landscaping to soften profiles and blend sites into their surroundings. Microsoft, for example, has begun applying “biomimicry” – borrowing strategies from local ecosystems to guide land, water, and restoration plans – to improve how some of its newest data centers look and function. The company first employed the approach at a site in Noord-Holland, the Netherlands, in 2022, planting 150 native trees and more than 2,000 square meters (about 21,500 square feet) of shrubs and grasses around the campus. Microsoft says it has since expanded the practice to more than 20 sites across the US and Europe. Microsoft’s director of global land strategy, Kaitlin Chuzi, told Data Center Knowledge that biomimicry is about more than aesthetics or traditional landscaping. “We start by understanding how the local ecosystem functions, combining ecological research with community input and then [using] those insights to inform land, water, and restoration plans that mimic and enhance natural systems,” she said. “The goal is to design for multiple benefits at once, from locally appropriate, biodiverse plantings that improve the viewshed to healthier soil, better stormwater management, and stronger habitat for local species." Here, “viewshed” refers to the area that is visible from a specific vantage point. There is growing interest in whether better-designed facilities can help win over residents. On June 11, the UK Government announced a national Data Center Design Challenge in partnership with the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA). The competition asks architects, designers, engineers, and communities to collaborate on high-quality design, meaningful public engagement, and sustainable outcomes. “As data centers become increasingly critical to the UK’s economic and technological future, we have a responsibility to consider how they are designed, located, and experienced,” said RIBA president Chris Williamson in a statement. “Data centers will be needed across the country, and this presents a major opportunity for architects to reimagine what they can be, while supporting sector growth.” Underground and Low-Profile Designs Challenging the standard “big shed” template, some proposals explore alternative materials and even partially buried or fully underground designs with little or no visible footprint. The potential benefits range from security to cooling efficiencies, and the reduced above-ground profile can ease local opposition. “Nobody’s going to oppose a data center in a mine,” Max Smolaks, a research analyst for Uptime Intelligence, told Data Center Knowledge earlier this year. What Residents Say: Design Factors that Change Acceptance A 2026 research report by the design firm Gensler also highlights the role of design in public acceptance. “Design emerged as a decisive factor in community acceptance. When asked about their top design concerns, residents prioritized issues architects can directly address: overall building appearance, massing, materials, and height,” the report states. Co-Designing with Communities Community participation is another theme. Carl Walker, head of societal insights at engineering consultancy Hoare Lea, said that it is not simply about better aesthetics but about integrating community input from the outset. “Co-creating data centers with residents is essential if they are to become valued community assets rather than simply being perceived as large, anonymous warehouse buildings,” he told Data Center Knowledge. “Co-creating data centers with residents is essential if they are to become valued community assets rather than simply being perceived as large, anonymous warehouse buildings.” – Carl Walker, head of societal insights, Hoare Lea Hoare Lea has developed a Social Charter for data centers that provides guidance for social engagement, including design. “Rather than imposing a standardized ‘one-size-fits-all’ warehouse model, co-creation enables data centers to reflect the character, identity, and needs of the communities they serve, helping them contribute positively to placemaking, local pride, and regeneration,” Walker said. Brownfield First: Regeneration Over Greenfield Sprawl Regeneration can be a powerful lever. While greenfield developments often face criticism for environmental impact, some operators argue that building on brownfield sites – previously developed land that may be disused or blighted – can reduce opposition and accelerate timelines where grid connections and transport links already exist. artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council on Monday faced a chamber packed with residents opposed to a data center that is proposed to go up next to their neighborhoods, even as the city attorney reiterated that the site is an industrial zone district where data centers are permitted. The city attorney also noted that, if an application meets zoning standards, Aurora could face potential liability if administrative officials denied it. Recommended Stories The council heard from about 40 Aurora and Denver residents who are upset about the plans for Trident Data Center, which would go up near Green Valley Ranch if approved. Before the public comment period began, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked everyone attending who opposed the Trident Data Center to stand up. Almost everyone in the room did so. When Schulte asked if anyone in the room supported the data center, nobody stood. Broadly speaking, supporters have argued that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities as well as new tax revenues. They have also insisted that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers: The Colorado counties that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums lean progressive. Plans for the new data center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, an Aurora spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. Vantage Data Centers submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. If built, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. Residents said they feel “totally blindsided” by the proposal. The Aurora residents opposed to the data center claimed that, until early September, they had not heard a word about the plan from the city or Oakwood Homes, the real estate developer for the community. The property where Trident is proposed is in an industrial zone district, where data centers are a permitted use and can be approved administratively as long as no major adjustments are requested, a city spokesperson said. Residents from both Aurora and Denver spoke at the meeting, with those in Denver saying they are close to the data center’s location but have no say in its location. Bre Kennedy, 16, told council members that the data center plan is “ridiculous,” asking councilmembers to raise their hands if they would want to live next to a data center. None of the councilmembers did. “You don’t want this near your neighborhood, so why is it OK for it to be near others’?” Kennedy said. “When you’re writing new regulations, please think about the people who are actually going to have to live next to these facilities.” “We the residents of The Reserve and the groups impacted by this were never informed,” added Dan Bergander, who has lived at The Reserve 55+ community since 2021. In fact, Aurora officials were not required to notify area residents of the plans for a data center because of the land’s zoning, according to Schulte, the city attorney. When applications go to the city for use of land that’s zoned for that use, it goes to administrative approval. “If the council had to approve every project that had to go through, our meetings would be two days long,” Schulte said. “That’s why we have zoning laws.” If an application meets the zoning standards, the city is subject to potential liability if administrative officials deny it, he said. Development and zoning information is public record, Schulte added. “We’re not in the game of hiding the ball,” he said. “Everything we do is open, on our website and can be searched. I encourage any homeowner with parcels of land by their neighborhood to figure out what the land is zoned for.”

artigo.texto: Jackson City Hall meeting called to educate residents on data centers "What we did not hear was the actual benefit, because there is none," said a Jackson Resident Jackson City Hall was filled Wednesday night as residents attended a special meeting to discuss data centers. It's a topic that has sparked intense debate in recent months and led city council members to impose a moratorium on their development. Councilman Vernon Hartley stressed the importance of educating the public about data centers. "We can't have our head in the sand concerning data centers," Hartley said. "We need to understand it. There is a huge data center being built on the northern border of the city of Jackson." Former IT entrepreneur Gerrad Gibert, invited by Councilman Kenneth Stokes, gave an overview of data centers, explaining their purpose and how they are already a part of daily life. "Gain a better understanding of what these sorts of obscure, windowless buildings are and what's in them and how they affect our lives," Gibert said. Gibert, who was involved in building Mississippi's first commercial data center in the 1980s, said data centers are integral to modern life and should not be feared. "I think Jackson can benefit quite a bit from a data center investment," Gibert said. "Jackson is poised well for it. Every business around uses IT systems that are typically housed in data centers." Despite the presentation, some residents, including Natalie Speaks, voiced dissatisfaction with the meeting, saying it lacked opportunities for public input. "People think when you're anti-data center that means you're anti-advancement, and that's not the case," Speaks said. She added that the presentation failed to address the benefits of data centers for the community. "We just heard a presentation about what data centers are and how you build them, [about] venture technologies and what he's done," Speaks said. "But what we did not hear was the actual benefit, because there is none." While city leaders viewed the meeting as a way to inform the public, some attendees left feeling puzzled and unfulfilled, underscoring the ongoing debate over data center developments in Jackson.

artigo.texto: Abbott says data center permits frozen until power, water concerns addressed HEMPHILL, Texas (KTRE) - Two AI data centers, AmpZ and Hyper Data Grid, are targeting Angelina County, but state permits for the facilities remain on hold. Governor Greg Abbott placed a moratorium on new data centers statewide earlier this month to assess their strain on local resources. During a stop in Hemphill, Abbott drew a hard line on electricity. “They must provide their own power as opposed to taking power off the Texas power grid,” Abbott said. Utility costs and firm purchase agreements Abbott said new facilities must prove they will drive down utility costs for neighboring residents. “Firm purchase agreements for buying a certain amount of electricity. Knowing full well they will not all the time buy that electricity, and that additional supply on the marketplace will then drive down the cost of electricity rates,” Abbott said. Abbott also said cities and counties need more control over where these facilities build, a power local leaders currently lack. Local control over land use Without tax abatement agreements, county leaders have no say on land use. That prompted both Angelina County commissioners and the Lufkin City Council to lobby state lawmakers for regulatory oversight. “And the reason we’re doing this - if we can’t get an abatement, if there’s not going to be an abatement, then there are zero control that we have over these data centers,” said Keith Wright, Angelina County judge. Abbott said he supports giving communities that authority. “Local communities should have the authority and the independence to make their own decision about whether they do or do not want data centers,” Abbott said. Abbott said the state Legislature and the Texas Water Development Board are drafting new rules to prevent data centers from draining local water supplies. The Texas Legislature’s next regular session begins Jan. 12, 2027. Copyright 2026 KTRE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The expert speaker slated to address the City of Sheboygan on data center issues cancelled out on Monday, but tomorrow’s meeting will still be held. From 6-7 PM Wednesday at Uptown Social there will be a review of the previous three speakers and a question-and-answer session. In previous sessions the meetings included the President of Alliant Energy, Becky Valcq, who told attendees that while there are tangible benefits to data centers, challenges to the grid are inevitable. Dr. Ben Green, co-author of “What Happens When Data Centers Come to Town” gave an overview during the second session of local impacts on economies of energy and resources, and how local governments need to craft careful zoning laws to manage those impacts. The Senior Policy Coordinator for the Great Plains Institute, Bridget Williams, was the speaker at last Wednesday’s session and warned that while some data centers use only as much electricity as a hotel, the largest can use almost 3 times the capacity of the entire Point Beach Nuclear Plant. Those and other discoveries will be used to eventually craft zoning laws to regulate data centers should one ever want to locate in Sheboygan.

artigo.texto: Por Conrad Fonseca, Head de Energia da Tractebel Brasil, Chile e Canadá. A publicação da Portaria Normativa MME nº 136, de 1º de junho de 2026, consolida as diretrizes e a sistemática do primeiro leilão brasileiro dedicado à contratação de potência elétrica a partir de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. Mais do que uma inovação regulatória, a medida transforma o BESS em instrumento formal de planejamento da segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), justamente quando o Brasil vive sua maior expansão solar e eólica da história, mas ainda desperdiça parcela relevante da geração renovável potencial por limitações de flexibilidade, transmissão e operação. O primeiro certame, previsto para 2 de dezembro de 2026, será o LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento Nacional, restrito a sistemas que atendam a requisitos mínimos de nacionalização, conforme critérios de credenciamento no Sistema CFI do BNDES. O segundo, previsto para 4 de dezembro de 2026, será o LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento, aberto aos demais projetos elegíveis de armazenamento em baterias. Juntos, os dois leilões podem representar um passo relevante na formação de um novo mercado de armazenamento no país, associado à queda de 93% nos custos das baterias nos últimos 15 anos e à necessidade crescente de flexibilidade operativa no sistema elétrico brasileiro. A Portaria MME nº 878, de novembro de 2025, cumpriu o papel de abrir a consulta pública e testar o desenho inicial do certame. A Portaria Normativa MME nº 136/2026, agora, consolida a estrutura final: contratação de disponibilidade de potência em megawatts, a partir de novos sistemas de armazenamento eletroquímico conectados ao SIN, com potência mínima de 30 MW, capacidade de operação contínua por pelo menos quatro horas, eficiência total mínima de 85%, tempo máximo de recarga completa de seis horas e atendimento aos requisitos técnicos de conexão definidos por ONS e EPE, incluindo funcionalidades de grid-forming. Os contratos deverão ter prazo de 15 anos, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A realização dos leilões se apoia na evolução recente do marco legal e regulatório do setor elétrico, que passou a reconhecer o armazenamento como categoria própria e a abrir espaço para sua contratação como recurso de potência, flexibilidade e segurança sistêmica. Na prática, a Portaria Normativa MME nº 136/2026 aproxima o BESS do centro do planejamento operativo e de expansão do SIN, ao transformá-lo em uma alternativa contratável para atender necessidades sistêmicas específicas. O mercado global de BESS viveu em 2025 seu ano mais transformador. O mundo instalou 247 GWh em novos sistemas de baterias no ano passado, um salto de 35% sobre o ano anterior. A projeção para 2035 é de 7,3 TWh, oito vezes o nível atual. Por que o curtailment tornou o BESS urgente Entre 2023 e 2025, o Brasil cortou 48,7 TWh de geração solar e eólica, o equivalente a dez meses inteiros de produção da usina de Belo Monte, ou 8% do consumo nacional anual. Em 2025, segundo a consultoria Volt Robotics, o curtailment médio foi de 20% da energia renovável potencial, com pico solar de 34,1% no terceiro trimestre, e concentração geográfica no triângulo Minas Gerais-Ceará-Rio Grande do Norte, que sozinho acumulou R$ 2,24 bilhões em perdas. O problema tem três causas que se alimentam mutuamente: gargalo de transmissão Nordeste-Sudeste, atualmente 13,8 GW, com 16,4 GW planejados para 2027; sobreoferta ao meio-dia; e critérios operativos mais conservadores adotados pelo ONS após o apagão de 15 de agosto de 2023, quando tecnologias conectadas por inversores falharam em entregar o desempenho dinâmico esperado. Estima-se que apenas 5% dessas perdas sejam efetivamente ressarcidas aos geradores hoje. Um sistema BESS de 500 MW com quatro horas de autonomia, instalado em um ponto adequado do Nordeste, poderia absorver parte relevante do excedente solar que hoje é cortado entre 10h e 14h e devolvê-lo ao SIN no horário de ponta, quando a demanda ultrapassa 100 GW e os preços tendem a se elevar. Em termos financeiros, cada MWh deslocado do piso para o pico pode capturar parte relevante do spread do PLD (Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças), criando uma fonte adicional de receita que, no agregado, pode contribuir para viabilizar o investimento ao longo do tempo. O curtailment, portanto, não é apenas um desperdício contábil: é um dos sinais de mercado mais claros que o sistema elétrico brasileiro tem produzido em favor do armazenamento. A nova portaria reforça essa lógica ao prever mecanismos de competitividade locacional: projetos conectados em pontos do SIN que proporcionem benefícios sistêmicos adicionais poderão receber bonificação para fins de competição no leilão, conforme estudos da EPE e do ONS. Na prática, o desenho regulatório começa a reconhecer que o valor de uma bateria não depende apenas de sua potência ou duração, mas também do ponto exato em que ela reduz restrições de transmissão, alivia áreas críticas, aumenta a confiabilidade do atendimento e melhora a integração das fontes renováveis variáveis. As cinco aplicações que o BESS pode assumir no SIN A aplicação mais consolidada no Brasil é o chamado peak-shaving, que consiste em usar baterias para aliviar a sobrecarga da rede nos horários de maior consumo. O Brasil pode seguir o exemplo do vizinho Chile, onde a Usina Tamaya BESS, localizada em Tocopilla, na região Antofagasta, no norte do país, armazena a energia excedente gerada pela Usina Solar Tamaya para ser injetada no sistema elétrico nos horários de pico de demanda. A usina, que conta com 152 contêiners de baterias de lítio tem um sistema de 68 MW e capacidade de 418 MWh capaz de abastecer mais de 50 mil residências. A segunda aplicação, a arbitragem energética, explora a diferença de preço entre os horários de sobra e de escassez no sistema. artigo.texto: For much of Gov. Wes Moore’s first term, he worked to “supercharge” the development of data centers, seeing them as just the kind of rocket fuel Maryland needed for its stagnating economy. AI’s endless appetite for computing power had the industry booming in nearby Northern Virginia, the data center capital of the world. And building these server farms held even more appeal after President Donald Trump’s moves to dismantle federal agencies hit Maryland’s tax base. But then data center politics rapidly shifted. Now, Democratic- and Republican-led counties across the state have passed development moratoriums, and Moore is trying to balance the allure of an economic driver that has labor support against opposition from environmentalists and community groups. The space between courting data centers and public demand for regulation has narrowed. With Moore considered a 2028 presidential contender, his decisions today could be viewed in a different light by primary voters in two years. Last week, the governor laid out a new review process for data centers and argued that the state needs to change its approach in response to the industry’s expanding scale. Read More “If you’re not protecting your people from this,” he said, “then I think you’re derelict in your duty.” This tough talk on data centers contrasts with the governor’s previous approach. At points, he has smoothed pathways for large-scale data center projects. He’s also opposed legislation to bolster regulatory reviews of data centers, vetoed a study of their energy and environmental impacts, and warned against the repeal of a 2020 industry tax break that has cost the state tens of millions of dollars in forgone revenues. Moore now seems more open to a data center slowdown. Though he has not called for a statewide moratorium, he said last month that he would “absolutely” sign a pause or ban if lawmakers pass one next year. Moore’s recent action follows other governors across the country who have looked to crack down on data centers in response to a public backlash. New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott have imposed sweeping development stoppages in their states, while others have looked to tighten regulations on data centers’ use of land, water and energy. Chris Borick, a political scientist at Lehigh University, sees similarities in how Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro — another 2028 contender — have evolved on this issue. Both Democrats followed a timeworn playbook. It’s typical for governors to roll out a red carpet for tech investment, using fiscal incentives and relaxing regulatory barriers for industries that promise community investment and lots of jobs. But Borick said the desire for economic success meant both governors turned “a little bit of a blind eye” to data centers’ downsides. One report by the pro-data center Maryland Tech Council estimated that the industry could deliver $16 million annually in state revenues for every million square feet of new development, while counties stand to gain even more from property taxes and benefits packages. “They were primed to buy into the sales pitch,” Borick said. A ‘bright future’ for data centers In the span of a few years, Moore has gone from pitching Maryland as prime territory for data centers to assailing the boom he invited. When state utility regulators in 2023 denied fast-track reviews for massive, diesel-powered backup generators at Maryland’s first hyperscale data center development — a 2,000-acre campus in Frederick County — Moore promised to rewrite policy to “ensure the industry has a bright future” in Maryland. He pushed a bill the next year to roll back reviews of those controversial generators, legislation that the General Assembly approved unanimously. Moore’s office also lent a hand to a wealthy entrepreneur and campaign donor hoping to build a massive data center at an old coal-fired power plant on the Potomac River. After repeated requests from the developer, the state’s top environmental official sent a letter offering expedited approvals for the project. And while Moore’s order last week instituted a new vetting process for data centers, in 2025 he vetoed legislation to study the industry’s energy and environmental consequences. Lawmakers overrode him months later. As the data center debate heated up, Moore said he wanted to prioritize projects that could check certain boxes: employing local union workers, prioritizing clean power and paying for their own electricity needs. Maryland could court economic opportunity without becoming the next “Data Center Alley,” he maintained. In legislative testimony this year, Moore’s Department of Commerce defended the state’s data center tax exemption and opposed a bill to establish new reporting requirements for data center developers, arguing that the measures would “send a message” to data center companies that the “cost of doing business in Maryland is too high and burdensome.” But in recent weeks, Moore’s rhetoric has shifted. On a podcast last month, he said he would sign a statewide pause or ban on data centers should lawmakers put one on his desk next year. At his executive order signing the following week, the governor said Maryland should repeal its data center tax credit, which lawmakers adopted before his term. Asked in an interview about his administration’s reversal, Moore said the state must constantly “pressure test” its laws and that his administration had found this one to be “outdated.” The governor has attributed his pivot to the Trump administration’s recent rollbacks on data center regulations and to the industry’s expanding scale. The impact of today’s data centers “is different,” he said last week. “As a state, we’ve got to have a different type of posture, because we are seeing how the landscape has changed.” Some don’t see it that way. artigo.texto: A Rússia atacou neste domingo (27) a sede da Kyivstar, maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, localizada na capital Kiev. Segundo a empresa, que confirmou o episódio à agência de notícias Interfax Ucrânia, o prédio foi danificado, mas nenhum funcionário ficou ferido. A estrutura já havia sido atingida em outros ataques realizados ao longo deste mês. O bombardeio faz parte de uma ofensiva russa mais ampla contra data centers e a infraestrutura de comunicações do país, intensificada nas últimas semanas. De acordo com o ministro das Relações Exteriores ucraniano, Andrii Sybiha, o objetivo de Moscou é interromper o fluxo de informações, o que afeta também os alertas sobre mísseis e drones enviados à população. Leia mais: - TIM segue na bolsa após Correios da Itália não atingir 90% das ações - Vero amplia portfólio B2B com nuvem, móvel e câmeras com IA - Empresas tentam comprar a Oi Soluções ‘fiado’ mas Justiça do Rio rejeita VODAFONE UCRÂNIA TAMBÉM FOI ALVO O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia afirmou, também no domingo, que atingiu um data center da Vodafone Ucrânia, segunda maior operadora de telefonia celular do país. A companhia não respondeu aos pedidos de comentário e não havia confirmado o ataque à agência Reuters. Até o momento, não há informações sobre possíveis impactos no serviço prestado aos clientes da operadora. No mesmo dia, o presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, relatou que a Rússia atingiu duas vezes um data center em Kiev durante a manhã. Segundo ele, duas crianças e um adulto ficaram feridos na ação. Não foi divulgado qual empresa é responsável pela instalação atacada, nem se houve interrupção nos serviços de conectividade oferecidos a partir do local. PROVEDORES DE INTERNET NA MIRA A ofensiva de domingo não foi um caso isolado. Na semana anterior, Moscou já havia atingido data centers de provedores de internet ucranianos, provocando interrupções no serviço para cerca de 100 mil residências em Kiev e nos arredores, segundo o Ministério da Transformação Digital da Ucrânia. Algumas operadoras precisaram recorrer a instalações de backup para manter os clientes conectados. Empresas de telecomunicações atingidas recentemente: - Kyivstar: sede em Kiev atingida no domingo (27), sem feridos - Vodafone Ucrânia: data center atingido, segundo o Ministério da Defesa da Rússia - UTELS, Pavutyna e Datagroup: provedores com data centers danificados na última semana Quer acompanhar tudo em primeira mão sobre o mundo das telecomunicações? Siga o Minha Operadora no Canal no WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, X e YouTube e não perca nenhuma atualização, alerta, promoção ou polêmica do setor! O PAPEL ESTRATÉGICO DAS TELECOMUNICAÇÕES Para o chanceler ucraniano, a estratégia russa tem um alvo claro e coloca vidas em risco. Em publicação feita na rede social X na quarta-feira (23), Sybiha escreveu: “A Rússia tem como alvo os principais data centers ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais. Eles salvam vidas”. Os ataques evidenciam a vulnerabilidade da infraestrutura de comunicações da Ucrânia, que tem se mantido em funcionamento durante a guerra graças a redes redundantes, instalações de backup e trabalhos rápidos de restauração. Em um país sob bombardeios frequentes, manter a telefonia móvel e a internet ativas é essencial para a circulação de informações e para os alertas de segurança.

artigo.texto: Building Resilience Into Digital Infrastructure As infrastructure expands beyond traditional regions, organizations will be better positioned by using a lifecycle approach to network resiliency. September 28, 2026 Sponsored by SES AI Growth Is Changing Infrastructure Assumptions Major hyperscale cloud providers have launched over 50 cloud regions in the past five years, and the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure is forcing data center operators to rethink long-standing assumptions about site selection and deployment. Growth in cloud services and AI workloads is pushing infrastructure into a wider range of geographies, exposing operators to new risks as facilities move beyond traditional connectivity hubs. While considerations of power, land acquisition, cooling, and permitting all remain important, connectivity readiness in some geographies can be just as consequential as power readiness. Connectivity Risk Is Changing Beyond well-documented financial impacts of outages, operators must also consider the potential cost to customer trust. If a fiber or power cable is cut, can you answer questions about the security systems in the data center? Can you tell a customer if their cage door was recently opened? Operators must also account for disruptions that occur well beyond the data center itself. As AI infrastructure footprints expand into new regions, connectivity can be affected by subsea cable failures, natural disasters, regional infrastructure disruptions, geopolitical events, civil instability, and other factors out of a facility operator’s control. For example, in 2024, a rockslide off the coast of West Africa caused multiple subsea cable breaks, disrupting service in West Africa. The Red Sea has experienced two incidents of simultaneous fiber cuts. As operators expand into new geographies and new risk environments, connectivity resilience is becoming a core design consideration. From the operator perspective, the question isn't whether connectivity outages occur but how critical management systems will remain reachable when those outages occur. Resilience Beyond Redundancy Traditional planning suggests that multiple fiber providers deliver resilience. But subsea routes and regional infrastructure concentration can create hidden dependencies. Resilient designs will look at carrier, path, and infrastructure diversity. Operators should consider if their resiliency plans provide: - Guaranteed capacity to help avoid consumer-grade congestion concerns. - Private routing options to avoid public internet exposure. - Flexible traffic routing that can support in-country routing, specific cloud destinations, and recovery sites outside a potential disruption zone. - Meaningful upload throughput for continuous support and visibility of operational systems, infrastructure management, and security platforms. Sovereign Infrastructure Is Raising the Stakes As both governments and enterprises place more emphasis on compliance, data control, and transparency, connectivity decisions now extend beyond uptime and resilience. During outages or failover events, organizations may also need visibility into where traffic is routed and how network paths align with jurisdictional requirements. This is driving interest in network designs that combine resilience with greater visibility into routing decisions. One Planned Connectivity Lifecycle Joining Construction, Commissioning, and Operational Resilience Resilience is most effective and cost-efficient in the long term when it is designed into a facility from the outset. By viewing connectivity as a lifecycle consideration rather than a series of point solutions, operators can take a more consistent approach to ensuring critical management, monitoring, and security systems remain accessible throughout the life of the facility. For example, a facility’s connectivity requirements may evolve like this as it moves from construction to operations: - During construction, delivering communications, site monitoring, security support, and temporary operational access before permanent infrastructure is in place. - As the facility approaches launch, enabling initial network access, testing, commissioning, and operational readiness. - Once the facility enters production, a shift from enablement to resilience with satellite serving as an independent management path, operational backup, and recovery communications channel. Conclusion Old connectivity assumptions are becoming harder to sustain as operators expand into new geographies and face new sources of infrastructure risk. In the AI era, the impact of lost connectivity grows, and connectivity resilience is a design decision that should be made well before a facility's first workload goes live. Successful infrastructure projects will evaluate connectivity with the same rigor applied to power, land, and cooling infrastructure. About the Author: Robert Hegblom is Sr. Principal Product Manager for Land and Sovereign Enterprise at SES, where he builds multi-orbit satellite connectivity offerings for global businesses and telco partners. He also has a decade of experience expanding data centers to underserved locations for hyperscale cloud providers, content delivery networks.

artigo.texto: A primeira etapa do plano prevê US$ 24 milhões para a aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual parque fabril da WEG em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e tem início das operações previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. A WEG já tem outras operações industriais no México. Além de Atotonilco de Tula, onde mantém atividades relacionadas à fundição e revestimentos, a companhia tem uma unidade em Huehuetoca voltada à produção de motores de baixa e média tensão, geradores, painéis, transformadores e subestações. Também mantém, em Monterrey, a operação incorporada com a aquisição da Marathon, que produz motores e geradores e realiza atividades de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Na segunda fase, a companhia investirá os US$ 141 milhões restantes na construção de duas instalações industriais em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte. A nova estrutura terá produção verticalizada, com processos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Segundo a WEG, a segunda etapa do projeto deverá ser concluída em 2030. A expansão ocorre em um momento de aumento da demanda por infraestrutura de energia nos Estados Unidos. A WEG encerrou 2025 com receita líquida de R$ 40,8 bilhões. A companhia possui unidades industriais em 18 países, presença comercial em mais de 135 países e mais de 49 mil funcionários. Cerca de 59% da receita de 2025 veio de vendas realizadas fora do Brasil. Data centers O movimento anunciado nesta segunda-feira reforça uma frente de negócios que vem ganhando importância para a WEG: o fornecimento de equipamentos para a infraestrutura elétrica dos data centers. Um relatório do BTG Pactual aponta que a exposição da companhia ao setor não se limita aos geradores. Cerca de 20% da receita de transmissão e distribuição (T&D) da WEG nos Estados Unidos já está relacionada a clientes de data centers, segundo informações da própria empresa. Os geradores são outro ponto dessa exposição. Data centers precisam de sistemas de geração de energia de emergência para manter suas operações em caso de interrupções no fornecimento da rede elétrica. A WEG atua nesse mercado por meio de suas próprias operações e da Marathon Electric. Juntas, as duas marcas têm cerca de 10% do mercado global de alternadores e grupos geradores, de acordo com o BTG. A companhia também fornece outros equipamentos utilizados nesses empreendimentos. Entre eles estão sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias, conhecidos como BESS, além de motores industriais e inversores de frequência usados nos sistemas de refrigeração dos data centers. A demanda por esses equipamentos ocorre ao mesmo tempo em que a WEG amplia sua capacidade de produção de transformadores, outro negócio ligado à infraestrutura elétrica necessária para esses empreendimentos. A companhia tem projetos de expansão nos Estados Unidos, México, Colômbia e Brasil. Nos EUA, uma nova unidade de transformadores especiais receberá US$ 77 milhões, com conclusão prevista entre 2027 e 2028. No México, uma nova fábrica está prevista para o fim de 2026 ou início de 2027. Em conjunto, os projetos devem aproximadamente dobrar a capacidade de produção de transformadores da WEG em relação ao fim de 2023. Segundo o BTG, a capacidade adicional deve entrar nos resultados de forma gradual, à medida que as novas fábricas comecem a operar. A utilização total da estrutura ampliada é esperada apenas para o fim de 2027. O tema deve estar entre os assuntos discutidos no WEG Day, evento anual da companhia marcado para sexta-feira (2), em Jaraguá do Sul (SC). Além da expansão de transformadores e da exposição aos data centers, o BTG espera informações sobre o impacto das tarifas de importação nos Estados Unidos e os próximos passos da estratégia de crescimento da companhia. A WEG vem adaptando sua produção para o mercado americano em resposta às mudanças tarifárias. Segundo o BTG, aproximadamente 41% do fornecimento relacionado às vendas nos EUA vem do México, 33% da produção doméstica americana e entre 20% e 21% do Brasil. O que o investidor deve acompanhar Apesar do aumento da demanda por equipamentos elétricos, a expansão da WEG também traz pontos de atenção. Um deles é a possibilidade de aumento da oferta nos próximos anos. WEG e outros fabricantes estão ampliando a produção para atender ao aumento da demanda por eletricidade, transformadores e equipamentos para data centers. O BTG Pactual avalia que a entrada simultânea de novas fábricas em 2027 e 2028 pode aumentar a oferta e pressionar os preços em alguns segmentos. O risco, segundo o banco, é maior nos produtos em que novos concorrentes conseguem adicionar capacidade com mais facilidade. As tarifas americanas também continuam no radar. A WEG vem compensando parte dos custos com reajustes de preços e mudanças na origem da produção, mas uma alteração nas tarifas ou na capacidade de repasse para os clientes pode afetar as margens. Outro ponto é o tempo necessário para que os novos investimentos se transformem em receita. Parte relevante da capacidade adicional de transformadores e geradores só estará disponível nos próximos anos, enquanto os desembolsos começam antes. A exposição aos data centers também merece acompanhamento. A WEG tem diferentes linhas de produtos relacionadas a esse mercado, mas o ritmo de expansão desses projetos será importante para determinar a velocidade com que a nova capacidade instalada será absorvida.
