artigo.texto: SAN DIEGO, Sept. 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Beam Global (Nasdaq: BEEM), a leading provider of innovative and sustainable infrastructure solutions for energy storage and security, electrification of mobility, and smart city infrastructure, will share developments in its advanced battery technologies for high-power applications, including AI data centers and electric aviation, during the Company’s presentations at The Battery Show North America, in Detroit, on October 12th through the 15th. Beam Global is developing battery energy storage systems designed to manage the extreme power fluctuations generated by the rapidly increasing workloads of AI data centers. The research focuses on high-speed, multi-timescale control strategies that can reduce peak utility demand and required grid capacity while using less battery capacity than conventional approaches. The Company is also applying its proprietary passive thermal management technology to support frequent, high-rate battery cycling while managing battery temperatures and degradation. Beam Global is evaluating its proprietary solutions to address thermal runaway initiation and propagation in high-power and high-energy lithium-ion battery systems for applications including electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. Testing includes side and bottom nail penetration, external heating and overcharge to evaluate thermal and electrical behavior during cell failure. At the module level, Beam’s engineering and science teams are evaluating how battery architecture, enclosure design, thermal coupling, liquid-cooled cold plates and Beam’s phase-change composite (PCC™) technology affect cell-to-cell thermal propagation. Electro-thermal modeling is being used alongside physical testing to further characterize failure mechanisms and support the development of next-generation battery systems. "Beam’s core competency and protected IP are centered on our ability to deliver high power bursts under extreme operating conditions using our superior engineering and proprietary thermal management solutions,” said Desmond Wheatley, CEO of Beam Global. "These capabilities are becoming increasingly essential for data centers and electric aviation applications like drones and eVTOLs. We are seeing significant increases in demand for our unique approach to these challenges. The Battery Show North America gives us the ideal opportunity to share the advances we are making to the very audiences who are seeking solutions to these critical challenges.” Beam Global's Chief Battery Scientist, Dr. Said Al-Hallaj, and Donald Gilmore, Director of Energy Storage Systems, will present preliminary findings from two of the Company’s research programs. Research into AI data center power transients will be presented by Donald Gilmore on October 13, followed by Dr. Said Al-Hallaj's presentation on thermal runaway in drone and eVTOL battery systems on October 14. Both presenters will be available at Beam’s Booth 3403 for further discussion. The markets for advanced battery technologies are expanding rapidly. According to MarketsandMarkets, the global data center energy storage systems market is projected to grow from $5.17 billion in 2026 to $10.48 billion by 2032, representing a 12.5% CAGR. The global eVTOL battery market is projected to grow from $6.90 billion in 2025 to $26.26 billion by 2032, representing a 21.0% CAGR, according to Fortune Business Insights. About Beam Global Beam Global is a sustainable technology innovator that develops and manufactures infrastructure products and technologies. The Company operates at the nexus of innovative and reliable energy, transportation and smart city solutions with a focus on sustainable energy infrastructure, rapidly deployed and scalable EV charging solutions, safe energy storage, energy security and intelligent infrastructure. With operations in the U.S., Europe and the Middle East, Beam Global develops, patents, designs, engineers and manufactures unique and advanced technology solutions that power transportation, provide secure sources of electricity, enable smart city services, save time and money, and protect the environment. Beam Global is headquartered in San Diego, CA, with facilities in Yuma, AZ; Broadview, IL; Belgrade and Kraljevo, Serbia; and Abu Dhabi, UAE. Beam Global is listed on Nasdaq under the symbol BEEM. artigo.texto: WEG investirá R$ 840 milhões em geradores para atender data centers A WEG anunciou na segunda-feira (28) um investimento de US$ 165 milhões, cerca de R$ 840 milhões, para ampliar a produção de geradores na América do Norte. O plano mira a procura por energia para operações críticas nos Estados Unidos, especialmente data centers. Segundo o comunicado ao mercado, a expansão ocorrerá em duas etapas. A companhia prevê chegar a uma capacidade global de cerca de 50 geradores por dia em 2030, ante os atuais 10. A meta considera as fábricas no México, nos EUA, no Brasil e na China. O investimento amplia os negócios incorporados com a aquisição da Marathon. A expansão dos centros de dados abre mercado para fabricantes de equipamentos elétricos, além de fornecedores de chips e servidores. Expansão começa pelo México A primeira etapa terá US$ 24 milhões para comprar e adaptar um prédio ao lado do parque industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade fará a montagem de geradores, com início previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. A segunda fase receberá US$ 141 milhões para construir duas instalações industriais. A WEG ainda definirá a localização na América do Norte. O projeto inclui a fabricação de componentes, como eixos, carcaças e enrolamentos elétricos. Energia acompanha expansão da IA Os data centers abrigam equipamentos que processam e armazenam informações. A expansão da inteligência artificial aumenta a necessidade de eletricidade e de infraestrutura capaz de manter essas operações. Em relatório publicado em abril de 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE) estimou que o consumo mundial de eletricidade dos centros de dados quase dobrará até 2030. A projeção passa de 485 terawatts-hora em 2025 para 950 terawatts-hora no fim da década, cerca de 3% do consumo global. A agência também identificou restrições no fornecimento de equipamentos elétricos e atrasos na conexão de novos projetos às redes. Nos Estados Unidos, essas dificuldades levam desenvolvedores a buscar geração de energia no próprio local. Para a WEG, o plano anunciado busca atender a esse mercado com mais capacidade industrial. O cronograma distribui a expansão até 2030, quando a companhia prevê concluir a segunda etapa. Fonte: WEG, Agência Internacional de Energia. artigo.texto: WASHINGTON — The Senate on Wednesday rejected separate bills to regulate data centers and limit stock trading by members of Congress. Battleground Republicans were hoping to campaign on the bills, but Democrats blocked both measures, saying they don’t go far enough. The two votes failed on the Senate floor in a final burst of business before senators headed home for the election, now less than five weeks away. Republicans scheduled votes on the two campaign issues, hoping to deliver something for battleground Republicans to campaign on. The Stop Insider Trading Act would prohibit most members of Congress and their spouses from trading stocks. The Ratepayer Protection Act is designed to prevent data centers from driving up local electricity rates. “It would simply promote the adoption of a standard that would require data centers to shoulder the electricity costs associated with their operation and construction,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said of the data center bill. Democrats argued the data center bill lacks teeth and is more about political messaging. On the stock trading bill, they accused Republicans of adding a poison pill in the form of new voter ID requirements, and criticized the measure for not forcing lawmakers to sell stock they already own. “The Republican toothless stock trading bill is as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. The spread of data centers has emerged as a potent campaign issue in states such as Ohio. Incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, sponsored the bill in part to counter relentless attack ads from his opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, focused on Husted’s past support of data centers. “If Democrats block this bill, they will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that they do not care about affordability,” Husted said on the Senate floor. Despite failing in the Senate, both bills had bipartisan support in the House. The Ratepayer Protection Act won the support of nearly all House Democrats, but in the Senate, just four Democrats backed the legislation.

artigo.texto: Publicidade A Samsung concordou em investir US$ 1 bilhão na Helix Digital Infrastructure, empresa de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial (IA) apoiada por KKR e Nvidia, em mais um aporte na corrida global por data centers, energia e redes capazes de sustentar a demanda por IA. O investimento eleva o capital já assegurado pela Helix para mais de US$ 11 bilhões, a ser usado na estratégia de entregar uma nova geração de data centers, geração de energia e transmissão. A Helix foi criada em junho por um consórcio liderado pela KKR, com investidores-âncora que incluem Nvidia, a Kuwait Investment Authority e a Vistra, empresa de geração e varejo de eletricidade. Leia também: OpenAI segura lançamento de novo modelo de IA após falhas em testes de segurança O CEO e cofundador da Helix, Adam Selipsky, disse que o compromisso da Samsung é um “voto de confiança” na estratégia da companhia para atender a uma demanda sem precedentes de grandes provedoras de nuvem por infraestrutura de IA cada vez mais complexa e em alta velocidade. Gigantes como Microsoft (MSFT34), Amazon (AMZO34), Meta (M1TA34) e Alphabet (GOGL34) vêm gastando centenas de bilhões de dólares para expandir infraestrutura de IA. O gasto de capital das quatro empresas chegou a US$ 410 bilhões no ano passado, quase o triplo do nível de 2022. Estimativas do economista Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, publicadas pela Brookings Institution, projetam US$ 10,3 trilhões em investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionada entre 2025 e 2032. Leia também: AMD compra startup de pioneira da IA por US$ 8,2 bilhões Continua depois da publicidade A Helix afirma que, além do papel da Nvidia em tecnologia e infraestrutura de ponta e da Vistra em energia, pretende aproveitar capacidades da Samsung em tecnologia avançada, construção, armazenamento de energia e refrigeração para desenvolver infraestrutura em escala. A Samsung disse que o aporte ajudará suas afiliadas a avançar de fornecedoras de componentes para funções de maior valor em sistemas e infraestrutura de IA. O movimento também ocorre enquanto empresas sul-coreanas ampliam investimentos para capturar o boom de IA. Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix planejam investir mais de US$ 520 bilhões em um polo de semicondutores no sudoeste do país, como parte de uma iniciativa liderada pelo governo estimada em US$ 2 trilhões para desenvolver capacidades domésticas completas em IA. Analistas da BMI, da Fitch Solutions, apontam que a competição deve se intensificar e que projetos maiores podem pressionar preços. Eles também alertam que a rede elétrica pode não acompanhar o ritmo e que regras recentes de licenciamento exigem padrões de eficiência energética, elevando as dificuldades para garantir energia para instalações de IA, intensivas em consumo. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – San Antonio leaders are looking at whether data centers should be required to use recycled water instead of drinking water as concerns grow about the potential impact of future artificial intelligence facilities. San Antonio’s District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan filed a council consideration request (CCR) almost a year ago to have city staff look into the impact data centers have on city resources and look at the possibility of requiring data centers to use recycled water. Water is used to cool down the industrial servers that data centers use for extended periods of time. Water is also used to produce power for the facilities. KSAT attempted to speak to Galvan about the recycled water proposal, but his office sent a statement. In it, Galvan said he wants to keep data centers from using any drinking water, and in order for a mandate on recycled water usage by data centers can move forward, San Antonio Water System (SAWS) must adopt a policy first, specifically outlining that that is what data centers must do. Donovan Burton, the senior vice president of water resources and governmental relations for SAWS, said when talking about data centers in the city, there must be a distinction made between existing data centers and future AI data centers and their water consumption. He said 23 of the existing data centers in the city account for a very small amount of the water pulled from the city’s water supply. “The existing data centers are very small (and have a) very, very small footprint. In fact, they’re using about .1% of our potable water supply,” Burton said. He said it is the future AI data centers that could potentially use a lot more water, and added SAWS’ Recycled Water Network could help data centers comply if the recycled water use became an official requirement. “Our Recycle Water Network has been in place for over 20 years,” he said. He explained that it is 130 miles of purple pipeline that specifically carries recycled water that is used and paid for by contracted, non-residential customers. “The recycle water programs, after (water) has been used, we treat it and put it into a purple pipe network that goes around ... a good portion of the entire city,” Burton said. “That network then takes it from three different plants, and we can move water back and forth.” SAWS headquarters, CPS Energy, Toyota, the San Antonio Zoo and the River Walk are among the multiple big entities and attractions that are connected in part or entirely to SAWS’ Recycled Water Network, and you can tell by the designated purple pipes present on or near the respective properties. Burton said if a recycled water use restriction is implemented, data center owners would have to choose to obtain a permit from SAWS and enter into a contract for a specific amount of water to connect to the purple pipeline. But he shared there is another option data centers have that can be a conservative measure. “Some of them are going to a closed loop (water) system, which will end up using a lot less water,” Burton said. An internet search on what a closed loop water system is yielded a general definition, describing how data center use the same water or a cooling liquid through sealed pipes to absorb heat and as it moves along the pipe path it removes heat from servers over and over again without pulling in or using fresh water. Until further notice, Burton said SAWS will continue its forward strategy. “It’s a matter of making sure that that works for all future customers, not just a very few one or two or five data centers or anything else,” he said. In the statement sent to KSAT, Galvan said he asked SAWS leadership to come up with a possible plan to move forward with the water usage restriction for new data centers. The statement went on to say he is interested in hearing from SAWS this week as to whether or not the board has made any movement on the proposal over the summer.

artigo.texto: Granbury residents stage walkout during city council meeting amid data center controversy GRANBURY, Texas - Dozens of Granbury residents walked out of Monday night's city council meeting as city leaders pushed back on petitions for their removal over alleged plans to build a data center in the city. Granbury data center concept Granbury data center concept What we know: Earlier in 2026, Granbury City Council voted to annex 2,200 acres of land near Meadow Wood Road. Now, there are plans for a data center to be built on the land. The city says it has received concept plans for the center, which is called Project Patriot. Project Patriot's website says the data center is being planned as a "self-sufficient campus with on-site power generation and privately funded infrastructure designed to minimize impacts on local utilities, public services, and taxpayers." Recall petition Local perspective: Some Granbury residents believe their city's leaders didn't disclose enough information about the potential data center before the land was annexed. Those concerns led to 15% of the city's population signing a petition to recall Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt and four city council members, with over 1,300 signatures on the petition. "They tend to do this. We speak, they don’t hear what we’re saying," Rachael Jacobson, a resident, tells FOX 4's David Sentendrey. "Maybe they hear it, but they don’t hear what we’re saying — and then the rest of this show goes on and they just do whatever they want." "The city council, whatever their intentions may be, neglected to listen to the citizens and the citizens have decided they’re not going to tolerate than anymore — to the tune of over 1,300 signatures on multiple recall petitions," said Alex Wolf, a Granbury resident and Granbury City Council-elect. Granbury Mayor Jim Jarratt "A circus" The other side: "I will not resign." At Monday's Granbury City Council meeting, Jarratt and city council members defended themselves. Jarratt said he believes there are procedural issues with the recall petition. "The petition against me does not explain any substance whatsoever, which makes it impossible for me to defend my public record against a generic accusation that could potentially span over the past five-and-a-half years. That’s how long I’ve been your mayor." When Granbury City Councilman Skip Overdier began speaking against the recall petition, dozens of Granbury residents walked out of the meeting. Rachael Jacobson described the meeting as "a circus." "You could tell they weren’t listening when we spoke during public comment." What's next: Petitioners are hoping to get the recall on the November ballot. A court battle over the proposed data center is also looming. City officials say any official development plans for the data center would go through the city's normal review process, and would need to meet zoning and development standards before approval. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Granbury City Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia is offering carbon market incentive schemes to global business leaders investing in green projects across the archipelago, Coordinating Minister for Food Zulkifli Hasan announced during the 81st UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC 2026. Addressing more than 20 global corporate executives at the High-Level and CEO Forum on Low-Emission Rice and Sustainable Agriculture in New York, the minister emphasized that carbon pricing mechanisms would allow investors to unlock additional financial value from verifiable emissions reductions in Indonesia. "Indonesia is facing a waste emergency that must be addressed immediately, one of which is through waste-to-energy. Therefore, the government is encouraging green investment in the waste sector as a priority," Zulkifli said in a statement on Tuesday (September 29). Zulkifli outlined three primary sectors open to green investment: sustainable agriculture through low-emission rice cultivation, waste-to-energy processing, and marine conservation through blue carbon development. As chair of the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, he said Jakarta is streamlining regulatory frameworks and strengthening carbon trading governance to ensure high-credibility carbon assets. A key step came on July 6, 2026, when the Financial Services Authority (OJK) enacted POJK No. 10/2026, mandating that all exchange-traded carbon units be formally registered under the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). OJK data as of August 31, 2026, revealed that 159 service users have registered on the Indonesian Carbon Exchange since its inception on September 26, 2023. Total transaction volume reached 1.98 million tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e), with a cumulative value of Rp93.90 billion (approximately US$5.24 million). Government projections indicate that the carbon pricing framework could mobilize up to US$5.80 billion in green investment while reducing greenhouse gas emissions by roughly 570 million tCO2e. Beyond waste management, Indonesia is seeking various international partners to scale up low-emission rice production to strengthen domestic food security while reducing agricultural methane emissions. Zulkifli noted that implementing low-emission rice cultivation on a large scale requires technological support, financing, market certainty, and clear economic benefits for farmers. He added that climate action must translate into concrete, field-level projects that directly benefit farmers and coastal communities. artigo.texto: Data Center On-Site Power Brings Pollution Risks Closer to Home The data center industry’s shift to on-site power generation to overcome grid constraints is creating new environmental compliance challenges. New Jersey’s recent $1.07 million penalty against a Vineland, New Jersey, AI data center operator has put a broader challenge for the industry into focus: Operators seeking alternatives to constrained electricity grids must also account for the environmental consequences of generating power on-site. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the facility installed and operated 62 natural gas generators without required permits. A state official announced the enforcement action on Sept. 22. The operator, identified as DataOne, disputed NJDEP’s determination regarding the temporary generators but said it would apply for air permits and is communicating with regulators, according to the New Jersey Monitor. As AI buildouts accelerate, on-site generation is changing what communities need to understand about proposed computing facilities. Electricity supply, air emissions, cooling demand, and noise increasingly belong in the same discussion. “AI data centers are increasingly becoming power plants as well as computing facilities,” said Abhijit Sunil, senior analyst at Forrester, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “AI infrastructure can now be deployed faster than traditional permitting and inspection processes were designed to oversee.” Behind-the-Meter Power Doesn’t Eliminate Environmental Costs Sunil said on-site generation, often using natural gas, has emerged in conversations with data center vendors as one response to grid constraints. Other approaches include battery storage and shifting workloads to align with grid availability. Generating electricity behind the meter can reduce a facility’s demand on the utility network, but that does not, by itself, establish an environmental benefit. “Taking pressure off the grid doesn’t eliminate an environmental cost,” Sunil said. “Taking pressure off the grid doesn’t eliminate an environmental cost." – Abhijit Sunil, senior analyst, Forrester For nearby residents, relevant effects include combustion-related air pollutants (such as NOx, CO, and particulate matter) and continuous or frequent noise. Evaluating a project, therefore, requires more than comparing a data center’s electricity demand with available grid capacity. Sunil recommends assessments that encompass electricity consumption and grid upgrades, as well as water use, land use, emissions, and noise. Those impacts should be weighed alongside a project’s socioeconomic benefits. The broader accounting also helps distinguish different concerns: greenhouse gas emissions, local air pollution, water consumption, and continuous noise are separate issues requiring different measurements and responses. Operator Priorities Skew Toward Power and Uptime Power availability and operational reliability can dominate investment decisions, leaving other environmental issues with less attention. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers within enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that a recent IDC worldwide operator survey found energy efficiency and renewable energy among the leading resilience and sustainability priorities. He noted that waste heat reuse ranked last, while reducing water usage was third from the bottom. “We see operators more concerned about rising power intensity and operational risk, and less inclined to commit to environmental and sustainability targets,” Fernandes said. Those findings suggest that improvements in energy performance should not be treated as a proxy for progress across every environmental measure. An operator’s efficiency strategy does not explain how it manages cooling demand, local noise, or the operation of on-site generators. For communities and customers, the distinction makes facility-level information important. Broad sustainability commitments offer limited insight into how a particular site operates and how its impact changes over time. Make Site-Level Impacts Transparent Sunil suggested that large facilities with on-site generation disclose their equipment, fuel, capacity, and permitting status. Reporting should also cover runtime, electricity generated, greenhouse gases, and relevant local air pollutants. Material changes to generation or cooling capacity should trigger updated disclosures, he said, because information presented during initial project discussions may no longer describe the operating facility. “The goal for new projects should be that communities [are not] surprised at any given stage,” Sunil said. He argues that monitoring should make impacts visible before residents experience consequences, rather than leaving neighbors to identify changes through generator noise or other observable effects. That recommendation goes beyond publishing an annual corporate environmental report. It requires information that connects a specific operation to the surrounding community. Permitting Lapses Can Halt Operations Across the industry, environmental obligations depend on the equipment and activities at each site. Speaking generally about data center operations, Pat Fanning, a trial attorney at Lathrop GPM, distinguished computing equipment from associated power infrastructure. “The servers in operation within a data center would not typically be associated with the generation of environmental pollutants,” Fanning told Data Center Knowledge. He noted that complaints about facilities often concern continuous low-frequency noise from cooling or HVAC systems, as well as demands on electricity and water resources. It also highlights how early integration of IT and physical infrastructure planning, supply chain management, standardized designs, and advanced tools such as EPMS, DCIM, and digital twins can help reduce project risk and improve capacity management. artigo.texto: ABEGÁS DEFENDE GÁS NATURAL NO REDATA E ALERTA PARA RISCO DE INSEGURANÇA JURÍDICA A Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado (Abegás) defende a inclusão do gás natural na regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), argumentando que o combustível pode desempenhar papel complementar às fontes renováveis na garantia da segurança energética necessária à operação dos data centers no Brasil. Segundo o diretor executivo da Abegás, Marcelo Mendonça, o gás natural não deve ser tratado como concorrente das fontes renováveis, mas como uma alternativa complementar diante da necessidade de fornecimento contínuo de energia. “Ele atua de forma complementar para garantir a segurança energética indispensável à viabilização dos data centers. Defender a neutralidade tecnológica é permitir que esses projetos avancem sem sobrecarregar o sistema de transmissão nem encarecer a conta de energia para os demais consumidores”, afirmou. A entidade argumenta que a característica intermitente de parte das fontes renováveis reforça a necessidade de alternativas capazes de assegurar o fornecimento contínuo exigido pela operação dos centros de processamento de dados. Para a Abegás, a geração a gás pode contribuir para a implantação de projetos de forma mais descentralizada, especialmente nas regiões Sudeste e Sul, onde a expansão dos data centers poderia exigir investimentos elevados em transmissão de energia devido à concentração de parte da geração renovável no Nordeste. Na avaliação da associação, a possibilidade de utilizar geração a gás próxima aos centros de consumo também pode reduzir a necessidade de novos investimentos em linhas de transmissão e evitar a transferência de custos adicionais para os demais consumidores de energia elétrica. A entidade defende, assim, que a regulamentação do Redata adote o princípio da neutralidade tecnológica e considere as diferentes alternativas disponíveis para garantir a segurança energética dos empreendimentos. Ao mesmo tempo, a Abegás manifesta preocupação com a possibilidade de a regulamentação do regime ultrapassar os limites estabelecidos pelo Congresso Nacional. Segundo a associação, a inclusão de medidas que extrapolem o escopo da legislação aprovada poderia provocar questionamentos por meio de Projetos de Decreto Legislativo (PDLs), aumentando a insegurança jurídica e dificultando a implementação dos projetos de data centers. “Contudo, nos preocupa que uma regulamentação que extrapole o que foi decidido pelo Congresso crie insegurança jurídica e trave esses investimentos essenciais para o país. Reiteramos nosso compromisso com o desenvolvimento do setor e com a construção de um ambiente regulatório que reconheça os benefícios e as externalidades positivas do gás natural para a infraestrutura digital do país”, declarou Mendonça.

artigo.texto: Two Workshops on EU-China ETS Cooperation Successfully Held in Wuhan On 16 September, the EU-funded project ‘EU-China Dialogue and Cooperation on ETS-related Policies and Measures’ organised two public workshops as official side-events during the 2026 China Carbon Market Conference in Wuhan. The workshops were hosted jointly by the European Commission and the Chinese Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE). It brought together senior officials, experts, and crucial stakeholders from China, the European Union, Brazil, the World Bank and UNEP, offering the audience engaged in China's national carbon market and observers from other parts of the world the latest policy developments and insightful opinions on the EU, Chinese, Brazilian, and international carbon markets, as well as the priorities of ongoing EU-China ETS cooperation. European Union, 2026 The morning workshop presented the main outcomes of the Joint Research Activity (JRA) on the conception and implementation of allowance auctioning in China's national ETS. Mr. LU Shize, Deputy Director-General of the Department of Climate Change of MEE, received three joint research reports on behalf of MEE from Mette QUINN, Deputy Director for Carbon Markets and Clean Mobility at DG CLIMA, and thanked the EU for its continued support to the joint research. The afternoon session turned to the important role and challenges of cap setting, a fundamental element for the credibility and environmental integrity of any emissions trading system. Following opening remarks by Ms QUINN and Mr LU, Ms QUINN shared the European Union's experience of setting the cap under the EU ETS. A highlight of the afternoon was the formal launch of the Joint Research on cap-setting supported under the EU project. European Union, 2026 Both workshops underscored the value of lessons-learnt from EU ETS on core ETS design elements. By combining international experience with China's specific institutional context, the project's joint research activities aim to provide a solid evidence base to support the inauguration of allowance auctioning and cap setting under China's national carbon market. Learn more about the ETS project https://www.eu-chinaets.org/

artigo.texto: MAHOMET — When you ask communities if they’re interested in data-center development, responses can vary, says Clean Cloud Energy CEO Raj Keswani. “You have some communities that say, ‘Yes, absolutely. This solves a lot of problems for us. The tax revenue’s important. We really welcome you,’” he told The News-Gazette. “Other times, communities say, ‘We want to hear what you have to say, no promises. We’re willing to listen.’ And then there are other communities that say, ‘You’re the 15th data center. We have no interest in anything more than the 14 we already have. No, thank you.’” Keswani said that when the company started to gauge interest in Champaign County, the response was in the middle: “No promises, willing to listen.” The village of Mahomet announced Monday that it has been in preliminary talks with Clean Cloud Energy, which is interested in potentially building a data-center campus “in a rural area west of Champaign.” This has included discussions around language for a possible development agreement. The company referred to the potential project as the Rising Edge Data Center. The area being considered by the company is outside of village limits but within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, which grants the village “certain planning and subdivision authority involving the property,” Mahomet officials said. “The Village has a responsibility to consider economic-development opportunities that could strengthen our tax base and support the long-term financial health of our community,” said Mayor Jason Tompkins. “At the same time, the size and nature of this proposal require careful and thoughtful evaluation. We must fully understand its infrastructure needs, financial benefits, environmental considerations and effects on residents before making any decision.” Tompkins added that the public will have the opportunity to review “any officially submitted proposal,” as well as to submit questions and comments to the planning and zoning commission and the village board. Village officials emphasized that, at this point, all conversations have been “strictly preliminary and exploratory,” with no formal proposal submitted to the village board at this time. Clean Cloud Energy likewise said in a statement Monday that it is “in the early stages of clarifying whether a data center is possible.” The company added that, if approved and built, the project would be expected to generate millions of tax dollars annually “to support schools, emergency services, and community infrastructure.” Maggie Bruns, executive director of the Prairie Rivers Network, said that the environmental nonprofit has been aware of Clean Cloud Energy’s past interest in developing a data center in the area. “We were surprised to learn today about the steps being taken by the Village of Mahomet to further explore the development of a data center just outside village limits,” she said. “We are, of course, concerned by this possibility and are seeking more information as we assess its potential impacts. Their interest underscores the simultaneous need for strong protections locally as we work to pass statewide protections in Springfield.” When asked about the size of the potential project, Clean Cloud Energy Director of Development Clark Bixler said that Ameren is studying the transmission system to determine what size of project could be supported at this location. According to the company’s website, Clean Cloud Energy develops campuses for hyperscale data centers. Bixler said that, in addition to being within the village of Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, the potential project area is also within Champaign County’s jurisdiction. The county currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is currently set to end in April. The county has also created a data-center activities task force to draft planning and zoning regulations for such developments. According to Bixler, the timing of the project also will depend on the company’s work with Ameren, though he said that Clean Cloud Energy would like to see the first phase online in late 2028, with construction starting in late 2027 to early 2028. “Data centers are built in phases based on the amount of power that’s available and the amount of infrastructure they can construct in a year,” he explained. “So depending on what’s available to be delivered through Ameren’s Rising substation, there could be more than one stage that’s built. We’ll still ultimately be talking about the total project in terms of one size, but it may be more than what could be built in a particular, individual phase.” Clean Cloud Energy said in its announcement that the project’s energy usage would not affect “the price or availability of power to the community.” “The project would pay for any needed upgrades and bear the full burden of any improvements to the local energy and transmission infrastructure,” the company said. “The energy that we’re talking about is coming from the grid. It’s not energy consumed by the county now; it’s coming from beyond the county along transmission lines,” Keswani said. “And all that is being studied as we speak. So our power and energy needs are not cannibalizing anything the county is using now.” “In order to support a data center, you need a strong grid infrastructure,” Bixler said. “So this area has that through the Rising substation.” The company also said that it will use “zero water” to cool the project. “The coolant is an engineered solution that will be trucked on-site with a small amount of water that may be used during the initial fill,” company officials said. “The only potable water used would be for the needs of the employees in the building — sinks, bathrooms, and canteen — just like any other business or manufacturing facility. artigo.texto: Alabama data center law takes effect Oct. 1: Here’s what it means for your power bill BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC) - Kirsten Allen bought her home in Birmingham’s Oxmoor Valley for quiet streets and long-term equity. Now, a data center and substation are planned near her property and she has broad concerns about what’s ahead. “We got notified through our HOA that Oxmoor Valley was targeted for a data center,” Allen said. “There was a meeting at our community center so we could learn more about the impact it would have. That’s where I got really involved, because I realized a lot of the impact was going to be on our resources and that the residents were going to pay the price, while the data center was getting tax incentives and cheap property.” Those concerns also involve whether the data center will increase her utility bills. “Both Alabama Power and Birmingham Water have said, ‘Oh, there won’t be any rate increases,’” Allen said. “But none of us homeowners have gotten any contracts saying this is a guarantee.” The closest thing Allen may get to that guarantee is a new law that goes into effect Oct. 1, which sets the rules the state must use to decide whether a data center’s contract keeps its costs off other customers’ bills. A WBRC 6 News investigation examined the law, the contracts filed since the commission began reworking its review process and how much of that process the public is allowed to see. The reason it matters to every ratepayer: Traditionally, electric utilities build infrastructure and spread the cost to everyone who uses the grid. “The utility builds all that infrastructure and then it spreads the cost to everyone, and we all pay for that infrastructure through our monthly bills,” said Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard Law School’s Electricity Law Initiative, which studied whether regulators can shield residential customers from data center costs. “Figuring out the right formula to apportion these costs among all different users is always a source of controversy.” What the law requires The law applies to data centers that need 150 megawatts or more of electricity at peak demand in Alabama Power’s service territory. For perspective, that’s about as much electricity as roughly 95,000 average Alabama homes use in a month while running around the clock, based on federal energy data. Those data centers sign large-load contracts with the utility and those contracts must be approved by the state’s utility regulators, the Alabama Public Service Commission (APSC). Under the law, the APSC can approve a data center energy contract if it’s expected to: - Pay the extra costs the utility takes on to serve it: Power generation, transmission lines, fuel and taxes. - Benefit the utility’s other customers, weighing whether the deal could lower costs for other customers, makes Alabama Power’s system more efficient, and benefits the local economy. APSC President Cynthia Almond explained the law isn’t much different than customer protections the commission had already put in place to consider these contracts. “We require that data centers pay their fair share of any incremental costs that are incurred from their project,” Almond explained, noting all additional costs for transmission, energy generation or infrastructure to service this data center must be paid by the company bringing the data center. “The second thing is that, due to the increased revenue from the data center, there be downward pressure on rates for existing customers. That’s you and me.” Other items include billing requirements, minimum contract lengths and some costs to be paid up front, according to Almond. The public versions of the contracts are heavily redacted. The pricing, contract length and minimum billing terms are blacked out. There’s no public hearing and no public vote. The APSC and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office, which represents ratepayers in the proceedings, receive unredacted copies. Alabama Power declined an on-camera interview, but defended the redactions in writing. “Publishing negotiated terms could weaken Alabama Power’s ability to secure strong protections for existing customers in future negotiations, as well as the data center customer’s ability to negotiate elsewhere,” stated company spokesperson Teisha Wallace. When asked what Almond would tell people who are wary of that secrecy, she said “Times are changing. Transparency is important, and we have ways of being more transparent than we used to be able to do, frankly. So, I’m hopeful that we will be able to put anything out in the open, that we’re able to put out in the open.” Energy Alabama, a clean energy nonprofit, believes there’s a way to build data center infrastructure in a way that won’t impact residential ratepayers, but says transparency is key. “Even if everybody is doing the right thing, if you’re not showing your work, no one’s going to believe you,” said Energy Alabama’s executive director, Daniel Tait. While the law goes into effect Oct 1, the APSC still has broad authority to determine how it will review these contracts and how much access the public will have. On July 8, the APSC opened a proceeding asking the public how it should review these contracts. It also extended the review window for data center contracts filed during that proceeding to 45 days, up from the 10-day review that’s been standard since 1996. (If the APSC doesn’t disapprove a contract within the review period, it’s automatically deemed approved.) The commission has proposed a 60-day window going forward. The Alabama Attorney General’s Office, Alabama Power, Energy Alabama and other businesses and residents filed written statements in that proceeding. Three large-load contracts have been filed since the proceeding began in July: - ADC Holdings, LLC - connected to the Nebius AI project in Oxmoor Valley, near Allen’s home has been deemed approved. - Wooster, LLC and APLD BHM-01 LLC (tied to Applied Digital in Tuscaloosa County) are still under review. American Battery Technology entered the present session with a clear catalyst: small speculative companies are attracting selective interest where financing visibility or a tangible commercial milestone supports the story. Investors now have to separate a tradeable reaction from a development that changes how the business should be understood. That distinction depends on company evidence, not on the direction of the broader tape. Readers tracking Penny Stocks can use this development as a starting point while keeping the analysis tied to American Battery Technology and its own disclosures. A fresh signal with conditions attached At its heart, American Battery Technology is exposed to battery materials and recycling. The market will want a direct link between todays attention and the operating model. That link could appear in customer activity, a clearer product cycle, stronger execution or more disciplined use of capital. Where execution becomes decisive For American Battery Technology, proof should arrive through repeatable operations rather than a single announcement. Readers should listen for specific explanations of demand, delivery and spending. Consistency across several updates would show that the company is building a pattern instead of benefiting from one favorable moment. The sector comparison The comparison with other penny stocks names is useful but limited. Businesses in the same category can face very different funding needs, customer cycles and competitive pressures. American Battery Technology must earn its own valuation through evidence that fits its model. What could reverse sentiment For American Battery Technology, the cautious view starts with timing. A sound strategy can still disappoint when adoption, delivery or approvals take longer than investors expect. Any shift in priorities or unexplained change in language would make the current case harder to defend. Evidence to seek next For American Battery Technology, a practical watchlist includes customer activity, competitive responses, capital allocation and the reliability of management guidance. No single item settles the case, but together they reveal whether the company is creating a repeatable advantage. What the setup means For now, American Battery Technology offers a credible watch item rather than a settled verdict. The decisive issue is whether management can turn attention around battery materials and recycling into consistent delivery. The next disclosure should make that judgment easier. How to read the next update For American Battery Technology, investors can keep the review grounded by separating fresh information from the share-price reaction. The useful questions are straightforward: did management clarify the source of demand, explain the resources needed to deliver, and identify the risks that could interrupt progress? Answers supported by operating detail deserve more weight than broad optimism. If the next update connects those points to battery materials and recycling, the thesis may become easier to defend. If the discussion stays general, the market may continue to debate the quality and durability of the opportunity. A closer company-level reading A useful reading of American Battery Technology begins with the mechanics of battery materials and recycling, not with the popularity of the wider theme. The company has its own customer mix, execution history and set of constraints. Those features determine how quickly an opportunity can become a repeatable business result. The next update should therefore be judged for specificity: who is responding, which priority comes first and what could still interrupt delivery.

artigo.texto: Pune, 28th September 2026: COEP Technological University is set to establish India's first indigenous battery prototyping and pilot-scale research and development centre at its Research Park in Chikhali, with an investment of over ₹800 crore. The university has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with JSW Projects, part of the JSW Group, to develop the facility in two phases. The proposed centre will focus on developing indigenous lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced battery technologies. It will support battery cell design, simulation, prototyping and testing, providing a platform for research and innovation in India. The project is expected to strengthen the country's battery manufacturing ecosystem and reduce dependence on imported technologies. The project will be developed in two phases, with a combined investment of more than ₹800 crore. The first phase will focus on establishing a cell research and development centre to design, simulate and prototype lithium-ion, sodium-ion and other advanced chemistry-based battery cells. The second phase will establish a cell validation facility capable of developing battery cells with capacities ranging from 100 to 600 ampere-hours (Ah). The facility will support testing and validation, helping develop battery technologies suited to Indian conditions. The partnership is expected to create more than 1,000 employment opportunities across the battery technology ecosystem. The centre will also provide students with access to advanced battery research and practical training, strengthening industry-academia collaboration. The project is expected to support the development of electric vehicles, grid-scale energy storage and clean energy solutions. It will also contribute to India's long-term goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2070. JSW Group Chairman Sajjan Jindal said, "Battery cells will become the new fuel of this century, and the time has come to manufacture them in India. Our partnership with COEP, which has a 172-year legacy in engineering, will bring a new dimension to industry-academia collaboration. It will also help design, test and validate battery cells suited to Indian climatic conditions." COEP Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud said, "This project has the potential to develop indigenous alternatives for battery manufacturing. It will give students an opportunity to learn advanced battery technologies while providing a platform for research, innovation and technological development." The MoU was signed by COEP Registrar Dr D. N. Sonawane and JSW Group Executive Vice-President Naresh Lalwani. Vice-Chancellor Dr Sunil Bhirud, RIIL Director Dr S. P. Mahajan, Dean Dr P. A. Sadgir, Dr Ranjit Date, Dr Sarika Kelkar, Mandar Bhatwadekar and Officer on Special Duty Dr Avinash Joshi were among those present.

artigo.texto: Commission Endorses Milwaukee Data Center Moratorium After Fiery Hearing After two hours of testimony, planners unanimously backed a one-year halt on new facilities citywide. A proposed data center moratorium for the City of Milwaukee received its first endorsement Monday, but only after nearly two hours of discussion on the proposal’s legal limits and testimony for and against it. The proposal would prohibit construction of new data centers for up to one year. Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic said AI and data centers have become some of the public’s hottest issues. “That’s what this is all about. Listening to what the people wanted,” said Dimitrijevic. “What’s happening is technology is moving at such a fast speed. We’re in an interesting time to live right now. Government can’t keep up, but we’re being asked to, though, and we need to rise to that occasion.” She framed the proposal as a “pause” and not an end to data center development. The pause, she said, would allow the city to craft zoning regulations to respond to the energy and water use of data centers, as well as their design and noise impacts. “This is not us closing the book,” said Dimitrijevic. The moratorium would be rescinded after one year or after a zoning framework is adopted, whichever comes first. The alderwoman has already introduced a draft framework, but the proposal has yet to move through the public hearing process. Department of City Development Planning Manager Tanya Fonseca said the moratorium is a “stopgap” measure because the current zoning code doesn’t even define what a data center is. The proposal has the support of Mayor Cavalier Johnson and his administration. A number of the individuals who spoke in support of the moratorium, including Stacy Smiter and Mabel Lamb, also showed up to oppose the redevelopment of the vacant Midtown Center Walmart, 5825 W. Hope Ave., into a mixed-use facility with a library, self-storage complex, affordable housing and a 19,000-square-foot data center. Dimitrijevic’s proposed data center zoning regulations, developed before the proposal was revealed, wouldn’t have affected it because it was under 20,000 square feet. Support for a moratorium is far from unanimous. Joel Roberts, a tech entrepreneur who founded Shepherd Traffic and a doctoral student at UW-Milwaukee, said data centers would provide the city tax revenue and that a number of facilities already existed in the city, like the Forest County Potawatomi Community‘s data center at 3135 W. Highland Blvd. “We’re not morons. We’re smart. We can do this,” he said. But the general manager of the Potawatomi data center, Data Holdings CTO Ryan Brooks, said he supports the moratorium. “It is a public data center, not a hyperscaler. It has been here operating in Milwaukee since 2013. We have about 80 customers,” said Brooks. Unlike the billion-dollar “hyperscale” campuses that Microsoft, Oracle and others are building, Brooks said the Potawatomi facility is modest in scale, solar powered and a good neighbor. A pending amendment to the proposal, listed as being offered by Ald. Robert Bauman, would exempt Potawatomi from the moratorium. It previously appeared in the council’s legislative file but is no longer included. Potawatomi did not respond to an earlier request for comment on the proposed exemption. Letters in opposition to the moratorium were submitted by Andrew Davis of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce and Chris Mambu Rasch of Building Advantage. “The city should reject the moratorium and instead act promptly through its existing public-review process to establish clear, predictable and enforceable standards that address community concerns without sacrificing economic growth, job creation and Milwaukee’s regional competitiveness,” wrote Davis in a letter to the council. “Rather than implementing industrywide pauses or reverting to overly restrictive de facto bans, the Common Council should use the special use or conditional use zoning process. A formalized special use review ensures the city can rigorously evaluate legitimate concerns — such as energy grid capacity, noise, sustainability and neighborhood compatibility — without shutting the door on high-value, responsible development,” wrote Mambu Rasch. But many supporters spoke to concerns about unknown impacts. “We need a pause. What we can’t do is approve development when we don’t know what the impact would be,” said Metcalfe Park Community Bridges Deputy Director Melody McCurtis. She said if development was allowed to occur immediately on land already zoned for heavy industrial use, it would disproportionately impact Black and Brown residents because of where that land is located. Ald. Alex Brower said the economy has become a “techno-nightmare” and he’s committed to working to address the resulting issues. After more than an hour of public testimony, acting Commission Chair Allyson Nemec and Commissioner Ranell Washington thanked all of the participants for presenting a wide range of viewpoints. The commission voted unanimously for the moratorium. Commissioners Stephanie Bloomingdale and Catrina Crane were excused from the meeting. The proposal next heads to the Common Council for review. In addition to Dimitrijevic and Brower, the proposal is cosponsored by Sharlen P. Moore, Bauman and Russell W. Stamper, II. artigo.texto: Located in Terang, in the state of Victoria, the project has a capacity of 100 MW/200 MWh, helping to strengthen the stability and resilience of the electricity grid. The commissioning of Terang marks a crucial milestone for FRV Australia, as it becomes the company’s first standalone battery energy storage project, increasing its portfolio of operational assets in Australia to nine and adding dispatchable energy capacity to FRV Australia's predominantly solar generation portfolio. The project was further bolstered by an $7 million grant awarded through the second round of the Victorian Government’s Energy Innovation Fund (EIF), supporting the deployment of new grid-forming inverter technology. This initiative forms part of the Victorian Government’s efforts to achieve its target of 65 percent renewable energy generation by 2030. Canadian Solar served as EPC contractor for the project, with TEC-C delivering the balance-of-plant works. The facility incorporates 48 SolBank 3.0 e battery containers, manufactured by e-Storage, and 38 SMA inverters. The project supported approximately 40 full-time-equivalent roles during the construction and generated business and procurement opportunities for local companies and suppliers. As part of their commitment to the communities in which they operate, FRV Australia supported several social initiatives throughout the development of the project, including sponsorship programmes for the Australian Indigenous Education Foundation (AIEF) and the Terang Mortlake Netball Club. “The commissioning of Terang marks a defining moment for FRV Australia” said Michael Steiner, CEO of FRV Australia. “The project demonstrates our ability to develop and operate utility-scale dispatchable energy infrastructure that supports Australia’s energy transition. It provides critical firming capacity during peak hours while helping to strengthen grid reliability. We are proud to contribute to Victoria’s energy future through a solution that combines sustainability, innovation and benefits for local communities.” Terang forms part of FRV Australia's expanding battery energy storage portfolio in Victoria. The company is developing the 250 MW/500 MWh Gnarwarre Battery Energy Storage System, currently under construction and targeted for completion by the end of 2027. artigo.texto: St. Louis officials say they will analyze financial estimates for a data center that is projected to generate millions in tax revenue for the city and impose fines on the project if it doesn’t meet them. Development group TerraWatt has told the city that its planned $3 billion data center in Midtown near the historic Armory building will generate $445 million in tax revenue over the next 10 years. A 120-megawatt data center will be built in the old Famous-Barr warehouse on Market Street as part of the campus. The tax revenue estimate comes from the developer and its consultant, Steadfast City, which provided the numbers to the city’s Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority earlier this month. But Mayor Cara Spencer and other city officials say they want to ensure the city receives the tax revenue developers have promised from the project. They plan to do so through a recently agreed-upon community benefit agreement and financial analysis from the city’s development arm. “This was a first of its kind for the city, so it was important to set a strong precedent for accountability and enforcement for environmental, workforce and revenue,” said Casey Millburg, Spencer’s chief of staff, of the agreement. “It was negotiated over many months.” The data center has been a focal point of conflict among anti-data center groups, concerned residents and city leaders over the past year as the project has slowly grown from proposal to reality. Previously, Spencer and other city leaders have said the project’s revenue could have significant benefits for the city, St. Louis Public Schools and other local taxing authorities that would receive revenue from it. “I think where we need to land here — where I want us to land as a city — is recognizing the economic benefit and protecting the community to the best of our ability,” Spencer said in July. City spokeswoman told St. Louis Public Radio that Spencer believes the city needs to keep a “keen eye” on the project. As a result, the project will undergo a financial analysis by St. Louis Development Corporation, the city’s development arm. Typically, SLDC conducts analysis only if developers seek tax incentives. In a statement, Steadfast City CEO Cecilia Dvorak said an independent assessment by the city would be welcomed. Jamboretz said city officials believe the project will be the first to undergo an analysis by SLDC while not seeking incentives. Per the recently agreed-upon community benefit agreement between the data center’s developers and city officials, it may not seek tax incentives from the city. The city sometimes uses tax incentives to attract developers to build, often delaying the city’s ability to see the full impact of a development for years. The agreement guarantees the city’s coffers will see an immediate impact from the project. The community benefit agreement also provides for the city to seek damages if the project fails to meet its annual tax revenue projections, Millburg said. She said fees will enforce the economic promises made by TerraWatt. For instance, the city will charge the developer $15,000 in damages for every $100,000 by which annual tax revenues fall short of the project’s projections. In a larger example, the city stated that if the actual tax revenue reported by the project in the first full year of operations is $60 million — nearly $3.1 million short of its goal — the developer will pay the city $476,249, or roughly 31 additional payments of $15,000 each. That amount must be paid within 60 days of reporting the shortfall. The community benefit plan also calls for TerraWatt to pay the city $15.7 million, with nearly $9 million of that paid by spring 2027, according to the agreement. Regarding jobs, the developers have agreed that by July 30 of the year in which the project’s building permit is issued, the center must employ at least 25 people. The center must employ at least 50 people by the second year, eventually increasing to at least 100. Millburg said the city will assess a $2,000 penalty for every job below the required target. The city also has the power to revoke the data center’s permits for uncorrected noncompliance on jobs, noise, utility and renewable energy requirements. Construction on the project, colloquially known as the Armory data center, is expected to begin next August. However, last week, David Daneshforooz, CEO and co-founder of TerraWatt, filed suit against the city, arguing that the city’s requirements exceed its powers and would make construction of the project impossible. Additionally, several data center opponents recently filed suit against the city to stop the development.

artigo.texto: A expansão da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e da digitalização das empresas está acelerando a demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados no Brasil. No eixo São Paulo–Campinas, esse movimento já aparece nos números: a capacidade operacional de data centers cresceu 91% em apenas um ano, passando de 346 megawatts (MW) no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 661 MW no mesmo período de 2026. O avanço coloca São Paulo como o terceiro mercado primário das Américas com maior crescimento percentual no período, atrás apenas de Atlanta e Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, segundo levantamento da Cushman & Wakefield. A perspectiva é de uma nova rodada de investimentos. Atualmente, o corredor São Paulo–Campinas possui 250 MW em construção e outros 2.066 MW planejados. Redata pode acelerar novos projetos O crescimento ganha um novo componente com o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), sancionado em 15 de setembro. O regime prevê a suspensão de tributos federais sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação, ampliação e modernização de data centers, incluindo Imposto de Importação, PIS/Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Importação e IPI sobre itens elegíveis. O incentivo contempla estruturas direcionadas à computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e inteligência artificial. “O mercado brasileiro já vinha apresentando crescimento consistente antes da sanção do Redata. A redução dos custos de implantação pode favorecer o avanço dos projetos, mas sua viabilidade continuará dependendo de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conectividade, terrenos adequados, licenciamento e segurança regulatória”, afirma Dennys Andrade, Head de Market Research & Business Intelligence da Cushman & Wakefield. 96% da capacidade está ocupada A expansão ocorre em um mercado com pouca capacidade disponível. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a capacidade operacional avançou 6%, de 623 MW para 661 MW. Ao mesmo tempo, o volume em construção saltou 69%, passando de 148 MW para 250 MW. Mesmo com a ampliação da oferta, a vacância ficou em apenas 4,1%, o que significa que aproximadamente 96% da capacidade de colocation estava ocupada. Os 2.066 MW atualmente planejados representam mais de três vezes a capacidade operacional do eixo São Paulo–Campinas. O pipeline brasileiro também supera a soma dos projetos previstos em Querétaro, Santiago e Bogotá, que alcança aproximadamente 1,47 GW. O volume planejado, porém, não significa que todos os projetos serão efetivamente construídos. Além do capital necessário, a expansão depende de disponibilidade de energia e acesso à rede de transmissão, conectividade, equipamentos especializados, licenciamento e demanda contratada. “O impacto do Redata será medido pela capacidade de transformar projetos planejados em infraestrutura operacional. O Brasil reúne demanda e potencial de expansão, mas energia, conectividade e velocidade de execução determinarão quais empreendimentos efetivamente sairão do papel”, acrescenta Dennys Andrade. São Paulo lidera infraestrutura na América Latina Com 661 MW operacionais, o eixo São Paulo–Campinas possui quase o dobro da capacidade de Querétaro, no México, que registra 336 MW. Santiago, no Chile, aparece com 272 MW, enquanto Bogotá, na Colômbia, possui 58 MW. A escala ainda é distante dos principais polos norte-americanos. A Virgínia soma 12.338 MW em operação e Atlanta, 3.488 MW. Em velocidade de crescimento, porém, São Paulo se aproxima desses mercados: enquanto o corredor brasileiro avançou 91% em um ano, Virgínia cresceu 97% e Atlanta, 106%. Energia pode definir próximo mapa dos data centers Embora São Paulo e Campinas concentrem a maior infraestrutura do setor no Brasil, a próxima etapa de crescimento pode abrir espaço para outras regiões. Locais com disponibilidade de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão, conectividade de alta capacidade e terrenos adequados tendem a entrar no radar dos novos projetos. Segundo o estudo da Cushman & Wakefield, a capacidade paulista poderá atingir aproximadamente 1,6 vez o volume atual até 2036. Mais do que incentivos tributários, a capacidade de transformar o volume recorde de projetos anunciados em data centers efetivamente operacionais dependerá, portanto, de uma combinação entre energia, conectividade, licenciamento e velocidade de implantação. Com IA e nuvem aumentando a necessidade de processamento, esses fatores tendem a ganhar peso na disputa pelos próximos investimentos do setor.

artigo.texto: The 15 MW/60 MWh Albispark battery energy storage system, located in Castelo Branco, is integrated with an existing 34.4 MWp solar plant, making it one of the largest battery energy storage systems currently in operation in Portugal. The project represents an important milestone for both companies. For Prosolia Energy, Albispark is its first international utility-scale battery storage [DF1] hybridisation project, while for Trina Storage it marks the company's first commissioned battery storage installation in Portugal, supporting the country's transition towards a more flexible, renewable-based electricity system. “The successful commissioning of Albispark represents an important milestone for Trina Storage in Portugal” said Gabriele Buccini, Head of Trina Storage Europe at Trinasolar. “As our first operational battery storage project in the country, it demonstrates our ability to deliver integrated utility-scale storage solutions that support Europe's evolving energy landscape. We are proud to partner with Prosolia Energy on this landmark project and look forward to supporting many more storage deployments across Portugal in the coming years.” Under the project, Trina Storage supplied an integrated utility-scale battery energy storage solution, including Elementa battery cabinets, power conversion systems (PCS), medium-voltage skids, power plant controller (PPC) and commissioning services, delivering a complete solution designed to maximise renewable energy utilisation while supporting grid flexibility. As Portugal continues to increase renewable generation, battery energy storage is becoming essential for improving grid stability, increasing renewable utilisation and providing greater operational flexibility. The Albispark project demonstrates how hybrid solar-plus-storage systems can enable renewable energy to be stored and dispatched when demand is highest, helping maximise the value of renewable generation while strengthening grid resilience. “Albispark is an important milestone for Prosolia Energy and demonstrates the value that battery storage brings to the energy transition” added Pedro Pereira da Silva, Country Manager of Prosolia Energy in Portugal. “Together with Trina Storage, we have delivered a project that improves grid flexibility and reinforces the foundations for future hybrid renewable projects in Portugal.” The commissioning of Albispark marks the beginning of Trina Storage's expansion in Portugal. In addition to this project, the company is currently supporting several battery energy storage projects across the Portuguese market[FT2] [CC3], reflecting growing demand for utility-scale storage as the country accelerates renewable energy deployment and grid modernisation. The project also forms part of Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), supporting the country's efforts to increase grid flexibility and accelerate renewable energy integration. artigo.texto: A autonomia da bateria é uma queixa comum entre os utilizadores de iPhone, que reportam sobretudo que a capacidade de armazenamento de energia vai reduzindo progressivamente ao longo dos anos. Lembrar que este tipo de degradação é normal em baterias de telemóveis e é também normal que, caso queira manter o seu dispositivo durante mais tempo, tenha de considerar a hipótese de trocar este componente se quer manter uma autonomia semelhante à que tinha quando o comprou. Mas como saber se a bateria do seu iPhone está de tal forma degradada que a substituição deve ser considerada? Para começar, deverá basear-se sobretudo na sua utilização do equipamento. A bateria ficar sem energia demasiado rápido é um sinal evidente que uma troca pode ser necessária, mas há outras “pistas” em que se pode basear. Uma maior lentidão em tarefas mais exigentes ou enquanto joga, por exemplo, é um sinal que o telemóvel está a evitar um encerramento, sendo que um sobreaquecimento da bateria quando esta não está a ser carregada também deve servir como um sinal de alerta. Felizmente, o iPhone conta com uma forma de saber o estado da sua bateria e pode ter acesso a esta informação diretamente a partir das definições do telemóvel. Para tal, só terá de entrar nas Definições e ir até à área dedicada à Bateria. Uma vez aqui, vá até ao Estado da bateria, onde poderá encontrar mais informações sobre a degradação da sua bateria. Se não tiver problemas, o estado da bateria aparecerá como Normal, com a Apple a apresentar uma mensagem onde indica que “a bateria deste iPhone está a funcionar como esperado”. Contudo, se aparecer outra mensagem, significa que está na hora de trocar a bateria para obter um melhor desempenho. Esta área dedicada à bateria conta ainda com outras informações e que lhe permite ver a Capacidade máxima de armazenamento de energia (com 100% a ser capacidade original com que adquiriu o telemóvel) e também poderá ver a Contagem de ciclos (que lhe permite saber quantos ciclos de carregamento já completou desde que adquiriu o telemóvel). Uma vez reunidos todos estes dados e se decidir proceder com a substituição da bateria, recomenda-se então que vá até uma loja da Apple ou a uma loja de reparações autorizadas para que o componente seja trocado. Leia Também: Ecrã partido ou bateria fraca? Eis quando vale a pena trocar de telemóvel

artigo.texto: Key takeaway:In the third quarter of 2026, the solid-state battery industry is at a critical stage of transition from “pilot-scale validation” to “the eve of mass production.” National-level special plans have been implemented, and the standards system is being accelerated and improved. On the materials side, sulfide electrolytes are seeing “rising volume and falling prices,” entering a transition period of ton-level volume ramp-up. On the technology side, solid-liquid (semi-solid) batteries are the first to be deployed in scenarios such as commercial vehicles, energy storage, and eVTOL, while pilot lines for all-solid-state batteries are being built intensively. Capital and industry are collaborating deeply, equipment orders continue to be secured, and downstream application scenarios are flourishing in multiple areas. At the same time, however, risks such as insufficient capacity utilization, lagging orders, and interface and manufacturing bottlenecks remain, requiring a rational view of the pace of industrialization. Foreword: Material Price Analysis—Policy Side Hot, Spot Side Cold, Sulfide “Rising Volume, Falling Prices” In Q3 2026, the solid-state battery sector showed a striking divergence: “hot on the policy side, cold on the materials spot side.” On September 28, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and six other departments issued the “15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New Battery Industry,” clarifying preliminary large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, which drove the battery sector and solid-state battery sector stronger on September 29. However, on the materials spot side, the pricing anchor centered on lithium salts declined unilaterally, and sulfide electrolytes showed a typical pattern of “rising volume, falling prices.” On lithium salts, the average spot price of battery-grade lithium carbonate in Q3 was about RMB 148,000/ton. At the end of the quarter, the quotation on September 29 for battery-grade lithium carbonate was RMB 123,000/ton, with a Q3 cumulative decline of -22.9%. On solid-state-battery-specific materials, sulfide electrolytes were the segment with the most obvious “price collapse” this quarter. From January to August 2026, China’s cumulative output of sulfide electrolytes was 70 tons, up 119.7% year-on-year, already exceeding the full-year 2025 output of 58.29 tons, but only 19.6% of the annual forecast target of 360 tons was completed. In August, capacity utilization was only 5.82%, product prices continued to plummet, and LPSC fell by more than 24% in a single month. Lithium sulfide also ramped up simultaneously: in August, China’s battery-grade lithium sulfide output was 7.79 tons, up 3.6% month-on-month and up 143% year-on-year; the January-August cumulative total was 52.9 tons, already exceeding the global full-year 2025 output of 34 tons. China’s output accounts for about 95% of the world total. It is expected that monthly output in Q4 will rise to 9–10 tons, with full-year output of 85–95 tons. On the supply side, Q3 saw the concentrated landing of “hundred-ton-level” production lines: Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and put into production in Q3; Shandong Chuanglu’s 150-ton/year solid electrolyte production line completed installation and commissioning; Capchem’s oxide electrolyte will put thousand-ton-level capacity into operation in 2026. However, in the first half of the year, both supply and demand for lithium sulfide and sulfide electrolytes were weak, and price pressure was the main theme of Q3. Anode materials were relatively resistant to decline, and additives were structurally strong. Overall, the solid-state battery materials sector has entered a transition stage from “kilogram-level transactions” to “ton-level transactions,” with the price center moving downward. Q4 needs to verify the quality of ton-level volume ramp-up. I. Solid-State Battery Materials - Electrolytes: Sulfide Upstream Volume Rises but Prices Remain Under Pressure; Oxide Capacity Takes the Lead in Scaling; Halides Accelerate Reserve The sulfide route was the most intensively expanded direction on the materials side in Q3. The high-purity lithium sulfide pilot line of a subsidiary controlled by Semcorp has been completed, with plans to achieve thousand-ton-level mass production of sulfur-halide solid electrolytes in 2026–2027. Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and entered trial production in Q3, using a self-developed liquid-phase method with costs 30%–40% lower than the mainstream solid-phase method. XTC New Energy’s high-purity lithium sulfide entered trial production. Yahua Group’s lithium sulfide pilot line entered the demonstration and design stage and has been sent to customers for samples. Tianqi Lithium’s 50-ton lithium sulfide pilot project is under construction and is expected to be completed in the second half of the year; most processes for argyrodite-type sulfide electrolyte preparation have been removed from glove boxes. Gotion Holding’s world’s first ten-thousand-ton-level high-purity lithium sulfide line started in Anqing, with plans to complete pilot testing by the end of 2026 and full mass production in 2027, with purity reaching 99.99%. Qinghai Weixiang’s 3,000-ton lithium sulfide project completed filing, with Phase I of 500 tons and Phase II of 2,500 tons, planned for completion in July 2027. Easpring’s sulfide electrolyte has entered small-scale validation with leading solid-state battery customers and has scalable supply capability. Guoci Materials’ sulfide solid electrolyte automated production line was completed, with a strategic focus on sulfides. Langu New Energy’s sulfide and halide solid electrolytes have achieved hundred-ton-level capacity, with the next step planned to expand to thousand-ton or even ten-thousand-ton levels.
