artigo.texto: Gas prices, AI data centers and Trump’s long shadow: Top takeaways from the governor’s race debate - Click here to listen to this article - Share via See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred The two candidates to become California’s next governor painted vastly different portraits of the state they want to lead during a televised CNN debate Wednesday night — though they both agreed the state faces tremendous challenges. Democrat Xavier Becerra, leading in polls, cast the state as an economic engine and a critical bulwark against the disastrous economic policies and creeping authoritarianism of the Trump administration, but also a victim of Trump policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran, that have made life less affordable and the nation less safe. Becerra said he would work hard to help struggling Californians — including by cutting red tape on housing and regulating AI to ensure it doesn’t destroy jobs — while his challenger, Republican Steve Hilton, would harm them further by backing President Trump’s agenda at every turn. Hilton, endorsed by Trump, blamed the state’s most entrenched ills on years of Democratic governance, awash in unnecessary state bureaucracy and regulation that have made it wildly unaffordable, and wrongly obsessed with fighting the president instead of bringing down costs and fixing related local issues like homelessness. Hilton said he would help struggling Californians by cutting taxes, cutting the cost of building new housing, eliminating fraud and bringing common sense back to state policy-making. Both candidates came out of the gate on offense, and at times it got intensely personal, particularly on immigration — with Becerra accusing Hilton of welcoming white immigrants into the country while rejecting Latino immigrants, and Hilton accusing Becerra of handing migrant children over to sex and labor traffickers during his time as U.S. Health and Human Services secretary. With ballots soon arriving in voters’ mailboxes and the Nov. 3 midterm election rapidly approaching, the hour-long debate — moderated by CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash in Burbank and aired live by the national news network — provided the public with its latest look at two candidates vastly different both in politics and campaign style. Becerra, a former Congress member from Los Angeles, California attorney general and Health secretary under President Biden, surged past a slate of other Democrats to win the June primary after onetime front runner Rep. Eric Swalwell dropped out of the race amid sexual assault allegations. Hilton placed second after Republican voters and others coalesced behind his message to shake up Sacramento — earning him the right to face off against Becerra in November. Hilton, a former British political aide, former Fox News host and Silicon Valley entrepreneur, has been crisscrossing the state looking for votes anywhere he can find them — an uphill battle given registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a nearly 2-to-1 margin, and opposition to Trump is widespread in the state and growing even among Republican voters. A poll this month by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times found 58% of likely voters surveyed said they support Becerra, compared with 33% who back Hilton — a slight increase to Becerra’s lead compared with an August IGS poll. California voters identified the high cost of living as their top concern, but that was followed closely by opposition to the Trump administration. The same poll found found that 76% of Republican voters in the state approve of the president’s performance, down from 83% last year. Becerra has taken a less visible approach to campaigning, with critics accusing him of intentionally keeping a low profile in an effort to cruise to victory in a state that last elected Republicans to statewide office two decades ago. “I just want to say thank you to CNN for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” Hilton said at the beginning of Wednesday’s face-off. “He’s barely been seen in public since the primary four months ago; it’s very important we have this debate.” During the debate, both candidates seemed prepared to focus on the lack of affordability — namely by blaming the other’s political party for it. But they also discussed artificial intelligence and data centers, immigration policy and, of course, Trump. Tackling gas prices, high cost of living California has some of the highest housing and energy costs in the nation, and affordability tops the list of concerns for likely voters. It also was the first issue the candidates debated. Hilton has made the cost of living a central theme of his campaign, with a plan he calls “Califordable” to cut gas prices and end income taxes on earnings up to $150,000. He blamed California’s high costs on Democrats, who have controlled the Legislature and statewide offices for more than 15 years. Hilton says he can lower costs by slashing onerous state regulations on businesses. Hilton said the “quickest way to get more money in people’s pockets is for the government to take less out” and to reduce regulations to allow more housing to be built — including in “10 new cities” he said he would help build in the state. Becerra has blamed higher prices on Trump’s tariffs and the war against Iran. In response to attacks from the U.S. and Israel, Iran has for months choked off a major oil trade route, sending global gas prices soaring — to a national average of $4.48 per gallon this month. Becerra said Hilton’s plan to end income taxes would amount to a massive tax cut for “billionaires and millionaires” that would take money from schools, healthcare and other critical services. “The math doesn’t add up to what he’s talking about. He’s going to have to take it out of somewhere. It will come out of our schools,” Becerra said. artigo.texto: $200M Indiana Battery Storage Plan Gains County Approval A planned 200-MW battery storage project in deep southwestern Indiana cleared an important local hurdle this month. Vanderburgh County Commissioners approved a request to site the $200 million Elliot Battery Energy Storage System near a Centerpoint Energy utility substation in Scott Township. The project reportedly would store excess wind and solar energy to deploy during periods of peak demand and high prices. The concept of the Elliot BESS was created by German-based RWE’s Americas renewable energy division in 2024. RWE Americas has or is developing more than 13 GW of wind, solar and battery storage capacity in the U.S. “Elliot BESS adds critical capacity to Indiana’s power grid, helping to stabilize electricity supplies and strengthen the state’s overall energy infrastructure,” reads RWE Americas website detailing the project still under development and with no announced timeline. “Through its advanced battery technology, Elliot BESS can discharge stored energy instantly, providing much-needed backup during emergency events such as storms or unexpected outages. By offering rapid-response power and improving the integration of intermittent generation like wind and solar, this project reduces reliance on imported fuels and supports state-of-the-art grid resiliency.” Total U.S. battery storage installed capacity topped 52 GW nationwide this summer and has risen 70% over the past three years, according to federal data. Energy storage systems are valued both for storing renewables and smoothing out intermittencies of solar and wind, but also having versatility to deal with fluctuations in data center loads. The facility is named after nearby Elliot Road in Vanderburgh County. The 41-acre project still requires other regulatory approvals before going into construction. RWE Americas has not named a specific battery supplier for Elliot BESS, but companies such as Samsung and SMA Americas were selected to supply the developer’s Cartwheel and Crowned Heron battery installations under way in Texas. EnergyTech is focused on the mission critical and large-scale energy users and their sustainability and resiliency goals. These include the commercial and industrial sectors, as well as the military, universities, data centers and microgrids. Many large-scale energy users such as Fortune 500 companies, and mission-critical users such as military bases, universities, healthcare facilities, public safety and data centers, shifting their energy priorities to reach net-zero carbon goals within the coming decades. These include plans for renewable energy power purchase agreements, but also on-site resiliency projects such as microgrids, combined heat and power, rooftop solar, energy storage, digitalization and building efficiency upgrades.

artigo.texto: SMM, September 30: Key points: In Q3 2026, the solid-state battery industry is at a critical stage transitioning from "pilot verification" to "pre-mass production." National-level special plans have been implemented, and the standards system is accelerating its improvement. On the materials side, sulphide is seeing "volume growth with falling prices," entering a transition period of "tonne-level" volume ramp-up. On the technology side, solid-liquid (semi-solid-state) batteries are taking the lead in commercial vehicles, energy storage, eVTOL and other application scenarios, while pilot lines for all-solid-state batteries are being intensively constructed. Capital and industry are deeply aligned, equipment orders continue to be secured, and downstream application scenarios are blossoming across multiple fronts. At the same time, risks such as insufficient capacity utilization rate, order delays, and interface and manufacturing bottlenecks remain, requiring a rational view of the pace of industrialisation. Foreword: Material price analysis – policy side hot, spot side cold; sulphide sees "volume growth with falling prices" In Q3 2026, the solid-state battery sector showed a notable divergence of "hot policy side, cold material spot side." On September 28, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other departments issued the "15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New-type Battery Industry," specifying initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, which drove the battery sector and solid-state battery sector higher on September 29. However, on the material spot side, the pricing anchor centered on lithium chemicals trended downward unilaterally, and sulphide electrolytes exhibited a typical pattern of "volume growth with falling prices." For lithium chemicals, the average spot price of battery-grade lithium carbonate in Q3 was approximately 148,000 yuan/mt. Quarter-end quotes: battery-grade lithium carbonate was 123,000 yuan/mt on September 29, down 22.9% cumulatively in Q3. For solid-state battery-specific materials, sulphide electrolytes were the segment with the most pronounced "price collapse" this quarter. From January to August 2026, China's cumulative production of sulphide electrolytes reached 70 mt, up 119.7% YoY, already exceeding the full-year 2025 total of 58.29 mt, but only 19.6% of the annual forecast target of 360 mt was achieved. In August, the capacity utilization rate was only 5.82%, and product prices continued to plummet, with LPSC falling more than 24% in a single month. Lithium sulphide ramped up in tandem: in August, China's battery-grade lithium sulphide production was 7.79 mt, up 3.6% MoM and 143% YoY. The January-August cumulative total was 52.9 mt, already exceeding the 2025 global full-year total of 34 mt. China's production accounted for approximately 95% of the global total, and monthly production is expected to rise to 9-10 mt in Q4, with a full-year total of 85-95 mt. On the supply side, Q3 saw a concentrated rollout of "hundred-tonne-level" production lines: Tinci's hundred-tonne-level lithium sulphide and solid-state electrolyte pilot line was completed and put into production in Q3; Shandong Chuanglu's 150 mt/year solid-state electrolyte production line completed installation and commissioning; Capchem's oxide electrolyte is set to bring thousand-tonne-level capacity online in 2026. However, supply and demand for lithium sulphide and sulphide electrolytes were both weak in H1, and price pressure was the main theme of Q3. The anode was relatively resilient, while additives were structurally strong. Overall, the solid-state battery materials sector has entered a transition phase shifting from "kilogram-level transactions" to "tonne-level transactions," with the price center moving lower. Q4 will need to verify the quality of tonne-level volume ramp-up. I. Solid-state battery materials 1. Electrolytes: Sulphide upstream capacity release but prices under pressure, oxide capacity first to scale up, halide reserves accelerating The sulphide route is the most intensive direction for material-side capacity expansion in Q3. SEMCORP's controlling subsidiary has completed construction of a high-purity lithium sulphide pilot line, with plans to achieve kt-level mass production of sulphide-halide solid-state electrolytes from 2026 to 2027. Tinci Materials has completed construction of a 100mt-level lithium sulphide and solid-state electrolyte pilot production line and began trial production in Q3, using a self-developed liquid-phase method with costs 30%-40% lower than mainstream solid-phase methods. XTC New Energy Materials (Xiamen) has entered trial production of high-purity lithium sulphide. Yahua Group's lithium sulphide pilot line has entered the feasibility and design stage and samples have been delivered. Tianqi Lithium's 50mt lithium sulphide pilot project is under construction, with completion expected in H2; preparation of sulphide electrolytes of the lithium argyrodite type has achieved most process steps outside the glovebox. Gotion High-tech's controlling subsidiary has launched the world's first 10kt-level high-purity lithium sulphide production line in Anqing, with plans to complete pilot testing by the end of 2026 and achieve full mass production in 2027, with purity reaching 99.99%. Qinghai Weixiang's 3,000mt lithium sulphide project has completed filing, with Phase I at 500mt and Phase II at 2,500mt, planned for completion in July 2027. Easpring Technology's sulphide electrolytes have entered the small-scale validation stage with top-tier solid-state battery clients and the company has large-scale supply capability. Sinocera Materials has completed an automated production line for sulphide solid-state electrolytes, with a strategic focus on sulphides. artigo.texto: A expansão de data centers no Brasil abriu uma discussão sobre o risco de pressão na conta de luz, conforme indica reportagem do Valor Econômico. O governo federal avalia como atender ao consumo dessas cargas, aproveitando a oferta de energia renovável do país, sem elevar os custos para os demais consumidores, e discute alternativas como o uso de gás natural e de baterias para armazenar energia nos momentos de maior geração. No setor, há divergências, entretanto, sobre o impacto desses investimentos sobre as tarifas de energia. Nos Estados Unidos, onde esses empreendimentos avançaram em escala muito maior, os preços da energia estão entre os fatores que alimentam a resistência de comunidades. No Brasil, cálculos de agentes do setor apontam para um custo adicional de cerca de R$ 7 bilhões por ano na conta de luz. O cenário considera um crescimento de 3,5 mil megawatts no consumo de energia causado pelos data centers em 2026 e parte da premissa de que a demanda será atendida pela expansão da matriz, com novas usinas eólicas e solares. A regulamentação, porém, ainda não definiu se será exigida nova geração ou se poderá ser utilizada a oferta renovável que já atende ao sistema elétrico. Setor de gás entra em alerta com possível decreto do Redata sem o insumo Reportagem da Agência Infra indica que o setor de gás natural entrou em alerta com a possível publicação de decreto nesta segunda-feira (28) para a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) sem a inclusão do insumo como fonte de suprimento energético. Segundo interlocutores do governo, o Ministério da Fazenda está articulando a edição do normativo com o entendimento de que o gás não atende à exigência de “baixa emissão de carbono”. Do outro lado, agentes do setor se apoiam no MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia), que já fez a defesa pública da inclusão da molécula na lista de fontes para atendimento dos data centers. A pasta estaria tentando segurar a publicação do decreto e ganhar tempo para que o insumo seja contemplado, disseram fontes da Esplanada. Marcelo Mendonça, diretor executivo da Abegás (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Distribuidoras de Gás Canalizado), disse à Agência Infra que os “rumores” de que o gás não será contemplado no Redata preocupam. “Existe uma falta de sintonia nesse discurso entre os ministérios, têm chegado informações equivocadas em relação ao tratamento do gás natural”, aponta. EPP pede que a Aneel retire documentos da Eneva e Global em leilão A CNN Brasil informa que a disputa sobre quem vai levar quase 2 GW em termelétricas do leilão de reserva de capacidade ganhou um novo capítulo. A EPP (Evolution Power Partners) pediu à diretoria da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) que desconsidere e retire dos autos os memoriais e documentos apresentados por Eneva e Global Participações em Energia na disputa pela habilitação dos consórcios ION. Para a EPP, a Eneva e a Global manifestaram fora do prazo previsto para responder ao recurso contra a inabilitação de seus projetos. A EPP lidera os consórcios ION que ganharam projetos termelétricos que somam 1.685 MW. Total Energies apresenta plano de crescimento até 2035 A TotalEnergies apresentou seus objetivos de crescimento para ampliar sua capacidade de energia após 2030, apoiada por bilhões de dólares em investimentos anuais. A companhia francesa de energia afirmou que pretende investir entre US$ 14 bilhões e US$ 17 bilhões por ano entre 2027 e 2032. A empresa espera que seu segmento de petróleo e gás registre crescimento de produção de cerca de 2% a 3% ao ano entre 2030 e 2035, sustentado por seu portfólio de projetos orgânicos. Para o segmento de eletricidade, a companhia prevê geração líquida de energia de 10 a 12 terawatts-hora por ano entre 2030 e 2035. A TotalEnergies espera que a eletricidade represente cerca de um quarto de sua matriz energética — que também inclui petróleo e gás — até o fim desse período. (Valor Econômico – por Dow Jones) Proposta para novas regras de transmissão pode beneficiar data center O diretor-geral da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, propôs uma regra de transição na Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) para atender cargas como data centers. A proposta teria alcance até 2029 e beneficiaria os centros de processamento de dados que têm implementação por etapas, o que levaria ao aumento do consumo de energia nos próximos anos. Conforme voto-vista apresentado na quinta-feira (24), o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) deverá priorizar, no acesso ao sistema de transmissão de energia, os empreendimentos que já tinham parecer positivo de viabilidade técnica emitido antes das novas regras, que começaram a valer em dezembro de 2025. Sandoval argumenta que o decreto que criou a Pnast, ao ter vigência imediata, impediu a “adoção de providências prévias” por consumidores como data centers, que têm previsão de acesso escalonada à carga. Ou seja, aqueles que já tinham acesso ao sistema e estavam aumentando o seu montante de uso de energia ano a ano teriam sido prejudicados pela criação da política, que substituiu a análise dos pedidos de forma cronológica pelas Temporadas de Acesso. O processo era relatado pelo ex-diretor Fernando Mosna, que apresentou voto em julho deste ano, quando Sandoval pediu vista. O assunto está na pauta do circuito deliberativo da Aneel, marcado para amanhã (29). Se aprovado, será iniciada consulta pública de 45 dias. (Agência Infra) Justiça limita votos, e plano de recuperação judicial da Unigel pode ser rejeitado Em decisão anunciada sexta-feira (25), a Justiça paulista reconheceu que determinados credores da Unigel não podem participar da deliberação sobre o plano de recuperação judicial da petroquímica, abrindo caminho para que seja rejeitado em assembleia que será retomada na próxima quarta-feira (30). artigo.texto: Elsewedy Electric has connected a 50 MW / 100 MWh battery energy storage system to Greece’s transmission grid, marking a step toward the national goal of between 5 GW and 7 GW by 2030. The government is also providing support for batteries for small and mid-sized firms, to be integrated with solar panels. In addition, deadlines for BESS investments in coal regions are set to be extended. While its neighbor Bulgaria is at the top of the chart on a global scale in battery energy storage systems, Greece is rushing to become a major player itself. The country has some 600 MW of operating power from the 13 active facilities in the system controlled by Independent Transmission System Operator (IPTO or Admie). The goal is 5 GW to 7 GW by 2030. In 2027, the total would need to reach 1.5 GW. Elsewedy adds 100 MWh to Greece’s battery storage fleet Elsewedy Electric energized a standalone BESS early this month. The project was developed by Elsewedy Energy and EPC and implemented by Elsewedy Electric Power Systems Projects and BMS. The battery facility has 50 MW in capability and a two-hour duration, which translates to 100 MWh in storage capacity. It is the Egypt-based firm’s first BESS in Europe. Elsewedy won government support three years ago at the country’s first auction for standalone energy storage, in the form of a contract for difference (CfD). Connected to the 150 kV network and a new 33/150 kV substation, the facility is located in Oinofyta in the municipality of Tanagra, part of the regional unit of Viotia in Central Greece. The investment was worth EUR 41.9 million. In early 2025, Elsewedy obtained a EUR 18.2 financing package from the National Bank of Greece. It also benefits from a EUR 10 million grant and EUR 5.5 loan, both from the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). SMEs win subsidies for BESS backup for solar power Expansion is underway in other segments of battery storage as well. The ministry recently published the provisional list of beneficiaries of the support program for small and mid-sized enterprises. The subsidies total EUR 8.15 million. Overall operating power for 209 firms is 28.2 MW, with 49.3 MWh of storage. BESS facilities will support 30.8 MW of photovoltaics altogether. It took almost eleven months since the applications deadline for the first list. The package was intended to cover 333 MW of battery capability with EUR 153 million. More time for projects in coal regions in transition Futhermore, the Ministry of Environment and Energy is prolonging a deadline for the winners of the third auction. The beneficiaries would be able to submit the so-called declarations of readiness to the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) by mid-December, according to a bill of law, Energypress reported. The procedure is for four-hour BESS projects in the coal regions of Western Macedonia and the Peloponnese. HELLENiQ Renewables and government-controlled Public Power Corp. (PPC) were the biggest winners, with two plants of 25 MW and one 50 MW system, respectively. The rest of the list comprises Amber Energy (18 MW), Plain Solar (7.9 MW), Enercoplan (25 MW), Eunice Group’s Arkadia Storage (10 MW), EDF’s subsidiary Heliothema (10 MW) and Ardassa Energy (18 MW). The three standalone energy storage tenders resulted in contracts for 900 MW overall.

artigo.texto: Crestview bans large-scale data centers, but mayor says decision could be revisited CRESTVIEW, Fla. -- The City of Crestview voted to ban large-scale data centers Monday evening. They aren't the first municipal government in the region to pass a similar law. Escambia and Walton County commissioners have also passed bans. The City of Pensacola has said there's no place for them in the city's plans. And Okaloosa County commissioners voted to regulate data centers rather than ban them. RELATED STORIES - Escambia County moves forward with ordinance banning AI data centers - Okaloosa County commissioners opt to regulate data centers, not ban them - Pensacola passes one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers as debate grows WEAR News spoke with the Crestview Mayor JB Whitten ahead of the meeting who describes the move as a precautionary effort. "Our city council is being very cautious," Whitten said. Crestview city council members unanimously voted to ban large-scale data centers from setting up shop in city limits. "I look at my own county," Whitten said. "[Okaloosa] County commissioners are talking about it and they're getting a lot of pushback on that. And I look over in Santa Rosa County and I look at Escambia County, all the other counties. And it could be because there's not a clear understanding of what they are." Whitten says while large scale data centers would bring money into the city, it wouldn't necessarily bring more jobs. "It can't always be about money," Whitten said. "One of the cons though is you think if you have a big data center, you have a lot of employees. You really don't. It's not a big workforce generator for the city." Whitten says while the ban passed, all it would take is another vote to revoke it. "I compared this very much to five or six years ago when they authorized medical marijuana," said Whitten. "We banned them the first year. There was not enough information to know what was going on. A year later, we authorized them." Whitten says if the city gets more information on the data centers, the ban could be revoked. "I think that what we have right now is the city council is taking a seat back, examining everything, determine where do we want to go with this," Whitten said. "So it could change in the future." For now, he says it's the council's job to listen to its residents. "We're seeing reactions of citizens right now don't want them," said Whitten. "They really don't. So I think the people [councilors] are trying to listen to the citizens." "So like I said, if it's not all that bad, maybe sometime in the future, it could be a change," he said. In 2025, Gov. Ron DeSantis passed a bill that allows local governments to decide where data centers can be built. The legislation also requires large data centers to pay for their own power and infrastructure to keep costs from being passed on to residents. Watch Mayor Whitten's full interview below:

artigo.texto: O Fórum Nacional de Secretários Estaduais de Minas e Energia (FNSME) pediu ao presidente Lula (PT) a abertura de um diálogo institucional com os estados antes da conclusão da regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) e o reconhecimento do gás natural como alternativa energética potencialmente elegível como fonte de baixa emissão incentivada pela política. O FNSME entende que o Redata deve preservar condições isonômicas entre os estados na atração dos investimentos em data centers. “Uma política pública de alcance nacional deve preservar condições isonômicas de participação entre os estados, evitando que critérios tecnológicos previamente definidos produzam, ainda que indiretamente, concentração regional dos investimentos”, cita o ofício enviado ao presidente da República nesta quarta-feira (30/9). O posicionamento ocorre em meio ao tensionamento, dentro do governo federal, sobre a regulamentação do Redata. A Fazenda, responsável pelo desenho do programa, tem pressionado para que o presidente Lula sancione o decreto regulamentador sem incluir o gás como fonte energética incentivada, mantendo assim a ênfase em fontes renováveis. O grupo de secretários defendeu também que os empreendimentos beneficiários do Redata devem “assumir adequadamente os custos de conexão, potência, infraestrutura e eventuais reforços sistêmicos que decorram de sua implantação”. O objetivo, nesse caso, é evitar a transferência indevida desses custos aos demais consumidores. Diversidade energética não pode ser fator de exclusão O Fórum defende a neutralidade tecnológica na definição das soluções de suprimento energético e a possibilidade de utilização de soluções híbridas envolvendo gás natural, fontes renováveis, armazenamento e outras tecnologias. A entidade alega que o Brasil possui diferentes realidades energéticas, com estados com expressiva disponibilidade de recursos renováveis e outros com reservas de gás natural, além de diferentes níveis de infraestrutura de transmissão e distribuição de energia e distintas condições de conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). “Essa diversidade não deve ser transformada em fator de exclusão. O gás natural possui papel relevante na segurança energética brasileira e pode, em determinadas configurações, integrar soluções de suprimento que combinem geração térmica, fontes renováveis, armazenamento, resposta da demanda e outras tecnologias”. Antes de o FNSME fechar posição sobre o assunto, diferentes estados já vinham se mobilizando para pleitear a inclusão do gás como fonte elegível aos incentivos do Redata. Esta semana, o Comitê de Planejamento Energético do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul (Copergs), em conjunto com o governo estadual, já havia enviado ofício ao presidente Lula reforçando o pleito. O Rio Grande do Sul tem atraído investidores interessados em investir em data centers no estado – a principal iniciativa, nesse sentido, é o Projeto da Scala AI City, com capacidade prevista de até 4,8 GW. Com capacidade de suprimento de gás natural limitada pelos gargalos do Gasbol, o estado defende que possui alternativas de diversificação do suprimento – como a conclusão do trecho do gasoduto Uruguaiana-Porto Alegre, que permitiria a chegada do gás de Vaca Muerta, na Argentina, ao mercado gaúcho, além da avaliação de rotas de gás natural liquefeito (GNL) e comprimido (GNC). Na semana passada, aliás, a Edge assinou com o governo do Rio Grande do Sul um memorando de entendimento para a estruturação de um terminal de GNL no estado. Antes dos gaúchos, os governos do Amazonas e Sergipe também já haviam solicitado formalmente a inclusão do gás na regulamentação do Redata.

artigo.texto: Five-Day Training on Solar Energy and Battery Storage Systems Begins in Nepal Kathmandu. A five-day training has started on promoting solar energy in Nepal's industries and making battery storage systems safe, effective, and sustainable. The training will provide participants with knowledge on the current status of solar and battery storage systems in Nepal, industrial carbon emission reduction, energy management, grid services, battery technology, safety standards, cyber security, environmental and social security, and other important topics. The training, organized by the Alternative Energy Promotion Center (AEPC) under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, has the participation of 45 engineers. The high-level training on 'Solar PV and Battery Energy Storage Systems for Industrial Sector: Design, Installation and Safety' is in collaboration with Practical Action and Ghampower Nepal. Representatives from the private sector, educational and research institutions, and related government and non-governmental agencies from across the country are participating in the training. The Alternative Energy Promotion Center has stated that in addition to theoretical knowledge, participants will be provided with practical experience through group exercises based on real industrial scenarios and field observation tours. In the context of Nepal prioritizing clean energy expansion, security, and green industrialization, the center expects to reduce overall energy consumption and make electricity supply reliable through the use of solar energy. In the context of climate-induced disasters exposing the risks to energy infrastructure, as highlighted by the Rusuwa flood, the center has pointed out the need to analyze the risks associated with monsoon-related events, as hydropower-based energy production, transmission, and distribution infrastructure are connected to river systems. Board member of the center, Ankita Shah, said that solar energy and battery storage systems can play a significant role in enhancing climate resilience if they can produce and store energy locally, given the risk of floods and landslides to electricity projects. According to her, promotion programs for energy production and storage will help create green employment and open up new entrepreneurial opportunities. artigo.texto: JAMES CITY — James City County residents on Tuesday learned more about a proposed battery energy storage system that could transform an abandoned industrial site in the county’s southeastern community of Grove. Pelican Energy Storage LLC has applied for a special use permit that would allow the construction of a battery energy storage facility on parts of a 220-acre industrial waterfront site in Grove. Pelican, a subsidiary of Tenaska based in Omaha, Nebraska, hosted a public informational meeting at the Abram Frink Jr. Community Center. Tenaska spokeswoman Jamie Wagner said the company seeks public engagement early and frequently when approaching a project like this and seek to ensure that they’re a good neighbor. “As with any new project, we understand that members of the Grove community may have questions,” she said. Pelican has touted benefits that would come with the redevelopment of the former BASF Corp. site, but some Grove residents are concerned about industrial redevelopment. The county’s planning commission is slated to consider and hold a public hearing on the special use permit application on Oct. 7. The proposed facility would consist of what Pelican describes as purpose-built battery energy storage system enclosures capable of storing 650 megawatts of energy. The lithium-ion batteries would hold energy that power plants generate and that can be fed back into the power grid when demand is highest. The battery site would connect to Dominion Energy’s 500-kilovolt Surry-Skiffes Creek transmission line, which crosses the property. Pelican officials say James City County and the wider southeastern Virginia community would benefit from the construction of an energy storage facility. Construction would create more than 275 direct and indirect jobs, Pelican estimates. The facility will have no emissions, use no water during operation and provide $90 million in direct revenue to the county, according to company estimates. “We find many communities are open to this type of investment,” Wright said. But some Grove residents feel as though they’re being overlooked as this proposal moves forward. “Why does Grove continually seem to be the part of James City County where things are put, rather than the part of the county that gets invested in?” Joshua Blue, a Grove resident since 2008, asked on Tuesday. He was one of a few dozen residents who attended the meeting. Grove lacks public amenities such as sidewalks in many areas and has no public access to the James River despite being adjacent to it. Redeveloping industry at the BASF site locks in industrial use for decades. “I would much rather see the county seriously explore whether this land could become a public park, natural area, river access or some other permanent community asset,” Blue said. Blue said the county has invested in public access elsewhere and wants the same consideration for Grove, an area populated by many descendants of people displaced in the 20th century to make way for federal military installations. “I’m not categorically opposed to battery storage,” he said. “But I am very concerned about permanently giving up one of Grove’s last opportunities for meaningful public riverfront access without first having a serious conversation about what that land could mean for the people who actually live here.” Once used for the manufacture and burial of synthetic fibers, which led to soil and groundwater contamination, the BASF Corp. site underwent cleanup and in 2021 was declared remediated by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, according Grant Weaver, an environmental analyst with Tenaska. Weaver said public waterfront access would not work for the site because of its prior use. Public beach access would be “very difficult given the residual contamination,” he said. Wright said the company nevertheless values the feedback from the community and wants to know their concerns and observations. John McGlennon, chairman of the county’s Board of Supervisors, attended Tuesday’s meeting and said some of the citizens he spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the site’s redevelopment, but that most simply wanted to know more about the proposal. McGlennon said a project like the proposed battery energy storage system would be increasingly important for feeding energy into the electrical grid, but whether this is the right location and project to do that has yet to be determined. Another energy company, Charlottesville-based East Point Energy, in July withdrew a request to bring a major battery storage facility to Chesapeake, saying it wanted “to continue sharing information and answering questions” for residents before proceeding. At the time, proponents emphasized that these type of facilities don’t pose the same risks as data centers. Chesapeake’s planning commission had recommended denial of the project. artigo.texto: The Science Newswise — Battery materials called electrolytes allow ions (charged particles) to move from one end of a battery to the other. This process is necessary for charging and discharging. Superionic conductors (SICs) are materials that are solids, but some of their ions move like liquids. As a result, they conduct electricity very well. One SIC, lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride, is a promising type of solid-state battery material. Using neutron scattering and computer simulations, researchers gained a better understanding of this material’s atomic dynamics. By raising the material to more than 400 K (260 F), they put it in the superionic state where ions act like a liquid. In that state, the scientists found that lithium ions can hop quickly through the material’s crystal structure. The team also documented how specific types of vibrations in the crystal enable ions to jump through vibrating crystal bottlenecks. The scientists discovered that these vibrations enable long-range flow and significant improvements in conductivity. The Impact These findings show researchers how to improve ion flow inside a solid-state battery material, which would increase its performance. This information could enable a solid-state battery material that offers very high quantities of mobile ions as well as good chemical and thermal stability. This structure would enable a battery to use solid electrolytes that could perform as well as liquid ones. (Ions move more freely through liquid electrolytes than solid ones.) As such, this change could enable faster and safer battery charging. The ability to tailor SIC materials could also guide researchers in developing and improving other devices, such as fuel cells and computers. Summary One class of materials, superionic conductors (SICs), has the properties of both a crystalline and liquid electrolyte. When warmed above a specific temperature, the material remains partly crystalline, but also develops ion flow properties like those of liquids. This study combined machine-learning simulations with inelastic and quasielastic neutron scattering at the Spallation Neutron Source, a DOE Office of Science User Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The researchers investigated lithium-ion dynamics in the SIC lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride. The team found the crystalline framework facilitated fast, liquid-like hopping of lithium ions between stable crystalline lattice sites. Additionally, they documented significant enhancements in lithium-ion diffusion across a range of temperatures through the dynamic breathing (unified relaxation) of vibrating diffusion bottlenecks. They also observed how the vibrational spectra of mobile lithium ions in Li₆PS₅Cl evolve from a crystal-like to liquid-like phase. The research bridges conventional diffusive and lattice vibrational models. These findings offer important insights into the rapid ionic motion in SICs for potential use in solid electrolyte batteries, fuel cells, and computing systems. Funding The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation (DMREF project); the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Basic Energy Sciences, Division of Materials Sciences and Engineering; and the German Research Foundation. This work used resources at the Spallation Neutron Source and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, both DOE Office of Science User Facilities.

artigo.texto: What’s it like living in the shadow of an AI data center? These Vineland residents know. They are some of the first in the Philly area to experience firsthand what it’s like to live near the massive facilities. Some of their neighbors have sold their homes to the data center developers. When Amber Ayrer bought her Vineland home 25 years ago, she envisioned growing old there, enjoying lazy afternoons with the windows open and a view of farmland from her front door. After her adult daughter, Ally, suffered a traumatic brain injury, Amber made the rancher accessible, installing a ramp that aides use to push Ally’s wheelchair outside for her daily walks. The place had all the makings of a forever home, Amber Ayrer said — until a massive AI data center moved in across the street. Now, the 71-year-old looks out her front windows at the hulking DataOne facility, a windowless compound surrounded by walls and metal fences. In recent months, Ayrer said, the 2.4-million-square-foot complex has emitted a near-constant hum. She struggles to sleep, she said, and has suffered from headaches. She turns the TV on to mask the sound. Residents who live farther away have also complained about the noise, including in a recent lawsuit that was thrown out due to procedural issues. In the suit, residents said the Cumberland County Department of Health measured the hum as higher than 50 decibels a mile away in the middle of the night. A sound higher than 50 decibels is equal to a running refrigerator and is 10 times louder than a typical suburban area at night. Ayrer, who was not involved in the lawsuit, said she doesn’t want to move, even as she sees neighbors sell their homes to the data center developers. “In order to get another home, I’d have to get one built” to be accessible, Ayrer said, standing in her entryway. She shrugged, adding, “I need to be here for my daughter.” The noise has quieted, she noted, since around Sept. 22. That’s when the New Jersey DEP ordered the data center to pay a $1 million fine for running 62 gas generators without the required permits. She isn’t sure why the hum stopped, or whether it is related to the fine. » READ MORE: Vineland AI data center hit with a $1 million fine But the sound will eventually return, she assumes, perhaps even louder when the center is fully operational. The Ayrers are some of the first Philly-area residents to live in the shadow of a massive AI data center. Only a handful of homeowners live within eyesight of DataOne’s South Lincoln Avenue complex in Vineland. They used to have more neighbors. But since 2025, DataOne Vineland and LJR Real Estate — which is registered to the address of Northeast Precast, a local company that has partnered with DataOne — have purchased at least five surrounding homes for a combined $3 million, according to online property records. DataOne and Northeast Precast did not respond to requests for comment about the acquisitions. Several former Vineland residents who sold their homes to these companies could not be reached or declined to comment. Asked about residents’ concerns, DataOne spokesperson Naomi Rice shared a previous statement, which said in part that the facility was “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells.” These generate energy through an electrochemical reaction rather than combustion, pistons, or rotating machinery. Nebius Group, which is operating the center’s internal AI infrastructure, says the fuel cells from Bloom Energy — a company expanding locally — and enhanced sound mitigation will make for a quieter environment than what residents experienced during construction, according to spokesperson Ava Iuliucci. Charles-Antoine Beyney, DataOne’s founder and chief executive officer, previously said the Vineland center would use “breakthrough” technology to reduce its environmental impact. He said the complex would be a good neighbor, promising a vertical farm — which uses technology to grow crops indoors — to help feed Vineland residents in need. “Most of the data centers that are being built today suck, big time,” Beyney said in January. “No freaking way am I going to do what the entire industry is doing … just killing our communities and killing our lungs to make money.” What it looks like near a South Jersey data center The dark exterior of DataOne abuts busy South Lincoln Avenue, towering above homes and farms on the outskirts of Vineland City. In spots, rows of crops extend to the data center’s walls. On a recent day, the data center appeared abuzz with activity, although residents said it was relatively quiet, as cars and yellow school buses drove in and out of its gated-off parking lot. Giant “no trespassing” signs are prominently displayed. While the front portion of the data center appeared complete, cranes farther back reached into the sky. Meanwhile, several large homes across from the entrance — purchased by the data center developers and associates — appeared abandoned, with recycling cans askew in the driveways, indoor and outdoor lights on in the middle of the day, and swing sets sitting empty in the backyards. No one answered the doors. At another home, a woman shook her head, saying she’d lived there forever and would never speak publicly about the development across the street. Who is behind the Vineland data center? Data centers like this one handle the cloud-storage and computing needs of increasingly sophisticated AI tools. DataOne, a French company that manages advanced data centers, is the owner, operator, and builder of the Vineland data center. Its client, Nebius Group, an Amsterdam-based AI-infrastructure company, operates the center’s internal technology, which fuels Microsoft’s AI tools. As demand for these facilities has surged, so has the controversy surrounding them. Across the country, proposed complexes have received fierce pushback from nearby residents concerned about environmental, noise, quality-of-life, and property-value impacts. » READ MORE: Human reporters explai

artigo.texto: Publicado em 28 de setembro de 2026 O segundo dia de ROG.e contou com a participação do presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, na mesa “Implementação das políticas públicas e regulamentos para diversidade energética e soluções de baixo carbono no Brasil". Um dos maiores eventos sobre óleo e gás da América Latina, a ROG.e foi realizada de 21 a 24 de setembro, no Riocentro, na Barra da Tijuca. A EPE participou da feira com um estande, apresentação de mais de 20 trabalhos e debates sobre o setor. Em sua participação, Prado dividiu o painel com o Subsecretário de Implementação da Sec. Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, Thiago Barral, e com o Diretor Executivo de Desenvolvimento de Negócios da Prumo Logística, Mauro Andrade. A discussão foi moderada pela fundadora e CEO da New Gaia Strategies Investments, Raphaella Gomes. O presidente da EPE destacou que o PDE 2035 e o PNE 2055 apontam uma matriz com bastante espaço para biometano, SAF, hidrogênio, captura e estocagem de carbono, entre outros. “Ambos os planos põem o hidrogênio como uma rota confirmada no longuíssimo prazo e com políticas concretas já aprovadas no Congresso. Temos o ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), a Lei do Combustível do Futuro, a questão dos mandatos de biometano e o Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) que também tenta organizar um pouco esse mercado em relação à oferta e a demanda", enumerou. “Em comparação a todas as outras opções de recursos e aproveitamentos energéticos, eu colocaria a captura e estocagem de carbono como aquele aluno na sala que necessita de um pouquinho mais de atenção", avaliou. Em relação ao carbono biogênico, originado de matérias-primas renováveis, como a biomassa e os biocombustíveis, Prado enxerga uma “grande oportunidade". “Você pode ter combustíveis renováveis com pegadas negativas de carbono", afirmou. Neste sentido, ele destacou a necessidade de maior aproximação com os estados que possuem a maior produção de biocombustíveis. Thiago Prado falou ainda sobre a importância fundamental de avançar no detalhamento regulatório e sobre a atuação do Brasil na Global Coalition for Energy Planning (Coalizão Global para o Planejamento Energético), criada no âmbito do G20, e na Olade (Organização Latino-Americana de Energia). “A maior mensagem que o Brasil pode passar é de diversificação, mas principalmente de vocacionamento. A transição energética tem que respeitar as vocações. Esse desenho de mercado tem que ser suficientemente capaz de representar não só o Brasil como outros países para que isso faça sentido para todo mundo e não vire uma discussão de rotas tecnológicas". Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) O Plano Nacional Integrado das Infraestruturas de Gás e Biometano (PNIIGB) foi tema da apresentação do analista de pesquisa energética Henrique Rangel, no painel Planejamento, Governança e Organização Institucional do Mercado. Ele apresentou o plano, a metodologia utilizada em sua elaboração, abordando etapas como os estudos de oferta e demanda, seleção de projetos, análise socioambiental, dimensionamento e Capex e estimativa de emprego e renda. A edição do PNIIGB apontou a necessidade de 15 projetos, com investimentos da ordem de R$ 35 bilhões e 2.200 km de dutos. “A análise integrada dos diversos elos do setor de gás natural demonstra que a expansão coordenada pode reduzir gargalos estruturais", concluiu. Rangel também destacou que a inclusão do biometano no planejamento reforça a convergência entre o setor e as metas nacionais de baixo carbono. A programação do segundo dia de ROG.e também contou com a participação do Superintendente Adjunto de Petróleo e Gás, Marcelo Alfradique, que mediou a mesa Distribuição, Regulação e Mercado Livre de Gás. Já no palco técnico, o analista de pesquisa energética Ederaldo Godoy apresentou trabalho sobre o estado da arte do BioGL no Brasil, com foco nas principais rotas tecnológicas e os insumos. O BioGL é sustentável e drop-in ao Gás Liquefeito de Petróleo (GLP), ou seja, quimicamente idêntico, sem necessidade de alteração nos equipamentos de queima, prometendo ser a molécula verde com potencial para ser adicionada na descarbonização do GLP. No estande da EPE, o analista de pesquisa energética Igor Veneroso apresentou o panorama dos investimentos em inovação no Brasil, enquanto a analista Pamela Vilela falou sobre o Zoneamento Nacional de Recursos de Óleo e Gás (ZNMT) 2023-2025.

artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County Commissioners approve $200 million battery storage facility EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Vanderburgh County Commissioners this week approved a series of agreements that clear the way for a new battery energy storage system, or BESS, next to the Elliott Station substation in Scott Township. Project details The developer, Elliot Battery Storage, an affiliate of RWE Clean Energy Development, plans to invest about $200 million in the project. The facility will store roughly 200 megawatts of power. This power could be used to help utilities manage high-demand periods. “So it’s a large station on the far east side of Vanderburgh County... they’re key to peak load... they’re a modern way of dealing with the peak load, and they need to be next to a substation, which this one is,” said Mike Schopmeyer, Vanderburgh County attorney. Zoning approval and neighbor notification The project already passed a Board of Zoning Appeals vote, 5-0. Schopmeyer said people living near the site off East Baseline Road were notified and briefed before that vote. “Everything’s approved now, so the petitioner... can move ahead with the construction. They’ve got to go through a building permit process,” Schopmeyer said. Payments to the county and timeline As part of the deal, the company will pay the county $250,000 for local development projects, plus cover the county’s legal costs for negotiating the agreements. The company must break ground by the end of 2029 or the deal falls apart. The facility is expected to be up and running no later than November 2031. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: “Ratepayer Protection Act” sets a standard intended to keep data center power costs off ratepayers’ bills. Opponents call the bill “toothless.” clarification: This article has been updated to reflect the 57-43 cloture vote on a motion to proceed HR 9340, which would have allowed the bill to move forward in the Senate. WASHINGTON, D.C. (WTAP) - A bill that passed the U.S. House earlier this month aims to keep the cost of powering data centers off the bills of ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Act would set a federal standard that, if considered and adopted by states, would require utilities to design rates so that data centers using 100 megawatts or more recover the full cost of any new generation, transmission or distribution needed to serve them. That includes cases where a data center later ends its contract, so utilities and ratepayers aren’t left holding the bag. Utilities would also have to collect financial assurances required to cover the cost of any upgrades up front. West Virginia Congressman Riley Moore co-sponsored the bill and said he encouraged House leadership to bring it to the floor. “It’s trying to ensure that people’s utility bills are not going to go up, that my citizens and citizens around this country are not footing the bill for data centers that are being built in their area,” Moore said. The bill sets a federal standard but few hard requirements, leaving the details and implementation to the states. State regulators would have a year to begin considering it and two years to make a decision. Moore said that scope is intentional, to avoid federal preemption of state laws, though he said he’d be open to the Senate adding more teeth. Democrats have criticized the bill for only requiring states to “consider” the proposal intended to protect ratepayers. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Shumer (D - NY) on Tuesday said the bill doesn’t go far enough to ensure data centers are held accountable. “Americans are demanding real guard-rails on AI and data centers, but all the Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill,” Shumer said on the Senate floor. “The bill is a fraud” The House passed the bill Sept. 16. A 57-43 cloture vote on a motion to proceed stalled the bill in the Senate on Sept. 30. The Senate also has its own version of the bill, introduced by Sen. Jon Husted (R - Ohio). A separate bill, the GRID Savings Act, introduced by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D - N.M.) seeks to have federal regulators, rather than the states, set rules for how utilities bill data centers for the cost of connecting to the power grid, preempting the consideration of state regulators. That bill has been referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Moore’s Democratic opponent for his seat in this year’s general election, Morgantown community organizer Ace Parsi, drafted a bill called the “Neighbors, Not Servers Act,” which he says will be the first piece of legislation he introduces a lawmaker if elected. The bill would go further than the Ratepayer Protection Act, requiring local community consent before any data center could receive federal permits or grid interconnection approval, and would override state laws, like West Virginia’s, that currently limit local control over data center siting. Parsi announced the proposal last week. Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment on it, though a spokesperson reached out afterward to highlight his work on the Ratepayer Protection Act. artigo.texto: A DHL está a expandir a sua rede mundial de logística de baterias, que integra já mais de 20 instalações especializadas. A operação acompanha todo o ciclo de vida destes equipamentos, desde o apoio à produção e transporte até ao diagnóstico, reparação, logística inversa e preparação para reciclagem. A eletrificação dos setores automóvel, industrial e energético está a criar novas cadeias de abastecimento e a aumentar a procura de soluções logísticas especializadas. Para responder a esta transformação, a DHL está a desenvolver uma rede integrada de Centros de Excelência de Veículos Elétricos e Baterias nos principais mercados mundiais. A plataforma reúne competências da DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express, combinando logística de produção, transporte, armazenagem, serviços pós-venda e gestão do ciclo de vida das baterias. A rede liga já mais de 20 instalações, estando prevista a abertura de novas localizações. A expansão surge num contexto em que as baterias deixaram de estar associadas apenas aos veículos elétricos. Os mesmos sistemas são cada vez mais utilizados em equipamentos industriais, operações mineiras, infraestruturas de rede elétrica e projetos de armazenamento de energia renovável. Algumas destas unidades ultrapassam as 50 toneladas, exigindo soluções de transporte pesado, equipamentos específicos e um planeamento logístico próprio. A classificação como mercadoria perigosa, as diferenças regulamentares entre mercados e modos de transporte e as exigências de documentação e controlo aduaneiro aumentam igualmente a complexidade das operações. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirma Francisco Milián, Head of Inbound to Manufacturing da DHL Supply Chain EMEA. Segundo o responsável, os clientes necessitam de capacidades especializadas em todas as fases, desde a logística de entrada e o apoio à produção até ao armazenamento, distribuição, recondicionamento, devolução e reciclagem. As instalações especializadas da DHL combinam áreas de armazenagem preparadas para baterias com serviços técnicos, entre os quais diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento, reparação, logística inversa e preparação dos equipamentos para reciclagem. Em Halle, na Alemanha, o operador disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de espaço de armazém adaptado a este tipo de produto. Na Hungria, está a ser preparada uma nova instalação dedicada à logística de baterias, cuja entrada em funcionamento está prevista para 2027. A DHL está também a construir um hub europeu em Holtum, nos Países Baixos. A infraestrutura contará com 17 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem e serviços especializados para baterias de alta tensão e deverá iniciar atividade no princípio de 2027. A proximidade à operação automóvel já existente permitirá criar um campus integrado, dedicado à mobilidade elétrica e aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Muitas destas instalações integram transporte, serviços aduaneiros e operações transfronteiriças, procurando concentrar num único parceiro várias etapas da cadeia de valor. A proposta dirige-se a fabricantes de baterias e automóveis, mas também a empresas de energia, operadores industriais e projetos ligados à exploração de minerais críticos. Eletrificação cria novos corredores logísticos A concentração de uma parte significativa da produção de baterias na Ásia, conjugada com o crescimento da procura na Europa e noutras regiões, está a alterar os fluxos comerciais. Ao mesmo tempo, a instalação de novas gigafábricas gera movimentos de equipamentos produtivos, matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes e baterias acabadas. “A transição energética está a criar corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, sublinha Hendrik Venter, Global CEO da DHL Supply Chain. Para o responsável, as empresas estão a redesenhar as suas operações para apoiar a mobilidade elétrica, o armazenamento de energia e a expansão das fontes renováveis. A logística de baterias ganha ainda uma nova dimensão com o crescimento dos sistemas BESS – Battery Energy Storage Systems – utilizados para armazenar energia e apoiar a estabilidade das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a DHL entregou mais de 1100 destas unidades em diferentes mercados. Estes projetos podem envolver sistemas de grandes dimensões, transporte multimodal, operações de elevação de cargas pesadas e entregas em locais remotos, além do cumprimento das regras aplicáveis às mercadorias perigosas. A área New Energy é um dos setores de crescimento definidos pelo DHL Group na sua Strategy 2030. O grupo desenvolve soluções logísticas para oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, sistemas BESS, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestruturas de rede, hidrogénio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: A ABB anunciou o lançamento do Infinitus, um portfólio de soluções de corrente contínua (CC) projetado para gerenciar as crescentes demandas de energia dos Data Centers de IA. O portfólio acelerará a adoção de arquiteturas CC em Data Centers, melhorando a eficiência energética e reduzindo a área ocupada pela infraestrutura de energia, ao mesmo tempo em que aumenta a capacidade de computação disponível. A ABB espera que outros setores de alto consumo energético façam a mesma transição. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) prevê que a demanda global de eletricidade dos Data Centers mais que dobrará até 2030, e a ABB estima que aproximadamente 25–40% da nova capacidade instalada em 2030 poderá utilizar distribuição CC. Espera-se que os chips de IA de próxima geração consumam 1 MW ou mais por rack, um aumento em relação aos quase 200 kW atuais, exigindo uma mudança para uma arquitetura CC capaz de sustentar o desempenho e, ao mesmo tempo, impulsionar a eficiência energética. Com a distribuição em 800 VCC, a pegada é mais compacta, eliminando etapas redundantes de conversão e reduzindo as perdas de calor dos sistemas convencionais de corrente alternada (CA). Um relatório recente da BCG/ABB calculou que a distribuição CC gera ganhos de eficiência energética superiores a 5% e aumenta o espaço disponível para racks de computação. Para um Data Center de 500 MW, um ganho de eficiência de 5% pode significar 25 MW adicionais de energia para cargas de TI geradoras de receita e mais de US$ 300 milhões em receita adicional potencial por ano. Com ganhos de eficiência de 5% em um campus de data center de 500 MW, a economia de energia ao longo de um ano seria equivalente a abastecer Washington D.C. por quase uma semana inteira. “A ABB é pioneira em tecnologia CC há mais de 25 anos em diversos segmentos. Estamos trabalhando em estreita colaboração com fabricantes de chips, clientes hyperscale, parceiros de fornecimento e entidades do setor para definir os padrões e o ritmo da implementação de arquiteturas CC de alta eficiência. O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio a fornecer os blocos de construção para qualquer arquitetura de data center — seja CC nativa ou híbrida CA/CC — para alimentar com eficiência os chips de IA de próxima geração. Essa tecnologia trará ganhos de eficiência energética semelhantes a outros setores de alto consumo, como manufatura em larga escala, energias renováveis e operações marítimas”, disse Giampiero Frisio, presidente da área de negócios de Eletrificação da ABB. O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio integrado source-to-rack de CC do setor. Em seu núcleo está a inovadora tecnologia de transformador de estado sólido Infinitus da ABB, que permite que as instalações operem com uma pegada menor e maior eficiência energética. Como o único grande fornecedor de eletrificação com o primeiro disjuntor de estado sólido totalmente certificado pela IEC do mundo e um UPS estático de média tensão pioneiro no setor em produção, a ABB oferece uma amplitude de tecnologia incomparável no mercado. O portfólio CC Infinitus da ABB inclui cinco blocos de construção principais: – Powertrains de Média Tensão fornecem energia estável e resiliente da rede elétrica ou de geração no local; – Fontes CC e Qualidade de Energia convertem CA em CC, eliminando a conversão do white space; – Distribuição de Energia CC entrega energia de forma segura e confiável, permitindo maior densidade de potência em uma pegada menor; – Proteção de Energia CC fornece proteção para operadores, servidores de IA e hardware contra sobrecorrentes CC; – Otimização de Resfriamento reduz o consumo de energia no grey space e no white space com acionamentos de velocidade variável e motores conectados em CC. A ABB trabalha com os clientes para projetar soluções adaptadas às suas demandas específicas de energia, layout das instalações e matriz energética. Essa abordagem de parceria garante que cada implantação seja otimizada para máxima eficiência e confiabilidade. O portfólio Infinitus complementa os sistemas CA tradicionais com a flexibilidade da CC, apoiando os clientes em todas as arquiteturas de energia e, ao mesmo tempo, permitindo eficiência, confiabilidade e escalabilidade sem precedentes para os data centers da era da IA. Para Data Centers de próxima geração, essa arquitetura integrada permite a entrega de energia de alta densidade e alta eficiência que os futuros chips de IA exigem. Com vários componentes principais produzidos nos próximos 12 meses, espera-se que as primeiras instalações nativas em CC que utilizam o portfólio Infinitus completo sejam instaladas e operacionais em dois a três anos. O lançamento do portfólio amplia o apoio à colaboração contínua da ABB com a Nvidia, anunciada pela primeira vez em outubro de 2025, para desenvolver arquiteturas de energia de 800 VCC para instalações de IA em escala de gigawatts. A ABB traz mais de 25 anos de experiência em CC e mais de 700 patentes abrangendo energias renováveis, geração de energia, armazenamento de energia, motores e inversores de frequência. artigo.texto: Politics Energy Benchmarks, Possible Moratorium Among the Topics Driving Chicago’s Data Center Discussion Large, resource-intensive data centers have drawn increased public attention in recent years as their construction ramped up around the country. But in an urban environment like Chicago, data centers of all sizes can have a big impact. Noise from cooling systems and air pollution from backup generators are two examples of data center impacts that can have an outsize effect in a densely populated city. Now, as a city task force explores the right guardrails on data centers, policymakers are shifting into gear as they work to catch up with the emerging industry. At last Wednesday’s City Council meeting, alderpeople voted to remove exemptions for data centers from the city’s Energy Benchmarking Ordinance. That move — a key recommendation from the city’s working group on sustainable data centers — is intended to provide transparency around data centers’ energy efficiency and water usage. But despite the support for benchmarking requirements, City Council members failed to get behind other proposed data center regulations — including a moratorium. In August, Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order addressing noise controls and air pollution permitting for data centers. Johnson’s order also called on alderpeople to enact a temporary moratorium on new data center development. That moratorium, introduced Wednesday, would have applied to data centers bigger than 1,000 square feet with more than 20% of their floor space dedicated to servers. But its fate is uncertain, after two alderpeople promptly routed it to the Rules committee upon its introduction. According to Angela Tovar, the commissioner of Chicago’s Department of Environment as well as the city’s chief sustainability officer, a temporary moratorium could give policymakers time to get the right guardrails in place. “The city was very transparent in saying, ‘The regulations we have in place today are not adequate for how we should regulate the modern data center,’” Tovar said. “This presents an opportunity for the city to course-correct.” But for Brad Tietz, the Midwest director of state government affairs at the Data Center Coalition, a pause on data center development isn’t necessary to work with the industry on regulations. “What (a moratorium) is doing is sending a signal to the industry that this might not be the best place to put forth a multibillion-dollar investment,” Tietz said. “We don’t believe you need a moratorium in place to spend all that time doing this. Quite frankly, we could have reached an agreement on these regulations pretty quickly.” While the Data Center Coalition opposes the moratorium, Tietz said the industry group did not oppose the mayor’s executive order, or the benchmarking requirements the City Council approved last week. Working quickly to bypass a moratorium was the goal of a separate ordinance introduced by Ald. Bill Conway (34th Ward), which was also sent to the Rules committee. That ordinance would have zoned data centers as planned developments, subjecting them to the public review process prior to approval. Currently, data centers are permitted by right in most commercial areas of the city. As data needs for business and personal use change, Tietz said he expects Chicago’s market for new development to shift toward smaller data centers that value proximity to end users. But Tovar said existing data centers in the city vary in their size and use. “From our perspective, I would say that all sizes of data centers matter here in the city because we’re in an urban area,” Tovar said. “We have data centers that are in mixed-use communities, that are existing right next to residential communities. … We can’t ignore some of the concerns we’ve heard from residents.” Heather Cherone contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Proteção para data centers: AXA apresenta sua solução integrada no INSUMMIT 26 O Brasil concentra 48% dos data centers da América Latina, segundo Arthur Mitke, vice-presidente de Subscrição e Sinistros da AXA no Brasil, e é a proteção dessas estruturas que o executivo leva ao INSUMMIT 26 na palestra "Data Center, nova solução integrada da AXA no Brasil". A conversa com a jornalista Thaís Ruco, da Insurtalks, acontece no dia 7 de outubro, às 10h, no evento online e gratuito de inovação no mercado de seguros promovido pela Segbox com apoio da Insurtalks. A solução dá sequência ao produto de Power & Energy, voltado a energias renováveis, que a AXA lançou no ano passado. Arthur vai explicar por que essas instalações, que sustentam bancos digitais, aplicativos, serviços públicos, ensino a distância e computação em nuvem, se tornaram infraestrutura crítica para a economia digital, e por que o país reúne as condições para atrair esse tipo de investimento, com matriz energética majoritariamente limpa, água em abundância e incentivos ao setor. Inteligência artificial e novos riscos O executivo vai explicar como o crescimento da inteligência artificial mudou o perfil de risco dessas instalações. A densidade computacional exigida pelos novos equipamentos gera um volume de calor muito superior ao da TI tradicional e impõe a migração para sistemas de refrigeração líquida, o que traz para a subscrição pontos de falha como o vazamento de fluidos. "Quando a escala muda, o risco muda", antecipa Arthur. A palestra também vai abordar os desafios de transportar e instalar equipamentos de alto valor, que podem pesar uma tonelada e ainda assim são extremamente sensíveis, e as interdependências entre riscos, como o ataque cibernético capaz de provocar superaquecimento e dano físico à estrutura. Da obra à operação Um dos pontos centrais da conversa será o desenho da solução, que acompanha o empreendimento desde o transporte dos equipamentos, com a central própria de gerenciamento de riscos da AXA e empresas especializadas em cargas sensíveis, até a fase de engenharia, com subscrição personalizada. Arthur vai detalhar as coberturas incorporadas à apólice de riscos operacionais, como os danos materiais causados por ataque cibernético e os danos ocorridos durante os testes de redundância, além do seguro cyber com cobertura de erros e omissões para danos a terceiros e do seguro garantia para diferentes fases da obra e para contratos de compra e venda de energia. O vice-presidente vai explicar por que faz sentido contratar engenharia e operação na mesma seguradora em projetos entregues por etapas, nos quais uma parte entra em funcionamento enquanto outra segue em construção, e como a AXA organizou a oferta de forma modular, sem obrigar o cliente a contratar o pacote completo. Prevenção e resposta rápida ao sinistro A palestra vai tratar dos riscos considerados mais críticos na operação, entre eles falhas em sistemas elétricos e de resfriamento, oscilações na rede, ataques cibernéticos e lucros cessantes por paradas não programadas, além do peso crescente dos eventos climáticos extremos. Arthur vai apresentar o trabalho da engenharia de riscos da AXA antes mesmo da contratação e o uso de sensores, termografia e monitoramento de vibração na calibragem da subscrição. "Evitar o sinistro é tão importante quanto estar pronto para indenizá-lo", afirma. Na frente de sinistros, o executivo vai explicar por que a regulação tradicional não atende um ambiente em que cada minuto de indisponibilidade pode gerar prejuízos milionários, e como a seguradora estruturou um protocolo de resposta pré-desenhado, com equipe multidisciplinar e acordos com reguladores. Ele também vai contar como a experiência da AXA XL em mercados como o da Virgínia, nos Estados Unidos, contribuiu para a construção do produto. O corretor como parceiro consultivo Na parte final, Arthur vai abordar o papel do corretor no atendimento a empresas do segmento e o apoio que a AXA oferece, com capacitação sobre as soluções, capacidade técnica e especialistas que acompanham o corretor em reuniões com clientes corporativos e investidores. O executivo vai revelar ainda como corretores especialistas participaram do desenho do produto e deixará uma mensagem para as empresas que investem em infraestrutura tecnológica. artigo.texto: Massachusetts awards more than $40 million for energy storage projects The Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (DOER) has awarded more than $40 million to a group of 36 energy projects across the state, officials from the department announced Sept. 18. Delivered through the DOER’s Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Program, the funding aims to bolster the Bay State’s grid through distributed energy resources. Specifically, the 36 projects all focus on one or more of three focus areas: Community Resilience, Safety and Education, and Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES). Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey says the projects cover a variety of community infrastructure and local businesses, including affordable housing, schools, community centers, and public works facilities. “This is about lowering energy costs and keeping the lights on when communities need it most,” she says. “These investments will help schools, affordable housing, community centers and other critical facilities stay powered during outages while strengthening our grid for the future. We’re also making sure first responders and local officials have the training and tools they need as more energy storage comes online across Massachusetts.” Bolstering community resilience As extreme weather events continue to rise due to climate factors, and area-wide brownouts and blackouts become commonplace across parts of the U.S., community energy resilience is a top priority. A sizable piece of the $40 million in grant money will go toward these efforts, as Massachusetts aims to install battery storage in schools, as well as affordable housing developments and community centers. Together, the projects will add about 10 MW / 44 MWh of storage across the state. “Communities need reliable power and the confidence that new energy technologies are being deployed safely,” says Massachusetts Lieutenant Gov. Kim Driscoll. “These grants will help cities and towns strengthen critical infrastructure, prepare first responders and local officials, and take advantage of storage technology that can save money and improve resilience.” A safe, educated state for installations Paired energy storage has gone from “nice to have” to “absolute necessity” for the solar project world in record time. Another piece of the Bay State’s new grant money will support first responders, as well as municipal officials, electricians, and other installation contractors. The grant funding, going to sites like the Metropolitan Area Planning Council and the Boston Fire Department, will train officials on battery safety, fire codes, permitting, inspections, and other crucial areas. “Batteries supplied more electricity to the grid in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025 – we’re bringing that momentum to the Massachusetts communities that need it the most,” says Massachusetts Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “We are also excited to be supporting two innovative zinc- and sodium-based storage systems to help us get through major storms, showing that Massachusetts is a great place to deploy and scale the latest tech.” Pushing innovation forward for the Northeast Long-duration energy storage ties into the first priority for Massachusetts with this particular grant fund: community resilience. LDES projects are on the rise in the Northeast at large, and this grant section will support a duo of sites using sodium-iron chloride and zinc-based technologies, officials say. These projects could potentially store electricity for 10 to 20 hours, representatives add. The grants, going to community businesses like the Berkshire East Mountain Resort and Mystic Place Apartments, can also help companies scale and test innovative LDES technologies throughout the state. “This investment recognizes that emerging energy technologies require a coordinated public-safety response,” says Tracy Rogers, director of emergency management for the Franklin Regional Council of Governments in western Massachusetts. “By providing specialized battery energy storage system training to first responders across the region, this grant will build shared knowledge, improve preparedness, and help protect the people who respond when communities need them most.”
