artigo.texto: The 200 GW Moment: Reinventing the Grid for the AI Economy As AI pushes rack densities into unprecedented territory, utilities, hyperscalers, and developers are rethinking how to deliver reliable, affordable power at massive scale. Global data center power demand is projected to exceed 200 gigawatts (GW) by 2030. AI workloads are driving typical rack densities from roughly 10-30 kW into 80-150 kW, with advanced deployments approaching 1 MW per rack. Individual campuses are scaling into the hundreds of megawatts and beyond. The pace of growth is unprecedented. At the Data Center World Power conference in Dallas, held Sept. 21-23, leaders from utilities, power producers, hyperscalers, data center developers, operators, and supply chain partners discussed how to scale capacity while safeguarding grid reliability, protecting ratepayers, and accelerating economic development. Bill Kleyman, executive chair of the Data Center World Power Advisory Board and CEO and co-founder of Apolo.us, opened an early session by laying out the realities of deploying Nvidia DGX-class servers. He noted that a standard rack can accommodate six such systems, each built around eight Nvidia H100 accelerators, with individual accelerator cards costing up to $40,000. “Sixty-nine percent of respondents to AFCOM’s State of the Data Center 2026 survey expect that rack density is going to increase like nothing we've seen in the past,” Kleyman said. “In parallel, we are seeing 36% growth in liquid cooling adoption in data centers, and that's continuing to expand.” Utilities Confront the Gigawatt-Scale Campus Scott Hart, executive vice president of NRG Business, a major provider of retail electricity, natural gas, and demand response in North America, described how customer requirements have escalated. “Traditionally, data centers would be a grid-connected, 20- to 40-MW facility,” he said. “Then we saw the cloud campuses in the 100 MW range, but now conversations have pivoted to a gigawatt and beyond.” With projects of that scale, it can be challenging for a utility to commit to constructing a power plant. Hart explained that there are two clocks running during data center development: a technology clock that operates on timelines of months or a few years, and a power infrastructure clock that operates on decades. That creates friction when customers want capacity on near-term timelines, but utilities must plan and finance assets over 15-30 years. “A utility needs a minimum 15-year time horizon and commitment with a secured [offtake agreement] that can pay for that entire period,” Hart said. Some sites will remain grid-only. Increasingly, however, projects are pursuing hybrid arrangements that combine grid supply with on-site generation and storage, Hart noted. That can involve mixing technologies such as geothermal, gas turbine plants, and renewables. Hart added that incorporating demand response – programs in which customers curtail load or shift to on-site resources during grid stress in exchange for incentives – is becoming more attractive. “Most of the data center projects we work on are excited about being part of a demand response program,” he said. Site Selection: Power and Community Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives at Switch, said the site selection calculus has changed. A few years ago, proximity to major metro areas and robust fiber connectivity often dominated decisions. Today, available and reliable power is paramount. “Everything now revolves around power,” Porto said. “And more recently, the scope has expanded to both power and community – it is those two together that now coordinate where you go, how big you go, and what you do.” “Everything now revolves around power.” – Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives, Switch Utilities, initially surprised by multi-hundred-megawatt and gigawatt-scale requests, are increasingly engaging earlier and collaborating on flexible solutions, Porto noted. That can include agreeing to reduce power draw during peak conditions or temporarily switching to batteries or backup generators to support local grid reliability when needed. To maintain optionality as chip roadmaps evolve, Switch is pursuing designs that accommodate both current and future cooling methods and densities. “Depending on the type of chips our customers have, they can deploy air cooling now and utilize liquid cooling later,” Porto said. She added that Switch’s “AI factory” design targets up to 2 MW per rack, with modularity to allow cabinet-level power draw to scale as denser server architectures enter the market. Developer and Operator Economics Dado Slezak, executive vice president of energy capital and strategy at QTS, emphasized the capital intensity of AI data centers, particularly when on-site power is part of the plan. “For every dollar you've got of generation, you've got multiple dollars of data center infrastructure,” he said. “With that scale of investment, there must be a decades-long financial return secured contractually.” Slezak also cautioned against rigid long-term prescriptions. “There is no point when you can look three or four years in advance and know what you should build,” he said. “A lot can change in that time, and decisions keep shifting, each with a downstream impact.” He urged deep collaboration among partners to manage evolving technology targets and interconnection realities.

artigo.texto: Os bastidores de ser rainha de bateria Para elas, a coroa exige mais do que samba no pé Atualizado Antes do samba-enredo começar, da bateria entrar e das câmeras se voltarem para ela, existe uma história que quase ninguém vê. O carnaval mostra apenas o fragmento mais luminoso da vida de uma rainha de bateria. Por trás dele, há mulheres para quem aquele posto não é vitrine, mas o reconhecimento de um laço construído com a escola, e a realização de um sonho. Tania Bisteka, Patricia Costa e Fabíola Andrade sabem bem o que é isso. Tânia, por exemplo, soube exatamente o que queria desde o dia em que a Mangueira anunciou um concurso para escolher a rainha de bateria em 1999. Não tratou como brincadeira, encarou como se concorresse a um cargo político. Espalhou faixas com o próprio nome pela quadra, abordava os integrantes da bateria para contar sua trajetória com a escola e, a quem estivesse por perto, defendia com convicção que merecia sair vencedora. Na época, o concurso reunia dez candidatas e um júri escolhido pela própria bateria, que avaliaria três entradas de cada uma. Durante o mês entre a inscrição e a disputa, Tânia lutou à sua maneira e sonhou com o que viria. Pôs em prática as ideias para viver o que define como uma festa: “Eu fiz blusas com a minha cara. Eu entrei, fiz uma roupa linda, fiz um biquíni lindo e ganhei. As pessoas desciam o morro para assistir! Só que você imagina, o morro todo lá embaixo gritando, berrando e falando.” A emoção foi grande quando descobriu que o que tanto queria se realizou. E deixa claro que ser rainha não é fácil. Estava o ano todo presente em ensaios, na academia e no boxe. Cuidava da alimentação, mesmo que reconheça que ter nutricionista não era tão acessível quanto hoje. E estava sempre na quadra, sem desculpas, para sambar até o fôlego acabar. Tudo na intenção de melhorar a resistência. Esse era seu preparo. Mas além da preparação em relação a exercícios e alimentação, Tania também se preparou psicologicamente e com a sua fé. A partir da espiritualidade, tomou uma atitude totalmente inusitada antes do desfile para que entrasse na avenida com energia boa. Conta que a Mangueira estava na concentração em um local que existia um valão, onde tirou sua roupa: “Eu fiquei pelada. Convoquei a todos, e quando as pessoas passavam e me viam diziam “meu Deus, a rainha está pelada!” E foi muito louco. Eu estava só com uma canga, eu arranquei a canga e comecei meu ritual.” Nascida no morro da Mangueira, foi muito bem recebida pela bateria. Algumas pessoas a chamam de rainha até hoje e, ao lembrar daquele ano, ela percebe que o processo é diferente para uma rainha cria. "É um trabalho árduo, mas que vale muito a pena. Principalmente quando você é da comunidade, uma rainha pé no chão. Quando eu digo pé no chão, quero dizer uma rainha do povo, né? Quando a rainha é cria da escola, ela é mais cobrada do que quando não é. Porque está ali para mostrar que realmente mereceu estar naquele lugar de rainha." Patrícia Costa, rainha de bateria da Viradouro de 1991 a 1998, também sentiu essa diferença. Ela conta que as pessoas famosas pareciam ter mais abertura para ocupar esse espaço. Quando foi chamada, já fazia balé, jazz e sapateado. O convite veio de forma surpreendente, quando foi prestigiar o mestre Maçal, com quem já havia feito um trabalho, e acabou sambando muito com os passistas. Foi um verdadeiro teste de fogo. Naquele dia, o então presidente da escola viu o movimento e ficou interessado em conhecê-la. No fim, a chamou ao camarote e fez o convite, quando teve que assumir uma postura: "Eu precisei me colocar assim, com muita responsabilidade e auto valorização da minha posição como uma artista do samba, uma artista, uma sambista que sabia o que estava fazendo ali à frente da bateria. Não foi fácil. Assim, fui conquistando a comunidade com a minha presença e dedicação." Patrícia explica que a relação com os mestres de bateria e os ritmistas é essencial. Durante os ensaios, a sintonia vai sendo construída. A partir das frases musicais e dos sons da bateria, surge uma criatividade que forma combinações capazes de ajudar a rainha a se movimentar em harmonia com os ritmistas. Nem tudo, porém, são flores. Sobre os perrengues, ela lembra de um ano em que desfilou com o sapato fechado e arrasou na avenida, mas terminou o desfile carregada no colo pelo namorado. Se sente neta da Águia da Portela, já que o avô foi um dos fundadores da escola. Cresceu ouvindo as histórias e foi ali que o amor pelo samba começou. Durante o desfile, essa paixão mantinha qualquer desconforto longe: “Nunca aconteceu de eu sentir alguma dor durante o desfile. O corpo fica quente, acontece uma troca de energia maravilhosa com o público, uma energia tão boa que não tem muito lugar para sentir dor. Para mim, naquele palco tem uma magia, o show acontece. Sem dor.” Energia essa também que também guia Fabíola Andrade. Foi rainha de bateria da Mocidade Independente de Padre Miguel de 2024 a 2026 e hoje é rainha da escola. Desde criança, já se encantava com a festa, o ritmo e a energia das escolas de samba. Para ela, ser rainha de bateria é fazer parte da história viva do carnaval carioca, levar alegria e garra a uma comunidade inteira. Pensando nas fantasias, diz que é um trabalho artesanal e demorado, feito em equipe com o carnavalesco e estilistas renomados do Carnaval. Segundo ela, os costeiros podem pesar de dez a vinte quilos e o salto alto exige estrutura. Então, garantir que nada saia do lugar é uma verdadeira engenharia. A rainha lembra que já precisou até de uma costura de última hora na fantasia, na concentração, com o coração aos pulos e frio na barriga. Assim como Patrícia, acredita que a adrenalina é um anestésico natural inacreditável, fazendo com que a garra da comunidade e a troca de energia impulsionem toda a animação: "É uma relação de puro amor, cumplicidade e respeito. O mestre de bateria e os ritmistas são o coração da escola, e eu estou ali para ser a energia vibrante daquele ritm

artigo.texto: With the rising tide of data center developments showing no sign of receding, a new Linn County Data Center Advisory Committee will soon be in place to help evaluate possible changes to the county’s existing data center ordinance. Preliminary plans for the committee were discussed during Wednesday’s Linn County Board of Supervisors meeting. The committee was suggested by Supervisor Brandy Z. Meisheid, who said Wednesday it will give local residents a say in how data center decisions are made at the county level. “This process is really something that allows… our constituents to have a voice in how Linn County grows,” Ms. Meisheid said, noting that residents and constituents should “help drive how we make decisions, how we look at these projects.” The move comes as Linn County is three months into an 18-month moratorium on consideration of any new data center proposals in the county’s unincorporated areas. Once formed, the new committee is expected to complete its work before that moratorium expires at the end of December 2027. Linn County Planning and Development director Charlie Nichols outlined the committee’s framework at Wednesday’s meeting. He said the committee will consist of 40 members, including a “substantial portion” representing Linn County cities and regional partners, each chosen by those areas’ governmental bodies. Bordering counties, including Benton County, will also be invited to provide members. Residents of Linn County’s rural areas would then fill the remaining seats through an open application process. Linn County staff will review applications and recommend names, with supervisors making the final choices. Mr. Nichols said the county will seek a geographic balance of committee members, as well as a balance of views and related experience. Applicants will be required to live in Linn County, be 18 or older, and be able to make evening meetings consistently. Each meeting is tentatively set for 6-8 p.m. No formal action was taken on the proposal Wednesday, as the board decided to postpone an official vote until Monday’s work session. Board chair Kirsten Running-Marquardt asked for the delay because the agenda item didn’t tell the public how the committee would be set up. “It’s been three months since the moratorium vote, so I think waiting a couple extra days isn’t going to materially change the process,” Ms. Running-Marquardt said. Ms. Meisheid agreed. “I’d rather do it right than speed it along too quickly,” she said. Once the committee is formally approved, membership applications will be open for about two weeks in October, Mr. Nichols said. Committee members will then be appointed in November, with the first committee meeting in December. The group is expected to meet six to eight times, with all meetings in the evening. Meetings will be open to the public. Potential meeting topics include energy issues, water resources, siting and land use, existing county regulations, and the life cycle and decommissioning of data center facilities – all issues mentioned in the county’s data center moratorium. The committee’s scope will also cover “larger industrial or energy-related development,” not just data centers, Mr. Nichols said. Each meeting will open with a presentation to the full 40-member group, with outside experts as needed. Members will then split into eight groups of five, each with a facilitator taking notes, and report back to the full group – an idea borrowed from the county’s earlier solar moratorium process. Ms. Meisheid said the facilitator model came from the Alburnett School District. She said facilitators are “not to influence… but just to guide conversation” and to manage the “differing views on how we grow.” Materials and notes from each meeting will be uploaded to a dedicated page on the county’s website. “Maximum transparency is what we are going for,” Mr. Nichols said. Before the final meeting, an open house will be held, allowing the public to talk with committee members about the draft recommendations. The committee’s work will then conclude with a set of statements guiding the board on how to update the county’s data center zoning ordinance, which was approved in February after extensive public input. Also Monday, the board will consider a facilitation contract with the East Central Iowa Council of Governments (ECICOG). Ten Linn County staffers, plus Ms. Meisheid, have already agreed to serve as committee facilitators, but under the proposed contract, ECICOG would fill any gaps if staff members can’t attend a meeting. The ECICOG facilitators, which may never be needed, would be paid $225 each per meeting, county officials said. A formal decision to establish the committee, and to approve a contract with ECICOG for backup facilitators, will be made at the board’s meeting Monday, and the application period is set to open Monday as well. “By our residents and constituents (helping to) drive how we make decisions, how we look at these projects, how we look at the growth of Linn County – I think that is the fairest and most transparent way to look at how we how we grow as a community and how we work together beyond just jurisdictional boundaries,” Ms. Meisheid said. “I’m really excited to have the collaboration with our towns, but also to have resident input as well.” To learn more about the committee and the application process, contact Mr. Nichols at (319) 892-5139 or by email at [email protected].

artigo.texto: CFMoto Ibex 450: ela rouba vendas da Himalayan 450 e da Honda NX500? | Teste A CFMoto Ibex 450 chegou ao Brasil para disputar um dos segmentos mais interessantes do mercado de motocicletas. Com motor bicilíndrico de 450 cm³, 44 cv de pot. Crédito: Estadão 30 de setembro de 2026 era a data de abertura do quinto lote de motocicletas da CFMoto, mas a marca cancelou a venda de 700 motocicletas, que seria feita online, por conta de “instabilidades técnicas no servidos do banco de dados”. A promessa de abertura foi feita no último dia 25 de setembro, e as vendas abririam hoje a partir das 12h. Seriam oferecidas unidades da Ibex 450, Ibex 700, CL-C 450 e CL-C 450 Bobber. Ainda não há uma nova data para abertura do quinto lote. Contudo, a reserva continuará sendo feita exclusivamente pela internet, por meio da plataforma da marca. A marca afirmou em nota: “Devido a instabilidades técnicas no nosso servidor de banco de dados, informamos que a abertura de vendas do Lote de Motocicletas, originalmente prevista para hoje (30/09) às 12h00, foi adiada. Tomamos essa decisão de forma preventiva para garantir a estabilidade da plataforma, assegurando que todos tenham as mesmas chances de participação e realize suas reservas com total segurança, sem falhas no processo. Em breve, divulgaremos a nova data e horário de abertura. Agradecemos a compreensão de todos." Inicialmente, a fabricante planejava dedicar o novo lote apenas à Ibex 450. Segundo a CFMoto, a procura pelos outros modelos fez a empresa ampliar a composição da remessa, incluindo novamente as quatro motos que formam atualmente sua linha no País. O lote, quando estiver disponível, será distribuído pelas operações da marca em São Paulo, Campinas, Piracicaba, Rio de Janeiro, Curitiba, Florianópolis, Porto Alegre e Caxias do Sul. LEIA MAIS: - GWM Ora 5: SUV elétrico mais barato do Brasil anda bem, mas dinâmica não combina com o visual - Exclusivo: estas 5 motos da CFMoto podem desembarcar no Brasil em 202 - CFMoto, a ‘BYD das Motos’, fatura mais de R$ 80 milhões em apenas 4 meses no Brasil Os preços atualmente anunciados para a linha são: - CL-C 450: R$ 32.990; - CL-C 450 Bobber: R$ 33.990; - Ibex 450: R$ 35.990; - Ibex 700: R$ 44.990. A Ibex 450 é equipada com motor bicilíndrico de 450,6 cm³ e 44 cv. Já a Ibex 700 utiliza motor de 693 cm³ e 67,9 cv. As quatro motos têm ABS, controle de tração e painel TFT com conectividade Bluetooth. Como reservar uma CFMoto? As reservas começam às 12h de 30 de setembro de 2026. O processo será feito pela plataforma oficial da fabricante. O interessado deverá: - acessar a plataforma de reservas; - escolher a concessionária; - selecionar o modelo; - preencher os dados cadastrais; - concluir o pagamento via Pix. Depois da confirmação, a concessionária escolhida dará continuidade ao processo de compra. A CFMoto mantém o sistema de reservas exclusivamente digital para os lotes. A fabricante afirma que a plataforma foi criada para centralizar as vendas e evitar listas paralelas. CFMoto já vendeu 500 motos em três minutos O novo lote chega depois de uma sequência de remessas esgotadas rapidamente pela CFMoto. No quarto lote, aberto em agosto, 500 motocicletas foram vendidas em três minutos, segundo a fabricante. A maior parte das reservas foi da Ibex 450, e o site registrou 9.347 usuários únicos durante a abertura. O número, porém, precisa ser analisado considerando o tamanho reduzido das remessas. A própria reportagem do Jornal do Carro destacou que a quantidade limitada ajuda a explicar a velocidade do esgotamento. Como comparação, a Honda CG 160 supera 40 mil emplacamentos em um mês. Nos três primeiros lotes, a CFMoto havia colocado pouco mais de 1.700 motocicletas à disposição. O primeiro tinha 700 unidades e acabou em pouco mais de 40 minutos; o segundo, de aproximadamente 500 motos, terminou em menos de cinco minutos; e o terceiro também teve mais de 500 reservas em poucos minutos. CFMoto amplia produção no Brasil A abertura do novo lote acontece enquanto a CFMoto aumenta a capacidade de sua operação brasileira. A fabricante informou que implementou um segundo turno de produção em Manaus no fim de agosto, com o objetivo de ampliar a capacidade de fabricação. A empresa também vem expandindo a rede de concessionárias. Além das operações que atenderão o novo lote, foram anunciadas lojas em cidades como Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Recife, Fortaleza, Salvador, Goiânia, Vitória, Belém e Manaus. Entrevista com Head de Motocicletas da CFMoto para o Jornal do Carro Entrevista com Head de Motocicletas da CFMoto para o Jornal do Carro. Crédito: Isadora Carvalho CFMoto tem mais de 1.400 motos emplacadas A expansão ocorre poucos meses depois do início da operação de motocicletas da CFMoto no Brasil. Até o momento retratado nos dados da Fenabrave, a marca acumulava mais de 1.403 emplacamentos, com a Ibex 450 respondendo por 1.091 registros entre julho e agosto. Em outro levantamento publicado pelo Jornal do Carro, os lotes vendidos nos primeiros meses de operação foram estimados em mais de R$ 80 milhões em faturamento. Esse valor, porém, é uma estimativa baseada nas vendas dos lotes, e não um balanço financeiro divulgado pela empresa. Carregando ofertas... Os comentários são exclusivos para cadastrados.

artigo.texto: Trending LANSING - Stormwater runoff at the sites of data centers is another environmental challenge facing developers because the runoff contains particulates harmful to the public and the ecosystem, according to Reese Dillard, the Michigan Environmental Council's water policy coordinator. Amidst growing public concerns about possible adverse climate effects of data centers such as high energy use and greenhouse gas emissions, the lesser-known threat in stormwater runoff and waste could be just as dangerous, Dillard said. Data centers are facilities used to store, process and transmit digital information. Construction sites need to "upgrade stormwater infrastructure," she said. She said that due to climate change there is increased precipitation and subsequently more flooding at data centers. Data centers use large amounts of water, most drawing from municipal systems, treated wastewater or directly from surface or groundwater. That water is used to absorb heat generated by the computer servers and equipment, and then cycled into cooling towers where some of it evaporates into the atmosphere. The remaining water is cycled back through to absorb more heat. "The pollutants that may be present in data center wastewater discharges depend upon several factors," according to a July report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. They include the "source and quality of the water being used for cooling, the cooling technology being used, site-specific operations and whether the discharges are from normal operations or from construction and commissioning phases," the report said. Data centers typically use a variety of chemical treatments for their cooling systems. They include, but are not limited to, acids, disinfectants, biocides, corrosion inhibitors and dispersants, according to the report. And data center discharges may include those chemicals during maintenance or center start-up. Discharges are typically released into wetlands or streams, introducing harmful pollutants into the nearby ecosystem, the report said, and they could end up in the water lines if not properly treated. "Wastewater discharges may also contain pollutants that are products of metal pipe corrosion, such as copper, nickel and chromium," the report said. Ingesting these chemicals raises public health concerns as they can cause problems such as severe nausea, vomiting, headaches and dizziness, as well as harm to liver, kidneys, respiratory systems, stomach and intestinal lining, according to the National Library of Medicine.

artigo.texto: Gabe Evans rips Democrats for blocking data center bill Critics say bill ‘has no teeth’ Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans tore into Senate Democrats on Wednesday after most of the party’s lawmakers blocked a measure designed to rein in electricity costs associated with building large new data centers. Opponents have insisted the legislation “has no teeth.” Recommended Stories The Senate failed to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act on a 57-43 procedural vote, falling short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a Democratic filibuster. Four Democrats joined every Republican voting in favor of the legislation. Colorado’s two Democratic U.S. senators, Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, voted against moving the legislation forward. Earlier this month, the bill passed the House, where Evans was a prime sponsor, on a nearly unanimous bipartisan vote. Evans accused the opposition party of playing politics, while critics countered that the “toothless” legislation was an attempt to hand a symbolic win to its vulnerable Republican sponsors. Although the bill doesn’t require that data centers “pay their own way,” as some of its Republican backers have claimed, the legislation gives state utility regulators two years to “consider” whether to adopt federal standards that would force new data centers to cover the “full incremental cost” of upgraded electrical generation and transmission infrastructure associated with the facilities. Evans is seeking reelection to a second term in Colorado’s most competitive district against Democratic nominee Manny Rutinel, a former state legislator. Decided by less than 2,500 votes two years ago, the race has already drawn nearly $10 million in outside spending, making it the most expensive toss-up seat in the country so far this cycle. The bill’s Senate sponsor, Republican Jon Husted, is seeking reelection in Ohio, where former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown is attempting to unseat him. “Rather than joining the House in putting Americans first, Senate Democrats choose to prioritize political games over a commonsense solution that protects ratepayers across the country,” Evans said in a statement after the Senate killed his bill. Evans said that the Democrats who backed the bill in the House — including the Democratic members of Colorado’s delegation — “understand protecting hardworking families from costs they didn’t create shouldn’t be controversial. The House proved that this wasn’t a partisan issue. Senate Democrats decided to make it one.” Hickenlooper said in an online video that it was Senate Republicans who were standing in the way of making data centers pick up the tab for increased utility costs. “(The) Republicans’ Ratepayer Protection Act has no teeth,” Hickenlooper said in a social media post. “It won’t actually protect families like yours from paying more on your energy bills.” “Families like yours shouldn’t be forced to pay for their new infrastructure needs,” Hickenlooper said in a video. “Republicans say their bill fixes that. It doesn’t.” Hickenlooper added that Republicans blocked a Democratic amendment “with real teeth” that, he said, would have required that “big new power users pay their fair share of costs.” “If big tech wants a data center, Big Tech should pay for it,” Hickenlooper concluded. “Congress needs to get serious and actually protect ratepayers now.” Evans responded to Hickenlooper on X, pointing out that Colorado’s House Democrats supported the bill. “You had the opportunity to join your Colorado colleagues and protect ratepayers,” Evans posted. “Shocker — you chose not to. One thing is for sure: given the choice, you put your partisan political games over the American people every time.” The exchange continued, with Hickenlooper accusing Evans of voting to approve “$70 billion in tax cuts for data centers” and Evans firing back that Hickenlooper had voted to raise costs for American consumers. The Republican-controlled House adjourned earlier this month until after the November election, and the Senate was expected to conclude its business later on Wednesday, without plans to return until after voters have weighed in.

N.C. Regulators Nix Duke Request Duke Energy Corporation has an ambitious capital construction program in North and South Carolina: it wants to spend at least $34 billion to construct roughly 50,300 megawatts (MW) of new generation capacity by 2041. For more on that, see August 24, 2026, article - Duke Energy Files 2026 Carolinas' Resource Plan. All of Duke's proposed Carolina project activity can be viewed in these project reports and plant profiles. Those plans include adding a 255-MW, gas-fired combustion turbine unit at the company's Sherwood H. Smith, Jr., Energy Complex in Hamlet, North Carolina. That proposed generator, which also could burn hydrogen, has an estimated total investment value of about $584 million. Duke plans to begin construction in September 2027, and finish construction by October 2029. But the schedule for that unit addition could be pushed back. On September 18, the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC) voted 2-1 to deny Duke a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CCN) for that planned unit addition. The commission cited a lack of specificity in Duke's application, particularly around planned data centers, and how the utility would implement the White House "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" it signed in March 2026 to protect captive residential and business customers from paying for the cost to serve data centers. "We are disappointed by the North Carolina Utilities Commission's decision regarding the Smith Energy Complex CPCN application and are reviewing the order and assessing potential next steps," Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton told Industrial Info Resources in an email. "We believe we have demonstrated that the Smith CT is part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina." The North Carolina regulators flagged other issues as well. For example, how would the plan to add this gas-fired generator, with its attendant carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, affect Duke's ability to meet state laws that require utilities to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050? Also, the request was filed before the panel ruled on Duke's integrated resource plan (IRP), a decision expected later this year. The NCUC majority pointed out that state law required utilities to pursue the lowest-cost resources to meet customer electric demand. Would investing more than half a billion dollars be the least-cost option, as required by state law? The North Carolina regulators are scheduled to issue their decision on that IRP by the end of this year. The commission's decision to deny a CCN is not the final word. The commission order would allow Duke to re-apply at a future date. By the Numbers - 584: The total investment value (TIV) in millions of US dollars, that Duke plans to invest to add a new generating unit to its Smith Energy Complex. - 255: The generating capacity, in megawatts, of the planned unit addition Duke wants to build. - 24,500: The amount of new generating capacity, in megawatts, that Duke plans to add to its resource base by 2035. - 70: The estimated proportion of Duke's electric load growth to 2035 that will come from data centers, according to regulatory filings. Big Plans to Build Data Centers in the Carolinas Industrial Info Resources is tracking 120 active and proposed data center projects in the Carolinas, currently slated to begin construction between the start of 2026 and the end of 2041. Not all these projects will be built in Duke's service territory. But as the utility is the largest provider of power in both states, serving more than 4.8 million customers, a majority, if not a significant majority, of those proposed projects likely are slated to be built in Duke's service area. The total investment value (TIV) of these 120 data center projects is about US$102 billion. Readers can learn more from a full list of related project reports. Data Center Issue Called Out by One N.C. Commissioner In a concurrent opinion to the September 18 NCUC decision, Commissioner Tommy Tucker wrote, "the proposed facility's significant and 'staggering' costs, as described by the public staff, are certain, while the proposed facility's value and need is overall uncertain due to the insufficiency of the evidence of record." He added, "As noted in the order, the speculative (electric load) growth noted by (Duke Energy) and the public staff includes significant data center growth, and the record does not adequately establish the specific extent to which the proposed facility is intended to serve the anticipated growth in data center customer demand. While the public staff witness panel indicated that the proposed facility was not being built for a particular customer, it is not lost on me that the proposed facility will be built in the same county as a transmission project previously approved by the Commission to support the load needs of a new customer data center campus." The utility "should provide additional evidence regarding the extent to which the Proposed Facility is needed to provide service to data centers, and how much those data centers will contribute to costs," Tucker wrote. artigo.texto: Understanding Thermal Runaway to Build Safer Battery Energy Storage Systems Editor’s Note: The following article is based on the FDNY Plenary Session, “Considerations for promoting the safe utilization of various lithium-ion battery technologies in the advancement of public policy initiatives in today’s world,” presented at ISPCE 2026 in May 2026. Lithium-ion batteries have become so common that they are easy to take for granted. They power phones, laptops, tools, e-bikes, and electric vehicles, and are associated with convenience and portability. That familiarity makes it easy to overlook the amount of energy these batteries store and how quickly that energy can be released when something goes wrong. New York City began seeing a sharp increase in lithium-ion battery fires beginning in early 2021. Investigations showed that these fires were occurring at an alarming rate, particularly in micromobility devices such as e-bikes and e-scooters. Fires involving lithium-ion batteries were growing rapidly, producing severe conditions earlier than expected and contributing to deaths and injuries across the city. Data from the Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) later documented 268 lithium-ion battery-related fires in 2023 and 277 in 2024, with 18 deaths in 2023 before prevention efforts began to reduce that number. The severity of these incidents also showed in the types of rescues firefighters were being forced to perform. One of the clearest examples was the increased use of the life-saving rope, a high-risk technique used only in extreme circumstances to lower a firefighter from a floor above to rescue someone trapped at a window. In normal conditions, this is a rarely used tactic. It is the kind of rescue that might happen once a decade. Seeing multiple deployments in a single year showed lithium-ion battery fires were trapping occupants before they could reach an exit more frequently than other fire types. Like micromobility devices, battery energy storage systems (BESS) share the same underlying fire hazards. These systems generally use the same lithium-ion technology, but they can scale that energy storage into larger, more complex installations that support buildings, infrastructure, and power systems. As the scale increases, the importance of managing the hazard increases with it. Conditions that drive battery failure do not change, but the consequences depend more heavily on how the system is designed, installed, used, and controlled. Therefore, safe deployment of BESS depends on how these systems are built to perform, not only during normal operation but also when something goes wrong. Understanding how lithium-ion batteries function, how they fail, and how system design influences those outcomes is essential to evaluating risk and supporting safe installation and operation. Known Hazards Battery-powered products are filling the space between small consumer devices and large stationary systems. Portable power packs, battery‑supported appliances, and plug‑in photovoltaic systems with portable storage all raise similar questions about stored energy, use environment, and safety expectations. As lithium-ion batteries appear in more forms, the safety discussion becomes less about product category and more about how the system stores energy, controls failure, and interacts with its surroundings. The Battery Fundamentals Behind the Risk A lithium-ion battery stores and releases energy by moving lithium ions between two electrodes inside a cell. The basic internal structure includes a cathode, an anode, a separator, and an electrolyte. The cathode is typically made from metal oxide-coated aluminum foil. The anode is usually carbon-coated copper foil. The separator is a very thin plastic layer that keeps the two electrodes apart while still allowing ionic movement. The electrolyte is usually made up of an organic solvent, lithium salts, and additives that support charge transfer. That arrangement allows energy to move efficiently during charging and discharging, which is one reason lithium-ion batteries became so central to modern electrical products. The battery can be recharged many times, can deliver power quickly, and can be built in different shapes for different applications. Pouch cells are common in smartphones and laptops. Prismatic cells are used in some electric vehicles and large-scale battery energy storage systems. Cylindrical cells, including the commonly used 18650 format, are used in power tools, e-mobility devices, and some laptops and vehicles. Thermal Runaway Lithium-ion batteries can fail for many different reasons. While the initiating causes may vary, many serious battery safety incidents involve a phenomenon known as thermal runaway. Thermal runaway occurs when an internal short circuit or other condition destabilizes the cell, causing an uncontrolled charge movement across the separator between the anode and cathode. This uncontrolled flow of electricity creates a lot of heat. As the flow continues, the cell generates heat faster than it can dissipate it. That process accelerates internal decomposition, releases more heat, and pushes the cell further into failure. Once thermal runaway begins, it often spreads to adjacent cells. That chain reaction is known as propagation. This is the point at which lithium-ion batteries become fundamentally different from many other electrical hazards. The battery is not simply overheating from the outside. It is generating heat internally in a self-accelerating way. That process can continue until all affected cells are consumed or until sufficient cooling slows the reaction. In large systems, the difference between a single failing cell and a propagating event is one of the most important risk distinctions to understand. artigo.texto: BROKEN BOW, Neb.— The Custer County Board of Supervisors met in regular session for just short of two hours on Tuesday morning starting at 9 AM. Toward the end of the meeting, public hearings were held for the possible closure of road 351 outside of Sargent, data center regulations that were passed to the board from the planning commission, and a possible temporary moratorium on battery energy storage systems. Landowners alongside road 351 came before the board to express their support of the closure, saying the road hasn’t been graded since the floods that happened several years ago. They did express an interest in an easement agreement since a party would be land locked with the closure of the road. Ultimately the board decided to give the township its 120 days time to decide if they want to maintain the road. During that time, they will check to see if the county is to have involvement in the easement process or if the private parties handle it themselves. Ahead of the public hearing regarding data center regulations that were put in the hands of the supervisors from the planning commission last week, Zoning Administrator Darci Tibbs made a statement regarding the process. “The purpose of these regulations is to not encourage or attract data centers, but to make sure that if one is proposed in Custer County, we have appropriate standards and safeguards in place to protect the health, safety, and welfare of our citizens, and to protect the ag and rural character of the county,” said Tibbs. Hear the full statement from Tibbs here: No members of the public came forward to make a statement during the public hearing and a resolution will appear for consideration by the board at an upcoming meeting. Tibbs also made a statement expressing the planning commission’s desire for a 12 month moratorium on battery energy storage systems so that ample time could be given to researching them and working toward regulations. Tibbs explained that the systems typically include battery units or containers, inverters, transformers, cooling equipment, electrical controls, monitoring systems, and safety equipment. The facilities can range from small systems serving one property to large commercial or utility scale facilities that can occupy multiple acres and connect to the electrical grid. No members of the public came forward to speak and a resolution that would put the moratorium in place will be on an upcoming agenda. The initial amount certified, including interest and fees was $52,611.63. The Sheriff’s office collected $36,314.60. artigo.texto: O Ministério do Planejamento, Orçamento e Gestão (MP) está exigindo que todos os órgãos governamentais apenas contratem serviços de cloud computing que tenham data centers localizados no Brasil. Ou seja, nada de armazenar os dados via nuvem baseada em computadores estrangeiros. A decisão surgiu por meio de um manual de "boas práticas, orientações e vedações". "A nossa expectativa é que os próprios fornecedores tenham o total interesse em resguardar o sigilo das informações quando assim for exigido. Se, eventualmente, houver problemas de judicialização, é importante que isso seja feito na jurisdição brasileira”, comentou o secretário de Tecnologia da Informação da pasta, Cristiano Heckert, segundo o CW. Para reduzir os gastos, o manual também diz para os órgãos do Sistema de Administração dos Recursos de TI (SISP) não contratarem salas-cofre e salas seguras. O documento tem o apoio de Heckert, que comenta que essas orientações devem otimizar os recursos de infraestrutura. Espionagem? Se alocar os dados de servidores em data centers nacionais é um medo de espionagem ou vazamento de informações, é necessário lembrar que a tecnologia de espionagem internacional está bem na frente. artigo.texto: The U.S. data center boom has entered a new, contradictory phase. On the one hand, both data center construction activity and credible forecasts for near-term capacity additions to the electric grid to serve data centers remain robust. The Electric Power Research Institute, for example, said in February that data centers will represent up to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and as much as 20% in 2035. On the other hand, data center and utility infrastructure projects face a host of challenges. These include both physical constraints, such as equipment and labor shortages, as well as mounting public opposition driven by concerns about large-scale computing facilities’ impact on water supplies, the cost and reliability of power and natural gas supplies, and the quality of life in host communities. The upshot is that even some data center development projects advanced enough to appear in utility load forecasts with a named hyperscaler attached are not certain to move forward. Near Grand Rapids, Michigan, for example, a Microsoft data center touted by Consumers Energy faces an uncertain future amid local permitting delays. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground." Blake Nixon President and CEO of Geronimo Power Another Microsoft-backed data center in Vineland, New Jersey, was recently hit with a $1 million fine for running dozens of gas-powered generators without the proper permits, and ordered to obtain them within 45 days or shut down. A proposed Google data center that would interconnect in Xcel Energy’s Minnesota territory faces a court-ordered work stoppage to allow time for environmental review. Even projects that sought to circumvent interconnection delays by building off-grid generation have seen setbacks. Last week, Oracle moved to protect itself financially from the delay or cancellation of Project Jupiter, a massive, 2.5-GW data center campus planned for Doña Ana County, New Mexico, after state regulators blocked a gas pipeline proposed to serve it. Data center opposition “has reached a pitch I have never seen before in my 20-plus years in development,” Blake Nixon, president and CEO of Geronimo Power, told Utility Dive in an interview. This spring, officials in Nobles County, Minnesota, shot down a proposal by Geronimo to build a 400 MW “data park” there, despite the company’s efforts at community outreach. Now, Nixon said his team is considering alternative sites in nearby communities. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground,” he said. In May, Goldman Sachs said only 50%-60% of planned data center capacity will come online as expected in the next two years amid delays and cancellations. And while the 36 GW of capacity added to the development pipeline in the first quarter of 2026 sounds impressive, that’s down 19% from the last quarter of 2025 as developers “continue to shift their focus to existing … pipelines in the face of an increasingly challenging development and regulatory environment,” Caitlin Connelly, a senior analyst with Wood Mackenzie, said in a July note. Experts say these developments raise questions about just how much data center load will come online in the near term — injecting unwelcome uncertainty into utility planning cycles that must look years, even decades, into the future. Working around grid constraints with flexibility, BYO capacity It’s increasingly difficult for developers of large-scale data center campuses to find sites with the hundreds of megawatts, let alone gigawatts, of spare grid capacity they expect their projects to need at full build-out. In the PJM Interconnection, real or perceived power scarcity is a major driver of both local opposition and top-down political backlash to the industry. The independent market monitor in July blamed data centers for 38% of charges at the most recent capacity auction. The Democratic governors of Pennsylvania, Virginia and New Jersey have taken action in recent months to push regulators to require data centers to bring more generation and transmission capacity online. These moves are not only in PJM states with Democratic governors. Power scarcity and cost concerns have triggered organized opposition and political backlash to data centers in places developers until recently believed were sympathetic to their cause, like Texas and Utah. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, R, successfully pushed for a sweeping pause on data center grid interconnections that threatens up to 20% of the total U.S. development pipeline, BloombergNEF said earlier this month. Utilities and data centers are responding in several ways. The most straightforward is through “bring your own capacity” arrangements in which computing facilities colocate with new generation or finance local capacity additions. Some of these arrangements are massive: OpenAI agreed earlier this month to take 8 GW of the capacity from a planned 10 GW power generation project in Ohio that includes 9.2-GW gas assets. The facility, which is being pursued by Japan’s SoftBank Group and the U.S. Department of Energy, would be the country’s largest generation source if built. If not, that title would go to Amazon’s proposed 7.7-GW gas-fired power plant in West Texas, which would also be larger than the current titleholder, Washington state’s 6.8-GW Grand Coulee hydroelectric dam. Smaller-scale capacity procurements are also in the works, like Google’s “first-of-its-kind” deal with Voltus for 100 MW of virtual power plant capacity in PJM. Elsewhere, utilities and data centers are pursuing asset-light alternatives using software to find previously untapped headroom on the grid or to ramp down computing loads during periods of peak demand. artigo.texto: The Science Newswise — Battery materials called electrolytes allow ions (charged particles) to move from one end of a battery to the other. This process is necessary for charging and discharging. Superionic conductors (SICs) are materials that are solids, but some of their ions move like liquids. As a result, they conduct electricity very well. One SIC, lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride, is a promising type of solid-state battery material. Using neutron scattering and computer simulations, researchers gained a better understanding of this material’s atomic dynamics. By raising the material to more than 400 K (260 F), they put it in the superionic state where ions act like a liquid. In that state, the scientists found that lithium ions can hop quickly through the material’s crystal structure. The team also documented how specific types of vibrations in the crystal enable ions to jump through vibrating crystal bottlenecks. The scientists discovered that these vibrations enable long-range flow and significant improvements in conductivity. The Impact These findings show researchers how to improve ion flow inside a solid-state battery material, which would increase its performance. This information could enable a solid-state battery material that offers very high quantities of mobile ions as well as good chemical and thermal stability. This structure would enable a battery to use solid electrolytes that could perform as well as liquid ones. (Ions move more freely through liquid electrolytes than solid ones.) As such, this change could enable faster and safer battery charging. The ability to tailor SIC materials could also guide researchers in developing and improving other devices, such as fuel cells and computers. Summary One class of materials, superionic conductors (SICs), has the properties of both a crystalline and liquid electrolyte. When warmed above a specific temperature, the material remains partly crystalline, but also develops ion flow properties like those of liquids. This study combined machine-learning simulations with inelastic and quasielastic neutron scattering at the Spallation Neutron Source, a DOE Office of Science User Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The researchers investigated lithium-ion dynamics in the SIC lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride. The team found the crystalline framework facilitated fast, liquid-like hopping of lithium ions between stable crystalline lattice sites. Additionally, they documented significant enhancements in lithium-ion diffusion across a range of temperatures through the dynamic breathing (unified relaxation) of vibrating diffusion bottlenecks. They also observed how the vibrational spectra of mobile lithium ions in Li₆PS₅Cl evolve from a crystal-like to liquid-like phase. The research bridges conventional diffusive and lattice vibrational models. These findings offer important insights into the rapid ionic motion in SICs for potential use in solid electrolyte batteries, fuel cells, and computing systems. Funding The research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation (DMREF project); the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Basic Energy Sciences, Division of Materials Sciences and Engineering; and the German Research Foundation. This work used resources at the Spallation Neutron Source and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, both DOE Office of Science User Facilities.

Ataque de Kiev a um navio iraniano no mar Cáspio expõe uma rede densa de inteligência militar circulando entre os dois conflitos. Maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia, a Kyivstar foi alvo de um ataque da Rússia no domingo (27), em meio a bombardeios lançados por Moscou contra a infraestrutura de telecomunicações do país vizinho. A ofensiva não resultou em vítimas, como informou a empresa à agência de notícias Interfax. Além do ataque à sede da prestadora em Kiev, um data center da Vodafone também teria sido atingido, como divulgado pelo Ministério da Defesa da Rússia. No entanto, a empresa que possui a segunda maior rede celular da região optou por não comentar o assunto. Ucranianos sem acesso à internet Os ataques do domingo, que também incluíram outro data center na capital ucraniana, ferindo um adulto e duas crianças, segundo o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky, não são casos isolados. Na última semana, os sistemas de comunicação do país sofreram diversos bombardeios. - Como relata a Reuters, centros de dados utilizados por operadoras locais estavam entre os principais alvos; - Em um dos casos, as explosões teriam interrompido a conectividade para cerca de 100 mil residências ao longo da semana; - Os clientes que ficaram sem acesso à internet residem principalmente em Kiev e cidades próximas, de acordo com o Ministério Digital da Ucrânia; - Autoridades do país disseram que os bombardeios afetaram sistemas críticos para a segurança, aumentando os riscos de mortes durante os ataques. “A Rússia tem como alvo importantes centros de dados ucranianos, buscando interromper o fluxo de informações. Alertas rápidos sobre ameaças de mísseis e drones são essenciais, eles salvam vidas”, afirmou Andrii Sybha, Ministro das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, em mensagem compartilhada no X. Na rede social, ele também disse que alguns dos ataques russos incluem drones Shahed com propulsão a jato, uma nova variante da aeronave não tripulada. Essas versões se destacam pela capacidade de alcançar mais de 600 km/h de velocidade e operar em altitudes mais elevadas, dificultando as ações dos sistemas de defesa aérea. Um drone guiado por IA lançado pela Rússia matou três civis na Ucrânia no mês passado, em um dos primeiros ataques realizados por aeronaves autônomas. Relembre o caso. Com informações da Reuters.

artigo.texto: Data centers have gained considerable attention in Upstate South Carolina and across the United States. The growing number of these facilities throughout the country supports the modern digital age, specifically the rising demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Despite this growth, many questions remain about how many data centers are in operation or planned. South Carolina has become an increasingly attractive location for data centers due to land availability, low regulatory barriers and economic incentives. However, public opposition to the development of these facilities has grown in recent years. Upstate Business Journal took a closer look at data centers to provide more information on what they are, where we think they are located and what local governments are doing about them. What are data centers? Data centers are facilities that house and operate computer systems, storage devices and network equipment. These facilities are used for the storage, management and processing of significant amounts of data. Types of data centers There are three main types of data centers: - Enterprise Data Centers: Private data centers owned and operated by a business or organization. - Colocation and Service Provider Data Centers: Shared data centers offering leasable space for multiple businesses and organizations. - Hyperscale Data Centers: Massive data centers operated by major technology companies for large-scale data processing, storage and computing. Source: Pew Research Center and International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Statewide tracking The South Carolina Department of Commerce does not track how many data centers are in the state. Instead, the agency monitors the number of facilities that apply for a sales tax exemption. This tracking method does not provide an accurate list of data centers in South Carolina. Alex Clark, the agency’s deputy director of communications, said not all data centers pursue this certification, and not all certified data centers begin operations in South Carolina. According to SC Commerce, the agency has received one sales tax exemption application since the beginning of 2026 and four applications in the past three years. Estimated data centers in SC The total number of data centers in South Carolina and where they are located remains unclear. Data Center Map, an industry database, estimates there are 48 data centers across 12 markets in South Carolina. Markets in the Upstate with data centers include Spartanburg, Greenville, Anderson, Seneca and Gaffney. National and regional breakdown More than 3,000 data centers are estimated to be in operation in the United States, with more than 1,500 new data centers under development. - South: 1,209 existing and 754 planned data centers - Midwest: 655 existing and 419 planned data centers - West: 807 existing and 277 planned data centers - Northeast: 397 existing and 106 planned data centers Source: Pew Research Center Environmental concerns Common environmental concerns regarding data center development include: - Water and energy consumption - Noise disruption - Air pollution - Large land use Source: Southern Environmental Law Center Energy consumption Powering and cooling the computer systems and equipment within data centers require vast amounts of electricity and water. According to the International Energy Agency, a 100-megawatt data center consumes: - As much electricity annually as 100,000 households. - As much water per day as around 6,500 households (an average of 2 million liters) Source: International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Fast fact The United States made up the largest share – 45% – of global data center electricity consumption in 2024. Data center energy consumption grew by approximately 12% between 2015 and 2024. Source: International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Notable local projects Valara Holdings High Performance Compute Center NorthMark Strategies, through its subsidiary Valara Holdings, is constructing a high-performance computing data center southeast of Spartanburg. The $2.8 billion project, announced in April 2025, redevelops the former Kohler manufacturing plant at 4000 S. Pine St. Spartanburg County Council approved economic incentives for the project in 2025. The new data center campus will feature an on-site power plant with 24 permitted natural gas generators and 11 proposed natural gas-fired turbines. An application was submitted in March to the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services for a second synthetic minor air construction permit for the additional turbines. If approved, the data center would have a power generation capacity of more than 450 megawatts. DartPoints Greenville Data Center DartPoints announced plans to invest $125 million into its existing data center in Greenville in November 2025. The enterprise-class data center is located at 78 Global Drive in Greenville’s Global Business Park near the intersection of Interstate 85 and Laurens Road. The expansion adds 88,000 square feet to the Greenville data center and creates 10 new high-tech jobs. The facility’s total capacity will be increased from 2.5 megawatts to 12.5 megawatts to support artificial intelligence, enterprise and edge applications. Data center moratorium Multiple government entities in Upstate South Carolina are considering or have approved a moratorium on approving new data center applications. - Spartanburg County: Spartanburg County Council has approved the first and second readings of a one-year data center moratorium. The third and final reading of the moratorium was expected to be held during County Council’s meeting on Sept. 21. - Anderson County: Anderson County Council gave final approval to a six-month moratorium on data center applications in August. - Greenwood County: Greenwood County Council approved the third and final reading of a one-year moratorium on data center applications in July. - South Carolina: House Bills 5526 and 5286 were introduced in early 202

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE — The Janesville City Council on Monday voted unanimously to enact a one-year moratorium on data centers within the city. The southern Wisconsin city is just the latest community to put the brakes on the rush of data center developments across the country. The ordinance comes as residents are preparing for a November referendum that if approved, would allow voters a say in any future major developments in the city, including data centers. According to a staff memo accompanying the ordinance, the moratorium would pause the acceptance, processing, review and approval of any application related to the development of a data center, including rezoning of property, permits, action taken on annexation requests, or other development approvals. During the moratorium, city staff would not solicit or actively encourage data center development, nor enter nondisclosure agreements related to such development projects. The purpose of the moratorium is to allow sufficient time to research environmental, economic, health, safety and land-use compatibility impacts; continue preparation of zoning code review, processes, and specific development standards for data center projects. It also would allow time for city staff to complete and the council to consider the Data Center Companion Ordinance.

artigo.texto: Archbald will hold back-to-back public hearings this week to gather testimony as council weighs developers’ applications for a power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road and seven data centers at a quarry. Council will convene at 5 p.m. Tuesday to continue to hear testimony on the 400-megawatt Essential Energy LLC natural gas power plant proposed near Staback Park and across from the same developer’s Project Boson data center. Then, the borough will hold a hearing Wednesday at 5 p.m. on Project Green Mountain’s proposal to build a data center campus across nearly 271 acres at the Stavola Quarry off the Casey Highway. Essential Energy Power plant representatives faced criticism and pushback during five preceding hearings over the conceptual nature of their plans as council considers Essential Energy’s March 12 application for a natural gas power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road. The debate over how much information is enough to satisfy Archbald’s zoning requirements has prevailed across data center and power plant hearings in the borough this year. Residents advocate for specific information during the hearings, while developers argue they can’t refine their plans until after they have approval. Developers’ representatives contend that permitting and regulations from agencies such as the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will protect the community. Archbald has held hearings on Essential Energy’s plans April 27, May 21, June 22, July 21 and Aug. 18. The most recent hearing concluded with testimony from Andrew Markle, the technical lead of power generation for KCI Technologies of Mechanicsburg, which is the engineering firm representing Essential Energy. Markle spoke broadly about the operations and safety features designed into power plants, touting his experience overseeing power plant development both domestically and abroad. The hearing concluded before cross-examination, so Tuesday’s hearing will likely open with questions posed to Markle. Cross-examiners include attorney Justin Richards of Elliott Greenleaf PC in Wilkes-Barre, who represents Archbald residents opposing data centers; Stop Archbald Data Centers co-founder Tamara Misewicz-Healey; Highlands Archbald residents Karen Timmons and Meg Nudelman; Valley View School District Solicitor Kyle Callejas; and Archbald’s special counsel, attorney Brett C. Flower of Eckert Seamans in Harrisburg. Project Green Mountain Representatives for Project Green Mountain will return to Archbald on Wednesday after a three-month hiatus. Green Mountain 6 LLC, using a Pittsburgh law firm as its address, filed a conditional-use application Jan. 26, making Project Green Mountain Archbald’s sixth proposed data center project, with plans for seven two-story data centers, each 65 feet tall with 138,000-square-foot footprints. Project Green Mountain’s data centers would span an L-shaped campus at the Stavola Quarry. It is the only application so far in Archbald that sites data centers opposite the Casey Highway away from residential development. The data centers would use a projected 525 megawatts of electricity, divided into 75 megawatts per building, while using up to 14,000 gallons of water daily from Pennsylvania American Water for domestic uses like sinks and toilets. During an outage, Green Mountain would use 196 backup diesel generators, each storing up to 10,000 gallons of diesel fuel, totaling 1.96 million gallons stored on site. Project Green Mountain’s initial hearing March 19 largely discussed the campus’s utility demands and potential economic incentives. On May 11, it focused on air emissions from backup generators, as well as traffic from the data centers. The June 18 hearing focused on the noise of data centers and their generators. Though Project Green Mountain’s sound study found that the campus would remain below Archbald’s 55-decibel residential daytime limit, even with all 196 backup generators running, it was heavily scrutinized in cross-examination During the latest hearing, Project Green Mountain attorney Jeffrey Wilhelm of Reed Smith LLP in Pittsburgh responded to a question from Councilwoman Lisa Osborne asking if the developer had finished any other data center campuses with a post-construction sound study to give the borough additional insight. Wilhelm told Osborne they would come back with an answer to her question at another hearing. Both hearings will be at the Valley View High School auditorium, 1 Columbus Drive, Archbald. Borough Solicitor Jay O’Connor announced the Essential Energy hearing at the conclusion of the last hearing on the power plant in August, and the borough announced the Project Green Mountain hearing via a public notice published Sept. 15 in The Times-Tribune. Both Essential Energy, which is tied to Archbald-based Kriger Construction Inc. and its executive leadership, and Project Green Mountain seek conditional-use approval from Archbald council, which requires the developers to testify at public hearings to explain how their projects abide by the borough’s zoning regulations for data centers and power plants. Other companies tied to Kriger and its leadership also proposed four data centers and three power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City. Affected residents who received party status and their attorney, borough officials and the Valley View School District’s solicitor all have the opportunity to cross-examine each witness presented by the developers. Once they conclude their testimony, any of the opposing parties can then present their own evidence. Council will accept public comment prior to voting, though it is unclear exactly when any decisions will occur. There are currently 51 data centers formally proposed in the borough across half a dozen projects, although two other data center developers look to expand in Archbald around the Valley View Business Park. Proprietary iron & saltwater electrolyte According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Flow Battery Energy Storage market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global flow battery energy storage market is entering a decisive commercial phase as utilities and developers seek long-duration storage solutions that can economically shift renewable generation across four to twelve hours or more. Unlike lithium-ion systems, flow batteries separate power and energy, allowing independent scaling of duration and capacity, which makes them attractive for grid operators facing rising renewable curtailment and peak-shaving needs. As of 2026, deployment remains concentrated in utility-scale projects and selected industrial microgrids, but the pipeline is broadening as vanadium supply chains mature, project bankability improves, and grid interconnection standards become clearer. The market is supported by ambitious decarbonization targets, renewable portfolio standards, and the need for resilient grid infrastructure. However, growth is tempered by vanadium price volatility, competition from lithium-ion and other long-duration technologies, and the complexity of project financing. This report provides a structured analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, pricing logic, competitive positioning, and regional outlooks. It is designed for manufacturers, integrators, utilities, investors, and policymakers seeking a commercially grounded view of where flow battery energy storage is heading and which segments will lead adoption. The baseline scenario for the world flow battery energy storage market through 2035 assumes continued policy support for renewable integration and long-duration storage, steady improvement in vanadium electrolyte supply, and gradual cost reduction as manufacturing scale increases. Under this scenario, the market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 18.5% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 520 by 2035 (2025 = 100). Growth is expected to be front-loaded in Asia-Pacific, particularly China, where large-scale vanadium redox flow battery projects are already being deployed for grid balancing and renewable time-shifting. North America and Europe will follow, driven by utility procurement mandates and the need to replace retiring thermal peaking capacity. The baseline assumes no major breakthrough in alternative long-duration technologies that would displace flow batteries in the 4–12 hour duration range, but it also assumes that lithium-ion will continue to dominate shorter-duration applications. Key uncertainties include vanadium price spikes, delays in grid interconnection queues, and the pace of cost declines in competing technologies. The market outlook remains positive, with flow batteries carving out a durable niche in long-duration, high-cycle applications where safety, scalability, and longevity are paramount. Electric utilities and grid operators are the primary adopters of flow battery energy storage, driven by the need to integrate high shares of variable renewable generation and maintain grid reliability. Flow batteries are increasingly chosen for renewable time-shifting, peak shaving, and ancillary services where discharge durations of four to twelve hours are required. Utilities value the independent scalability of power and energy, which allows them to size systems precisely to grid needs, and the long cycle life that matches asset lifetimes. As of 2026, several large-scale projects are operational or under construction, particularly in China and the United States. Through 2035, demand will be supported by capacity auctions, clean energy standards, and the retirement of coal and gas peakers. Key demand-side indicators include renewable curtailment rates, peak demand growth, and the volume of storage capacity procured in utility integrated resource plans. The segment's growth is also tied to the increasing need for grid resilience amid extreme weather events. Current trend: Growing. Major trends: Rising procurement of long-duration storage in utility integrated resource plans, Policy mandates for renewable integration and grid resilience, Shift from pilot projects to commercial-scale deployments, Growing use of flow batteries for peak capacity replacement, and Increased focus on domestic content and supply chain security. Representative participants: Sumitomo Electric Industries, Rongke Power, VRB Energy, Invinity Energy Systems, and Stryten Energy. Renewable energy developers and independent power producers (IPPs) are increasingly incorporating flow batteries into solar and wind projects to improve project economics and meet grid requirements. Co-locating storage with renewables allows developers to shift generation to high-price periods, reduce curtailment, and provide firm capacity. Flow batteries are particularly attractive for projects requiring durations beyond four hours, where lithium-ion becomes less cost-effective. As of 2026, several large solar-plus-storage projects with flow batteries are in advanced development, especially in Australia, the Middle East, and Africa. Through 2035, demand will be driven by falling renewable costs, corporate power purchase agreements with 24/7 clean energy goals, and grid connection rules that require storage. Key indicators include the levelized cost of storage, renewable penetration rates, and the share of new renewable projects paired with long-duration storage. Developers value the modularity and safety of flow batteries, which simplify permitting and insurance. Current trend: Growing. artigo.texto: O edital para a segunda parte da concessão da Floresta Nacional do Bom Futuro, em Porto Velho (RO), foi publicado. A área de quase 40 mil hectares será usada para restaurar áreas degradadas, gerar empregos locais e produzir créditos de carbono, ajudando o Brasil a cumprir sua meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até 2030. O Serviço Florestal Brasileiro (SFB) e o Ministério do Meio Ambiente (MMA) divulgaram as regras para a venda do segundo lote de gestão da Floresta Nacional (Flona) do Bom Futuro, localizada em Porto Velho, no estado de Rondônia. O processo foi preparado com ajuda técnica do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e tem como objetivo principal recuperar áreas que foram degradadas na região da Amazônia, permitindo que empresas privadas gerenciem o espaço de forma sustentável. O documento do edital mostra que a área disponível é muito grande, ultrapassando 39 mil hectares. Para dar uma noção do tamanho, isso equivale a quase 55 mil campos de futebol. Deste total, cerca de 6,4 mil hectares serão usados especificamente para plantar árvores e restaurar a floresta. As empresas interessadas devem entregar suas propostas na sede da bolsa de valores B3, em São Paulo, entre 10h e 12h do dia 4 de novembro. A abertura das propostas, para ver quem ganhou, está marcada para o dia 18 de novembro. - Área Gigante: São mais de 39 mil hectares, o que é maior que muitas cidades do interior. - Meta Climática: A ação ajuda o Brasil a cumprir a promessa de recuperar 12 milhões de hectares de vegetação até 2030. - Carro de Ouro: A empresa vencedora poderá vender créditos de carbono, o que ajuda a pagar pela restauração. - Empregos Locais: O projeto exige contratação de moradores da região e compra de sementes locais. - Primeiro Caso: O lote anterior foi ganhado pela empresa Re.Green, marcando a primeira concessão de restauração no Brasil. Modelo de concessão e impacto social Este é o segundo leilão para recuperar a floresta neste local. O primeiro lote foi arrematado pela empresa Re.Green em março. Naquela ocasião, foi a primeira vez no Brasil que uma empresa ganhou o direito de cuidar de uma floresta pública principalmente para gerar receita com a venda de créditos de carbono (prova de que a atividade removeu poluição do ar). Agora, com esse segundo lote, o governo espera repetir o sucesso e ampliar a restauração. O contrato da concessão não fala apenas de plantio. Ele exige que parte do dinheiro ganho com o projeto seja investida em pesquisa científica, educação ambiental e proteção da floresta. Além disso, o edital manda que a empresa ajude as comunidades que moram no entorno da reserva, incluindo a população indígena Karitiana. Há regras para garantir que mulheres tenham chances iguais, que povos indígenas sejam incluídos no processo e que a economia local seja fortalecida com a compra de insumos e contratação de mão de obra da região. Desafio nacional de recuperação da vegetação Esta concessão faz parte de um plano maior do Brasil para recuperar a mata nativa. De acordo com os dados divulgados, essa ação contribui diretamente para a meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até o ano de 2030, estabelecida pelo Plano Nacional de Recuperação da Vegetação Nativa (Planaveg). Atualmente, o país já tem 3,4 milhões de hectares em processo de recuperação. Isso representa quase um terço da meta total. O novo lote da Flona do Bom Futuro vem justamente para impulsionar esse número, focando em uma das regiões mais importantes e frágeis da Amazônia.
