artigo.texto: HSBC maintains bearish stance on Ola Electric despite battery manufacturing gains While acknowledging the electric vehicle maker's progress in cell localisation and gigafactory capacity, the brokerage cited weak financial performance and balance sheet concerns in maintaining a reduce rating. Global brokerage HSBC has maintained a bearish Reduce rating on Ola Electric Mobility Ltd., setting a target price that implies a nearly 38 per cent downside, despite acknowledging significant operational progress in the company's battery manufacturing and localisation efforts. The divergence between Ola Electric's technological advancements and its financial realities was laid bare in a recent brokerage note following visits to the company's manufacturing facilities. While HSBC praised the electric two-wheeler maker's vertical integration and proprietary cell technology, it cited weaker-than-expected recent financial performance and low confidence in management's near-term estimates as primary drivers of its cautious stance. Gigafactory milestones and technological optimism HSBC analysts recently conducted site visits to Ola Electric's Gigafactory and its future electric vehicle assembly plant. The brokerage noted that the Gigafactory's capacity has successfully reached 6 gigawatt-hours (GWh), a critical milestone in the company's strategy to reduce reliance on imported battery cells. The firm expects the facility's manufacturing yields to improve to approximately 90 per cent from the current 70 per cent over the next six to nine months. The brokerage specifically highlighted Ola's development of the 4680 cell utilizing proprietary dry-cathode technology. Management asserts that this innovation can reduce operating costs by 20 to 30 per cent compared to traditional wet-cathode processing. Furthermore, HSBC observed that the future factory reflects a high degree of automation and vertical integration, which supports management's claims of achieving better operating margins in the long term. On the retail front, the company is aggressively expanding its footprint. Ola Electric's dealer network is projected to jump from 30 to approximately 150 outlets by the Navratri festival, a crucial sales period for the Indian automotive sector. Notably, HSBC does not currently view the company's unsold inventory levels as a red flag, attributing them to the transitional phase of new product rollouts. Balance sheet realities and market reaction Despite the operational positives, HSBC's financial modeling remains deeply conservative. The brokerage set a target price of Rs 24 per share, implying a steep 37.6 per cent downside from recent closing levels. This bearish valuation reflects the firm's pricing of weaker-than-expected performance metrics and a fundamental lack of confidence in the company's aggressive forward estimates. The market reacted swiftly to the brokerage's assessment. Ola Electric's stock took a significant hit in Monday trade, falling as much as 3.5 per cent to Rs 36.53. This decline notably outperformed the broader market downturn, with the benchmark Nifty index falling 0.86 per cent and the overall auto sector slipping 0.7 per cent. The company's first-quarter results for the current fiscal year reflect the ongoing transition following a major operational reset undertaken previously. While the consolidated net loss narrowed to Rs 336 crore, revenue from operations fell sharply by 45 per cent year-on-year to Rs 455 crore. Management described the quarter as the first full period reflecting its restructuring efforts, emphasizing a sequential recovery in the automotive business. The road to operational restructuring For Ola Electric, the immediate challenge lies in reconciling its heavy capital expenditure on localisation with the need for near-term revenue growth. The company's diversification attempts beyond China for equipment sourcing and its focus on higher energy density cells are viewed positively as long-term strategic moats. However, rebuilding brand image and ensuring consistent delivery commitments remain key monitorables for investors. The broader electric two-wheeler sector in India is also navigating a period of moderated growth. Slower penetration rates and intense competition from legacy automakers and emerging startups have forced companies to prioritize unit economics over sheer volume accumulation. Until Ola Electric can demonstrate that its battery manufacturing prowess translates into sustained market share and improved cash flows, brokerages like HSBC remain cautious, advising investors to weigh the promise of vertical integration against the immediate realities of the balance sheet. artigo.texto: AURORA | Monday’s Aurora City Council meeting featured three hours of public comment opposing what would be Colorado’s largest data center. Around 100 residents of The Reserve, a local senior housing community, and the surrounding Windler and Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods attended the meeting to voice their concerns and disagreement with the planned Trident data center, located at 23001 East 48th Ave in northeast Aurora. Before public comment started, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked the audience to stand if they opposed the data center and nearly every attendee stood. No one stood in support of the data center. Speakers, who ranged in age from 16 to 86, were emphatic in their requests for council to impose regulations on data centers, including residential buffers, and require the Trident data center to have more safeguards for health and the environment. Dan Bergander, a resident of The Reserve, highlighted the potential health and quality of life impacts the data center will have on older and disabled neighbors. As he spoke, 50 or more people in the audience stood to support him while he spoke and then burst into applause when he finished. “I’m here speaking for the other at-risk neighbors in the audience and at home, and surprisingly enough, I’m also speaking for your future,” Bergander said. “You on city council will one day settle into retirement and I certainly hope you’re not betrayed by developers and government officials.” When the comments reached the typical hour limit, council voted 9-1 to hear all of the speakers who signed up, with Council member Curtis Gardner opposed. Other than some council members thanking the public for attending, the council did not respond to the wave of comments or address the Trident project at Monday’s meeting. Council did unanimously approve a ban on evaporative cooling, which is a more water intensive cooling system used by some data centers. Planning documents show the Trident data center will be around 860,000 square feet and located in Airport District zoning, which allows data centers as a use by right, which means the project can be approved administratively by the city without a public hearing, unless the project is requesting a variance. While Trident is not requesting a variance, city spokesperson Jennifer Soules said the city is working with the developer, Vantage Data Centers, to schedule a community meeting, but a date has not yet been set. A development application and site plan for the data center were first submitted in August 2025 and the project is on its third round of reviews, according to the city. Neighborhood opposition has grown swiftly, with a local town hall on Sept. 22 drawing about 150 people, while a Change.org petition against the project has more than 2,500 signatures. Ray Czaplewski, a resident of The Reserve whose home will be about a quarter-mile from the data center, said he found out about the project just two weeks ago from his neighbors. Czaplewski described feeling appalled and betrayed when he found out about the data center. “We were blindsided by it,” he said. “Never in our wildest dreams would we expect our city government to be complacent with putting in a hyperscale data center literally right next to residential areas.” Czaplewski said he has a lot of unanswered questions and he raised concerns about noise, air pollution and the toll of the facility on water and energy resources. He also disapproves of the city’s development process allowing data centers without public hearings or notification. “The use by right categorization in the airport district is designed to be opaque,” Czaplewski said. “If we had known a year ago and knew the magnitude of this, we could have started working with Vantage.” Czaplewski and other residents want the city to require a fourth review period to ensure all of the concerns are mitigated. Should they not be addressed, the group is considering legal action for possible damages to health and property values, Czaplewski said. Vantage’s Misty Allen, vice president of public policy for North America, said the company is planning more community outreach as the project moves into construction, including neighborhood meetings and a public website where construction updates will be shared. “It’s perfectly reasonable when people have questions of new developments coming into their community and it’s our commitment that we will be having open community conversations as the design for the project moves forward,” Allen said. “All of that engagement will start to kick off as the project moves forward, so we’re just at the beginning of this.” Allen said the meetings will include subject matter experts to answer questions and connect residents to company representatives. “We’re going to be here for the long-term, so it’s important for folks to get to know the new neighbor in town and to make sure that we have that relationship,” Allen said. In response to concerns from the community, Allen said the facility will have setbacks which will provide at least a 350-foot buffer from homes, as well as a brick wall and water-wise landscaping surrounding the property. Aurora also restricts the noise level at data centers to the same level as other businesses, with different allowances based on zoning and time. The data center is expected to use 334 megawatts of energy for computing capacity, which would be more than twice the state’s current largest data center — the 160 megawatt QTS facility, also in Aurora. The facility would use a closed-loop cooling system, which is less water intensive than other cooling systems, and it’s expected to have 28 emergency generators, as well as battery energy storage, Allen said. “(The generators are) far less than what you would see in a comparable size data center because we’re using the battery storage as well,” Allen said. “We definitely took into consideration how we can be most efficient in this environment.” Allen said Aurora attracted Vantage’s attenti

Partilhar Acordo de 10 anos, estruturado através de um modelo de tolling, que atribui à Statkraft a gestão comercial da utilização das baterias nos mercados de energia e flexibilidade. Abrange os projectos Ełk e Turośń Kościelna, ambos na Polónia, com 200 MW / 800 MWh de capacidade cada. É o maior acordo de BESS do género publicamente comunicado na União Europeia até à data A Greenvolt e a Statkraft, o maior produtor europeu de energia renovável e um dos principais fornecedores de PPAs na Europa, assinaram um acordo de tolling com uma duração de 10 anos, abrangendo 400 MW de capacidade de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em dois projectos na Polónia. O acordo é, até à data, o maior publicamente comunicado na União Europeia e marca o primeiro contrato de grande escala da Statkraft para BESS no mercado polaco. O acordo abrange dois parques de baterias: o Ełk (200 MW/800 MWh) e Turośń Kościelna (200 MW/800 MWh), localizadas, respetivamente, em Nowa Wieś Ełcka e Turośń Kościelna. A estrutura de um acordo de tolling confere à Statkraft o direito de decidir quando as baterias carregam e descarregam nos mercados de energia e de flexibilidade, proporcionando simultaneamente à Greenvolt uma fonte adicional de receitas previsíveis e de longo prazo, a par das receitas já asseguradas através do Mercado de Capacidade da Polónia. “Este acordo com a Statkraft traz uma sofisticada capacidade de optimização de mercado para estes projectos, permitindo monetizar a flexibilidade das baterias em diferentes mercados de electricidade e desbloquear receitas adicionais”, sublinha Łukasz Zagórski, business origination and market regulation director da Greenvolt Power. “Com a maior transacção de BESS realizada até à data no país, continuamos a desempenhar um papel activo no apoio à transição energética da Polónia. Os dois projectos de BESS complementam o nosso portefólio de activos eólicos e solares de terceiros, a partir do qual podemos oferecer preços competitivos e estáveis a grandes consumidores de energia”, acrescenta Kornel Koronowski, head of origination poland da Statkraft. À medida que o sistema eléctrico da Polónia integra quantidades crescentes de energia renovável, prevê-se que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias desempenhem um papel cada vez mais importante. Ao armazenarem o excedente de electricidade renovável e libertá-lo quando a procura é mais elevada, as baterias de grand escala contribuem para equilibrar a oferta e a procura, estabilizar a rede e facilitar a integração de mais energia eólica e solar no mix energético da Polónia.

artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. — Tampa Electric says it filed a plan with the Florida Public Service Commission aimed at protecting customers from potential costs tied to future data centers and other large-load electric users. The filing, called a tariff, is required under a data centers law Gov. Ron DeSantis signed in May. DeSantis said the law is meant to protect consumers from having to pay for one of those facilities. Tampa Electric spokesperson Cherie Jacobs said the tariff would require large-load customers, such as data centers, to pay for the electric infrastructure that powers them. Those facilities would also be responsible for some of the cost of maintaining and operating the broader electric system. “We are seeing interest from large-load customers for potential opportunities in the future,” Jacobs said. “Right now, Tampa Electric does not serve any large-load customers, but this plan does pave the way for the future to make sure that our customers remain protected and that reliable service is maintained.” Electricity use has been a recurring topic at meetings about data centers across Tampa Bay. Residents have raised concerns about whether local electric grids can handle the power required by large facilities and whether their own utility bills could increase. According to Tampa Electric, requiring companies to help maintain the overall system could also help lower bills for existing customers. Jacobs said the plan still needs approval from the Public Service Commission, which could happen late this year or early next year. Duke Energy has also submitted a tariff to the Public Service Commission. A Duke spokesperson said the company was the first utility in Florida to present its plan. In a statement, Duke said it does not currently have a large-load client in Florida and was a signer of President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. The company also said it requested a rate cut for customers on Sept. 3 that could take effect in 2027.

artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) propôs à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) uma mudança na metodologia de rateio do encargo que custeará os leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) para baterias, com redução da cobrança dos geradores conforme a contribuição de potência de cada usina na janela crítica do sistema. Pelo ajuste de critérios proposto, usinas solares sem armazenamento continuariam com o coeficiente cheio, por praticamente não contribuírem com potência na ponta noturna. Já termelétricas inflexíveis e nucleares, que também ficam sem desconto na metodologia proposta pela área técnica da Aneel, passariam a ter sua contribuição de potência reconhecida e tenderiam a pagar menos. A sugestão foi apresentada pelo ONS em reunião com o gabinete do diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator do processo, em 14 de setembro. O operador quer substituir o Índice de Flexibilidade previsto pela área técnica da agência como critério de graduação do encargo por um indicador que meça quanto cada empreendimento entrega de potência nas horas em que o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) mais precisa. A discussão ocorre a pouco mais de dois meses dos dois leilões de armazenamento, marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A regulação do rateio ainda precisa passar por consulta pública e deliberação da diretoria da Aneel. A proposta da área técnica prevê 30 dias de consulta e outros 30 dias para consolidação das contribuições. Proposta da Aneel A metodologia elaborada pela área técnica da Aneel prevê que todos os geradores participem do custeio do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade associado aos sistemas de armazenamento, o Ercap-SAE, mas com valores diferenciados conforme a flexibilidade de cada usina. Os empreendimentos seriam divididos em quatro patamares. Usinas classificadas como inflexíveis teriam coeficiente de 100% do encargo. O percentual cairia para 75% no segundo patamar, 50% no terceiro e 25% para os recursos classificados como de flexibilidade muito alta. A forma de medir a flexibilidade varia conforme a fonte. Para as hidrelétricas, a proposta compara a geração entre as janelas das 10h às 14h e das 18h às 22h, com menor cobrança para as usinas que reduzem a produção no período de menor demanda líquida e ampliam a geração na ponta. Para as termelétricas, o índice considera parâmetros como tempos de acionamento, permanência em carga e desligamento, além da capacidade de modular a geração. Os parâmetros operativos têm peso de 70% no índice e a modulação intradiária, de 30%. Na simulação feita pela Aneel, toda a geração nuclear foi enquadrada no patamar de menor flexibilidade, com coeficiente cheio. Eólicas e solares sem armazenamento também ficaram nesse grupo. As termelétricas foram distribuídas entre os quatro patamares, mas as de operação contínua ficam entre as mais oneradas. Em uma simulação feita pela agência apenas para testar a metodologia, nucleares, eólicas e fotovoltaicas teriam encargo médio de R$ 10,82/MWh. As termelétricas ficariam, em média, em R$ 8,53/MWh, enquanto as hidrelétricas pagariam R$ 5,65/MWh. Na apresentação, o ONS ressaltou que a proposta não substitui a estrutura desenhada pela Aneel, mas altera o critério usado para diferenciar a cobrança entre os geradores. Permaneceriam o rateio entre todos os geradores, a energia gerada como base de incidência, a graduação do encargo e o piso de 25%. A mudança ficaria concentrada no coeficiente: em vez de refletir o Índice de Flexibilidade, ele passaria a considerar a contribuição de potência de cada empreendimento na janela crítica. Potência na hora crítica Para isso, o ONS propõe trocar a régua desenhada pelos técnicos da Aneel por um Índice de Contribuição de Potência na Janela Crítica, o ICP-JC. A diferença é que a metodologia da Aneel busca medir o quanto uma usina é capaz de flexibilizar sua operação, enquanto a proposta do ONS considera a potência que o empreendimento entrega no período em que o sistema mais precisa. O operador argumenta que o produto contratado nos leilões de baterias é disponibilidade de potência, por isso, o critério usado para graduar o encargo deve considerar a contribuição de cada usina nessa mesma condição. Isso altera principalmente o tratamento dado às usinas de operação contínua. Uma termelétrica inflexível ou uma nuclear pode ter baixa capacidade de modulação, mas permanecer gerando durante a ponta. Pela proposta do ONS, essa entrega passaria a reduzir sua participação relativa no rateio. Termelétricas despacháveis, usinas a biomassa e eólicas também tenderiam a pagar menos, conforme a potência entregue na janela crítica. Para as hidrelétricas, o efeito seria uma redistribuição dentro da própria fonte. A solar sem armazenamento tenderia a permanecer com coeficiente cheio se a janela crítica permaneçer no período noturno. Segundo cálculo da Aneel no relatório de Análise de Impacto Regulatório (AIR) elaborado neste processo, entre 18h e 22h, a geração fotovoltaica correspondeu a apenas 0,009 vez sua geração média anual no período analisado. Na eólica, a relação foi de 1,20 vez. Nova conta O índice proposto pelo ONS seria calculado a partir da relação entre a potência que a usina comprovar entregar na janela crítica e uma potência de referência. Quanto maior a contribuição, menor seria o coeficiente aplicado sobre a energia gerada pelo empreendimento para calcular sua participação no rateio. O operador apresentou como uma das alternativas uma escala contínua, com coeficientes entre 100% e 25%. Uma usina sem contribuição na janela crítica ficaria com coeficiente 1, enquanto uma usina cuja contribuição atingisse integralmente a referência teria coeficiente de 0,25. Outra possibilidade é manter os quatro níveis de 100%, 75%, 50% e 25% desenhados pela Aneel, mas definir o enquadramento pela contribuição de potência, em vez do Índice de Flexibilidade. A energia efetivamente gerada no mês continuaria sendo a base do rateio e todos os geradores permaneceriam responsáveis

artigo.texto: Publicidade 28 Set (Reuters) – A WEG (WEGE3) anunciou nesta segunda-feira um plano de investimento de US$165 milhões (R$840 milhões) para expandir sua capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte para atender à crescente demanda por soluções de geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos EUA, especialmente impulsionada pela expansão dos data centers. De acordo com comunicado ao mercado publicado pela empresa, o projeto será feito em duas fases, sendo que a primeira etapa contempla investimento de US$24 milhões para a compra e adequação de prédio industrial no México destinado à montagem de geradores. De acordo com a empresa, o início das operações está previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, a WEG investirá US$141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte. Ao fim da segunda etapa, prevista para ser concluída em 2030, a companhia terá capacidade global de fabricar cerca de 50 geradores por dia em suas fábricas no México, Estados Unidos, Brasil e China. Atualmente a empresa tem capacidade para produzir 10 geradores por dia, acrescentou.

artigo.texto: Oriana Power has completed the first tranche of its proposed divestment of a 74% equity stake in its subsidiary Truere Guj SPV Private Limited (T Guj) to Leo Energies Private Limited, formerly known as Helioact Power India 1 Private Limited, a group entity of Actis GP LLP. The subsidiary owns a solar project with an aggregate capacity of approximately 70 MWp, along with 30 MWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity. Oriana Power said it has received the consideration for the first tranche of the proposed divestment. The enterprise value of T Guj is approximately ₹325 crore, subject to closing adjustments in accordance with the Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) and subsequent amendments. The consideration has been determined after making the applicable adjustments to the enterprise value under the terms of the SPA. The first tranche has been completed in accordance with the agreed terms and conditions. The remaining tranches, where applicable, will be undertaken subject to the SPA, applicable approvals and other conditions. Oriana Power said the transaction supports its asset-recycling and monetisation strategy, while strengthening its balance sheet and liquidity position. The proceeds are expected to be redeployed into the company’s growing pipeline of solar, open-access and BESS projects. artigo.texto: Trending Communities hosting hyperscale data centers are seeing benefits even while the protests grow. "New recreational spaces, water and wastewater infrastructure, traffic lights, build-outs of local roads and grants for schools were among the pluses for communities hosting them. "Our roads around our data centers are beautiful," said Etta Lockey, director of Commercial Energy Supply, Meta, also known as Facebook, Instagram, What's App and maker of novel hardware such as tech glasses. "Growth can pay for growth," she cited at the 16th annual Marcellus Shale Coalition INSIGHT 2026 in Erie. "My team is responsible for bringing the high voltage and electrons to our data centers in partnership with our utilities and energy development partners," she said. The goal, she said, is "not to shift costs onto the families in the communities where the data centers exist." Meta also has placed a priority on its commitment to the community and ongoing community engagement. "None of this is possible without our communities more than the jobs that data center development can support, we want to be good neighbors and good community partners," she said. This is done through hiring local contractors, boosting local tax revenue, paying for local infrastructure, and adding new energy to the grid, she added. This phenomena is where electrons and molecules are meeting the real economy. The workers, the townships, the utilities, the producers, a consortium of folks that have been powering the U.S. for generations are now having to address national AI dominance and meet demand. To do this right, developers need community partners who are seeing the upside and serving as home to some of the most innovative technology in the world. Meta, she noted, provides millions of dollars in grants year after year to support schools and nonprofits. In fact, Meta has given $94 million supporting over 3,700 grants and communities where it has data centers around the globe. One criteria screened for site selection is the availability of natural gas "We are also investing in partnerships and solutions that reduce the footprint over time," Lockey said. That includes support for U.S.-produced low methane natural gas. At Meta, energy innovation has become as important as software or chip innovation. The evolution of artificial intelligence is changing how thoughts are evolving on infrastructure, pushing innovation at every layer, Lockey said. For those in Appalachia, this presents an enormous opportunity. "We have the resources, we have the expertise and the workforce to help meet that demand," said Jim Welty, president of Marcellus Shale Coalition Meta is a company helping drive a new era of energy demand, he said. Lockey, an attorney by training, continues to lead efforts to secure the affordable, reliable energy needed to support the company's growing data infrastructure, he said.

artigo.texto: ARCHBALD — Data center opponents challenged Tuesday whether changing conceptual plans for a proposed power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road is enough to prove the project meets the borough’s requirements for protecting public health and safety — continuing a months-long standoff between Stop Archbald Data Centers and Essential Energy LLC. “You are here to testify to this borough council that despite the fact that it is a conceptual design, it can be designed, constructed and operated in a safe way?” asked attorney Justin Richards, who represents residents challenging proposed data centers in Archbald. “There is a way that we can do this,” replied KCI Technologies Technical Lead of Power Generation Andrew Markle, testifying on behalf of Essential Energy. “We can do this — I’m not telling you how we’re going to do it — I’m saying that we can do this.” Borough council held its sixth conditional-use hearing to consider Essential Energy’s March 12 application for a 400-megawatt natural gas power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road. About 70 residents clustered throughout the Valley View High School auditorium, occasionally applauding or jeering during the three-hour hearing. There are 51 data centers proposed in Archbald across six projects, though more are likely on the way. Essential Energy is a firm tied to Kriger Construction Inc. of Archbald and its executive leadership — President Jim Marzolino and Vice President Dave Stiles. Other Kriger-linked firms propose the nearly 620,000-square-foot Project Boson data center across the street from Essential Energy, as well as four data centers and three power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City. Essential Energy’s plans have been contentious at hearings due to the power plant’s proximity to homes, schools, businesses and a popular borough park. The proposed power plant would nearly border Archbald’s Staback Park; it is opposite the Highlands Archbald residential community on Eynon Jermyn Road; and the Valley View School District’s campuses begin about half a mile away on Columbus Drive. There is also a preschool in the plaza in front of the Highlands, and a developer plans to build assisted living and skilled nursing facilities in the area. The debate over Essential Energy has largely revolved around the conceptual nature of its plans, with opponents pressing for more specific information and invoking Archbald’s zoning criteria for credible evidence, while power plant representatives counter that specifics will come later as the development evolves and navigates the regulatory processes. Markle, who cited his experience overseeing a fleet of 180 natural gas power plants in the United States representing about 5% of the grid, compared Essential Energy to a smaller version of the nearly 1,500-megawatt Lackawanna Energy Center in Jessup, characterizing natural gas power plants as “cookie-cutter” designs with specific protections and design elements tailored to the location and community. ‘Credible evidence’ Richards, of Elliott Greenleaf PC in Wilkes-Barre, opened his cross-examination by asking Markle to provide his Pennsylvania engineering license number; Markle authored the two-part report that was the subject of Tuesday’s hearing and the previous Aug. 18 hearing. “I do not have one,” Markle said, explaining he is a registered professional engineer in the province of Ontario, Canada. W. Casey Deller, a vice president at KCI Technologies in Mechanicsburg, reviewed and sealed the report as a professional engineer in Pennsylvania, Markle said. He later defended it as a standard practice in engineering due to the difficulty of maintaining licensing across individual states and provinces, each of which has its own licensure board. Richards also reiterated his contention that the hearing itself is a legally null because Essential Energy LLC did not exist March 12 when it submitted a zoning permit application in Archbald. The limited liability company organized with the state March 13. Markle said he had no idea about it. The attorney representing Stop Archbald Data Centers members referenced changing site plans and different testimony and reports from various engineers, changing the number of turbines and equipment multiple times. “If multiple different assumptions have been provided to the borough council based on wildly varying equipment, which one is the most accurate?” Richards said, listing multiple engineers who previously testified. It’s the normal progression of a conceptual design, where people examine different ways of approaching the same problem, Markle said. “We’re refining the design as we’re going,” Markle said. Citing Archbald’s zoning ordinance, Richards pointed to requirements for credible evidence, sufficient detail to indicate potential public health and safety hazards, and that the burden is on the applicant to demonstrate to the borough that the proposed use will not create a significant hazard to the public health and safety, such as fire, toxic or explosive hazards. “Merriam-Webster defines credible as, ‘Offering reasonable grounds for being believed or trusted,’ where you are the most recent in a line of witnesses that cannot state or affirm what the site layout will be, what the required equipment will be for this project … how can your testimony offer reasonable grounds for being considered trustworthy or believable?” Richards said. “Because this is the way things are normally done,” Markle said, drawing murmurs from the crowd. “We go from conceptual to preliminary to detailed to as-constructed to operational, and this is just the way that these these projects are produced.” Stop Archbald Data Centers co-founder Tamara Misewicz-Healey continued a similar line of questioning, in addition to cross-examining Markle on the yet-to-be-determined routing of a natural gas pipeline to fuel the power plant. “There’s natural gas on the site, and the pipelines are a part of this application, and you’re testifying that it’s safe — and pipeline s

artigo.texto: Delta Electronics Unveils AI Modular Data Center with 800 VDC In-Row Power for NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Microgrid Solutions at Data Center World Asia 2026 SINGAPORE, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Delta Electronics, a global leader in power management and smart green solutions, is attending Data Center World (DCW) Asia 2026 with its new AI Modular Data Center (AI MDC) and Microgrid Solutions to accelerate the deployment and enhance the energy efficiency and resilience of AI infrastructure. The prefabricated AI MDC integrates next-gen 800 VDC In-Row Power and liquid cooling systems for the fast deployment and scalability of AI data centers based on NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture. The Microgrid Solution integrates Delta's renewable energy, energy storage, and Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (SOFC) systems, as well as Solid State Transformers (SST), which are essential to directly convert medium voltage power to 800 VDC for the AI factories of the future. "AI workloads are scaling faster than most data centres were designed to handle, while their demands can be increasingly unpredictable. This means infrastructure planning must move from reactive to integrated and future-ready," said Jason Yuan, President, Southeast Asia & ANZ, Delta Electronics. "Our AI Modular Data Centers and Microgrids, both part of our Grid-to-Chip Solutions portfolio, are ideal to help our clients across Southeast Asia deploy and power their future-ready AI data centers. Moreover, Delta's solutions are engineered for energy efficiency, reliability and performance, while providing the flexibility to adapt to changing workloads and infrastructure demands." Visitors can expect interactive showcases spanning Delta Electronics' AI infrastructure portfolio, including its AI Modular Data Center designed for scalability, flexibility, and compatibility, high-voltage direct current (HVDC) 3.6MW in-row coolant distribution unit (CDU) technology to help manage the thermal demands of high-density AI workloads. The showcased 800 VDC In-Row Power architecture features 660kW output power, up to 98% AC-DC efficiency, 480kW capacity in battery backup units (BBU), and aluminium capacitors to optimize GPU workloads in next-generation AI data centres. In addition, Delta's prefabricated AI Containerized Data Center (CDC) Solutions deliver up to 60 kW per rack of AI compute within the footprint of a single parking space, as well as a seamlessly integrated Liquid-to-Air CDU system to achieve a PUE as low as 1.19. The unveiled Microgrid Solution demonstrates how on-site energy generation resources, energy storage, power conversion, and the new solid state transformer (SST) can support greater power resilience, efficiency and flexibility. Through real time coordination of multiple energy sources, uptime and power quality are maintained during grid connection delays or off-grid operation, with SOFC providing reliable on-site power 24/7. Its prefabricated DC coupled architecture combines SSTs, DC/DC converters and dynamic energy support to reduce conversion stages, enabling the system to respond to fluctuating AI loads while supporting scalable deployment. At the board-level, Delta's thermal management solutions include a dedicated state-of-the-art cold plate for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, with the latest microchannel and multi impinging flow design. See the Future of AI Infrastructure Live at DCW Asia 2026 Delta Electronics will showcase the In-Row Power at DCW Asia 2026, taking place from 29– 30 September at the Marina Bay Sands Convention Centre, Level 1, Singapore, at Booth D10. Sakda Sae-Ueng, SEA & Oceania Data Center Business Platform Head, will also be headlining the Data Centre World Keynote Theatre at 10:25am on Day 1, where he will discuss Delta Electronics' collaboration with NVIDIA and the roadmap for 800VDC power architecture. Singapore and the Southeast Asia region are increasingly viewed as a regional hub for next-generation AI infrastructure, with operators across the region under pressure to deploy at a pace and density that did not exist a cycle ago. Delta Electronics helps customers respond to this shift with integrated power, cooling and energy infrastructure engineered to support the rapid evolution of AI workloads, while providing the flexibility, efficiency and resilience needed to remain future-ready and accelerate the transition towards more sustainable data centers. As a world-class corporate citizen guided by its mission statement, "To provide innovative, clean and energy-efficient solutions for a better tomorrow," Delta leverages its core competence in high-efficiency power electronics and its ESG-embedded business model to address key environmental issues, such as climate change. Delta serves customers through its sales offices, R&D centers and manufacturing facilities spread over close to 200 locations across 5 continents. Throughout its history, Delta has received various global awards and recognition for its business achievements, innovative technologies and dedication to ESG. Since 2011, Delta has been listed on the Dow Jones Best-in-Class World Index (formerly the DJSI World Index of Dow Jones Sustainability™ Indices) for 15 consecutive years. artigo.texto: CHINA unveiled a new five-year plan for its battery industry on Monday, aiming for the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 as the country accelerates the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, together with six other government agencies, jointly issued the new development plan for the battery industry, outlining the sector’s development priorities over the 15th Five-Year plan (2026–2030) period. The plan comes as China continues to expand its role in the global battery supply chain and seeks to strengthen its leadership in the global energy transition, according to Chinese experts. The country already has strong battery manufacturing capacity, but industry experts said that it still needs to improve basic research and core technologies to maintain long-term competitiveness. To promote the high-quality development of the industry, efforts will be made to accelerate technological innovation, industrial transformation and upgrading, improve the industrial system, enhance the capacity of industrial science and technology services, and raise the quality and level of trade and investment cooperation, according to the document. China will seek steady growth in its new battery industry over the next five years, while making major breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. It also called for significant progress in new battery systems, with all-solid-state batteries moving toward initial large-scale deployment by 2030. New batteries refer to energy storage and conversion devices built on new mechanisms, materials, structures and manufacturing processes. They include lithium batteries, sodium batteries and flow batteries, which analysts said are becoming key parts of China’s push to develop new industrial sectors, build a new energy system and strengthen its capabilities. China’s battery industry has strong manufacturing capabilities but still needs to strengthen fundamental research, Sun Xiaohong, former secretary-general of the automotive branch of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, told the Global Times on Monday. All-solid-state batteries are one of the plan’s key technological priorities. Compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries, which typically use flammable liquid electrolytes, solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes and are considered safer and potentially capable of offering higher energy density, according to Sun. The plan calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, with a focus on improving ionic conductivity, cycle stability and cost efficiency. It also stresses the need to advance key materials and processes, including interface contact technology, high ionic conductivity, long life cycles and engineering pressure system design. China’s solid-state battery market is projected to grow from $42.5 million in 2025 to $384.8 million by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 44.4 percent, significantly outpacing the global average of 37.5 percent. Meanwhile, substantial research and development investments by domestic manufacturers such as CATL and BYD are accelerating solid-state battery commercialization and deployment, according to media reports. Sun said that solid-state battery technology worldwide is still in the research and testing stage, and has not yet entered large-scale commercial use. He noted that the main challenges remain manufacturing consistency and cost reduction. “Small-scale commercialization is already possible, but large-scale adoption still depends on lowering costs further and improving production processes,” Sun said.

artigo.texto: Investidores aguardam a regulamentação do Redata A PwC projeta US$ 11,4 bi investidos em centros de dados neste ano no país, um aumento de 49,3% em relação a 2025 A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), no dia 15 deste mês, estabelece uma política tributária importante para o mercado de tecnologia e de construção de data centers no Brasil. No entanto, investidores interessados em alocar capital para novos projetos de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) esperam pela publicação do texto que regulamenta o regime e por uma decisão sobre impostos estaduais que representam dois terços da carga tributária sobre equipamentos para centros de dados. A janela de aproveitamento da isenção dos impostos PIS e Cofins (9,25%) está ficando menor. Em janeiro, os impostos serão substituídos pela Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS), prevista pela Reforma Tributária, cuja isenção não está contemplada no texto do Redata, dizem os sócios da área tributária da consultoria PwC Brasil, Alvaro Pereira e Beatriz Vasconcellos, em entrevista ao Valor. Pereira diz que a demora na regulamentação surpreende o setor. “A expectativa era de que a regulamentação saísse na sequência [da sanção presidencial], tendo em vista que a isenção de PIS e Cofins acaba em dezembro e uma alíquota de quase 10% gera um impacto expressivo para os investimentos em data centers”, afirma. O executivo observa que o modelo de negócios de construção de centros de dados - que exige volume alto e imediato de gastos de capital (capex) - não se beneficia de imediato do crédito tributário sobre a receita previsto pelas novas modalidades de impostos no país. “Um projeto de data center leva tempo, então, você só vai abater esse crédito lá na frente, quando o data center estiver operando”, compara Pereira. “É como se você ficasse com o dinheiro parado na conta, sem correção em um cenário de juros altos”, ele completa. O prazo de regulamentação do Redata é essencial para que o país não perca investimentos em infraestrutura, afirmam os sócios da PwC que vêm atualizando investidores de capital privado interessados em investir no setor. “Se a gente não corre com a regulamentação, o dinheiro deixa de vir para o Brasil. Ele vai para outro país que está pronto para rodar essa infraestrutura”, diz Vasconcellos. O governo discute se o gás natural seria fonte de energia elegível para abastecer os data centers no programa O Brasil é o quinto maior destino de investimentos em centros de dados no mundo. Este ano, a PwC projeta US$ 11,4 bilhões investidos no setor, um crescimento de 49,3% em relação ao investido em 2025 (US$ 7,6 bilhões), segundo dados da PwC, obtidos com exclusividade pelo Valor (ver infográfico). O Redata também prevê a suspensão dos tributos Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação na compra de componentes eletrônicos, produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados a data centers. O impacto fiscal estimado pela Receita Federal é de R$ 5,2 bilhões em 2026, R$ 1 bilhão em 2027 e R$ 1,05 bilhão em 2028, somando R$ 7,25 bilhões em três anos. O decreto que regulamentará a nova lei deve definir critérios e procedimentos de habilitação das empresas no Redata, a lista de equipamentos elegíveis, o método de comprovação das contrapartidas e parâmetros ambientais e de sustentabilidade. O Valor apurou que uma das discussões dentro do governo federal é a inclusão ou não do gás natural entre as fontes de energia que poderão abastecer os data centers beneficiados pelo novo regime. Assim, não há, por enquanto, previsão de quando o decreto será publicado. Outra apreensão do setor envolve a demora na análise de propostas de incentivos estaduais a equipamentos para data centers. Conforme informou o Valor, a análise das propostas de redução de 80% a 95% do Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS) sobre os equipamentos pelo Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) ficou para o fim do ano, após as eleições. “O esforço federal precisa de contrapartida estadual”, disse a Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (TIC) e de Tecnologias Digitais (Brasscom), em nota logo após a sanção do Redata. A entidade, que reúne empresas do setor, informa que dois terços da carga tributária sobre os equipamentos de tecnologia referem-se ao ICMS. “Sem a adesão coordenada dos Estados, o esforço federal corre o risco de ser esvaziado”, afirmou a Brasscom. Para efeito comparativo sobre o impacto tributário nos custos de um data center no Brasil, um projeto com capacidade de 100 megawatts (MW) e investimento de US$ 5 bilhões, custa 26,7% mais no Brasil do que nos EUA, segundo um estudo produzido em julho pela Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV) para as empresas Scala Data Centers e Norgás. Com o Redata, a diferença entre os projetos cairia para 17,7% e a redução do ICMS equilibraria os custos, diz o estudo. A Brasscom lembra ainda da necessidade de revogação do aumento de alíquotas do Imposto de Importação para bens de capital e de tecnologia nas categorias de equipamentos incluídas no Redata. Em fevereiro, a decisão do Comitê de Gestão da Câmara de Comércio Exterior (Gecex/Camex) elevou as tarifas de importação sobre mais de 1.000 equipamentos de tecnologia e bens de capital. (Colaborou Giordanna Neves, de Brasília)

artigo.texto: Sungrow has announced the successful grid connection and completion of full acceptance testing for the Cambodia EDC Kandal Stueng station (GS79), a 108.4 MW/215.6 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Takmao, Kandal Province. The project deploys grid-forming technology at utility scale and is designed to support grid stability, black-start capability, and coordination with hydroelectric and thermal generation. The facility is located at a key point in Cambodia’s central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. During system-restoration testing, 516 grid-forming power conversion system (PCS) units successfully energized the entire BESS plant from zero voltage while establishing stable voltage and frequency. The system also supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations as the network was progressively restored. As part of the testing, the BESS supported the startup and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant. The restored network was subsequently operated with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, the energy storage system, and connected loads. The project remained stable during five transformer energization events, including one involving a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stable operation while synchronizing different power sources with a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees. The BESS demonstrated extended islanded operation for 3.5 hours, allowing it to continue supporting the local network while separated from the main grid. The project also completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded modes, with voltage deviation maintained below 2% and transient frequency fluctuations within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. Sungrow said the project was delivered under strict testing requirements, a compressed construction schedule, and rainy-season conditions with ambient temperatures reaching 40°C. The commissioning and testing activities were completed within 20 days. The project team carried out hot commissioning and three rounds of performance testing during the commissioning period to support timely grid connection. Sungrow provided services covering storage and monitoring system design, equipment design, commissioning, EPC-related support, and operations and maintenance. The company said the integrated approach was intended to address the project’s grid-level requirements across design, delivery, and operation. The project adds a large-scale grid-forming BESS installation to Cambodia’s power system and demonstrates the use of energy storage for grid restoration, islanded operation, and coordination with multiple generation sources. artigo.texto: Senate Democrats block bill to shield ratepayers from data center costs in 57-43 vote The bill, aimed at making data centers pay for their own energy infrastructure costs, passed the House 417-3 earlier this month WASHINGTON (Valley News Live) — The Senate failed to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act Wednesday afternoon in a 57-43 vote, falling short of the 60 votes needed to move forward. The bill was a GOP-led effort to shield Americans from energy costs tied to data centers. Most Senate Democrats argued it does not go far enough, though four Democrats voted with Republicans in favor of advancing it: Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Raphael Warnock of Georgia. The bill passed the House of Representatives earlier this month in a 417-3 vote. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is a cosponsor of the Senate version. What the bill would do The bill would amend the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 to establish a federal standard requiring “large-load customers” — non-residential electric consumers primarily operating data storage and computing facilities with a peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site — to cover the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrades needed to serve them. It would also require large-load customers to provide financial assurances or contributions before those upgrades are made, and would guarantee utilities can recover those costs even if a large-load customer later ends its contract. Under the bill’s text, state regulatory authorities and nonregulated electric utilities would be required to begin formal consideration of the standard within one year of enactment and complete that consideration within two years. The bill directs states to consider and decide whether to adopt the standard, rather than mandating that they do so. Support and opposition Hoeven said the bill is intended to shield ratepayers from costs tied to data center construction. “American families shouldn’t have to pay higher energy costs if a data center is built in their community,” Hoeven said in a statement. “Our legislation would protect consumers from these rate increases resulting from data center construction. Instead of passing on higher energy costs to families and small businesses, the Ratepayer Protection Act will help ensure that the data center is responsible for paying for the infrastructure upgrades as well as fixed costs as a result of their demand for energy.” Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Senate Democrats raised concerns that the bill would not deliver meaningful relief to ratepayers. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said he supports ratepayer protection but argued the bill fell short. “I support ratepayer protection. I have a bill to do it, the Grid Act, not this bill, which affords no real relief to ratepayers,” Blumenthal said. “It’s bait and switch. That’s what it is, a bait-and-switch bill designed to provide cover for Republican senators who have consistently opposed ratepayer protection.” Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., said the legislation amounted to a largely symbolic gesture. “It basically is a symbolic protest to data centers, and both parties joined in,” Durbin said. “But when you read it closely, you realize it has no teeth.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., argued the bill’s core protections are voluntary rather than required. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud. It does not require any protections at all,” Schumer said. “While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. ... Optional requirement on data center development, optional standards for safety against catastrophic risk, optional enforcement to protect the American people. An optional guardrail is not a guardrail at all.” Schumer said Senate Democrats want the bill’s standards to be mandatory rather than optional for states. “Senate Democrats want to ensure that American families, communities, small businesses aren’t left on the hook for massive infrastructure costs created by the new data centers because the state chooses not to adopt the standards,” Schumer said. “The core difference is simple. This bill makes the protection optional. Senate Democrats want to make it mandatory, plain and simple.” Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., criticized Senate Democrats for blocking the bill, saying in a social media post that North Dakota has some of the lowest electricity rates in the country and that residential electricity prices have risen nationally. artigo.texto: INTERVIEW Hooxi Partners seeks to turn emissions cuts into revenue Climate fintech firm eyes expansion amid tighter carbon rules, targets 2028 Kosdaq listing Cutting greenhouse gas emissions does not automatically generate revenue. Companies must first measure and verify the reductions, then have them recognized as carbon credits before they can sell them. For smaller businesses with limited staff and capital, navigating those steps can be difficult. Hooxi Partners, a climate fintech company, was founded to help close that gap. Before establishing it in 2021, CEO Lee Haeng-youl saw an opportunity in the environmental, social and governance (ESG) market as environmental gains were difficult to measure, and businesses had few ways to turn them into financial value. He believed reliable emissions data could provide the basis for tradable carbon credits. “For carbon reduction to be sustainable, those making the cuts must receive an economic reward. Telling companies to do it because it is the right thing will not work for long,” Lee said in a recent interview with The Korea Times. That idea is reflected in the company’s slogan, “We make money from carbon credits.” Since founding the company, Lee has sought to change how businesses view carbon management. Many treat it as a compliance exercise, calculating emissions at year’s end, filing reports and purchasing credits to cover any shortfall. Under that approach, carbon remains a cost. “We want to move carbon from a cost item to a manageable asset on the balance sheet,” he said. “Rather than looking at greenhouse gas emissions data once a year or quarter, companies should manage it continuously, like sales or inventory, and calculate in advance how much value an investment in emissions reduction equipment could generate in carbon credits.” With that information, decisions to invest in equipment or upgrade existing facilities could move beyond the environmental team and become part of a company’s broader investment planning. Lee sees a particularly strong case for financial incentives among businesses that are not required to participate in Korea’s emissions trading system. Hooxi Partners consolidated its services this year under a platform called Carbon AI. Its NET-Z module calculates and reports corporate emissions. Measurement, reporting, verification and creditization (MRVC) helps companies develop emissions reduction projects and obtain verification and certification. Hooxi Connect links project operators with companies and financial institutions seeking carbon credits or verified reductions. The platform is designed to carry data through each stage, from measuring emissions to selling the carbon credits a project generates. “The synergy comes from continuity of data,” Lee said. “Emissions calculated in NET-Z become the baseline for assessing reduction potential in MRVC, and reductions certified through MRVC become volumes available for trading on Hooxi Connect. This eliminates the cost of reorganizing and verifying data each time a project moves to the next stage.” The company began in transport, focusing on electric buses. Lee noted that mileage and charging records make it possible to estimate emissions reductions compared with diesel vehicles, but individual bus operators often lack the resources to develop carbon credit projects on their own. Hooxi Partners has signed agreements with 272 bus operators and submitted electric bus projects representing about 1.8 million tons of potential emissions reductions. Projects covering 450,000 tons have received government approval. The company said it was the first operator in Korea’s transport sector to win approval for an electric vehicle emissions reduction program. “We demonstrated that the entire process works in practice by combining the reductions of small bus operators into one project, securing government approval and converting the results into carbon credits,” Lee said. The company is also seeking to address a funding problem that can prevent such projects from getting started. Emissions reduction investments such as introducing electric vehicles or upgrading facilities require upfront funding, while revenue from carbon credits may be years away. Under its “future carbon credits” model, a business can sell credits it expects to generate through a forward transaction and receive funding earlier. The firm said it has carried out a forward transaction with Hyundai Motor Securities. The arrangement was featured as a case of Environmental Progress Credit (EPC), an incentive mechanism developed by the Center for Social Value Enhancement Studies to reward climate technology developers early and encourage greater emissions reductions. “Small and midsize businesses with limited financial resources may give up on emissions reduction investments because they cannot bridge that time gap,” Lee said. “Future carbon credits use finance to address that delay.” Lee expects demand for emissions management to grow during the fourth phase of Korea’s emissions trading system, which began this year, and following the implementation of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Companies covered by the trading system will need to secure credits, while exporters will need product-level emissions data. Lee said demand for such data is extending to suppliers. “We are working with Oriental Brewery and 15 of its suppliers to jointly measure and verify Scope 3 emissions, and demand for this kind of supply chain measurement, reporting and verification has been growing rapidly since CBAM,” Lee said. For its next stage of growth in Korea, Hooxi Partners is targeting solar installations and heat pumps. Although each project may produce relatively modest reductions, the company believes combining many projects could create volumes large enough for a carbon credit program. artigo.texto: The Chinese company Gotion buys 49% of Volkswagen's battery plant in Sagunto The Chinese manufacturer will invest €1,100M and will have 49% of the gigafactory - CAT - CAST BarcelonaThe Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and the Chinese company Gotion High-Tech have agreed to "deepen their strategic alliance" through a joint venture for the development and operation of the battery cell gigafactory currently under construction in the town of Sagunto (Valencian Community). In this way, the Chinese manufacturer is investing some 1.1 billion euros to obtain 49% of the gigafactory. The battery plant in Sagunto, which should start operating this year, had planned an investment of about 3 billion euros, with aid from the Spanish government within the PERTE for the electric and connected car. This plant should supply batteries to the Seat plant in Martorell and the Volkswagen plant in Landaben (Navarre). The German consortium is already manufacturing electric cars at both plants: the Cupra Raval and the ID Polo in Martorell, and the ID Cross and the Skoda Epiq in Navarre. The planned collaboration between the Volkswagen Group and the Chinese company Gotion "enhances the plant's technological capabilities, which represents a new milestone in the industrial development of the project and strengthens its role within the growing European battery value chain," company sources told Europa Press. The agreement signed this Monday maintains PowerCo (Volkswagen Group) with a majority stake of 51% in the Sagunto gigafactory, which guarantees "continuity in the governance, strategic direction and operational oversight of the project." In addition, the investment commitments and employment targets –3,000 jobs– previously announced "remain unchanged". The same sources point out that as the European automotive industry moves towards electrification, the demand for LFP battery technology (lithium iron phosphate batteries) is expected to grow significantly. According to market forecasts, LFP batteries will be dominant and could represent between 40% and 65% of total demand in Europe by 2030, driven by their competitiveness, safety, durability and suitability for high-volume electric vehicle segments. Currently, practically all LFP cells used in Europe are manufactured in China. With the joint venture, Volkswagen, PowerCo and Gotion are turning the Sagunto project into a key piece to establish a competitive European production base for this strategically important technology with cells destined for the European market. Its long-term competitiveness is reinforced thanks to a larger scale, manufacturing experience and supply chain resilience. First phase commitments The joint venture has been designed to "strengthen the long-term viability and competitiveness of the Sagunto project, while preserving the strategic commitments already made". The investment of more than 2.3 billion euros already in execution and the creation of more than 1,500 direct jobs in the initial phase –which includes the first two production blocks– remain unchanged, thus consolidating the gigafactory's position as one of the most relevant industrial projects currently under development in Europe. Sagunto will begin operations with two production blocks and a combined annual capacity of up to 30 GWh in a first phase.

artigo.texto: Note: Welcome To RCBJ’s “Your Voices” Column, an occasional column prompted by readers’ commentary. If you have something to say, in a well-reasoned essay of 500 to 700 words, email the editor at ttraster@rcbizjournal.com Battery Storage Projects Are Good For The Economy, Good For Reducing Energy Bills, And Safe By Justin Wilcox New York’s energy policy must be measured by more than the ambitions it sets. It must also deliver electricity that households and businesses can afford, a grid that remains reliable and an economy capable of supporting future growth. That requires practical investments in the infrastructure needed to meet the state’s energy needs. Battery energy storage is one of those investments. For years, batteries have held the promise of storing electricity when it is abundant and returning it to the grid when it is needed. Without substantial energy storage, the renewable mandates established by the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act become more difficult and more expensive to integrate reliably. They can also supplement dispatchable resources and displace generation from some of the least efficient and highest-emitting plants during certain hours. That is a legitimate grid function, and one that should not be overlooked simply because battery storage cannot solve every challenge facing the electric system. Upstate United has consistently argued that New York needs a diversified energy resource mix. Existing natural gas generation will remain necessary for years to maintain reliability, and the state should support strategic investments in generation and fuel supply that can reduce costs and emissions. Battery storage should be understood as part of that same practical approach. Yet as battery projects move from planning documents to individual communities, their promise is increasingly colliding with the public’s safety concerns. There are valid safety considerations associated with virtually every form of energy infrastructure. Natural gas pipelines, nuclear power plants and fuel storage facilities must all be engineered and operated with safety as a fundamental guiding principle. Battery storage should be held to the same standard. That principle was behind the creation of New York’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group in 2023. Following several battery fires, the state brought together fire safety experts and agencies to examine incidents, inspect operating facilities and identify improvements to safety standards and emergency response. The working group inspected 57 large, operating battery storage projects. Those inspections produced important lessons about fire code requirements, inspection procedures and coordination with local emergency responders. Many of the group’s recommendations were subsequently incorporated into New York’s updated Fire Code, which took effect in January 2026. The updated requirements address matters including emergency response planning, inspections, fire department coordination and independent review of project safety. These are not substitutes for careful local oversight. They are tools that can help communities evaluate proposed facilities with greater confidence and ensure that safety remains central to the process. New York’s Public Service Commission has approved a target of 6 gigawatts of energy storage by 2030. Meeting that target will require more than setting a number in Albany. It will require the state to provide communities with the technical resources, clear standards and support necessary to make informed decisions about proposed projects. Local governments should retain their authority to review land use and evaluate the impacts of development. At the same time, legitimate concerns should be addressed through rigorous standards, transparent information and meaningful engagement, rather than allowing uncertainty to become an indefinite barrier to investment. New York cannot afford an energy policy that encourages new resources in principle, while making it increasingly difficult to build the infrastructure necessary to support them. Battery storage is not a silver bullet. But it can help diversify our resource mix, improve grid efficiency and support a more orderly transition to lower emissions. Policymakers must acknowledge that new technologies can raise legitimate safety concerns, just as existing energy technologies carry risks of their own. But the answer should be to manage those risks, not to turn away from the benefits. New York needs to evaluate these investments on their merits, insist on strong safety standards and build the infrastructure that can deliver measurable benefits. If we are serious about an affordable, reliable and lower-emissions energy future, battery storage must be part of the solution. Justin Wilcox is executive director of Upstate United, a coalition of businesses, organizations and community leaders working to strengthen Upstate New York’s economy, improve affordability and create opportunities for growth.

artigo.texto: NLC India, the Indian PSU which was earlier primarily involved into thermal energy generation company is steadily moving towards green energy. After boosting its solar and wind portfolio, the listed company is now working towards making renewable energy firmer by steadily increased its energy storage portfolio. However, unlike the private companies engaged in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), this company is working towards building an integrated storage portfoli-comprising both BESS as well as Pumped Hydro Storage (PSP) projects. As per the company’s FY2025-26 Integrated Annual Report, NLC India and its wholly owned subsidiary NLC India Renewables Ltd. (NIRL) have secured multiple energy-storage projects, with the company reporting a contracted storage pipeline of 3,300 MWh across three arrangements. The portfolio includes a 250 MW/500 MWh BESS project in Tamil Nadu, which has progressed to a signed power purchase agreement. NLC has also secured a Letter of Award for a 600 MW solar project coupled with a 300 MW/1,800 MWh BESS from the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), while another 500 MWh BESS project has been awarded by Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (PSPCL). The company has subsequently won bids for a 50 MW/200 MWh BESS project from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. and a 275 MW BESS project from Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd, hintings towards its hunger for bet for more storage projects. First large-scale BESS project The 250 MW/500 MWh Tamil Nadu project represents NLC's first large-scale BESS deployment. NIRL secured the project from Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Ltd. (TNGECL) through tariff-based competitive bidding under the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. The Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA) was signed with Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Ltd., while the land lease agreement with TANTRANSCO was subsequently executed. The project is proposed to be financed by KfW Germany, and NLC has placed an order with Pace Digitek for the battery and other EPC activities. NLC says the project will enable renewable electricity to be stored and released when required by the grid, helping improve grid stability and increase the utilisation of clean power. Storage being integrated with new renewable capacity The company is increasingly combining storage with new renewable-generation projects rather than treating BESS as a standalone business. Its renewable project pipeline includes large-scale solar, wind-solar hybrid and battery-storage projects. NLC specifically identifies the 250 MW/500 MWh BESS project and the 600 MW solar project with 300 MW/1,800 MWh of battery storage as important steps towards firm renewable energy. This marks a shift in the company's renewable strategy from adding generation capacity alone towards combining generation with storage to improve the availability and flexibility of renewable electricity. NLC currently has 1,785 MW of operational renewable capacity and generated a record 2.26 billion units of renewable electricity in FY2025-26. It is targeting 10,110 MW of renewable capacity by 2030, with 5,810 MW of projects under implementation or active development. BESS alongside pumped storage NLC's storage strategy is not limited to batteries. The company is also pursuing pumped-storage projects, including two 50 MW projects in Neyveli mine voids, as well as larger projects at Palar-Porathalar in Tamil Nadu and Salandi in Odisha. The company says feasibility work has been prepared for the two 50 MW Neyveli projects, while the larger projects include a proposed 1,100 MW pumped-storage development at Palar-Porathalar and a 500 MW project at Salandi. This gives NLC two parallel storage pathways: battery systems for grid-scale short-duration storage and pumped hydro for larger, longer-duration applications. Renewable portfolio broadens NLC's expansion into storage comes alongside a significant increase in its solar and wind portfolio. During FY2025-26, the company commissioned its 300 MW Barsingsar Solar Project in Rajasthan and a 50 MW solar project at Neyveli. Its renewable pipeline also includes wind and wind-solar hybrid projects. NLC has secured a 450 MW ISTS-connected wind-solar hybrid project from NTPC and has been pursuing additional solar and wind projects through SECI, GUVNL, SJVN and other agencies. The company has therefore begun positioning storage as a component of a broader renewable portfolio rather than as a standalone diversification activity. Beyond generation The expansion into BESS is part of a wider diversification strategy at NLC. Alongside renewables and storage, the company is developing a 4 MW PEM electrolyser-based green hydrogen plant at Neyveli and has entered critical minerals, including blocks containing vanadium, titanium and aluminous laterite. For NLC, the emerging model is increasingly built around solar and wind generation, backed by BESS and pumped storage, with green hydrogen and critical minerals forming additional clean-energy businesses. The company has set aside ₹10,669 crore for diversification through 2030 and has received government approval for an additional ₹7,000 crore investment in NLC India Renewables Ltd. to accelerate its renewable ambitions.

artigo.texto: ORNL’s new 100,000-square-foot facility pushes the frontiers of quantum computing, battery tech The facility brings together once-scattered research teams under one roof, bridging fundamental science with real-world applications in quantum computing, advanced materials and next-generation battery storage. What This Story Is About - Oak Ridge National Laboratory has opened its fully operational, 100,000-square-foot Translational Research Capability facility, uniting multidisciplinary scientists to accelerate breakthroughs in quantum computing, grid storage and battery technology. Why It Matters - From keeping smartphones charged longer to building utility-scale batteries for AI data centers and deploying the nation’s first scientific-scale quantum computer, the research happening inside the TRC directly impacts consumer technology and national energy security. What Happens Next - Scientists have begun operating specialized testbeds, including the “Pathfinder” quantum computing testbed, with long-term plans to deploy a large-scale quantum computer within the next five to 10 years. For Context - The TRC features purpose-built spaces designed to eliminate vibration and electromagnetic interference, alongside one of the driest laboratory environments in the entire Department of Energy complex. OAK RIDGE, Tenn. (WVLT) - Just a few hundred yards from the historic Graphite Reactor that helped launch the atomic age more than 80 years ago, Oak Ridge National Laboratory has officially opened its newest scientific powerhouse: the 100,000-square-foot Translational Research Capability (TRC). The facility brings together once-scattered research teams under one roof, bridging fundamental science with real-world applications in quantum computing, advanced materials and next-generation battery storage. One of the Driest Rooms in America Among the TRC’s standout visual features is an ultra-specialized “dry room” engineered specifically for battery synthesis. With a dew point of minus 75 degrees and a moisture concentration of only 20 parts per million, it represents one of the most arid working environments in the world. “If you’re out in the warm Tennessee air, it’s thousands and thousands of water molecules,” explained Cynthia Jenks, Associate Laboratory Director for Physical Sciences at ORNL. “Here, for every million particles, there are only 20 of water. Water reacts with materials used to make new batteries. To make better energy storage devices, we must remove the impact of water.” The environment is so devoid of moisture that researchers can physically feel the air pulling hydration from their mouths and skin, requiring strict buddy-system safety protocols and limited shift durations to prevent dehydration. Consolidating into this space allows scientists to take materials from microscopic atomic arrangements to working prototypes. “Previously, our battery portfolio had grown, and we were in 10 different laboratories,” said materials scientist Andrew Westover. “Consolidating into this space gives us material synthesis and characterization capabilities, but the real enabling piece is this dry room. It allows us to actually make batteries at scale.” Powering Phones, Electric Vehicles, and AI Data Centers Inside the battery labs, researchers manufacture thousands of experimental coin batteries daily while engineering next-generation solid-state and lithium-ion cells for electric vehicles, smartphones and aviation. The facility is also tackling energy demands driven by the artificial intelligence boom. Tucked in the corner of the lab sits a prototype redox flow battery, a large-scale storage system designed to back up power grids and massive data centers. “We’re going through an AI revolution right now,” Westover said. “This prototype redox flow battery is specifically designed to enable data centers and that AI revolution, helping manage power consumption and improving grid reliability.” The Next Frontier: Scientific-Scale Quantum Computing Beyond energy storage, the TRC serves as the nerve center for ORNL’s quantum information science initiatives. The building features specialized quantum labs isolated from outside electromagnetic noise and ground vibration. A few months ago, teams deployed the “Pathfinder” quantum computing testbed inside the building, allowing material scientists, experimentalists and computer scientists to work side-by-side. “We are at the bleeding edge of quantum information science, and it takes a broad range of scientific domains to make quantum computing the next important chapter in scientific computing,” said Gina Tourassi, Associate Laboratory Director for Computing and Computational Sciences. Tourassi noted that the ultimate goal over the next decade is deploying the first large-scale scientific quantum computer dedicated to open science, accelerating discoveries across chemistry, physics, and national energy priorities. “We have always been at the bleeding edge, deploying what we call ‘serial number one,’” Tourassi said. “We see quantum computing as the next frontier.” The TRC is intended to accelerate collaboration and help translate fundamental research into technologies with real-world impact.
