artigo.texto: JA, a global leader in photovoltaic products and integrated energy solutions, is expanding its European range of commercial and industrial (C&I) battery storage systems (BESS) with the launch of JAPlanet Fusion and JAPlanet 2.0. JAPlanet Fusion is a DC-coupled hybrid solution for PV and battery storage that combines inverters, battery storage and backup functionality in one system. In parallel, JAPlanet 2.0 is the latest generation of JA’s established AC-coupled C&I battery storage system, adding higher efficiency, optimized thermal management, and improved operation and maintenance (O&M) capabilities to the JAPlanet platform. Both systems are designed to provide C&I customers and project partners with greater flexibility in the design of storage systems for different site, grid and operational requirements. JAPlanet Fusion: PV, storage and backup in one system JAPlanet Fusion integrates inverters, battery storage, and backup functionality into one coordinated system, simplifying system planning, installation, and commissioning. Component integration reduces system interfaces, cabling overhead, and reduces space requirements. It can also reduce the risk of compatibility issues between separately procured components. The system has a battery cabinet with a capacity of 261 kWh and a nominal power of 125 kW. Thanks to the modular architecture, up to 10 units can be operated in parallel in grid-connected operation and up to six units in island operation, allowing the system capacity to be flexibly adapted to project requirements. JAPlanet Fusion is particularly suitable for solar repowering projects. The system can accommodate a PV input power of up to 250 kWp, enabling the installation of additional PV power on the DC side with up to 20 strings and 10 MPP trackers, while keeping the AC output power within the grid power limit allowed at the site. For plant operators, this opens up the opportunity to make better use of existing solar systems and grid connections, integrate energy storage and increase operational resilience. At the same time, coordination with distribution system operators is simplified by reducing complexity and time required for projects that would otherwise require an increase in grid connection capacity. For backup applications, an integrated static transfer switch (STS) detects a power failure and switches the system to island mode within 10 milliseconds to maintain the supply of critical loads. The system also includes liquid cooling, continuous monitoring of temperature, smoke and gases, integrated aerosol fire suppression, and redundant dual-channel ventilation in accordance with NFPA 69. “Across Europe, there is a growing potential to upgrade aging solar installations with more powerful technology. However, grid constraints can make increasing generation capacity complex and time-consuming. At the same time, companies want more control over their energy consumption and greater resilience to grid disruptions,” says Ignacio Espinosa Gil, Head of the European Technical Team at JA. “JAPlanet Fusion was developed with this next generation of C&I projects in mind. By integrating PV, storage and fast backup functionality into a single system, we can offer our partners a more efficient approach to system planning and implementation, while enabling better utilization of PV generation and greater resilience based on existing site infrastructure.” JAPlanet 2.0: AC-coupled BESS of the latest generation In addition to JAPlanet Fusion, JAPlanet 2.0 brings the latest generation of JA’s AC-coupled C&I battery storage technology to Europe. The 261 kWh system achieves a maximum round-trip efficiency of over 90% and can operate at ambient temperatures of up to 50 °C without reducing power. Intelligent thermal management reduces auxiliary energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional systems, improving system efficiency while supporting operation in different environmental conditions. High product safety is ensured by cell-level monitoring as well as UL-9540A testing of the entire battery system. JAPlanet 2.0 is equipped with JANebula, a new integrated energy management system (EMS) for applications such as time-of-use optimization, peak shaving or a higher PV self-consumption rate. The system complies with EU regulations on product safety. JAPlanet Fusion and JAPlanet 2.0 will be available for pre-order in Europe from the second half of September 2026. The first deliveries of JAPlanet Fusion are scheduled for the end of the fourth quarter of 2026. Both systems will also be presented as part of the JA customer roadshow Journey Ahead 2026, which runs until the end of October 2026. Further information at www.journeyahead.eu. JAPlanet Fusion

artigo.texto: URBANA — Dozens of students and community members gathered in front of Foellinger Auditorium on the Main Quad at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to show their opposition to the construction of AI data centers in Champaign County. The protest on Friday, Sept. 25 was organized by the Students for Environmental Concerns (SECS), a registered student organization at the U of I. Gabi DelSanto, SECS president and a U of I senior, said the group got involved with data center matters after meeting the co-founders of Resist AI Data Centers in Champaign County — Ruth Yontz and Antonia Herbstreit. “So that really lit a fire under us,” DelSanto said. “We started planning out ways that we would get involved with them and involved with other organizations to stop [data centers] from being built in Champaign.” Yontz and Herbstreit were also at Friday’s protest. Herbstreit said she worries about the Mahomet Aquifer. “If our aquifer gets polluted, there is no way to clean that back up to drinking water,” she said. The Mahomet Aquifer supplies water to about 1 million people across 14 counties in central Illinois. Herbstreit said she worries that if this source were to become contaminated or drained by data centers, communities across the region would be harmed. Lauryn Barnett, a sophomore in political science at the U of I, said she attended the protest to voice her concerns about protecting nature more broadly. “I think it’s very important that we take care of our environment,” Barnett said. “We know what these data centers are doing, not only in Champaign, but in Chicago and all across the country. We want to make sure that we are protecting our environment the same way it has been doing for us for the last centuries.” The protest hosted speakers from Prairie Rivers Network, Black Students for Revolution and Students for Socialism, and the U of I’s Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science. The speakers shared personal testimony and insights about data centers and the harm they could cause to humans and the environment. Next steps for a local data center ordinance Emotions are high as community members await news from the Champaign County Data Center and Activities Task Force, which is developing a local ordinance to regulate new construction of data centers in the county. The county’s 12-month moratorium on data centers with at least 10,000 square feet of processing space expires in April 2027. Officials say that since Champaign County is not a home-rule county, its authority is limited by powers granted by the state. So, an outright ban is not possible, they say — but they can pass an ordinance to regulate land usage through zoning. While they wait for news about the ordinance, Yontz said she and Herbstreit will continue to provide public input at the Data Center Task Force’s meetings. The task force is considering adding a required decommissioning bond for data center developers, which would require developers to put money aside so that if the data center were to shut down, they can properly remove all internal equipment so the property can be repurposed for future use. “We are already talking to them,” Yontz said. “We are going to their meetings. We [are] providing all different aspects of the ordinance that they’re working on.” The task force discussed several potential regulations at its meeting on Monday, Sept. 21. Task force chair Emily Rodriguez, vice chair of the Champaign County Board, says they hope to have a draft ordinance finalized by November.

artigo.texto: Mucahithan Avcioglu 30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026 Volkswagen and Chinese battery maker Gotion High-tech plan to invest €3.22 billion ($3.66 billion) in battery and materials production projects in Europe and North Africa to develop a regional supply chain for the European market. The plan involves three joint ventures in Valencia, Spain; Surany, Slovakia; and Kenitra, Morocco, according to Gotion’s investment announcement and a Volkswagen statement released Monday. Gotion’s contribution totals approximately €1.598 billion. The Spanish and Slovak projects will produce battery cells, while the Moroccan facility will manufacture cathode materials for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary PowerCo will retain a 51% stake in the Valencia venture, with Gotion holding 49%. Gotion will hold 51% in each of the Slovak and Moroccan ventures, while PowerCo will own the remaining stakes. The Spanish project targets annual battery production capacity of 29.1 gigawatt-hours, while the Slovak facility is planned to produce 8.4 gigawatt-hours annually, according to Gotion’s filing. The Moroccan project aims to manufacture 100,000 metric tons of LFP cathode materials a year, primarily supplying the two European battery ventures. Investment will be made in stages. “This marks a major breakthrough for both companies,” said Volkswagen technology chief Thomas Schmall. Volkswagen said the partnership would diversify supplies of key cathode materials and strengthen the competitiveness of Europe’s battery industry. The projects are subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions, including approval by Gotion’s shareholders.

artigo.texto: There have been many instances of massive turnout at public meetings about data centers in communities throughout the state of Michigan. Angry and concerned residents are expressing frustration with their public officials about even the potential of a new build, or the concerns over facilities that are already under construction. In many cases, elected officials may have less recourse on the matter. A new survey from the Ford School for Public Policy at the University of Michigan shows most elected officials also have hesitations or skepticism themselves about new data center proposals. Stephanie Leiser, director of the Center for Local, State and Urban Policy at the U of M's Ford School (CLOSUP), led this survey and joined Stateside's April Baer to discuss. April Baer: Stephanie, welcome back to Stateside. It's good to see you. Stephanie Leiser: Wonderful to be here. AB: Before we get to the results, I'm just curious, were you able to get responses from very many local governments that you asked about this? SL: Yes. So we run this survey regularly, and it is our goal to achieve a 70% response rate. And there's 1,856 cities, villages, townships, and counties in the state. And so we hear from 70% of them. And I think one thing that allows us to do is hear from parts of the state that we don't often hear from. AB: Meaning to say smaller units of government. SL: Smaller communities, smaller townships. And and as we know, these are some of the people who have the strongest feelings about data centers right now. AB: I saw from the overview of the numbers that a majority of people who responded expected strong opposition. How did that line up with how they actually felt about the data centers themselves? SL: So we noticed a few interesting things. When you ask sort of generally, do you think data centers, you know, considering all the costs and benefits, do you think they're worth it? When you ask them just themselves in general, there's maybe some receptiveness to it, but still opposition more than support. But then when you sort of zoom in and say, how do you think your residents feel? Or how do you think your city council or your board feels about this? That's when the opposition gets a little bit stronger. There are all kinds of things to consider with data centers in the community and things that might be on the cost side and the benefit side. Not surprisingly, there's a lot of concern about fresh water and utility bills and public health and quality of life. But one thing we uncovered too is there's, you know, generally a recognition among public officials that this may still have some positive effects, like you know, they are thinking about economic competitiveness. They are thinking about impact on local property tax base. And still, well, while you weigh all of those things together, there is, you know, much more opposition than there is support. I think this is a more nuanced conversation than sometimes we hear about. AB: Did you get a sense of whether municipal leaders in rural settings felt very differently than people in more urban settings? SL: Yeah, definitely. We see stronger opposition in rural communities. It's partly a function of, you know, this is where they're being sited, right? You can't plunk down a gigantic data center in the middle of a city. And so they are looking at more rural parts of the state, you know, so that's part of it too, is that this is definitely something that is impacting their communities more, but also that you know, when you have smaller townships or smaller communities, it's sort of a David and Goliath situation. Like how can you expect them to bargain with and deal with these massive companies and massive developments. So it's also a sort of a capacity issue as well as a political issue for, for smaller and rural places. AB: Did you notice many responses to the survey that reflected a sense of inevitability? SL: I think there's definitely a sense of inevitability. And we did get a lot of comments to that effect. But I think that sort of could go one of two ways. Like it's inevitable. So we might as well take advantage of it, is I think maybe the minority opinion. And then the, you know, maybe we got more opinions to the effect of: this is inevitable. What can we do? We just sort of throw up our hands and accept our fate. AB: Were there any questions that were part of the survey that that might have given us some insight into how local leaders feel like they're going to decide these questions. SL: Well, I think one thing that's also really important that pops out of the survey is how much they are sort of begging the state for help. And this is actually somewhat surprising because local governments are often very, you know, like, stay out of our business, let us handle ourselves. But I think in this case, they're, they're really asking the state for help. So, what happens with decommissioning if these projects stop functioning? And this, you know, like they're so big and they're such large users of utilities, this is a big concern for down the road. They want help from the state to think through health and environmental impacts. They want the state to help them deal with regulations around water use and discharge. They don't want the state to interfere in their ability to do zoning and planning and siting of centers. They want to maintain that authority. But the types of resources that they're looking for; 57% say it would be very useful to have model ordinances. 57% say that they'd really like help, you know, guidance negotiating with data centers. They want to try to coordinate with the county and their other local governments. They need help figuring out how to do resident engagement. There's a lot of need. And I think there's a kind of frustration with the state that, you know, the state adopted these incentives for data centers, and now they're just sort of sitting on the sidelines, leaving local governments to fend for themselves and deal w

artigo.texto: 30 Setembro 2026 Data center é uma atividade de grande interesse de bilionários da IA contra o resto de nós, diante de seus impactos nocivos na poluição do ar e sonora, nos preços de energia e nas mortes de comunidades do entorno, além de outras promessas falsas e enganosas. O artigo é José Rodrigues Filho, publicado em seu blog, 28-09-2026. José Rodrigues Filho é professor da Universidade Federal da Paraíba e doutor pela Universidade de Manchester, Reino Unido. Eis o artigo. Data Centers A oposição pública aos data centers ganhou força rapidamente nos últimos meses, nos Estados Unidos, em meio a preocupações com o aumento dos custos de eletricidade, ceticismo quanto aos benefícios sociais da IA e receios sobre seus impactos ambientais. Se os data centers fossem algo vantajoso estariam sendo construídos nas vizinhanças de bilionários e da classe política e não nas comunidades menos favorecidas, vítimas de casos de asma infantil e outras doenças respiratórias. A questão tornou-se um ponto de disputa nas próximas eleições americanas de novembro, tendo um efeito negativo para os conservadores. Neste caso, conservadores e democratas são contra os data centers. Assim sendo, a reação negativa contra os data centers — que vem moldando eleições e discussões domésticas em todo o país — está agora chegando a Wall Street, que começa a ver com ceticismo o boom dos data centers. Neste caso, o apetite aparentemente insaciável dos investidores interessados na Inteligência Artificial está sendo afetado e alguns deles estão manifestando um ceticismo crescente quanto às expectativas de crescimento dos data centers e aos riscos associados à sua expansão. Isto pode forçar executivos do setor e seus consultores a recalibrar seus planos de captar dezenas de bilhões de dólares e arrefecer a expansão de data centers não só nos Estados Unidos, mas em várias partes do mundo. Aqui no Brasil, estranhamente, esquerda e direita se uniram para expandir a construção de data centers, com incentivos fiscais para beneficiar bilionários de IA, conforme lei criada e sancionada há poucos dias, pelo governo petista. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Vale mencionar que dois partidos políticos foram contra esta lei, ou seja, o Psol e Novo, sendo o primeiro de esquerda e o segundo de direita. Espera-se que estes partidos, mesmo com visões diferentes, tentem anular esta lei, pelo seu caráter destrutivo. A lei contempla os bilionários com incentivos fiscais que, em 2026, é estimado em mais de cinco bilhões de reais, mas não regulamenta os impactos danosos, em termos de poluição do ar e sonora e outros terríveis crimes ambientais e danos à saúde das pessoas. O mínimo que se espera é que o Ministério Público embargue a construção destes data centers no Brasil, até que a sociedade participe do debate e ofereça subsídios sobre uma regulamentação adequada. É absurda a forma como se coloca a responsabilidade das empresas pela energia consumida. Até parece que vivemos num país sem soberania. Não se pode camuflar os custos de energia para a sociedade e os riscos ambientais. Numa conferência sobre o clima a semana passada, em Nova York, a Governadora Abigail Spanberger, do Estado da Virgínia, onde se concentra o maior número de data centers dos Estados Unidos, fez severas críticas sobre a expansão destas construções em seu Estado, muitas vezes secretas e sem a devida regulamentação. Ela disse que alguns moradores “estão colocando colchões contra as janelas porque o ruído é muito intenso”, proveniente dos sistemas de refrigeração utilizados nos centros de dados. Afirmou também que os geradores a diesel de emergência, que abastecem muitos desses centros, têm gerado poluição do ar que agravou casos de asma infantil e outras doenças respiratórias. Para a Governadora da Virginia, a IA e data centers nos vários estados precisam ser regulamentados, considerando seus efeitos no ar, na poluição sonora, nos preços de energia e nas comunidades do entorno. Pesquisas realizadas no próprio Estado da Virginia já mostram os danos ambientais e à saúde da população. Além disto, são enganosas as promessas de empregos depois de construídos. É insignificante. Nesta mesma conferência, um representante do Tennessee, Justin Pearson, chamou a atenção dos efeitos sobre a saúde advindos da poluição do ar, citando estimativas do gás das turbinas e dos geradores a diesel, que já estão matando pessoas nas comunidades. Para ele, as comunidades que lutam contra a construção de data centers devem continuar firmes, alertando que estes projetos de promessas de bilionários já enganaram muitos e são nocivos às comunidades. Presente na mesma conferência, a atriz e ativista americana desde a Guerra do Vietnam, Jane Fonda, de 88 anos, crítica os dois principais partidos políticos do país pela inação em relação às mudanças climáticas. Para ela, seu país enfrenta duas crises existenciais – climática e democracia. No Brasil não é diferente e quando é de interesses dos bilionários, esquerda e direita se unem contra a população. As últimas notícias dão conta de que no Estado do Pará está sendo instalado um centro de dados, que pode ser o maior centro de poluição e destruição ambiental da região. Com certeza, os data centers são máquinas de se ganhar dinheiro das Big Techs, como já disse Trump, e um coice na cara não só da população indígena, mas de todos os brasileiros. Enfim, não há dúvidas de que os projetos da IA e data centers são projetos dos bilionários contra o resto de nós, ou seja, a maior sujeição humana.

The report, titled ‘From 1 GWh, RE battery storage systems charging to ~45-50 GWh’,covers bids awarded between fiscals 2024 and 2026 across nearly 100 renewable energy developers. However, around 8-9 GWh of awarded capacity faces a higher risk of delays, which could moderate the pace of deployment. It said that the growing need for storage is a direct consequence of the rising share of renewable energy to 39 per cent of India's installed power generation capacity and 15 per cent of energy generated last fiscal. He said that developers typically procure batteries about a year after securing project bids. “Most projects awarded in 2025 are now exposed to higher battery prices, which have rebounded from the lows witnessed in 2025. As the battery prices were consistently coming down till 2025, developers appeared to have bid aggressively on the assumption that prices would continue their downward trajectory,” he said. The report also noted that as by nature, the RE generation is intermittent which has increased the need for firm and peak-hour power supply. This has elevated the importance of energy storage solutions, particularly BESS. However, in reality, battery prices have increased and at these prevailing levels, project returns may be insufficient to achieve a typical target internal rate of return of 12-14 per cent. Consequently, developers may defer implementation in anticipation of more favourable battery pricing.

artigo.texto: The Walker County Data Center Development Standards Study Committee reconvened recently for its third meeting, undertaking a section-by-section review of the county’s initial draft data center ordinance. Key discussions focused on parcel size thresholds, conditional use options, water capacity limits, and a tense exchange regarding committee transparency and industry conflicts. Draft Ordinance Review: Parcel Minimums and Micro-Facility Rules Planning & Zoning Director Jon Pursley and Economic Development Director Stephanie Watkins opened the session by outlining updates to the draft ordinance. Following recommendations from prior meetings, staff added Section 15, which mandates upfront performance and decommissioning bonds to protect the county from abandoned infrastructure. Under Section 3 (Land Use), the draft restricts data centers to industrially zoned districts and establishes a 10-acre minimum parcel size. Committee members debated whether a 10-acre requirement is suitable for smaller “micro-facilities” or fiber “booster stations” which can occupy as little as 5,000 square feet and consume minimal power and water. District 1 Appointee Barney Danks said restricting data centers strictly to the industrial zone could make land disappear quickly. He questioned why would the county force an industry to locate on 10-acres, if it only needs two. “I think commercial sites, whether existing in the county today or in the future, may want to have a ‘data center’ that is small.” He encouraged the committee to focus industrial zone requirements on hyper-scale operations. “Not every data center is the same as another data center.” The other District 1 appointee, Jason Rader, suggested restrictions for data centers with a footprint greater than 50,000 square feet. “I think smaller ones should be allowed in commercial. It’s no different than other buildings. It could be a dollar store or anything else.” Pursley explained that developers seeking smaller footprints or commercial locations (such as C1 or C2 zones) can apply for a conditional use permit or variance, allowing the Board of Commissioners case-by-case oversight. County records show Walker County contains 63 industrial-zoned parcels with a majority of the acreage located within the Walker County Business Park (400 acres) and the Northwest Georgia Business Park in Rock Spring (50 acres). Appointees agreed to consult legal counsel to confirm whether restricting facilities strictly to established industrial parks is legally defensible. Closed Loop Cooling Systems and Committee Member Experience District 3 Appointee Laura Owsley questioned District 1 Appointee Barney Danks regarding his industry holdings. Danks mentioned he operates an 8-megawatt Bitcoin mining facility on 2.5 acres along Glentana Road using open-air cooling fans. Owsley raised concerns over a lack of prior disclosure and questioned whether Danks resides in Walker County. Danks clarified that while he owns commercial property and businesses in Rossville and Walker County, he resides elsewhere. He acknowledged that his 6-year-old facility relies on older open-air technology, which generates noise and would not comply with proposed modern standards, and expressed support for requiring closed-loop cooling systems for future developments. Committee members appear favorable toward recommending closed-loop system requirements in their report. Water Capacity Limits, Utility Easements, and Power Restrictions Resource protection remained a core focus. While Walker County Water and Sewer maintains an excess capacity of 4.5 to 5 million gallons per day, officials noted that upcoming commercial developments (such as the Pilgrim’s prepared foods facility) and residential housing growth will absorb much of that margin. To prevent unexpected grid strain, the committee agreed to require developers to submit utility capacity confirmation letters covering all project phases prior to permit approval. On power infrastructure, Danks noted the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) now requires major power users to pay $1.5 million per megawatt upfront for infrastructure expansion. The committee discussed prohibiting on-site fossil fuel power plants and requiring data center developers, and not utility companies or the county, to secure their own utility easements to prevent the use of eminent domain through residential neighborhoods. Setbacks, Green Space, and Environmental Protections The committee reviewed physical development standards under Section 4: - Setbacks & Buffers: The draft establishes a 100-foot setback between adjacent industrial properties and a 400-foot setback from residential properties, matching the county’s restrictive poultry house standards. - Green Space & Height: Parcels must maintain a 15% minimum green space buffer, and buildings are capped at a maximum height of 50 feet. HVAC units and generators must be placed on roofs or oriented away from residential borders. - Environmental & Historic Protections: Owsley advocated adding an anti-clustering clause to prevent cumulative air quality impacts and urged prohibiting data centers in historic districts such as McLemore Cove. Next Steps and Data Center Tour Committee members will take a tour early next month of regional data centers and booster stations to see operations firsthand. At their next meeting, they plan to discuss sound/noise and lighting restrictions. The committee is working toward a December 4 deadline to finalize its draft recommendations. Once complete, the proposed ordinance will move to the Planning & Zoning Board for public hearings before reaching the Board of Commissioners for a final vote in early 2027. artigo.texto: Fórum Científico sobre Economia Circular e Créditos de Carbono - Um Método para Construir Modelos de Produção com Emissão Zero Na manhã de 30 de setembro, a União de Associações de Ciência e Tecnologia de Thanh Hoa, em colaboração com o Departamento de Ciência e Tecnologia da Universidade Hong Duc e o Instituto de Agricultura de Thanh Hoa, organizou um fórum científico sobre economia circular e créditos de carbono – um método para construir modelos de produção com emissão zero. Os delegados presidiram o fórum. O fórum atraiu nove apresentações de cientistas e empresas, com foco em diversos temas-chave: gestão comunitária de riscos de desastres no contexto das mudanças climáticas; transformação do sistema agrícola de Thanh Hoa no contexto das mudanças climáticas, abordada a partir de uma análise de problemas e comparação de similaridades ecológicas; transição energética e tecnologias de captura e armazenamento de carbono em indústrias de alta emissão; e a aplicação da tecnologia digital na transparência e otimização de recursos circulares. Os delegados apresentam trabalhos no fórum. No fórum, cientistas e empresas se concentraram em discutir questões-chave, incluindo: a base científica e prática para o desenvolvimento de uma economia circular vinculada a créditos de carbono em Thanh Hoa; métodos para avaliar o estado atual do uso de recursos e energia, geração de resíduos e emissões de gases de efeito estufa em modelos de produção; soluções tecnológicas que podem ser aplicadas imediatamente na agricultura, indústrias de processamento, indústrias de materiais de construção, tratamento de resíduos e desenvolvimento de produtos OCOP; condições para a formação, mensuração, verificação e desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono a partir de florestas existentes e projetos de redução de emissões, reutilização de resíduos, energia renovável e sequestro de carbono; e mecanismos e políticas para apoiar as empresas no acesso a créditos verdes, tecnologia, mercados e instrumentos de financiamento de carbono. As opiniões expressas no fórum contribuíram para esclarecer questões teóricas e práticas, bem como soluções científicas e tecnológicas que servem ao processo de transformação verde da província. Ao mesmo tempo, criaram uma base para a proposição de modelos piloto, programas de pesquisa, serviços de consultoria e transferência de tecnologia adequados às exigências do desenvolvimento sustentável. artigo.texto: Clivet Targets High-Density AI Data Centers With Next-Gen Cooling at AI Infra Summit 2026 Clivet is reshaping data center cooling with advanced core technology, full-chain liquid cooling, and integrated power-cooling infrastructure for high-density AI systems. September 30, 2026 AI computing growth is driving higher rack power density and wider load variation. Clivet’s AI data center portfolio is designed around these operating demands, combining core cooling technology, liquid-cooling distribution, terminal products, and coordinated power-and-cooling solutions. At AI Infra Summit 2026 in Santa Clara, California, Clivet showcased a portfolio covering facility-side cooling and liquid-cooling applications. The company also made the global debut of its Next-Gen Magnetic Levitation Technology under the theme DUO POWER BOOST and jointly demonstrated a power-and-cooling solution with CLOU. A Full-Chain Liquid-Cooling Portfolio for AI Infrastructure Clivet presented a product portfolio built around cooling needs at different points in the data center system. Magnetic levitation cooling sources serve facility-side cooling; the magnetic levitation supplementary-cooling CDU combines cooling-source and liquid-distribution functions for liquid-cooling architectures that require supplemental cooling; and fan walls and terminal units extend the portfolio across additional cooling links. The 1350 CDU displayed at the summit handles secondary-side heat exchange and distribution, with capacity up to 3 MW at a 3K approach temperature (ATD) or 5 MW at 5K ATD. Predictive control limits temperature fluctuations to ±0.5°C, while key components support online replacement to reduce maintenance impact on uptime. Through different product combinations, Clivet can configure solutions according to project conditions including climate, rack density and liquid supply requirements. Next-Gen Magnetic Levitation Technology Debut Sets a New Benchmark for AI Cooling Clivet developed its next-gen magnetic-levitation compressor around three cooling challenges identified in AI data centers: high-temperature performance degradation, efficiency under partial-load conditions, and reliability risks that can lead to prolonged downtime. At the core of the technology is the DUO POWER BOOST dual-rotor variable-speed architecture. In its two-stage compression system, both rotors and their corresponding impellers independently adjust speed to suit different flow and pressure-ratio requirements. This breaks through the limits of a single-shaft architecture and enables a wider unloading range without relying on inlet guide vanes (IGVs), allowing the compressor to maintain high efficiency across a broader range of operating conditions. According to Clivet, the new compressor reduces high-temperature cooling-capacity degradation by 45% and raises the extreme surge temperature by 8–10°C. The wider operating boundary is designed to maintain cooling stability when extreme heat pushes conventional compressors toward capacity loss and surge, while IGV-free unloading supports more efficient operation as loads fall below peak levels. For data center operators, the combined advances extend the usable operating range from day-to-day load variation to extreme temperatures and from current demand to future expansion. A wider efficient range allows more electricity to be directed to computing rather than cooling, while stronger high-temperature stability and on-site serviceability help reduce shutdown and maintenance risks. The Synergistic Art of Power Supply and Cooling At AI Infra Summit 2026, Clivet and CLOU jointly presented a coordinated power-and-cooling solution for AI data centers. CLOU provided energy storage and power transmission capabilities, while Clivet supplied thermal management products and solutions for high-density computing and energy storage. As computing density increases, power configuration, cooling design, space allocation, and operations and maintenance planning become more closely interdependent. Decisions made in one area can shape the requirements and constraints of the others, making early coordination increasingly important to subsequent solution design and engineering delivery. By aligning power and cooling requirements from the outset, the integrated approach turns system-level synergy into tangible project value. Clivet’s solution supports optimized infrastructure configuration, improved space utilization, enhanced operational stability, and lower overall operating costs, while ensuring greater continuity from planning to delivery. Together, the technologies showcased at AI Infra Summit 2026 highlighted Clivet’s vision for the next phase of AI infrastructure: combining core cooling innovation with coordinated capabilities across liquid distribution, terminal cooling, system control, power, engineering delivery, and service. This synergy between power and cooling provides a stronger foundation for AI data centers built for efficiency, reliability, and scalability. To learn more, explore Clivet’s AI data center cooling technologies and solutions for high-density computing applications: https://www.clivet.com/en/products/application-area/data-center

artigo.texto: WEG (WEGE3) anuncia plano de investimento de R$ 840 milhões de olho na expansão de data centers; veja A WEG (WEGE3) anunciou nesta segunda-feira (28) um plano de investimento de US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões, para expandir sua capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte. De acordo com o comunicado ao mercado, o projeto se dará em duas fases, visando atender à crescente demanda por soluções de geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos Estados Unidos, especialmente impulsionada pela expansão dos data centers. “A iniciativa representa mais um passo na estratégia de crescimento dos negócios incorporados à companhia por meio da aquisição da Marathon”, diz a WEG. Vale recordar que, em setembro de 2023, a WEG anunciou a aquisição dos negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores da norte-americana Regal Rexnord no valor de US$ 400 milhões. A transação, conforme anunciado à época, teve como foco os negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores, vendidos sob as marcas Marathon, Cemp e Rotor. Receba gratuitamente as newsletters do Money Times As fases do investimento A primeira fase do projeto da WEG contempla investimentos de US$ 24 milhões para aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e contribuirá para a expansão da capacidade produtiva da companhia, com início das operações previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda fase, em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte, a WEG investirá US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais. O projeto prevê a implantação de uma estrutura produtiva verticalizada que abrangerá processos estratégicos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças, aumentando a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da operação. Ao fim da segunda fase, prevista para ser concluída em 2030, a companhia terá capacidade global de fabricar cerca de 50 geradores por dia em suas fábricas no México, EUA, Brasil e China, ante a atual capacidade de 10 geradores por dia.

artigo.texto: Why Calumet County hasn't passed a data center moratorium CHILTON (WLUK) -- While other cities and counties are passing data center moratoriums, Calumet County has not. It's because their zoning ordinance already doesn't allow data centers in the county. "We didn't need to [pass a moratorium]," said Calumet County Administrator Todd Romenesko. "Our current ordinance does not allow it as permissible use." A legal adviser said because it isn't allowed as permissible use, a moratorium would be redundant. "From my standpoint, you don't need a moratorium in Calumet County," said Rebecca Roeker, attorney at Attolles Law, who advised the county on Monday night. "Again, because of your existing ordinances and because of the modifications that the elected officials are going to consider in the near future." - RELATED: Manitowoc County Board votes unanimously to impose 18-month moratorium on data centers - RELATED: Winnebago County will pursue 12-month data center moratorium Any modifications would likely just be to close any potential legal loopholes. These zoning ordinances apply to townships in the county, but not necessarily villages or cities. For example, it'll apply in the town of Woodville, but may not in the city of Chilton, as villages and cities may have their own separate zoning ordinances. Romenesko said there are no current data center proposals in the county. The discussion comes as the Chicago-based Invenergy has proposed a natural gas energy project and wind energy project in the county, which has raised concerns from residents about the possibility of a new data center in the county. County Administrator Todd Romenesko says there's no link. "This just happened to be something we were trying to be proactive on regarding trying to regulate anything regarding data centers," said Romenesko. The county does already have several small data centers, according to Romenesko. Because Calumet County has lots of open land, it could be the target of a major data center development.

artigo.texto: VERNON — Residents of Vernon and the surrounding area asked questions about fire safety, chemical emissions, employment, taxes and noise during a recent public community forum put on by PowerTransitions, the Texas company that is studying the Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant site for potential reuse. The community gathering, held last Wednesday at the Governor Hunt House community center, drew a large crowd as PowerTransitions officials were questioned about their stated priority to build a battery energy storage facility on a portion of the site. Area residents asked questions about potential employment, noise, property taxes, and fire safety with the large batteries and PowerTransitions' timetable. One woman said the town is concerned about the impact of any battery storage facility's noise – both the frequency emitted by batteries that large or the sound itself, on the nearby organic dairy cows at the Miller Farm. Carrie Cullen Hitt, a spokeswoman for PowerTransitions, said the company is committed to following Vernon's wishes, and as a result, it had dropped earlier plans for a data center or even a solar installation. There was no mention of a modular nuclear reactor, which has been mentioned earlier. "We have heard loud and clear," she said, "no data center and no solar." Hitt said PowerTransitions was in the process of studying the site, evaluating it and coming up with a plan. She did say that as a result of questions raised in Vernon during earlier meetings, PowerTransitions brought a fire safety expert to Wednesday's meeting to address concerns. Rocky Edwards, an engineer with TetraTech, said that battery technology is changing rapidly, and the batteries are safer than they were 10 years ago. He told the gathering that any fire at a battery storage facility would be fought with water. Two fires at battery storage facilities in other parts of the country have led to concern about the projects' safety. The batteries themselves are about the size of a trailer on a tractor-trailer unit, and would contain smoke detectors. The batteries have a life of between 15 to 20 years. They are typically eight feet wide, 22 feet long and 10 to 12 feet tall. The outside is "very plain," Edwards said. "It's really just a white box," he said, and he noted the batteries would be spaced apart. "If there's a fire, it will not affect the one right next to it," he said. Another PowerTransitions consultant, Derek Porter of Miami, said the size of the battery facility could range from 110 megawatts to 440 megawatts, and as a result, Vernon and the state of Vermont would benefit, tax wise, on the amount of power stored and then released back on the grid. Hitt said an important role for battery storage facilities is to "smooth out the peaks and valleys" on the electric grid, and make the electric grid more stable and reliable. He said the company is thinking of applying to ISO-New England, the regional electric grid operator, for a place on its next "interconnect queue" for joining the grid, in preparation for its project. The battery storage facility would take electricity off the grid during low-usage times, and put it back on the grid at high demand times. PowerTransitions has a lease with NorthStar Group Services, the owner of the 140-acre Yankee site. While demolition and cleanup is almost complete at Yankee, its 42 years of high-level radioactive waste in the form of its old fuel rods, would remain in the steel and concrete casks. Kerrick Johnson, Vermont's commissioner of the Department of Public Service, said the state's position on PowerTransitions' plans would be made after a proposal is made. "Of course our Department’s position will be determined by what is actually, formally proposed and the facts in the matter," Johnson said via email on Tuesday. "My general view though is that done right, a battery could serve as an affordable reliability and grid flexibility asset, and could also serve as a complementary piece to a generator of some sort that could be co-located on that site." "In that way the site could be fully utilized in a manner that delivers the greatest value to the community, state and region," said Johnson, who has said previously he wanted Vermont ratepayers' investment in the VELCO switchyard to have some return. A battery storage facility has never been built near a nuclear fuel storage facility, the PowerTransitions people said, although they had consulted with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission about it. Hitt said that assuming PowerTransitions does go forward with the battery storage facility in Vernon, it would reserve the right to install some additional kind of power generation there as well. She didn't say what kind. No mention was made by PowerTransitions during the two-hour session about the possibility of a small modular nuclear reactor. But one women said at the end, "I don't think a nuke plant would be very welcome." Hitt had apologized at the beginning of the session for originally asking for RSVPs when the company first sent out notice of the meeting. She said the company backed off that request in the face of questions. She said PowerTransitions is not compiling a list of names, phone numbers or email addresses. Hitt said the Vermont Yankee site was a very complicated one. "You have a very unique site," she said. "Very interesting, very complex and very challenging. It's very challenging." But she emphasized that if the town is not supportive, PowerTransitions would not go forward, either in applying to the state for a Section 248 permit, or applying to ISO-New England. "We will be back," Hitt said at the end of the two-hour session. "This is Step One."

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. 1. BYD's Xi'an Battery Project Enters Full-Scale Production BYD's power-battery project in Xixian New Area, Xi'an, has entered full-scale production. Located in the Qinhan Autonomous Driving Industrial Park, the facility produces battery cells and packs and will supply BYD's vehicle manufacturing operations in Xi'an. The project's first battery cell rolled off the line on October 17, 2025, about 10 months after the project was signed. The base is among the first production sites for BYD's second-generation Blade Battery and a key production base for its flash-charging technology. Its lines cover the process from electrode preparation and cell formation to module assembly, battery-pack integration and system testing, supported by an MES intelligent manufacturing system. BYD and more than 40 supporting companies have also established operations in the surrounding Zhouling advanced manufacturing area, strengthening the regional NEV supply chain. 2. XPENG and Banma Develop an Automotive-Grade AI Cockpit At the 2026 Yunqi Conference, XPENG and Banma announced a joint automotive-grade AI cockpit solution combining XPENG's Turing AI chip with Banma's AutoOmni multimodal on-device large model. The system supports the local operation of 30B-class models, with the Turing chip providing up to 750 TOPS of effective computing power per chip, according to the source. The "on-device first, cloud-assisted" architecture is designed to handle core functions such as multi-turn conversation, multimodal interaction, offline Q&A and task planning in the vehicle, while using the cloud for lower-frequency services. The companies say this can sustain AI functions in weak or unavailable network conditions and help address connectivity and data-privacy requirements in overseas markets. They plan to continue model adaptation and toolchain development, with the solution intended for mid- to high-end vehicle models. 3. PATEO Signs Global Supply Agreement with Jeep PATEO has reached a global supply agreement with Jeep to provide high-end intelligent cockpit domain controllers and AI-based in-vehicle interaction systems for models under two of the customer's brands. The vehicles are intended for overseas markets including Europe, the Middle East and South America. Separately, under a new joint-venture framework between Stellantis and Dongfeng Motor Group, two electrified models are being developed for production at DPCA's Wuhan plant and planned global sales through Stellantis' international network. PATEO's cockpit technologies are expected to be used in the program, extending the company's work from Chinese brands to an international automaker's global supply system.

artigo.texto: DICKINSON The city council next month will consider for final adoption an ordinance that would place more stringent regulations on battery energy storage systems, replicating a similar ordinance League City passed in July 2024, officials said Tuesday. The proposed regulations would classify battery energy storage systems as major utilities, a category that includes electric and gas generation plants, require operators to obtain a conditional use permit and impose extensive fire, safety and emergency-response requirements. Battery energy storage systems are being developed all over the country and county because they can provide on-demand electricity to supplement traditional power generation during periods of peak demand. That proliferation has caused concern among residents and city leaders about where the facilities are built in relation to neighborhoods and the risk of fires. At the Sept. 22 meeting, the council amended the proposal to require developers to pay the cost of an independent safety review up front before unanimously approving the ordinance on first reading. The proposed regulations come about five years after a battery storage facility was first built in Dickinson. Built in 2021, Dickinson’s battery energy storage facility has a capacity of almost 10 megawatts, which is enough to power about 2,500 homes during peak hours, according to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas. Councilman Mark Townsend, who proposed the initial ordinance, said he did so out of an abundance of caution. While there haven’t been any incidents at the Dickinson facility, battery fires are among the primary safety considerations, Townsend said. “You can’t put them out,” Townsend said. “They’re like a chemical reaction; you just have to let them burn out.” Battery energy storage systems stockpile electricity when it is inexpensive, storing it in battery banks until it is sold and released back into the grid during periods of higher demand, Townsend said. Proponents of the technology say the systems can reduce the risk of blackouts and increase the reliability of electrical grids where they are installed. Opponents have focused on the possibility of thermal runaway, a chain reaction that can occur when batteries are damaged or malfunction and can result in uncontrolled heating and fire that can be difficult to extinguish. Fires involving lithium-ion batteries, which are commonly used in battery storage facilities, can release toxic smoke containing hydrogen fluoride, according to a 2017 study published in the journal Scientific Reports. Much of the ordinance under consideration in Dickinson was taken directly from League City’s ordinance, Townsend said. “There’s no need to recreate the wheel, if you’ve got an ordinance that you can look at and adjust to your own town,” Townsend said. As Dickinson considers new regulations for battery storage systems, some municipalities around the country have faced public resistance to the facilities. Dickinson Fire Marshal Amber Phillips made recommendations on the proposed ordinance, including requirements that comply with the provisionally adopted 2024 International Fire Code, which addresses battery energy storage systems, she said. “The codes the city adopted establish requirements for items such as separation distances, fire protection features, emergency planning, and overall system safety,” Phillips said. “If a proposed facility meets the applicable code requirements and successfully completes the required review and permitting process it would be evaluated under the same nationally recognized standards that apply to any similar situation.” The second and final reading is scheduled to go before city council on Tuesday, Townsend said. A meeting agenda had not yet been posted at the time of publication.

artigo.texto: O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, afirmou na terça-feira (29) que executivos do setor de tecnologia concordaram em estabelecer padrões voluntários para a IA e reiterou seu apoio à rápida expansão dos data centers, em meio a crescentes preocupações com a segurança da IA e com a crescente presença do setor nas comunidades. Trump fez essas declarações após se reunir com executivos do setor de tecnologia na Casa Branca. As empresas concordaram em trabalhar com “auditores independentes” para avaliar se os sistemas de IA estão funcionando conforme pretendido por seus desenvolvedores, de acordo com uma cópia do acordo publicada por Trump em sua rede social. As empresas também afirmaram que trabalharão para garantir que suas ferramentas de IA não “invadam ou acessem sistemas técnicos de maneiras indesejadas”. O governo enfrenta um escrutínio cada vez maior sobre os riscos apresentados pela IA avançada, depois que a OpenAI e a Anthropic relataram que seus agentes de IA haviam se rebelado e invadido os sistemas de outras empresas. Os data centers, que fornecem o poder de computação para treinar e executar modelos de IA, têm gerado oposição em comunidades por todo o país devido a preocupações com a demanda por eletricidade, custos de serviços públicos e outros impactos locais. A reação negativa representa um desafio político para os republicanos às vésperas das eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA, em 3 de novembro. “É quase como uma constituição, de certa forma”, disse Trump, referindo-se ao acordo entre as empresas. “E as pessoas mais importantes do mundo assinaram isso, e eu assinei como presidente. E isso realmente é uma forma de proteção.” O que começou como um almoço a portas fechadas com executivos do setor de tecnologia ganhou visibilidade pública quando Trump se juntou ao presidente da Câmara, Mike Johnson, e a um grupo de CEOs na entrada da Casa Branca, uma área raramente usada pelo presidente para falar com jornalistas. Ele respondeu a perguntas dos repórteres por cerca de 30 minutos sobre segurança da IA e outros temas, com os CEOs posicionados atrás dele. A cena incomum ocorreu em um momento em que a pressão sobre o governo para lidar com os riscos e a rápida disseminação da IA tem aumentado, e ressaltou a aliança que Trump cultivou com líderes do setor de tecnologia. Entre os executivos presentes na reunião estavam Greg Brockman, da OpenAI; Dario Amodei, da Anthropic; Mark Zuckerberg, da Meta; Sundar Pichai, do Google; e Jensen Huang, da Nvidia. Zuckerberg, chamado à frente do grupo de executivos bilionários por Trump para falar, disse que as empresas concordaram em desenvolver “controles internos robustos” para seus sistemas de IA. Trump afirmou que está considerando criar um conselho de 10 pessoas para fiscalizar a segurança das ferramentas de IA. Ele não especificou possíveis membros desse grupo. Acrescentou ainda que em breve nomearia um novo responsável para liderar as políticas da Casa Branca em matéria de IA. Aposta dobrada em data centers Questionado se estava preocupado com a possibilidade de seu apoio aos data centers prejudicar os republicanos em novembro, Trump disse que as empresas de tecnologia trabalhariam para deixar as comunidades “felizes” com a construção dos data centers. “Essas empresas grandes, poderosas, muito ricas e muito inteligentes vão fazer contribuições enormes para as comunidades”, disse Trump mais tarde aos repórteres reunidos na entrada da Casa Branca, cercado pelos executivos das empresas. Mas as empresas têm sido criticadas por não fazerem o suficiente para tornar a IA mais segura. Uma pesquisa nacional Reuters/Ipsos, realizada de 17 a 20 de setembro, mostra que cerca de 73% dos entrevistados temem que as empresas de IA não tenham feito o suficiente para impedir que a IA cause danos graves à sociedade, e 55% das pessoas afirmaram que seria bom desacelerar o desenvolvimento da IA. Executivos e investidores de empresas de IA estavam entre os maiores doadores individuais em 2025 para o MAGA Inc., um comitê de ação política alinhado ao presidente. Brockman, da OpenAI, e sua esposa, Anna Brockman, doaram juntos US$25 milhões ao comitê em 2025, de acordo com registros da Comissão Eleitoral Federal. Trump se reuniu com os CEOs no mesmo dia em que seus assessores anunciaram uma nova ferramenta de IA que, segundo eles, facilitará o uso dos serviços governamentais pelo público. Executivos do Vale do Silício participaram de um evento de lançamento da nova ferramenta, incluindo Dina Powell McCormick, da Meta, e Shaun Maguire, sócio da Sequoia Capital. O cofundador da Airbnb, Joe Gebbia, liderou o projeto da nova ferramenta. As empresas do Vale do Silício Google, SpaceX, Meta e 8VC foram listadas no programa do evento de lançamento como patrocinadoras. Trump, no evento de lançamento, afirmou que a ferramenta de IA não poderia, “em teoria, ser hackeada” por agentes mal-intencionados. Ele não apresentou evidências. Trump, nesta terça-feira, também instruiu as agências governamentais a usarem as palavras “superinteligência” em vez de “inteligência artificial” ao se referirem à tecnologia.

artigo.texto: SALT LAKE CITY — In central Utah, plans are underway to build the world’s largest data center. In northwest Utah, a proposed data center and its famous backer have garnered protests. Politicians who advanced the project lost reelection bids in the recent primary contests. Yet, data centers already enjoy a certain ubiquity. By one count, Utah has 48 of them. Most of them are much smaller than the hyperscale ones being developed today. “This is the trend moving forward is bigger, larger data centers,” said Shon Hiatt, a professor at the University of Southern California who has studied Utah’s data center landscape. The centers store electronic data and provide the computing that fuels modern life – emails, text messages, web searches and social media scrolling. Surging through discussions like ones and zeroes are concerns about electricity, gas and water. And there are questions about who really benefits from data centers. “We sort of solve one problem,” said Michele Beck, who advocates for ratepayers as the director of the Utah Office of Consumer Services, “then we identify the next problem.” A team of journalists at FOX 13 News has spent months looking at how data centers are impacting Utah – and how they could change the state. In the coming weeks, we will tell you: - The military ties to the most-controversial data center. - What it’s like to live next to a data center. - What really happens inside one. - How data centers are changing rural Utah. - What data about you is stored. - Whether data centers could one day increase what Utahns pay for their utilities. “It's a really polarized world,” said Mark White, a professor at the University of Illinois who has been studying the rise of data centers in rural communities. “And this is one of those issues that seems to be uniting people from all different political persuasions.”

artigo.texto: WASHINGTON (CBS19 NEWS) -- Virginia Sen. Mark Warner is calling for stronger federal requirements for data centers, saying a proposal expected to come before the Senate does not go far enough to protect communities and utility customers. The Senate is expected to vote Wednesday on the Ratepayer Protection Act. The measure would direct states to consider requiring certain large data centers to cover infrastructure costs associated with their development. States would have two years to consider the standard, but they would not be required to adopt it. Warner criticized that approach during remarks on the Senate floor Tuesday, arguing Congress should establish requirements rather than leave the decision entirely to individual states. “I think we need real legislation on this,” Warner said. “We need legislation that actually has some boundaries. This should not be optional.” Warner is instead promoting his Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act. His proposal would require greater public disclosure of information including data centers’ energy and water consumption, backup power systems and environmental impacts. The legislation would also connect certain federal tax benefits to whether developers meet standards involving energy, water use, building efficiency, setbacks from neighborhoods and community transparency. Warner pointed to Virginia’s large data center industry while explaining why he believes additional federal action is necessary. “Virginia is the capital of data centers in our country, and there is enormous concern from neighbors, from communities,” Warner said. Under his proposal, developers that fail to meet certain requirements could lose access to some federal tax benefits. Warner said Tuesday that he had not decided how he would vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act. He urged senators to consider his proposal as an alternative with mandatory requirements and penalties for companies that fail to meet them.

artigo.texto: A Unidade de Recuperação Energética (URE) de Barueri terá uma reunião aberta à comunidade no dia 27 de outubro para apresentar o projeto de créditos de carbono que será desenvolvido na usina. O encontro será às 14h, na Avenida Pirarucu, 3.891, no bairro Nova Aldeinha. A reunião será promovida pela Orizon Valorização de Resíduos, empresa responsável pelo empreendimento, e é aberta a moradores e demais interessados. A participação, no entanto, exige confirmação prévia, devido à limitação do espaço físico. Os interessados devem informar o nome completo pelo telefone (11) 91087-9116 ou pelo e-mail comunicacao.social@orizonvr.com.br. Segundo a companhia, serão apresentados os principais aspectos do processo de certificação do projeto junto à Verra, organização internacional que administra padrões para projetos do mercado voluntário de carbono. O encontro também abordará os benefícios ambientais previstos, a geração de energia renovável e a emissão de créditos de carbono. De acordo com a Orizon, haverá espaço para que os participantes tirem dúvidas sobre a usina e apresentem contribuições. O que são os créditos de carbono O projeto pretende transformar em créditos parte das reduções de gases de efeito estufa associadas à operação da URE. De forma geral, um crédito de carbono corresponde a uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) que deixou de ser emitida ou foi removida da atmosfera. A emissão dos créditos, porém, não é automática. O projeto precisa seguir uma metodologia reconhecida, demonstrar como as reduções são calculadas e passar por processos de validação e verificação. É nesse contexto que ocorre o processo de certificação junto à Verra que será apresentado durante a reunião. A Orizon estima que a operação da URE evitará a emissão de 128 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano. Documentos financeiros do empreendimento também consideram a futura comercialização dos créditos como uma das fontes de receita da usina. Como funciona a URE A URE de Barueri é uma usina projetada para transformar resíduos urbanos não recicláveis em energia elétrica por meio de uma tecnologia conhecida como waste-to-energy (resíduos para energia, em tradução livre). Depois da separação dos materiais que podem ser reciclados, os rejeitos são submetidos a tratamento térmico em altas temperaturas. O calor produzido nesse processo aquece água em uma caldeira e gera vapor. Esse vapor movimenta uma turbina ligada a um gerador, produzindo eletricidade. A unidade terá capacidade para processar cerca de 870 toneladas de resíduos por dia, aproximadamente 300 mil toneladas por ano, provenientes de Barueri, Santana de Parnaíba e Carapicuíba. A potência instalada será de 20 megawatts (MW), suficiente, segundo a empresa, para atender o consumo equivalente a mais de 75 mil residências. A proposta é reduzir a quantidade de resíduos destinada a aterros sanitários, aproveitando a parcela que não pode ser reciclada para a produção de energia. Questionada pela reportagem, a Orizon confirmou que a previsão é de que a URE entre em funcionamento no primeiro semestre de 2027. artigo.texto: Expansão dos data centers no Ceará acompanha avanço da IA Crescimento da IA aumenta demanda por infraestrutura de processamento e coloca o Ceará no radar de novos investimentos em tecnologia Resumo O avanço acelerado da inteligência artificial não está transformando apenas a rotina de empresas e profissionais. Por trás de ferramentas capazes de gerar textos, imagens, analisar dados e automatizar tarefas existe uma infraestrutura física cada vez mais necessária: os data centers, estruturas responsáveis por armazenar e processar grandes volumes de informações. No Ceará, o movimento começa a ganhar novos contornos. A região do Pecém, por exemplo, vem sendo considerada para a instalação de estruturas de grande porte. Em junho deste ano, estudo da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) apontou a necessidade de soluções de transmissão que permitam atender até 4 GW de cargas eletrointensivas no Ceará e Piauí, incluindo data centers e plantas de hidrogênio. Mais recentemente, foi aprovada a implantação de um novo projeto de data center na ZPE do Pecém, ligado à Voltalia Energia do Brasil. Para Daniel Monteiro, coordenador de Inteligência Artificial da Digital College, a expansão desse tipo de infraestrutura está diretamente relacionada ao crescimento das aplicações de IA.“Quando uma pessoa utiliza uma ferramenta de inteligência artificial, existe uma estrutura computacional enorme funcionando nos bastidores. Quanto mais empresas e pessoas utilizam IA, maior é a necessidade de processamento, armazenamento, conectividade e energia para sustentar essas operações”, explica. O próprio Governo do Ceará vem planejando investimentos em infraestrutura digital. O plano de negócios da ETICE para 2026–2030 prevê, entre outras ações, a expansão do Cinturão Digital com novas rotas de fibra óptica, a modernização do backbone para até 400 Gbps e melhorias na infraestrutura de data center, incluindo um cluster voltado para inteligência artificial. Para Karlos Morais, professor de Inteligência Artificial Generativa na Digital College, a movimentação também evidencia a necessidade de formar profissionais capazes de atuar nessa nova infraestrutura.“A discussão sobre inteligência artificial não pode ficar restrita aos softwares. Existe toda uma cadeia por trás da IA, envolvendo infraestrutura, computação em nuvem, dados, segurança, redes e profissionais especializados. À medida que essa estrutura cresce, também cresce a demanda por pessoas preparadas para trabalhar nesse ecossistema”, afirma. Essa transformação já desperta interesse entre estudantes da área de tecnologia. Juliane Azevedo, aluna da Digital College, conta que acompanhar o crescimento da inteligência artificial mudou sua percepção sobre as possibilidades de carreira no setor. “Quando comecei a estudar tecnologia, pensava muito na parte de desenvolvimento e programação. Hoje percebo que existe uma estrutura muito maior por trás da IA e várias possibilidades de atuação. Isso abriu minha visão sobre o mercado”, relata. Além da infraestrutura, a expansão dos data centers também traz discussões sobre energia, conectividade, sustentabilidade, segurança de dados e formação profissional. Em julho, a Assembleia Legislativa do Ceará aprovou um projeto de lei que estabelece procedimentos para o licenciamento ambiental de sistemas de armazenamento de energia e data centers no Estado. Com a inteligência artificial ganhando espaço em empresas, serviços públicos e diferentes setores da economia, a tendência é que a infraestrutura necessária para sustentar essas aplicações passe a fazer parte cada vez mais das discussões sobre desenvolvimento tecnológico no Ceará. Nvidia amplia seu programa de recompra de ações que chegará a US$ 235 bilhões, um recorde
Operação deve ser concluída em 2028 e supera a que foi feita pela Apple em 2024, até então a maior da História
A Nvidia, fabricante de chips que está no centro do boom de inteligência artificial, informou nesta segunda-feira que autorizou mais US$ 150 bilhões (R$ 781 bilhões) para seu programa de recompra de ações, tornando-o, segundo a própria empresa, o maior programa de recompra de ações da história, refletindo a confiança do CEO Jensen Huang na continuidade do crescimento da empresa.
- Nova ferramenta: Nvidia lança sistema projetado para impedir que agentes de IA saiam do controle
- ‘Coach’ de robô: Veja como brasileiros ganham dinheiro gravando tarefas como faxina para treinar IA
Com este acréscimo, o valor total de recompra de ações da companhia chegará a US$ 235 bilhões (R$ 1,22 trilhão). O anúncio supera em muito o recorde anterior da Apple, de US$ 110 bilhões (R$ 573,3 bilhões), autorizado em 2024.
A Nvidia espera concluir até a operação até 2028, informou a empresa em um comunicado divulgado na segunda-feira.
“O crescimento da Nvidia está sendo impulsionado por uma mudança de plataforma que ocorre uma vez a cada geração, em direção à inteligência artificial e à computação acelerada”, afirmou Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia, no comunicado.
“Nosso forte fluxo de geração de caixa nos dá capacidade para investir nas tecnologias que impulsionam essa transformação e devolver capital aos acionistas. Essa autorização reflete nossa confiança na oportunidade de longo prazo que temos pela frente”, acrescentou Huang.
As ações da fabricante de chips dispararam em meio ao boom de inteligência artificial. Os chips da Nvidia são o elemento central dos gigantescos data centers de IA, e a demanda por esses chips tornou-se um indicador da crescente demanda pela tecnologia.
Outras empresas vêm comprando dezenas de bilhões de dólares em chips da Nvidia, tornando a companhia a empresa de capital aberto mais valiosa do mundo, com uma capitalização de mercado de cerca de US$ 5 trilhões.
A recompra ocorre após a empresa informar, no mês passado, que sua receita mais que dobrou, para US$ 96,22 bilhões, no trimestre encerrado em julho. Apenas três anos atrás, o lucro trimestral da Nvidia era de US$ 6,2 bilhões.
Em agosto, a Nvidia informou aos investidores que sua receita projetada para o trimestre atual aumentaria 90% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, chegando a US$ 108 bilhões — um sinal de que o boom da inteligência artificial ainda tem bastante força.

Com este acréscimo, o valor total de recompra de ações da companhia chegará a US$ 235 bilhões (R$ 1,22 trilhão). O anúncio supera em muito o recorde anterior da Apple, de US$ 110 bilhões (R$ 573,3 bilhões), autorizado em 2024.
A Nvidia espera concluir até a operação até 2028, informou a empresa em um comunicado divulgado na segunda-feira.
“O crescimento da Nvidia está sendo impulsionado por uma mudança de plataforma que ocorre uma vez a cada geração, em direção à inteligência artificial e à computação acelerada”, afirmou Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia, no comunicado.
“Nosso forte fluxo de geração de caixa nos dá capacidade para investir nas tecnologias que impulsionam essa transformação e devolver capital aos acionistas. Essa autorização reflete nossa confiança na oportunidade de longo prazo que temos pela frente”, acrescentou Huang.
As ações da fabricante de chips dispararam em meio ao boom de inteligência artificial. Os chips da Nvidia são o elemento central dos gigantescos data centers de IA, e a demanda por esses chips tornou-se um indicador da crescente demanda pela tecnologia.
Outras empresas vêm comprando dezenas de bilhões de dólares em chips da Nvidia, tornando a companhia a empresa de capital aberto mais valiosa do mundo, com uma capitalização de mercado de cerca de US$ 5 trilhões.
A recompra ocorre após a empresa informar, no mês passado, que sua receita mais que dobrou, para US$ 96,22 bilhões, no trimestre encerrado em julho. Apenas três anos atrás, o lucro trimestral da Nvidia era de US$ 6,2 bilhões.
Em agosto, a Nvidia informou aos investidores que sua receita projetada para o trimestre atual aumentaria 90% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, chegando a US$ 108 bilhões — um sinal de que o boom da inteligência artificial ainda tem bastante força.

Empresário revela a lição sobre dinheiro que mudou sua visão sobre investimentos
À frente da Novo Ideal desde 2016, Léo Casellato conta como o contato com mais de 2.500 endividados mudou sua visão sobre dinheiro, e por que renda alta não é sinônimo de vida financeira organizada
Quando fundou a Novo Ideal, em 2016, o empresário e educador financeiro Léo Casellato tinha uma certeza que os anos seguintes se encarregariam de desmontar: a de que o problema de quem se endivida é, no fundo, falta de dinheiro. Depois de participar da negociação de cerca de R$ 1 bilhão em dívidas e atender mais de 2.500 clientes, ele chegou a uma conclusão diferente.
"Entrei achando que o problema das pessoas era falta de dinheiro. Depois de negociar cerca de R$ 1 bilhão em dívidas e atender mais de 2.500 clientes, entendi que raramente o problema é quanto a pessoa ganha: é a relação que ela tem com o próprio dinheiro", afirma.
Na prática, diz Casellato, a renda isolada explica pouco. Ao longo da operação, ele conta ter encontrado dos dois lados do balcão: profissionais de salário alto afogados em dívidas e famílias de renda modesta com as contas em dia e uma reserva montada. O que separava um grupo do outro, segundo ele, não era o valor do contracheque, mas os hábitos por trás dele.
Foi essa percepção que mudou também a forma como o empresário enxerga o investimento. Para ele, o erro mais comum de quem quer começar é pular etapas: procurar produtos financeiros antes de entender o próprio comportamento de consumo.
"Investir não começa na corretora, começa no comportamento. Antes de falar em ação, FII ou renda fixa, a pessoa precisa entender para onde o dinheiro dela vai todo mês", explica.
O primeiro passo que recomenda é menos sofisticado do que se imagina: acompanhar, por um ou dois meses, cada real que entra e sai. Sem esse mapa, argumenta, qualquer escolha de investimento vira aposta, porque a pessoa não sabe quanto sobra de verdade nem para onde o dinheiro está escapando. A educação financeira, nesse raciocínio, tem menos a ver com decorar produtos e mais com construir uma disciplina que sustente as decisões no longo prazo.
O ponto de virada da própria trajetória, ele reconhece, veio do contato diário com o endividamento, inclusive como lição pessoal.
"A dívida me ensinou que investir é, antes de tudo, uma questão de consciência e disciplina, não de sorte ou de 'ter muito dinheiro'", conclui.

Vorcaro e Motta conversaram sobre ‘sociedade’ e projeto de lei na Câmara, mostram mensagens analisadas pela PF
Presidente da Casa diz que diálogos não relatam irregularidades e que tem interlocução com ‘diversos segmentos do empresariado’
Mensagens trocadas entre o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do Banco Master, e o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), indicam que os dois discutiram uma “sociedade” relacionada à compra de um terreno em João Pessoa, capital da Paraíba. No diálogos, os dois se tratam como "amigo" e "irmão". Motta afirmou em nota que as conversas não retratam “ilícitos” e que ele mantém interlocução com “diversos segmentos do empresariado e representantes da sociedade”.
- Faça o teste do GLOBO: Com qual candidato a deputado federal do Rio e de SP você se identifica?
- Quer acompanhar de perto o noticiário das eleições? Participe da comunidade do GLOBO no WhatsApp
As mensagens, reveladas pelo portal Fato Online, foram extraídas do celular de Vorcaro, apreendido em novembro do ano passado. O conteúdo está sendo analisado pela Polícia Federal no curso das investigações que apuram as fraudes do Master.
As conversas extraídas mostra que Motta procurou Vorcaro, em 9 de março de 2024, para tratar da “negociação de compra de área aqui de JP”, possível referência a João Pessoa, capital da Paraíba, estado do presidente da Câmara.
“Boa noite, amigo! Tudo bem? Desculpe incomodar no sábado, estou aqui reunido com o pessoal para finalizar a negociação de compra da área aqui de JP. Conforme falamos, já temos os documentos assinados passando a empresa para minha cunhada. Ela iniciou a negociação com a Adriana, mas acredito que ela não tá sabendo do formato de sociedade que ficou combinado.Quando puder me orienta como devemos proceder pq o prazo é curto para saldar com Intercement (empresa que atua na produção de cimento)", escreveu Motta.
Vorcaro, então, responde: "Vamos fazer uma operação rápida com a Adriana. Em paralelo, organizamos a questão da sociedade”.
Motta perguntou na sequência se seria necessário “o pessoal” ir a São Paulo para finalizar os trâmites. Vorcaro disse que checaria o andamento do caso e que “entre nós, resolvemos depois”.
A negociação mencionada nas conversas ocorreu no mesmo mês em que a cunhada de Motta, Bianca Medeiros, contraiu um empréstimo de R$ 22 milhões com o Master para a compra de um terreno em João Pessoa, conforme mostrou reportagem do jornal “Folha de S.Paulo” publicada em março deste ano. O crédito é relacionado à aquisição do terreno mencionado nas mensagens.
Em nota, Motta afirmou que sempre manteve "diálogo com os diversos segmentos do empresariado e representantes da sociedade brasileira". "Enfatizo que não há nenhum ilícito retratado nos diálogos publicados e repudio a tentativa de atribuir conversas descontextualizadas a qualquer relação de interesse espúrio ou de favorecimento por minha parte. Tenho uma vida limpa, assim como é limpa a minha atuação política nesses 15 anos de vid
